The Nāṭyaśāstra composed by the sage Bharata.
First Chapter.
Having bowed my head to the two gods, Pitāmaha and Maheśvara, I shall proclaim the Nāṭyaśāstra as it was uttered by Brahmā. (1)
The *Abhinavabhāratī*:
A Commentary composed by the venerable Abhinavagupta.
[Salutation] to him who, through the process of conversing with his own heart, [makes all things] consist of that [divine essence].

I bow to that one who wears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament; he who instantly partakes in the divisions of the ground of the multitude of diverse powers, and who brings about the supreme transformation in those possessed by the joyous outburst of emotion.

I shall explain this *Bharata-sūtra*, which consists of thirty-six [verses], whose beauty is like a reflection kissed by the mass of rays of consciousness that illuminates the sky of the world composed of thirty-six [categories].
I bow to Śiva, the abode that discerns both the Vedas and their true meaning.
I bow to the Lord in the form of the Earth, who exists as the foundational support for the sprouting of the seeds of the universe and consists of the power of sustenance. (3)

For the sake of accomplishing the desires of seekers, [Abhinavagupta], established in the feet of Maheśvara Abhinavagupta, has proclaimed the true meaning of the principles of the Nāṭya-veda as understood by the six schools of thought.
He clarifies [this] by means of a concise method of exposition.
The recitation of what is to be adopted, the citation of its opposite,
a clear commentary, the resolution of contradictions, and complete fullness— these are the [five qualities]. (5)

Following the intended meaning, discerning the portions of the expression that possess double meanings, the connection [of parts], and the resolution of apparent repetitions—these constitute the complex process of interpretation. (6)
And this method of exposition, namely "compendium" (saṅgraha), has been adopted here.
The sage Bharata, preceded by a salutation to his chosen deity, primarily declares the purpose through the subordination of the subject matter; by means of his epithets,
he indicates the succession of teachers, while the subject matter, the purpose, and their relationship are shown as being implied by the sense.
By the words "having prostrated" and so forth—

here the term *deva* refers to the Grandfather (Brahmā), not the father of the father (the grandfather of the father), nor to Maheśvara or a king, because of their well-known status. Furthermore, this should not be doubted, as it is established by tradition that there is but one God who desires victory and is the originator of the drama.

The Blessed One, being fond of play due to his overflowing bliss, dances at the junctions of the day; thus, since the practice of drama (*nāṭya*) and its accompaniment, dance (*nṛtta*), originated from him, those two alone are the presiding deities and the teacher here, and are therefore to be saluted. Although the Lord of Lakṣmī is the creator of the *vṛttis*, nevertheless—
"Like Brahmā and others, he is devoted solely to his own duty;
thus acting, he does not subsist on this drama as people do in the world. Therefore, because of the absence of such gravity, he has not been saluted.
This [argument] is also incorrect, because it is inappropriate to define the grounds for a salutation in this manner.
Therefore, prostration (*praṇamana*) is the state of bowing down through body, speech, and mind. The first [mode] is indicated by the words "with the head" (*śirasā*);
the second is indicated by the words "to the gods" (*devau*). For it is improper to mention the name of one to whom prostration is made without an honorific title;
thus, the word "gods" was spoken first. Furthermore, because the dramatic performance is primary, the physical gesture is expressed by the words "with the head."

The vocal representation (*vākyābhinaya*) is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "O gods" (*devāvityādi*). Indeed, this representation is established in common worldly usage and is not of the nature of dramatic convention (*nāṭyadharma*). Just as one might show a person who is clever by pointing to his arms and so forth as being distinguished by their upward position and so on, that which is to be represented must likewise be displayed. However, mental humility (*prahvatā*), being accessible through the operations of speech and body, is not [exclusively] mental.
They are mentioned separately; the order "the Grandfather and Maheśvara" is for the sake of *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration),

and to demonstrate that a sentence accompanied by poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) is fit for dramatic performance (*abhinaya*), as well as to show that such a sentence is a cause for the gratification of the deities.
3) To demonstrate this: by the phrase "the Grandfather and Maheśvara," the desire for the welfare of the world on the part of the two deities is expressed.
[The work is called] the *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
"I shall proclaim the treatise (*śāstra*)—the means of instruction and the text—for *nāṭya*, the art of the actor.

Others say this is not so; for *nāṭyaveda* and *nāṭyaśāstra* are synonyms. In that case, if by the term *nāṭyaśāstra* a specific text is meant here, then the composition of that text is what is being undertaken now, and not [the art itself].

The *pravacana* (the teaching). For that, being in the form of an exposition, is distinct from the instrument [of composition], as in the expression "proclaimed by Kaṭha. Furthermore, if the treatise were the *Nāṭya-veda*, there would be an inconsistency in the question, because the fivefold set beginning with "origination" (*utpatti*), which pertains to it, is common to other texts as well. [This applies to] the subsequent text...

Nor is there a lack of logical consistency, because [the text] is not disconnected from its subject matter, as seen in such passages as "whatever may be visible or audible" (1.11) and "he took up the recitation from the Ṛgveda" (1.7). Therefore, it is both drama (*nāṭya*) and a treatise (*śāstra*).
Because it provides proficiency [in performance], I shall proclaim—that is, explain—that Veda known as drama according to its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇataḥ*).
The meaning is that [the author] will explain this.

But even this is not satisfactory; for it is impossible to teach [something] apart from its nature as sound, and drama (*nāṭya*) does not have sound as its essence. Furthermore, if "explaining" were merely "teaching," then the very composition of the book would also constitute teaching.

Furthermore, since the non-conceptual and external nature [of the object] would already be obtained simply by the fact that the drama (*nāṭya*) is being proclaimed, it would follow that the word "treatise" (*śāstra*) is redundant; moreover, this would result in an inconsistency with what will be stated at the end of the treatise: "Whoever should hear this proclaimed *Nāṭyaveda*. This is because [the object] does not exist apart from being an object of words.

Because the word "should hear" (*śṛṇuyāt*) is not [merely] expressive [of a command], my teachers say that it is thus: one who is engaged in performing what is beneficial for all and endowed with the perfection of enthusiasm,
for the sake of increasing that [benefit] and with the desire to dispel obstacles to it.

Having placed at the forefront the path of transitory emotions characterized by longing, anxiety, fortitude, intelligence, and so forth— which have as their object the Supreme Lord, the Universal Sovereign in the form of the Guru, who has ascended the stages of one's own consciousness—
and the group of emotions such as dullness and dissimulation directed toward external objects of action;

Having entered into the heroes of the Dharma, he first manifests the appropriate physical and verbal expressions (anubhāvas) and then defines the very purpose of his own undertaking; for it is the purpose alone that motivates action. As they say:
"That object aiming at which one acts is the purpose" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.24).

In this context, what is called "drama" (nāṭya) is distinct from worldly objects; it is unique from their imitation, reflection, mirror-image, resemblance, superimposition, determination, poetic fancy, dream, illusion, and the horn of a hare, for one who perceives it.

We shall explain that the object to be known through the experience of the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— which possesses a mode of existence distinct from right knowledge, error, doubt, non-determination, lack of resolve, and ordinary cognition— is essentially *rasa* itself.
Its treatise (*śāstra*) is its instruction (*śāsana*), distinguished by its difference from external objects such as vessels, dance, and so forth.

[He] thoroughly [applies] the means for understanding its true nature, by means of the removal of those useless elaborations uttered by the disciples of the Supreme Brahman (or: by the shaking off of those elaborations).
I shall speak. As he will say: "That man who should hear this Nāṭyaveda proclaimed by the Self-existent One, or who should perform its practice, or likewise study it."

"May he attain that destination which belongs to those who know the Vedas, that destination which belongs to those who perform sacrifices, and that destination which belongs to those whose nature is generosity. Thus it is said.
(...... a gap in the manuscript?)(Nā. Śā. A.

36) By this, the objection raised by some—that because of the rule "this group of ten born of desire" (Manu 7.47), drama (*nāṭya*) is to be avoided and thus is not to be adopted—is rendered untenable; for [the practice of drama] is found in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*, the Purāṇas, and other such works.

Because one hears of an abundance of praise; and because of the principle that dharma is not accessible through inference in the absence of scripture (āgama). This, however, is stated merely for the sake of dispelling the doubts of those who are timid out of place, though it is indeed superfluous. Likewise:

Indeed, this [actor's conduct] must simply be performed as it is handed down in its own tradition of duties; nor is it for us to deliberate upon his behavior. It is not appropriate for an injunctional statement teaching the purchase of Soma to exert itself in investigating the propriety or impropriety of the actions belonging to another Brāhmaṇa who is selling it. Not so.

Furthermore, it is taught that one should sing and dance; however, this is based on the personal practice of contemporary great actors, which has been transmitted through a lineage of disciples following the instructions of Sage Bharata— the originator of the words of Viriñca as they were set in motion during the first occasion of the dramatic performance— extending down to the present day.

It is primarily intended as an instruction for the rest [of the audience]. For this very reason, this treatise is primarily concerned with instructing on the attainment of success (*siddhi*) and its proper means as they pertain to that [actor].
Now, nothing at all is taught by this work to the actor himself, other than for the sake of benefiting him. As for the poet (*kavi*)...

[He is] one who possesses the power to manifest various unprecedented objects, arising from the grace of the Supreme Goddess of Speech— the expression of the ever-arising intuition residing in his own heart—
just as Prajāpati [creates] the world born of desire. Yet, there remains a further apprehension regarding another...
Only this wretched person remains here to be instructed;

for him, however, the instruction is given here that he should not sing, dance, play instruments, or be devoted to such things. Rather, [the instruction is directed] at one who is already naturally engaged in the enjoyment of pleasant objects, and for that very reason—

We shall explain that for one whose heart is bewildered by the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, and so forth, this particular subject has been introduced among those pleasing topics in such a way that, by its very power, it brings about the understanding of the means to the goals of human life.
As for the questions concerning the origin and other matters that will arise, they concern the Veda known as Nāṭya; they do not, however—
The subjects of the Nāṭyaveda-śāstra: For we shall explain in the passage beginning "O Brahmin, how did the Nāṭyaveda [arise]? (Nā. Śā. 1.4) that the Nāṭya itself is the Veda.
And this Nāṭyaveda-śāstra was proclaimed by Brahmā and spoken to me. As will be stated:
Having been thus commanded, [he approached] the practitioner who had completed his recitation and was surrounded by his sons.
Once, however, during a period when study was forbidden, [he approached] Bharata, who was skilled in dramatic arts.
In former times, the high-souled sages, headed by Ātreya and possessing restrained senses and intellects, attended upon him and questioned him.

"Having learned this Nāṭyaveda from my grandfather, I taught it to my sons" (Nāṭyaśāstra 1.25). Here, however, the compound *nāṭyaveda* means "the Veda of drama," that is, the treatise (*śāstra*), because otherwise teaching would be impossible.
Therefore, the meaning is simply that I am setting forth exactly what was proclaimed by Brahmā, according to its proper sequence.

It has been stated that drama (*nāṭya*) was extracted and brought forth by Brahmā from the various limbs of the Vedas, and thus the treatise concerning it is also cited as such. For if the "knowledge" (*veda*) of drama— meaning its attainment of existence— is the subject of inquiry therein, then that which takes drama as its basis, namely the *Daśarūpaka*, is called by the term "Drama-Veda."

As he will say: "The history has been seen by me" (Nāṭya Śāstra 1.19). In this view, the meaning is that what was uttered by Brahmā is the "exemplified" (*udāhṛta*), which refers to the "demonstrated example" (*darśita-dṛṣṭānta*) or the "shown illustration" (*kṛta-nidarśana*).

Others, however, maintain that drama (*nāṭya*) is simply the ten types of dramatic forms (*daśa-rūpaka*) which constitute the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) to be performed; this treatise is the science (*śāstra*) concerning that.

For this is indeed the definition of the ten forms (daśarūpaka). Thus, the ten forms are to be composed by the poet and performed by the actor; such is the purport of the treatise, because all categories such as aesthetic flavor (rasa) and the rest find their ultimate culmination therein. And that has been illustrated by Brahmā, providing a concrete example.

Others, however, say that by the very statement "I shall expound the science of drama" (nāṭyaśāstraṃ pravakṣyāmi), he has accepted its purpose; for he accepts it as something to be explained, which arrives at this moment in the form of what is to be abandoned and what is to be practiced, as set forth and defined by the Lord Brahmā, who is the aggregate of words known as the Veda.

Bhaṭṭanāyaka, however, says: "I shall describe that drama which was exemplified by Brahmā, the Supreme Self, as an illustration for the grasping of insubstantial distinctions created by ignorance. For it has as its essence mere imagination, and for that very reason, its form is not fixed."

In an instant, even that which is distinct from dreams and the like— being the cause of a profound capture of the heart and constructed through the artifice of conceptualizing Brahman as its own objective support— the unreal activity of Rāma, Rāvaṇa, and others, shines forth from some source of marvelous occurrence as if it were endowed with hundreds of thousands of crores of conceptualizations. Likewise:

And even while appearing, it becomes a means to the goal of human life; likewise, this very universe—though consisting of an unreal proliferation of names and forms—nevertheless brings about the supreme goal of human life through the power of hearing, reflection, and so forth.
Thus, by indicating the transcendent supreme goal of man...
"This will be an introduction to the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*).

'Taking each its own respective cause, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arises from tranquility. (Nāṭyaśāstra 6). By this, the ultimate purpose has been stated; thus the commentary in the *Hṛdayadarpaṇa* concludes.
As it is said (p. 6):
"This [work] which has been correctly composed by the Blessed One is equal to the Veda."
O Brahmin, how did the Nāṭyaveda originate, and for whose sake was it created?
How many limbs does it have, what is its measure, and what is its application like?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this according to reality.
"Salutations to Śambhu, the poet who fashions the three worlds, from whom every moment the person [of the world] takes delight in the performance of the drama of the universe. Thus [it is said].

Thus, the purpose of teaching the *Nāṭyaśāstra* has been stated. Its specific utility (*prayojana*) has already been demonstrated. The subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the *Nāṭyaveda*. And the relationship (*sambandha*) is characterized by the nature of the one to be instructed and the instructor. Furthermore, when someone desires to study a particular treatise, at that time, provided the author of that treatise is well-known—

Since he regards the authority [of the work] as already established—as if it were a proven fact—he proceeds without hesitation at that very moment toward the relationship, the subject matter, and the purpose as stated in the author's words.
Whether another person who has mastered the entire meaning of the treatise holds it in high regard or not is a different matter altogether; this concerns the first [type of person].
It is well known from one's own experience that the opening statement has already been employed as soon as [the inquiry] has commenced.
Therefore, what is the point of this [objection] that the opening statement is the motivator because it generates doubt regarding the subject matter, reasoning, curiosity, and so forth?
In this regard, the Sage is endowed with the excellence of zeal for acting for the benefit of the entire world.
Having entered the seat of Dharma, he first manifested the appropriate physical and verbal expressions of emotion,

and then explained the very purpose of his own undertaking. Furthermore, transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as recollection, longing, fortitude, and intelligence regarding his grandfather Maheśvara are perceived here.

Then the Sage, conceiving of himself as another, confirms through the demonstration of a past event exactly what was stated by Brahmā with the words "that which was uttered," using the two verses beginning with "having completed his recitation. [These qualities are:
being full of passion, fitness for the science of drama (*nāṭyaveda*), the faultlessness of the drama, its quality as a cause of diversion, and its ease of comprehension.

The opportunity to obtain the occasion for questioning; the renown of the teacher’s fitness; the authoritative status of the learned; the prior acquisition of the scriptures according to rule; the manifestation of the worthiness of the subject as inferred from its established reputation and the respect accorded to it; and the fact that this undertaking is not the first of its kind.
The non-redundant significance of the words, in their respective order, is the students' proficiency in reasoning through affirmation and negation (*ūhāpoha*) and their fitness for comprehension.
(2–3) To show what they asked, he says: "This one who... [referring to] "by the venerable teacher."
The sage Bharata spoke thus: "That particular work, which was composed by that sage Bharata—

woven together through the arrangement and collection of most beautiful materials— and which we have seen at the time of its performance, is referred to here as 'this' (ayam) by virtue of its being directly perceived."
And because its inner essence is unknown to us, even though it is perceptible, it is as if non-perceptible;

thus, its specific nature is said to be indefinable by means of the word "yat" (that which). For this very reason, the application of the word "tat" (that) is not sought here, as in the expression "he says something or other. Furthermore, this very [scripture] has reality as its object of investigation, since it is commensurate with the Vedas.
It is equal.
For instance: [the classification] of the *dhīrodātta*, *dhīralalita*, *dhīroddhata*, and *dhīrapraśānta* types.
Because the protagonists are engaged in complete means (*upāya*), the conduct of the antagonists— who resort to such incomplete means—

is directly perceived as being either fruitful or fruitless; [this is realized] through the heroic and the marvelous, the heroic, the erotic, and the comic, the heroic, the furious, the terrifying, and the pathetic, and the heroic, the loathsome, and the peaceful.

By means of the various subordinate sentiments (*rasāntara*) residing in the antagonist (*pratināyaka*), which become objects of extraordinary aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), it effects an entry into the heart,
producing an understanding of what is to be adopted through the fourfold means such as Dharma, and a turning away from non-Dharma and the like.

That this [Nāṭya-veda] is established by direct perception even for us who have mastered the truth of the Śruti is evident; its designation as "Nāṭya-veda" is well-known. For this very reason, because it serves as a source of instruction, it is a Veda. And thus, it is precisely this that ought to be investigated.

How has it arisen? In what manner has it arisen? Since its purpose is established from the Vedas alone—if it had arisen [as something] such that its meaning were already established like the Vedas from time immemorial, how indeed could this be questioned? The meaning is: "just as in the case of the four Vedas. Now, for that which has no instruction from the Vedas...

He asks, "Who is that perfected one (siddha) such as that?"—that is, for which qualified person? For what purpose? Is the one authorized for the Vedas alone the qualified person here, or is there another as well? This question concerns the subject of qualification. The former [question], however, is an objection based on the lack of purpose, since it would involve proving what is already established. [He asks: "How many limbs does it have?"

If it possesses very many constituent elements (*aṅga*), then because they are difficult to discern, its determination would be impossible. Thus, the third question is: among the visible singing, instrumental music, acting, and so forth, how many are its constituent elements? Furthermore, is *nāṭya* (dramatic performance) the nature of those constituent elements, or is it merely the collection of those constituent elements?
"What is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Well, first of all, drama is established by the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as he will say:
"That which is visible and audible" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 1.11).
Furthermore, the fact that it makes known the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*) is established through the self-cognition of the sages; otherwise, [it would not be so].
It has already been stated that this [object] cannot even be subject to investigation. So what is this question? True;
however, this question concerns the auxiliary means (aṅga). That is to say: by what means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is it established, and what is its auxiliary means?
If certain auxiliaries are to be known, by what means of knowledge is which auxiliary known?

Likewise, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the rule regarding the relationship between the constituent parts and the whole (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) to be known here? In this context, a *pramāṇa* is that which produces certainty.
Others, however, [ask] regarding the dramatic forms (*rūpaka*) and so forth contained within the drama, as well as the recitation, acting, aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), and songs: what...

They explain that this question concerns the scope of the classification: "What is the measure and what is the number? Regarding this [drama], they ask: "What is its mode of performance? If the constituent parts (aṅgas) were performed simultaneously, since there is no simultaneous perception of things perceivable by different senses, how could it be a single drama?"

[This concerns] the performance. Even in the case of sequential application, it is certainly not [fixed]; therefore, how is the application [to be understood]? Likewise, is the application made through a fixed relationship of primary and subordinate elements (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), or through an unfixed one? This is a question concerning the variety of dramatic forms—such as dramas (*nāṭaka*) and so forth—within the scope of general acting and diverse acting, by way of the application of the constituent parts of drama (*nāṭyāṅga*).
Having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata then replied with these words concerning the discourse on the Nāṭya-veda.
"Having become pure and with attentive minds, you must listen to the origin of the Nāṭya-veda as created by Brahmā. (7)

Fifth: Thus, from these five questions, it is indicated that this treatise is intended as an instruction for both the poet and the performer. Therefore, regarding the statement, "Therefore, this treatise is an instruction for the creator, the spectator, and the performer," the inclusion of "the spectator" (draṣṭṛ) therein is incorrect; for the audience member is not being instructed by this work, due to their lack of eligibility.

Furthermore, just as in the case of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and so forth, no instruction regarding that [science] is heard here [in this text]. If the "observer" (draṣṭṛ) is said to be one who initiates the examination, even for him there is no instruction provided systematically; rather, it occurs only occasionally, as in the cases of "the dancer," "the lord of wealth," and so on. And thus, regarding the status of being an object of instruction, [it applies to those such as] the architect, the carpenter, and the like.
Everything here might indeed be subject to instruction; therefore, enough of this.

Regarding the phrase "according to reality": we have no burden here concerning the sequence, nor regarding its extent. For we are but ignorant inquirers in this matter. For this very reason, the question is primarily directed toward the goal to be attained, just as in the case of a child.
He said, "Quell my suffering. But the knower of that [suffering] asks after the means: "From where is food to be obtained?
Thus, this treatise proceeds by way of the goal, through a sequence of questions regarding other goals presented as answers.

It should be understood that this exists as a continuous sequence consisting of the goal (*upeya*), the means (*upāya*), and so forth. Therefore, in whatever manner it is suitable for formal description, even if something has not been asked about, one should describe it oneself. Without overstepping reality, that which is appropriate to reality must be described, and reality itself must be described. This is what is meant by "this."
This concludes the examination of the characteristics (lakṣaṇaparīkṣā). (4–5) If they were to ask, "What did the sage Bharata do? he says: "But of them... (*teṣāṃ tu*).

The particle *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), meaning "having heard it immediately and not after a delay," since the suffixes *ktvā* and *lyap* are prescribed merely to indicate priority of time (*paurvakālya*).
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (therefore): because that sage is a knower of reality (*tattvavid*) and they are fit for his instruction, for that reason [the word is used].
The mention of "receiving the discourse" clarifies the very meaning of the phrase "according to reality.
As for the doubt raised regarding the question on practice—that the answer might consist in a manifestation of the practice through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—[this is addressed as follows:]
It is true that the mention of "discourse" (*kathā*) was intended to avoid [the charge of] contradiction; however, when it is said, "You ought to speak," what occasion is there for her [the Goddess]?

Thus, the sage Bharata, representing himself as another [person], composed this much of the text. Others, however, maintain that someone among his disciples composed this much of the text; in that context, the word "by Brahmā" refers to the sage Bharata.

It was indicated in the first verse. How Brahman arose—this very point is thus resolved as a single coherent statement. Immediately following that, however, is the text composed by the sage Bharata beginning with "śuciḥ" (pure).
In the middle of this [work]...
(9) O Brahmins, formerly, when the Kṛta Yuga had passed during the Svāyambhuva interval,
and then the Tretā Yuga of Vaivasvata Manu had arrived.
But when the world has turned toward vulgar ways, fallen under the sway of desire and greed, and is utterly deluded by envy, anger, and the like— whether experiencing happiness or suffering— (9)
Some say that those statements consisting of questions, answers, and formal compositions found in the thirty-six chapters are merely the words of his disciples;
but that is incorrect, because there is no evidence for the view that a single work should consist of a compilation of the utterances of multiple speakers.

This is because we observe the presentation of prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and conclusive replies (*uttarapakṣa*), and so forth, through the conventions of self and other even within treatises composed by a single author, such as the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, grammar, and logic. By this means— namely, the discernment of the three systems of Sadāśiva, Brahmā, and Bharata— it is established that the system of Brahmā represents the essential core.

As for what the preeminent teachers among the nihilists (nāstika) have said— that this treatise was composed by inserting fragments of their own works to analyze the essence and non-essence of the three systems of thought, and that it was not authored by the Sage (Muni)— that has been refuted;
for it contradicts the unassailable linguistic conventions of the world, which cannot be denied by anyone.

On this point, some say: "The five questions are first resolved within this very chapter; the subsequent chapters are devoted to their classification, definition, and examination, according to the established order of exposition. Others, however, say:
"By means of the five chapters, including those up to the 'Provision of Preliminary Rites' (*pūrvaraṅgavidhāna*), two questions have been resolved."

"By means of general gestures (*sāmānyābhinaya*) and ending with variegated gestures (*citrābhinaya*), the remaining [teachings] consist of three questions. However, we say: there is no fixed sequence here; rather, as the occasion arises, they exist primarily as the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) in the form of the *Ṣaṭsahasrī*.

The reality (*tattva*) is determined by a treatise devoted to the investigation of the five questions, but there is no specific sequence [of these questions]. We shall clarify this very point in the course of explaining the text itself. (6) In that regard, wishing to determine the meaning of "how" and "whose," he says: "By you," and so forth.

The production of jars and the like is established by worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) alone, and since this is followed by potters and others, it is logical to say "the jar is being made. However, this is not the case for drama (*nāṭya*). For its origin is established as having been first known by Viriñca (Brahmā); thus it has been said that its "coming into being" (*sambhava*) was created by Brahmā. Some, however, [assert] its beginninglessness (*anāditva*) here.
Those who explain the drama as being like the Veda employ terms such as "origination" (*utpatti*) and so forth figuratively in the sense of "recollection," "manifestation," and the like;
for in that context, when it is necessary to express "origination" by way of its cause, [the cause] is everywhere [found to be] time.

In order to demonstrate that, by virtue of being the prior cause, it pertains to the domain of those qualified for such [a practice] through its acceptance at the appropriate time, he says the five verses beginning with "pūrvam" (p.
When Jambudvīpa was overrun by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and mahoragas, and established under the guardians of the world; || 10 ||
It is said that the Grandfather was addressed by the gods, headed by Mahendra:
"We desire a plaything which may be both visible and audible. (11)
The connection of the great statement "At this time, the Grandfather was addressed thus by the gods" is as follows:

"At what time previously? means not only in this current kalpa, but also in previous kalpas. There are fourteen Manvantaras; such a period constitutes one kalpa, which is a single day of Brahmā. In that regard—

The first *manvantara* of the kalpa is named Svāyambhuva, while the seventh is the Vaivasvata *manvantara*, in which we currently reside. In all these *manvantaras*, the *Nāṭyaveda* was introduced by Brahmā during the occasion of the Tretā age; however, it was not so in the Kṛta Yuga.

The intended meaning is as follows. The construction [of the sentence] is: when that Kṛta Yuga which occurred in the first Manvantara of the Svāyambhuva period had ceased, and when the Itarā Yuga had begun more clearly with the complete passing of its transitional juncture (saṃdhi);
not only in that very Manvantara—but the word "tu" has the sense of "yāvat" (as far as)—until the [end of the] Vaivasvata [Manvantara].
Even when that period within the Manvantara known as the Tretā Yuga has commenced, by this examination of its beginning and end,
all the intermediate Manvantaras are included. By this, it is stated that the practice of drama occurs during all Tretā Yugas.

At this point, what was he asked? He replied: "We desire that which is a toy for play, pertaining to those people in Jambudvīpa—the land of karma—who are happy or suffering, by which the mind is distracted and led astray. The suffix *kṛtya* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulakāt*). And the mind [is led] from here and there."

Even while being led along a path, one is directed [toward it]; or rather, it is a toy suitable for play. In both cases, the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of "unknown" and so forth—that is, it is not known that this [world] is like medicine that is sweet on the outside but bitter within, having as its sole fruit the distraction of the mind. And that toy [of worldly existence] belongs to those who are happy and those who are suffering.

It is thus: for there is no play whatsoever in a time or place that is exclusively happy, nor in one that is exclusively miserable. Therefore, play does not occur among the inhabitants of Ilāvṛta and other such regions during the Kṛtayuga, nor at the end of the Kaliyuga, nor among those in hell. This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in which the meaning of the final member is predominant (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*). [The compound *duḥkhakrīḍā* means] "play consisting of suffering."
He speaks of abundance: "How is it known that the world is happy or suffering?

Because one whose heart is deluded and perfumed by envy, anger, and so forth—by the inclusion of "and so forth," [it means] by attachment, craving, and so on. He states the reason for this in sequence:

Envy and the like arise from being under the sway of desire, while anger and the like arise from greed for sovereignty and so forth. Why are desire and greed considered excessive? Because they are the cause of the state of being happy or miserable; that is, they are the cause of desire and the rest, which leads to engagement in vulgar conduct. "Vulgar" refers to that which is appropriate for people in regions crowded with those who have not heard the meaning of the scriptures.

Dharma is characterized by the non-transgression of one’s own specific duty (*svadharma*), because it is toward that end that the world has proceeded. This Vedic discourse is not to be proclaimed among the Śūdra castes.
Therefore, create another Veda, the fifth one, which is common to all classes.

[Objection: "But if this is so, how can there be happiness for these beings due to the abundance of unrighteousness? To this he says: "In Jambūdvīpa, which is overrun by gods such as the glorious Vijaya and Avimukta who have descended as Rudras, as well as by Dānavas and others whose hearts are filled with passion (rājasa) and who perform worship according to their own imagination."

And when [the world] is invaded by gods and others, and brought under their control—surely, in that case, while the means for accomplishing pure and mixed dharmas exist, how can there be *dharma*? For those [means] do not operate therein. True; however, by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*)...

When the world has been established by kings produced from portions of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and enjoined toward the accomplishment of their own duty (*svadharma*), [the world] consists of what is visible and what is audible—that is, worthy of being seen and heard. It is not merely a means to accomplish [worldly] duty; it is also possible [to experience it], yet it is not for the most part miserable or harsh. The world...
By this use of the singular number, it is indicated that whatever is suitable [for the object] is common to all, and that [suitability] does not consist of the nature of being tangible and so forth.
However, the possibility of being common to many applies more extensively to the visible and the audible; for when an object is uncommon, only envy, anger, and the like arise.

This is what is meant: in the Kṛta age, when *sattva* predominates, people are devoted solely to their own duty (*svadharma*) and do not exert themselves with a sense of rejection or acceptance toward pleasure and pain. But in the Tretā age, due to the presence of *rajas* and *sattva*, they seek to destroy suffering and desire happiness; this is because of the flickering nature of *rajas*. At that time, regarding those things prescribed by the scriptures...
It is set in motion by royal control; and therein, such a means must be devised by which their engagement occurs spontaneously. And that [means] is drama alone.
By the word "and" (ca), he says this: it is brought about through some such connection by a certain means.

By this, it is indicated that the performance (*prayoga*) has its life-force in the general representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*), such that even when the visible and the audible are apprehended by different sense organs, they do not lose their status as objects of a single unifying synthesis (*ekānusandhāna*). "Visible" means that which bestows delight (*hṛdya*);
"audible" means that which bestows etymological understanding (*vyutpatti*); thus, the meaning is that it bestows both pleasure and knowledge. By this—

[Objection: But what is the self-interest of Indra and the others by this much? [Reply: He says: Those people who have gone to Jambūdvīpa, which is presided over by the world-protectors (lokapāla), being established in their own duties, nourish heaven through sacrifice and so forth. "Therefore we desire it"—by this he expresses the consensus of all.

Therefore, Vindhyavāsin and others have described the divine and human creations as functioning through mutual assistance; others, however, say that for Mahendra and the rest, their own purpose alone is sport (*krīḍā*). By the phrase "when the Tretā age had begun and the world was in such a state," this has been stated:

It occurs thus: for even in heaven, at various times, because their hearts are made dusty by the connection with the qualities of kingship inherent in humans—such as the performance of sacrifices and other rites—the gods themselves long for something to play with. (10–11)

Having thus stated the purpose of the purpose— that even a person authorized by the scriptures is easily disciplined through drama— he states another purpose as well, beginning with "There is no Vedic practice," and so forth.
In the Kṛta Yuga, everyone [attained their goal] solely by the power of the excellence of the *sattva* quality.
Having said "So be it" to them and having dismissed the king of the gods,
he who knew the reality, resorting to yoga, called to mind the four Vedas. (13)
"These Vedas are not to be heard by those born among the classes of women, Śūdras, and others;
therefore, I shall create another fifth Veda that may be heard by all."

He maintains his own dharma. But nowadays, due to their rajasic nature, those of the śūdra class—such as the Karana and other castes—are all overcome by immense pride and do not follow the conduct of the three higher varnas.
They do not respect the teaching that "the scripture instructs you thus," regarding it as mere words; nor do they...

They are worthy of instruction in the Vedic scriptures; therefore, he says "properly here in this place. This has been taught to you by Śruti, so they are not [to be considered] unhearable. "Applicable to all castes" (sārvavarṇika) means that it provides proficiency even for those who are delicate, whether they are qualified or unqualified. All...
The phrase "that which has the phonemes as its purpose by way of those to be trained" constitutes a summary of everything previously stated and now stated.
Others, however, say that this is to avoid redundancy: [it refers to] all the phonemes being [expressed] in a manner that is flavorful and delicate.

That which exists in a poem where there is a delineation of one’s own duty according to the proper method is "dependent on that" (tadāśrita). By means of this, every person— whose mind is delighted by the charming and youthful [hero]—
utilizes even the knowledge of what ought and ought not to be done as an inseparable consequence of enjoying the work, just like the consumption of medicine situated within milk.
"Drama provides instruction for those who are already qualified, as well as for the delicate who are not yet qualified;
even for those who have not heard the scriptures, it establishes an unwavering discernment between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done through its correspondence with reality.
(12) "Let it be so," he said to them. "The king of the gods"—having spoken thus to them and having dismissed them, [he] dismissed the king of the gods.

This was stated because of its preeminence; the meaning is "having dismissed Indra and the others. Regarding the word *yogam*: it means that which causes all the Vedas to appear simultaneously. Regarding *tattvavit*: it means one who knows all the worlds and the Vedas. (13) He states with three verses beginning with *dharmyam* what he did after that. Thus (*evam*). (1-16)

Having conceptualized the meaning expressed by the pair beginning with "dharmyam" (righteous), [he] said "from that" (*tataḥ*) on the basis of the recollection of the four Vedas. He created the *Nāṭyaveda* from the four [Vedas]. The suffix *-śatṛ* is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetau*). Regarding "dharmyam": it is for the sake of instruction that is effective (*sādhu*) regarding *dharma*;
the same applies to the word "artha" (wealth/purpose). Others, however, hold that its purpose (*prayojana*) is fame (*yaśas*) which is not devoid of *dharma* and *artha*. In this regard:

In both of these two explanations, there would be an inclusion of other human goals (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, in this conception which contains the origin of drama as its embryo, that which has already been abandoned [in the previous explanation] remains abandoned. Moreover, since fame is a fruit of dharma, for what purpose is it mentioned separately? And there is a redundancy in the phrase "with instruction" (*sopadeśam*) and so forth.

Therefore, this is the meaning here: by the word *dharma*, all four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) are intended. That which is "good" (*sādhu*) or "efficacious" (*sādhaka*) with respect to them [is what is meant]. Now, is it direct? No, he says.

It shall be consistent with dharma, conducive to worldly prosperity, and conducive to fame; it shall contain instruction and include means of gathering followers, and it shall reveal all duties for the sake of future generations.
I shall compose the fifth Veda, known as Nāṭya, which is endowed with the meaning of all the Śāstras, which initiates all arts and crafts, and which includes the Itihāsas. || 15 ||

"Accompanied by instruction" means that which exists together with the means being taught (namely, the means for the four goals of human life and the ten dramatic forms), that is to say, that which demonstrates the means for the fourfold aims of existence. [Objection: But the Vedas and other scriptures are also like this. [Response: This is not so; "properly" implies a complete compendium. For beyond this...
No other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sought for the sake of a conviction free from doubt;

and that [conviction] consists precisely in direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). As they say: "And every means of valid cognition culminates in perception. "Together with that" means including that [perception]. Even so, since one observes right conduct, sacrifice, and so forth through perception, what is the distinction of this [scriptural authority]?

He said: "It reveals all actions. This means that it reveals all actions being performed immediately thereafter, within a short time—such as five or six days—in which there is a direct perception of the connection between auspicious and inauspicious actions and their results. To whom does this apply? He says:
"Whoever among the world"—that is to say, whoever shall exist in the world after this moment; the meaning is "of that [person] who is to be instructed.
Here, the word "shall exist" (*bhaviṣyat*) is explained with the intention of referring to the object of imitation (*anukārya*). And by the word "not" (*na*)...

The inclusion of the past and the present [in the definition] is refuted by the subsequent and preceding [arguments]. For it is appropriate that the narration of the lineages of royal sages and so forth be mentioned directly by the author himself as the primary subject; however, it is not so for the future—let this matter rest.
Therefore, the phrase "of the world" (lokasya) should be explained solely with the intention of those who are to be instructed.

Even so, he asks: by what means is the world set in motion therein? He says: "Desirable" (*arthya*). This means that because it is pleasing to the heart, it is to be longed for by all people, despite their various capacities. [Objection: But how can there be longing for something whose ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is not yet known? He says: "Glorious" (*yaśasya*). Everywhere...
It is renowned for its heart-pleasing quality.

Not only does it show the means to achieve the primary goals of human life, but it is also endowed with and joined to all the subjects of the arts—such as song, dance, instrumental music, and so forth—which constitute the contents of all treatises on the arts. Furthermore...

It sets in motion all arts, such as painting and sculpture, by including them through their utility; thus, that from which the accomplishment of all things occurs through a single effort is called *nāṭya* (drama). And that [drama] includes the *itihāsa* (epic history).
It takes the form of instruction based on *itihāsa*, along with its various divisions. The word *iti* is used here in the sense of "thus," referring to direct perception.
Having thus resolved, the Blessed One, recollecting all the Vedas,
then created the Nāṭya Veda, which originated from the limbs of the four Vedas. (16)
He took up the recitation from the Ṛgveda, the singing from the Sāmans,
the dramatic gestures from the Yajurveda, and even the aesthetic sentiments from the Atharvaveda.

It illuminates. *Ha* is the augment *iha*. *Āsana* means "seated. Thus, that *itihāsa*—in the reading *sa-heti*, the suffix *-a* denotes possession—is where such matters derived from scripture (*āgamika*), which are directly perceived and whose nature consists in the relationship between action and its fruit, reside. *Iti* means knowledge; its *hāsa* (laughter) is...
Some maintain that it is an expansion preceded by joy. And the *Itihāsa*—its definition is as follows:

"That wherein the various types of dramatic forms (*rūpaka*) are described. By the word "instruction" (*upadeśa*), one refers to the *Daśarūpaka*, which is indeed useful for that purpose, as well as the science of the *Nāṭyaveda* concerning the characteristics of the two hands and so forth. It is precisely that [science] which is accompanied by it.

The resolve [arises] from the sense of what must be done. Otherwise, how could a drama, even when conceived by the intellect, be transferred elsewhere? And without that, how could there be a performance? "The fifth" means he who, though being one, surpasses the four Vedas. "I" refers to him whose supreme task is indeed the upholding of the affairs of all the worlds.

The task [is as follows]: "Having thus resolved" means that this very operation of resolution—characterized by the unification of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*) through the intellect—is the production of the *Nāṭyaveda* by Brahmā. [Objection: But surely, by the mere recollection of the Vedas...
In that regard, how is its status as a cause established? He says: "Arising from the four Vedas and their ancillaries. There are four Vedas.

It is that from which the arising of the ancillaries—such as phonology (*pāṭhya*) and so forth—occurs; it is called "arising" (*sambhava*) because they arise from it. For this very reason, even the fourfold Veda is subordinate to the ancillaries therein; thus it is so described. (14)

He shows which Veda is employed for which part [of the ritual] by saying, "He took the *pāṭhya* from the Ṛgveda. Here, regarding the root *paṭh* (to recite), it is stated that its meaning is "articulate speech" (*vyaktā vāk*). This quality of being articulate (*vyaktatva*) consists in the capacity to convey one's own intended meaning as qualified by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). And that...

It comes about through the application of the totality of elements such as *kāku*, *adhyāya*, and the *svara-alaṅkāra*s to be described hereafter; thus, recitation (*pāṭhya*) is said to be "refined" by that. And because it is the most important, it is mentioned first.
For he will say:
"Effort must be exerted in speech, for this is considered the very body of drama; indeed, it is through gesture, costume, and inner disposition that the meaning of the words is manifested. (14-2, p.
It is joined with the Dharma, action, and purpose; it is accompanied by authoritative instruction and the means of integration;
it accords with the inclinations of all the world and demonstrates every form of activity.
He contemplated the fifth Veda, known as Nāṭya, which is endowed with the meaning of all scriptures and possesses all arts, and which is an Itihāsa.
Thus was the Nāṭyaveda, connected with the Vedas and Upavedas, created by the blessed and great-souled Brahmā, the knower of all things. 18.
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, the Great-Souled One created the Nāṭyaveda;
having produced the Nāṭyaveda, Brahmā spoke to the Lord of the Gods:
"This Itihāsa has been created by me; let it be assigned to the gods. (19)

For this very reason, although it is included within *abhinaya* (acting), it is treated separately. It is derived from the *Ṛgveda*, because that Veda—whose primary characteristic is the threefold tone (*traisvarya*)—contributes to the sacrifice by means of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns. Furthermore, the recitation (*pāṭhya*) is also endowed with the threefold tone; for in the case of monotony (*aikasvarya*), the quality of the accent arises through the presence or absence of intonation (*kākubhāva*).
"And because [it arises] from a single essence, it attains the form of song in the case of vowels and so forth," as we shall explain later (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 17).
Following the discussion on the notes belonging to recitation (*pāṭhya*), it was stated that "he took the song from the *Sāmans*.
Some maintain that its mention later is logical because it serves as an embellishment (*uparañjaka*). Song is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Because it will be stated that [this] depends on the *prayoga*, our teachers maintain that since *sa-carvaṇā* (relishing) is dependent upon that, its mention is appropriately placed right here.

By the word "ca" (and), he indicates that this is of equal status [with the other]. By the word "eva" (only/just), he indicates that from among those [elements], only the *gīti* (melodic movement) is grasped within the *gītis*.

This is according to the principle [of Jaimini] that "the name [indicates the source]" (sāmākhyā, Jaimini 2.1.36). It shows that the application of the words *dhruvā* and *ādhāra* originates from the Ṛgveda itself; therefore, it has been included right here based on the statement in the *Dhruvādhyāya*.

In this very [context], the general principle of *tāla*— which consists of time as the vital breath of the activity of singing by the ensemble of forms densely enveloped [in sound]— is accepted and enters [into the ritual]. However, in the Yajurveda, where the duties of the *adhvaryu* priest are primary,
the sequence of subsidiary acts, such as circumambulation and so forth, comes first.
"He shall recite the verses beginning with 'pāṇikā' (32-2)," and so forth. Furthermore, there is also the wind-instrument (*suṣirātodya*), because of the predominance of musical notes (*svara*).
However, in the *Atharvaveda*, during rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and killing (*māraṇa*), that officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is like an actor (*naṭa*).

Through the apprehension of the various *anubhāvas*— such as the shouting of "vaiṣuṇṇā" and so forth— by the subjects, enemies, and others, as well as through the wearing of the red turban and other such costumes (*nepathya*) in those respective actions, there arises *sattva*, which consists of the mental fortitude produced by men of exceptional effort.
Because of their possibility:
those who are skilled, wise, bold, and have overcome fatigue.
"Let this Veda known as Nāṭya be transmitted by you to them. (20)
Having heard those words uttered by Brahmā, Śakra,
becoming prostrate with palms joined in reverence, replied to the Grandfather.
"O Best of Beings, O Blessed One, the gods are incapable and unfit for the grasping, retention, understanding, and practice of this [art], as it pertains to the performance of drama. (22)
Next is the mention of the names of the [specific] representations. Verbal representation (*vācika-abhinaya*) has already been explained previously.

Because of the predominance of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and the transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*), such as fortitude (*dhṛti*) and joy (*pramoda*), which exist in ultimate reality, their synthesis is the primary [factor].

Since the experience of *carvaṇā* (relishing), which consists of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) produced by the totality of factors such as the *vibhāvas*, is possible [only through this process], it is said that the apprehension of that [flavor] occurs from that [process];
thus, these [factors] are not merely external. For this very reason, they are relished; and we shall explain later that they are indeed relished within that [very state].
Therefore, in this way, [the treatise] begins with the dramatic performance (*nāṭya*) and other forms of representation.

Drama (*nāṭya*) consists essentially of supreme delight, characterized by the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which is nourished by the categories of song, instrumental music, breath-control, and dramatic gesture. Therefore, it has been demonstrated in sequence that drama alone is the Veda, because proficiency in it arises from that [Vedic source]. Thus, by its very nature, it stands distinguished from those scriptures whose life-force lies in injunctions consisting of sequential arrangements and formal prescriptions.

It is established that the nature of the Vedas as vital breath (*prāṇa*) belongs to drama alone, for it is one who knows the names and designations of knowledge that has spontaneously ascended [into it].
He concludes this with the verse beginning "By the Vedas and Upavedas," etc. The Vedas have already been explained.

That by which the meaning of the Vedas is understood as being beneficial is the *upaveda* (subsidiary Veda). For example, Āyurveda is that which demonstrates the interpretation of the *mantras*, *arthavādas*, and so forth of the Ṛgveda, as well as [the methods for] initiation and the protection of progeny. Because he is the Great Soul (*mahātman*), he is therefore omniscient (*sarvavedin*). And because he is omniscient, he possesses the power to create such a world.
By concluding with "thus" (*evam*), he shows that the three questions have been answered;

for the purpose, the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), and the relationship between the auxiliaries and the primary subject (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) have already been determined.
Thus, by the poet who is like the Grandfather (Brahmā), there is always the construction of dramas in the form of the body of the Nāṭya-veda.
Having demonstrated that "it must be enacted," there is the king as the patron who employs the actors endowed with creative power;
and there is the director, who is like the sage Bharata, possessed of a complete retinue and omniscient.
The time for the performance is characterized by a great festival of the patron. These [actors] provide instruction under the pretext of introducing the dramatic play.

Free from passion and hatred, acting with impartiality, possessing the fitness for becoming one with that [sentiment] when the mirror of the heart is stainless, and skilled in the relishing of aesthetic flavor—such are the spectators (*sāmājika*).
This he demonstrates by means of a narrative from a former age through the following passage on instruction: "Having produced..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "But the Nāṭyaveda," the word "but" (tu) implies that only a king is capable of putting it into practice.
As for those sages who know the secrets of the Vedas and are firm in their vows:
These are capable of its grasping, as well as its application and its retention. || 23 ||
Having heard the words of Śakra, the Lotus-born One said to me:
"O sinless one, you, accompanied by a hundred sons, shall be the performer of this [rite]."
Having understood that I was commanded [to do so], I taught the science of drama (nāṭyaveda) and its practical application in its true essence to my sons from the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 25 ||

Itihāsa consists of the ten types of dramatic forms (*daśarūpaka*). "Skilled" means capable of grasping and retaining [the teachings]. "Eloquent" means capable of reasoning through induction and deduction (*ūhāpoha*). "Bold" means fearless in an assembly. "Conquered of fatigue" means fit, with a body suited for the task and one that is untiring. Regarding "in grasping": [this refers to] understanding previously from the mouth of the teacher.

Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the non-forgetting of that [knowledge]. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the investigation through reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*). Application (*prayoga*) is the manifestation [of knowledge] before an assembly. By the word "and" (*ca*), [it is implied] the practice of exercises, physical training, and so forth, which are conducive to those [qualities].
The gods (*devāḥ*) are so called because they abound in happiness. Even if they were to engage [in such practices] somehow or other by the command of their Lord, [they would not do so].
The meaning is that it is difficult for these [people] to reach the ultimate fulfillment of that [knowledge].
(19–22) To the question, "What then should be done? he says: "Those who... By "knowers of the Veda," he refers to the capacity for grasping and retaining [the texts].
By "knowers of the secret," he refers to the skill in knowing and retaining the meaning of the Upanishads concerning the supreme self (*adhyātma*).

This is the capacity produced by the *sattvic* [state] through the utilization of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth, as he will state: "The *sattva* is to be accomplished through mental effort," and so on. By means of that— One should fix the vital breath (*prāṇa*) between the eyebrows; there arises a stiffness and tears in the eyes.
Perspiration in the heart, trembling in the anus, horripilation on the head, and [salivation] from the mouth.
Discoloration occurs in the throat, a faltering tone in the voice, and a loss of consciousness within the nose.

Such is their fitness. For this very reason, as a secondary consequence (*anuṣaṅga*), even the actor attains the supreme human goal through the power of *dhāraṇā* and other practices. Regarding the term "seers" (*ṛṣayaḥ*): one is a seer because of seeing (*darśanāt*). They are those capable of reasoning and deliberation (*ūhāpoha-yogya*).
Regarding the term "those of firm vows" (*saṃśita-vrata*): [they are so called because their vows are sharpened].
Śāṇḍilya, Vātsya, Kohala, and likewise Dattila; Jaṭila and Ambaṣṭaka, as well as Taṇḍu and Agniśikha. (26)
Saindhava, Sapulomāna, Śāḍvali, and Vipula, as well as Kapiñjali, Bādira, and Yamadhūmrāyaṇa. || 27 ||
Jambudhvaja, Kākajaṅgha, Svarṇaka, Tāpasa, as well as Kaidārin, Śālikarṇa, Dīrghagātra, and Śālika. || 28 ||
Kautsa, Tāṇḍāyani, Piṅgala, Citraka, Bandhula, Bhallaka, Muṣṭhika, and Saindhavāyana; || 29 ||
"They are capable of practice. "In that way," means that the sequential order of these [stages], beginning with grasping (*grahaṇa*), must be demonstrated.

By saying "these," he shows that their nature is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself. Regarding "but having heard from me": by the word "but" (*tu*), he indicates that this [teaching] is superior even to that of other sages.
"Brahmā himself has commanded me"—this indicates an excess of reverence.

"Because of the union with a hundred sons" (or "the union with many others") indicates the presence of a vast retinue mobilized by another. By the address "O sinless one," it is indicated that there is the successful accomplishment of the correct application for one who has been honored by an assembly full of enthusiasm through their entreaty. He was thus commanded.

Thus, his speech is declared to be inviolable. By the phrase "from the Grandfather," he dispels any suspicion that he might not have been taught by a preceptor. *Prayoga* refers to the *Daśarūpaka*; it is called *prayoga* because it is employed (*prayujyate*) or brought into being (*nirvartyate*) by means of it—that is, the treatise on dramatic characteristics (*nāṭyalakṣaṇa-śāstra*). I caused my sons to study that.
"Prayukti" means application (*prayoga*). I taught my sons that [application] up to the point of mastery (*adhyavasāya*).
The meaning is that I acted in such a way that those sons properly attained that application.
By the two particles "ca" and "api," two repetitions are indicated.

The preoccupation with other duties appropriate for a sage is also indicated by the word *liṭ* (the periphrastic future). By the term *tattvataḥ* ("in reality"), the complete reliability of the teacher of drama (*nāṭyācārya*) is understood.
Taitila, Bhārgava, Śuci, Bahula,
Abudha, Budhasena, Pāṇḍukarṇa, and Sukerala.
Ṛjuka, Maṇḍaka, Śambara, Vañjula, as well as Māgadha, Sarala, Kartāra, and Ugra. || 31 ||
Tuṣāra, Pārṣada, Gautama, Bādarāyaṇa, Viśāla, Śabala, Sunābha, and Meṣa as well. || 32 ||
Kāliya, Bhramara, as well as the sage Pīṭhamukha, Nakhakuṭṭa, Aśmakuṭṭa, and Ṣaṭpada, who was likewise most excellent. || 33 ||
Pāduka and Upānaha, as well as Śruti and the cry of the blue jay (cāṣasvara); Agnikuṇḍa and Ājyakuṇḍa, and likewise Vitaṇḍya and Tāṇḍya. || 34 ||
Kartarākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, Kuśala, Dussaha, as well as Lāja, Bhayānaka, Bībhatsa, and Savicakṣaṇa. || 35 ||
He indicates the sons by their names, beginning with "Śāṇḍilya" and so forth. In this context, the primary purpose for mentioning the names is that the actors' renown is a cause for respect;
however, there is also a secondary purpose. For example, [this applies] to names such as Vidūṣaka, Tāpasa, and others.

The application of the specific stages [of practice] occurs through the reasoning that establishes the meaning obtained from the etymological derivation of *talākamīna* (or *tathākarmīṇa*). However, another says: "Only a hundred [verses] are recited here;
and among those to be enacted, there is the production of the *sthāpaka*..."

This is with the intention of emphasizing the primary status of fifty objects— consisting of the nine rasas, their thirty-three transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), and the eight *sāttvika* states— which are categorized as appropriate or inappropriate and relate to the hero and the antagonist. In that context, however, even the *kaiśikī* [vṛtti] may be employed.
Thus, there is no room for a subsequent passage; enough, therefore, with these explanations based on the dogmatic adherence of those lacking in aesthetic sensitivity. (26–39) p.
20) One who has a sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*) on the eyes and a sectarian mark on the nose, whether black or white;
Vidyujjihva, Mahājihva, and Śālaṅkāyana as well. || 36 ||
Śyāmāyana, Māṭhara, and likewise Lohitāṅga;
Saṃvartaka, Pañcaśikha, Triśikha, and Śikha as well. || 37 ||
(Śaṅkhavarṇamukha, Ṣaṇḍa, Śaṅkukarṇa, as well as Śakranemi, Gabhasti, Aṃśumālin, and likewise Śaṭha.
Regarding the phrase "in which": [this refers to] the activities of those of superior nature (*uttamaprakṛti*) and so forth. Regarding the word "as" (*yathā*): it refers to a certain person.
Another [type of performance] is appropriate by way of manifesting joy in his heart, whereas this [present one] is appropriate by way of manifesting his grief.
Now,
in order to withdraw the other implements employed for the *kaishiki* style— which is the life-force of all dramatic performance— the author begins:

"She reveals me as Bhāratī," and so forth. Regarding "vṛtti" (mode of action): when the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), such as *dharma* and the rest, are to be accomplished, it is the general activity of speech, body, and internal disposition (*sattva*). And that is fourfold according to its concise subdivisions.
For whatever action is undertaken, there is necessarily the operation of speech, mind, and body. Among these—

There is an entry into a certain sequence of graceful variety, because for those of superior nature, every activity consists solely of excellence. That itself is the fourfold movement (*vṛtti*). *Bhāratī* is the movement of speech;
*sāttvatī* is the movement of the mind, consisting of mental activity and characterized by goodness (*sattva*). "Good" (*sat*)...
Cognition is of the nature of manifestation. That which possesses this [manifestation] is the sentient mind (*manas*). "This belongs to that" means:

they go forth (*iyarti*), thus they are *arāḥ*—soldiers who are spirited and untiring. This is their *ārabhaṭī*, a bodily activity. Hairs, even though performing no collection of purposeful actions whatsoever, are useful for the beauty of the body; likewise, [this] is useful for beauty.

The primary sequence is that the *kaiśikī* style (*vṛtti*) constitutes the dramatic action (*vyāpāra*). As for the designation of other [styles] by that same name, it is because they are dominated by it—just as the term "sweet" is applied to things like *pānaka* (a syrup) when they are primarily composed of various flavors. We shall elaborate upon this further on.
By the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā), and out of a desire for the welfare of the world, we [created] Vidyuta, Śātajaṅgha, Raudra, and also Vīra. (39)
A hundred sons were employed according to the divisions of their respective domains;
each was appointed to that specific task for which he was suitable, and in the manner appropriate to him.
"O twice-born ones, this performance has indeed been executed by me, relying upon the Bhāratī, Sāttvatī, and likewise the Ārabhaṭī styles. (41)
Having accepted [the request] and bowed, Brahmā was then petitioned by me;
thereupon the Preceptor of the Gods said to me, "Employ the Kaiśikī style as well."
Thus, whatever grace there may be, all of that is the manifestation of the *kaiśikī* style;

and the word "but" (*tu*) indicates that it is impossible for those [men] to employ it. Therefore, the entire *daśarūpa* (the ten forms of drama), being devoid of such variety, has been applied to them. For this very reason, he expresses contempt for such a performance with the word "verily" (*vai*). It was employed...
Thus; the meaning is that it has been applied to their stage of practice.

(41) "Adequate" means that one employs it with skill, attentiveness, and variety. For this very reason he says: "substance"; "beautiful. Because that *kaiśikī* style has beauty as its very life-force. "In this way" refers to the cleverness of intellect.

He asked this of me in order to know my [intentions]. By the use of the particle *ca*, he demonstrates his possession of ready wit (*pratyutpannapratibhāna*). By this, he indicates that the quality of a dramatic teacher (*nāṭyācārya*) consists in being capable of instantly grasping the heart of the poet. (42–43)

Furthermore, it is not possible to infer the means [of realization] regarding an object that has never been perceived before. However, at the time of instruction, Brahmā merely stated that this heart-captivating variety should be applied therein. With this intention, he describes the direct realization of the Kaiśikī style.
By the pair of verses beginning with *nṛtāṅgahāra* and so forth: *nartanam* means dancing.
It is the casting [of the body] through the grace of the limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), and not by any part that must be performed [according to a rule].
Even common worldly people speak in this very way regarding such matters, saying, "He moves as if he were dancing," and so on. In that regard:

It is endowed with *aṅgahāras*, which are the movements of the limbs; by means of these, there is the attainment of appropriate positions in an unbroken form. It belongs to Lord Śaṅkara himself, whose body is filled with perfect bliss, and from whom a beautiful internal radiance issues forth; for this very reason...
I saw her as one being employed, dancing with pure joy because she was devoid of any other duty to be performed.
"O best of the twice-born, tell me what wealth is appropriate for her.
Thus was I addressed by him, and I replied to the lord. (43)

"O Blessed One, let the materials for the performance of the Kaiśikī style be provided; it is endowed with dance and bodily gestures, and consists of aesthetic flavors, emotions, and dramatic actions. (44)
I have seen the Kaiśikī style performed by the Lord Nīlakaṇṭha as he danced; it is characterized by delicate costumes and originates from the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa). 45.
But she could not be employed by men, being fit only for women;
therefore, the all-pervading Lord of great splendor created the Apsarases from his mind.

[Objection: But how is that [beauty] useful for drama? [Reply: He says: if that very same [beauty] is accompanied by appropriate, refined attire (*nepathya*), then—just as he will say, "The erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) consists of a radiant costume" (Nāṭyaśāstra 6.50)—the erotic sentiment (*rasa*) described in drama becomes possible; not otherwise. The mention of "attire" [is intended to include]...

This is also an illustration for those with delicate limbs and the like; therefore, even when the fourfold delicate acting (sukumāra-abhinaya), which is the cause for the manifestation of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), is employed, it is [accomplished] without [the need for] sweet, slow, twisting, turning, raising of the eyebrows, side-glances, and so forth.

There is not even the name of a tasting of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) here. To explain how this [tasting] occurs with such application, he says: "consisting of the essence of rasa, bhāva, and action. The state (*bhāva*) of rasas is their cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which is the pervasion of the hearts of the poet, the actor, and the audience. The "action" (*kriyā*) is its procedure (*itikartavyatā*); that alone is the essence (*ātman*).

This is its inherent nature (*svabhāva*). What is meant is this: even when the manifestation of sentiments such as the Furious (*raudra*) is to be performed, whatever acting (*abhinaya*) is employed must be characterized by a beautiful variety consisting of alliteration, rhythmic movement, circular gestures, and so forth, through their non-mixture [with other elements].

If poorly joined or not joined at all, it cannot be a cause for the manifestation of rasa; thus, the Kaiśikī [vṛtti] is the very life-breath in every instance. As he will say: "Its branches are dance and the subjects of dramatic representation" (Nāṭyaśāstra 8.15). Indeed, even the mention of the name of the *śṛṅgāra* rasa is not possible without it.
Regarding the phrase "disregarded by women," the intended meaning is this:

as long as the purity of the irrepressible wonder arising from the play of aesthetic flavor (rasa) within one's own heart has not been produced—just as it was in the case of the Blessed One—even by hundreds of instructions, such extraordinary charm cannot be acquired; and this is likewise true for the sages.
What wonder is there in the bliss of those whose mental fluctuations are naturally turned away from sense objects?

Even that bliss born of meditative absorption does not transcend the limits of the body; on the contrary, we flee from it. Therefore, women possess such a unique variety of being; for they are those whose tender emotions arise through contact with them.
Perhaps they might even be able to;
those skilled in dramatic ornaments gave them to me through practical application.
Mañjukeśī, Sukeśī, Miśrakeśī, and Sulocanā. || 47 ||
Saudāminī, Devadattā, Devasenā, Manoramā,
Sudatī, Sundarī, Vidagdhā, and likewise Vipulā— || 48 ||

As for those who say, "The Blessed One lacks the capacity for the performance of *kaiśikī* [sentiment]; therefore, the reading should be *tena dṛṣṭomayā* (she was seen by him together with Umā)," meaning that while the Blessed One was dancing with Umā, she was seen by me performing [the dance] herself, disregarding even the Blessed One—they are refuted by the reasoning already stated. Likewise—
"The Lord, with various graceful gestures (*aṅgahāra*) imbued with playfulness, bound his mass of hair; therein the *kaiśikī* [vṛtti] was fashioned" (Nāṭyaśāstra 20.13).
Thus, it would be inappropriate for the Blessed Viṣṇu to fashion the *kaiśikī*; enough of this prolixity.
By the word *jana* (people), he dispels the suspicion that they possess passion (*rāgitā*). "Then he created them" means "by means of his mind";
the sense is that they were fashioned according to his pleasure.
(44–46) *Kaiśikī*—which is the ornament of drama (*nāṭya*) and the cause of its variety (or consisting of playfulness, charm, and so forth)—is that in which they are skilled.

Others, however, hold that the dramatic ornaments (*nāṭyālaṅkāra*) to be mentioned in the section on general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*) consist of ten innate ones, such as *svabhāvajā*, *līlā*, and *vilāsa*, and seven effort-induced ones, such as *śobhā* and *kānti*.
By this, the unsuitability of the sage’s daughters for this [drama] has first been stated; for, in mentioning their names...

The purpose [of this] is to be determined as before. By the words "he gave to me," it is shown that the collection of requisites was under the control of the master of the dramatic art (*nāṭyācārya*). Furthermore, indicating that those [women] were accepted by me through the granting of instruction as was appropriate, he suggests that I also employed the *kaiśikī* style.

He demonstrates this: having shown that drama, complete with its four modes of performance (*vṛtti*), has been practiced in the rehearsal hall (*guṇanikā*), he now shows its conjunction with the two embellishments (*uparañjaka*)—song and instrumental music—beginning with "Svāti," and so forth.
Svāti was a particular seer (*ṛṣi*). By whom...

The meaning is that the construction of the *puṣkara* drum was accomplished by means of arranging various colors fashioned from the shimmering play of lotus petals struck by the diversity of waterfalls falling during the rainy season, according to their respective rules of form. "Together with his disciples" refers to [the instruction] of the *tripuṣkara*.
The inclusion of instruments played with the hands (pakṣātodya) has been stated through the employment of the āpūraka, paṇava, mṛdaṅga, jhallarī, and so forth.
Here, the lute (bhāṇḍa) is mentioned first because it is useful when that very instrument is employed in the circumambulation and other such movements. And here, the Kaiśikī [vṛtti] is present.
Sumālā, Santati, Sunandā, and likewise Sumukhī;
Māgadhī, Arjunī, Saralā, Keralā, and Dhṛti. (49)
He gave me Nandā, Sapuṣkalā, and Kalamā;
while Svāti, appointed to the care of the vessels, remained with his disciples under the self-existent one.
And the Gandharvas, headed by Nārada, were appointed to the art of singing;
thus, having thoroughly understood this drama, he [performed it] together with all his sons.
Accompanied by Svāti and Nārada, the cause of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
I approached Brahmā with palms joined in reverence for the purpose of practical application.
"The mastery of drama has been attained; tell me, what shall I do?
Having heard these words, the Grandfather replied: ||| 53 ||

It has been stated that [the musician] is appointed in the middle; therefore, this [work] does not have that as its primary focus. Regarding the phrase "the application of singing" (*gānayoga*), the word "singing" (*gāna*) includes wind instruments (*tatasuṣira*). By using the word "singing," he indicates that the art of music (*gāndharva*) is not applicable here.
By the word "appointed" (*niyukta*), he shows the dependence of instrumentalists, singers, and others upon the master of dramatic performance (*nāṭyācārya*).

With two verses beginning with "Thus, this is drama" (*evaṃ nāṭyam*), he shows that the performance should be carried out by merging dance, song, instrumental music, and acting into a single unity for the sake of achieving their harmony: "Thus, in this synthesis, this is drama"— it is merged and apprehended by a single cognition.
"Having understood and realized that [the art] was perfectly accomplished," means that he approached Brahmā together with his sons, Svāti, and Nārada;

the sense is that he stood before Brahmā for the purpose of an invitation. (47–52) He demonstrates the invitation with the words "of the dance. "Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) means that which has been grasped or learned.

The meaning is that it is a dance (*nāṭya*). "Grasping" means its observation; the sense is that it has become fit for viewing once it has been attained. Regarding the phrase "this, however" (*etattu*): the word *tu* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*. "Upon merely hearing" (*śrutvaiva*). For this very reason, it is "presented," meaning it has appeared before one spontaneously and by the stroke of fate. [This refers to] the banner, which signifies Indra.
