The festival of the banner (*dhvajamahaḥ*) is that wherein there is great worship and honor. By means of the epithet "having slain the asuras and dānavas," he shows the origin of this festival of the banner.
He demonstrates the sequence of its performance therein with the words, "First, the *nāndī* was performed by me. This refers to the [introductory rite] called *nāndī*.
This is the primary auspicious occasion for the commencement of this great practice; it has now arrived.
This glorious festival of the banner of the great Indra is now taking place.
Now, let this Veda known as Nāṭya be employed here;
then, during that festival of the banner, when the Asuras and Dānavas have been slain.
During the festival of Mahendra’s victory, crowded with joyful immortals, I first performed the *nāndī* accompanied by words of benediction. (56)

Some maintain that this is an indication of all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*). Others hold that the intent of this [text] is that even the *nāndī* alone may be employed from among the constituent parts of the *pūrvaraṅga*. However, our teacher [states]:
"As long as the demons had not yet committed any obstacles there, [the performance of] the *pūrvaraṅga*..."

What scope is there for that which is preceded by ritual injunction? For that [injunction] is primarily the cause for satisfying the deities stationed in their respective portions of the pavilion by warding off obstacles; and it is also, as a necessary consequence, the cause for satisfying the Daityas. But once the obstacles have arisen, from that point onward begins the *pūrvaraṅga* (the preliminary performance). Thus:

It will be stated in the fourth chapter (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.10): "When the preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) has been performed by me, it is presented to the Lord, the venerable Śiva. However, that which consists of the arrangement of the *kutapa* and so forth is not what is denoted by the term *pūrvaraṅga*. Therefore, in this context, there is the performance of the *nāndī* alone.

To the question "For what purpose is this [performed]?", he says: "It is fashioned according to the Vedas. For the Śruti states, "In that regard, one invokes auspiciousness," thus declaring that all ritual acts (*karma*) are preceded by an invocation of blessings (*āśis*). Therefore, there is the performance of the *nāndī*; however, it is not as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *pūrvaraṅga*. (53–56)

The eight constituent words that form either a sentence (*vākya*) or a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) are both those ending in nominal suffixes (*suptiṅanta*) and intermediate subordinate clauses (*avāntaravākya*); it is for this reason that they are described as "various" (*vicitra*). By this—[as in the example:
"Victory to the Lord of Stars! Salutations to the gods! May the best of the twice-born be free from calamity!"—it is shown.
And may the moon among kings, whose form is like the new moon, protect the earth abounding in grain.
(Ratnāvalī) Thus, this [verse] also, being well-known as belonging to the Indian tradition, becomes a *nāndī* as demonstrated by Kohala.
However, in this particular case—
"In these intervals between the *nāndī* verses, those two attendants (*pāripārśvika*) should always say 'So be it' with the words properly spoken [by the director]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.114).
In this verse, the word *antara* should be understood as signifying the interruption of intermediate sentences.
(26) Endowed with eightfold words, variegated and fashioned from the Vedas,
at its conclusion a mimicry was composed, just as the Daityas were defeated by the Suras. || 57 ||
It consisted of mutual conflict, flight, cutting, piercing, and combat;
then the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were gratified by his performance.
They indeed gave all kinds of implements to the sons of Mada;
Śakra, being pleased, first gave his own auspicious banner.
The discerning scholars, however, say: by the mention of the "limbs" (*aṅga*), it is the intermediate sentences themselves that are thereby included.
And therein, the numbers eight and twelve follow the square and triangular *tāla*s, with reference to the two types of *pūrvaraṅga*. In that regard—

Regarding the verse from the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (5.109), "The *nāndī* adorned with twelve or eight quarters," the word "also" (*api*) indicates that the four-quartered and sixteen-quartered forms belonging to the square [meter] are obtained;
likewise, the three-quartered and six-quartered forms belonging to the triangle are also included. Thus, even these minor varieties are each threefold according to their respective divisions.

The *nāndīs*. Beyond that, because there are many more [verses], this four-line verse begins with "By him the moon-lord was conquered. However, the sixteen-line version begins with "Victorious is the cause of the world," and so forth. "At its end" means at the conclusion of the *nāndī*. "Imitation" refers to drama (*nāṭya*). And therein, "bound" means it is composed as a rehearsal (*guṇanikā*), but not as a formal performance (*prayoga*).
But this is incorrect, because it contradicts what precedes and follows. For it was previously stated:

"In this manner, having performed the *nāndī* beginning with 'This is a drama' and ending with '...is done,'" and it will be stated later: "Brahmā and the others were gratified by the performance. Therefore, it was introduced as being "bound" (*baddhā*), but not yet completed; thus it is called the *prastāvanā*.
The meaning is that it is "performed" (*prayuktā*) for that duration.

Others, however, say that the *prastāvanā* is an imitation (*anukṛti*), consisting in the imitation of drama; they also read [the verse] as: "At its conclusion, the imitation is performed. It is precisely by taking this as their basis that ancient poets [begin] at the end of the *nāndī* with: "(Then enters...)"

The *sūtradhāra* (stage manager) writes thus in the manuscript: "What has been introduced? He says: "As for the Daityas," meaning that one of the dramatic forms—such as the *ḍima*, *samavakāra*, *īhāmṛga*, and so forth—has been introduced.
Although the sons of Bharata have practiced all ten types of drama (*daśarūpaka*), nevertheless, it is not possible to perform them all simultaneously.

It has been stated thus: "it is possible. Therefore, the objection raised by some—namely, that the preceding text is inconsistent because there is no occasion for the application of the *kaiśikī* style in a *samavakāra*—is entirely without foundation.
For it has also been stated that even in the *samavakāra* and other such works, the aesthetic variety consisting of beauty is indeed the manifestation (*vijṛmbha*) of the *kaiśikī*.
Brahmā [holds] the *kuṭilaka* (crooked staff), Varuṇa the auspicious *bhṛṅgāra* (water-pot),
Sūrya the parasol, Śiva success (*siddhi*), and Vāyu the fan. (60)
Viṣṇu gave him the lion-throne, Kubera likewise the crown,
and the goddess Sarasvatī granted him the quality of being worthy of hearing and seeing.
The remaining gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas,
in that assembly, desired various objects based on their diverse species and qualities.
Those delighted inhabitants of heaven bestowed upon my sons their own portions of existence, as well as aesthetic flavors, beauty, and strength. (63)
*Sampheṭa* (conflict) consists of speech strung together with anger. *Vidrava* (flight) is caused by suspicion, fear, and terror.
*Chedya* (the severable) is that which deserves to be cut; it is combat with weapons. *Bhedya* (the divisible) is that which deserves to be split;
it is wrestling (*niyuddha*) consisting of hand-to-hand combat. "Thereupon" means for the sake of pleasing the lord, [describing] the deeds of the lord.

Some say that sometimes in drama what is to be described may be understood from such [historical facts] as "the Daityas were conquered by the gods. That is incorrect, because it contradicts the logic of the definitions of the ten types of dramatic compositions (*daśarūpaka*).
For it will be stated therein that some [plots] consist of well-known events while others consist of invented events. And...

It is appropriate to imitate the deeds of the present; for if those to be trained (vineya) lack identification with them due to passion, hatred, neutrality, or the like, there will be no joy and consequently no realization. Furthermore, regarding the deeds of the present, if the connection between actions such as dharma and their fruits were perceptible, practice would be rendered useless. If it were imperceptible...
There can be no imitation [of the gods], because such an imitation is impossible due to the principle that "it would lack a basis for its derivation" (*pramāṇābhāvāt*).
We shall elaborate on this in the chapter on the *Daśarūpaka*; let it suffice for now.
But as for the gods today...
Because it is impossible for the characters being described to be [historically] well-known, this is a narration of the deeds of gods and asuras belonging to previous kalpas and manvantaras;

for since saṃsāra is beginningless, it is like the narration of gods and asuras authorized by Śruti and Smṛti. In that regard, the description of what exists [in the present] refers to those of that same class. Now...

We shall explain that the asuras, deluded by the confusion regarding his conduct, were agitated. Furthermore, the gods do not find satisfaction here through a description of their own deeds; for it says, "satisfied by the performance [of the ritual].
Regarding the word *dhvaja*: it is that which will later be employed for the purpose of worship in order to pacify obstacles. (58–59)
Regarding "kuṭilaka": it is a curved staff used by the *vidūṣaka*. The staff is the essence of Brahmā’s weapon; it is so called because it does not depart [from him]. (p.
When this application for the destruction of the Daityas and Dānavas had thus begun,
all the Daityas who were assembled there became agitated.
Having incited the obstacles headed by Virūpākṣa, they said:
"We will not tolerate this dance; come here! (65)
Then, together with those asuras, the obstructors resorted to their illusory power (māyā) and paralyzed the speech, gestures, and memory of those who were dancing.
Seeing such destruction, the King of the Gods said to the architect, "Why this discrepancy in the execution? and entered into meditation.
The meaning is: "also by way of its terrifying form. The *bhṛṅgāra* (golden pitcher) is for the use of the *pāripārśvika* (assistant actor). Here, the *chatra* (umbrella) is a canopy (*vitāna*);

because clouds originate from the sun, it is like them. As they say: "At the end of the season, a great mass of clouds pours forth" (or "from the gathering of clouds"). The [divine] powers are dependent upon the Blessed One.

The mention of "human accomplishment" (*mānuṣī siddhi*) in the middle [of the list] is intended to demonstrate the all-pervasive nature of divine accomplishment (*daivī siddhi*). The fan is for the removal of heat; the lion-throne and so forth are useful in the royal setting. Yakṣas and others who know the truth [are present] at the performance. Thus it is said.
"Training in speech" refers to that which is useful for each respective stage. "States" (bhāvān) refers to the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.

For instance, blood, flesh, and the like, which are the determinants of fear and disgust, become the determinants of joy and energy for yakṣas and *rākṣasas*; this is to be understood precisely from such instruction. "Flavors" (*rasān*) refers to...

The instruction regarding the group of *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions) and *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory emotions), which are conducive to the various *rasas* associated with their respective appropriate *sthāyibhāvas* (permanent emotions), has been shown. "Form" refers to the expression of the face; "strength" refers to the movement of the limbs. This was granted by one who was thoroughly satisfied on each stage. Finally, some further instruction (*śikṣā*) should also be given here to the members of the audience.
By the statement "knowledge of wealth," it is shown that one who wishes to acquire [wealth] and who desires to please the assembly must strive for this; (60–63) now,
in order to show that a worship with worn-out materials should be performed for the pacification of obstacles, he begins with a traditional narrative (itihāsa):

"Thus is the application": wherein the destruction of the Daityas and others is to be employed. "Come hither": let it be understood, or rather, let us come together. "Illusion" (māyā) means invisibility. "Movement" refers to physical action. Although everything becomes paralyzed by the paralysis of memory, nevertheless—

It is said that by virtue of the predominance of this or that dramatic performance, that very [state] is "stilled" (*stambhita*). "Of the *sūtradhāra*" means "together with his retinue. This means that this obstacle occurs precisely in the midst of the performance of the prologue (*prastāvanā*). "Meditation" (*dhyāna*) refers to that wherein illusion (*māyā*) has no power. (64–67)
Then he saw the sacrificial hall surrounded on all sides by obstacles;
along with the others, the master architect had lost consciousness and was rendered motionless. (68)
Rising quickly, Śakra seized his supreme banner;
his body was radiant with all kinds of jewels, and his eyes were slightly dilated.
The king of the gods, with his thunderbolt, rendered those obstacles and asuras who had taken their places upon the stage-pedestal into ones whose bodies were shattered and mangled.
When all the obstacles, together with the Dānavas, had been slain, all the inhabitants of heaven rejoiced and then spoke these words: || 71 ||
"Aha! This divine weapon has been acquired by you, by which these Dānavas have had all their limbs shattered to pieces. (72)
"Since those obstacles, along with the asuras, have been shattered by him, therefore he shall be known by the name Jarjara. (73)
Furthermore, whatever other assailants shall come for the purpose of doing harm,
upon merely seeing him thus decayed, they too will likewise depart.
"So be it," Śakra then said to those gods;
"and this Jarjara shall become the dice for everyone. (75)

Regarding the word *sada*: where it is used in its application, it means "that in which one sits" (*sīdaty asmin*). It is a form derived from the root *jṛ* with the suffix *ac* (after the elision of the *yaṅ* reduplication), meaning "to decay excessively. Thus, those whose bodies have been excessively worn out are described as such. The form *jarjareṇa* is likewise derived from the root *jṛ* after the elision of the *yaṅ*, followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, and then again by the suffix *ac*. In this way, [they were] by the king, who was an obstacle to their success.
It has been shown that they are to be punished.
For when such a vast festival of Indra is underway, as the performance proceeds... (p. 30) ...again.
The remaining obstacles cause terror to arise for those who are dancing. || 76 ||
Having seen the resolve of those Daityas born of their intent to cause harm,
I approached Brahmā accompanied by all my sons.
"O Blessed One, it is certain that obstacles will arise for the destruction of this dance;
O Lord of the Gods, please duly command the ritual for its protection. (78)
Then Brahmā spoke with diligence to Viśvakarman:
"O high-minded one, construct a theater hall endowed with all auspicious characteristics. (79)
Then, after a short time, Viśvakarman, having constructed a magnificent and auspicious theater hall endowed with every auspicious characteristic, [presented it]. (80)
Having gone to the assembly hall with palms joined in reverence, he spoke to Brahmā:
"O Lord, the theater is ready; you ought to behold it. (81)
Then, together with Mahendra and all the gods as well as others,
Druhiṇa arrived in haste to behold the theater pavilion.

Alternatively, a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be constructed from the very beginning for its protection. For those factors that are beyond the reach of the staff—such as wind, heat, rain, and so forth—it is by them that the obstruction to success is caused; however, when the pavilion exists, such an obstruction does not occur.
With this very intention, he states the ancient tradition (*purākalpa*), beginning with "the performance" (*prayoga*). As for the word "the rest" (*śeṣāḥ*):
The meaning is: "even though their bodies were reduced to a state of decay. As he will say: "O Blessed One, the obstacles are certain.

Likewise, at this time of being worn down, these [obstacles] became non-proximate. Regarding the word "terror": it means that they were in no way capable of destroying [him]. For it has been said: "His power, being decayed, will depart in this very manner. Then...
"Viśvakarman": this indicates his status as the chief architect (*sthapati*) in the theater (*nāṭyamaṇḍapa*), according to those who know the principles of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*).
"Druhiṇa" refers to Brahmā. The others are the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and so forth.
Having seen the theater hall, Brahmā then said to all the gods:
"This theater pavilion must be protected by you through your respective portions. (83)
Then, the Moon was appointed for the protection of the pavilion;
likewise, the world-protectors were stationed in the cardinal directions and the Maruts in the intermediate directions. (84)
Mitra was stationed on the stage for the dressing room, Varuṇa in the sky, Vahni at the protection of the altar, and all the gods in the vessel. (85)
Then the four castes were assigned to the pillars,
while the Ādityas and Rudras were stationed within the intervals between the pillars.
Then, the spirits were in the *dhāraṇīs*, the apsarases in the halls,
the yakṣiṇīs in all the dwellings, and the great ocean upon the surface of the earth.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the constituent parts" (*aṃśabhāgaiḥ*): it refers to those vessels or bases which consist of the constituent parts.
By those parts of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) which are your third, fourth, and so forth portions.
(68–83) He explains the very division of these parts with the word "protection" (*rakṣaṇa*). By this, the protection of the pavilion's parts is indeed equal to this.

It is shown that someone is to be appointed. For it is shown that Soma, who is of a gentle nature (*saumyaprakṛti*), is the presiding deity of the entire pavilion and is the primary one to be appointed—this is indicated by the word "the Moon" (*candramā*). Furthermore, by the word "also" (*api ca*), and by the phrase "in the intermediate directions" (*vidikṣu*):
not only in its own corner consisting of the west and north, but also in the other intermediate directions. By the word "and" (*ca*), [it is implied] in the cardinal directions as well. For they...

Some maintain that by this [verse], the making of windows is indicated, because they are extremely beneficial as protectors against the defects of heat. Since the word *mitra* is masculine when referring to the sun (*āditya*), the Vārttikakāra— indicated by that term— states that for the purpose of avoiding shame, a *napuṃsaka* (eunuch) is placed in the dressing room (*nepathyagṛha*) by the female dancers (*nartakībhiḥ*).
That is a designation not touched upon [elsewhere]. "Friend" (*mitra*) refers to brilliance that is useful for acquisition, such as that of jewels and the like.

"Altar" (*vedikā*) means a stage-altar; the meaning is that a sharp person presides there. "Vessel" (*bhāṇḍa*) refers to the *tripuṣkara* together with its accessories. "Celestial beings" (*divaukasas*) refers to clouds, for the purpose of producing a deep and resonant sound. Thus it is in all cases.

Even when a visible purpose is observed, one must consider whether it culminates in a similar perceived [result]. If such a result is not obtained in any way whatsoever, then by necessity, it is indeed a visible [purpose]. Regarding the term "syllables" (*varṇāḥ*): these are specific deities who preside over them. Regarding the phrase "in other pillars": this refers to those such as the four pillars of the syllables; the meaning is that they are not on other pillars.
(32) Kṛtānta and Kāla themselves were appointed to the gate-hall;
the two chief Nāgas of great strength were stationed at the door-panels. 88.
At the threshold stood the staff of Yama, and above it was fixed a trident;
both Niyati and Mṛtyu stood there as the two gatekeepers. (89)
And on the side of the stage-platform, Mahendra himself stood;
there, the slayer of the Daitya Vidyut was stationed within the *mattavāraṇī* (the elephant-stall).
In the pillars of the intoxicated female elephant, for the sake of her protection,
were stationed spirits, yakṣas, piśācas, and mighty guhyakas.
The thunderbolt, the destroyer of the Daityas, was placed within the joints of the staff;
indeed, the lords of the gods of immeasurable prowess were stationed at its various sections.

Regarding the phrase "in the halls": this refers to the two pillars in each of the eight chambers, due to the arrangement of the windows, the dressing rooms, and the second floor. Regarding the phrase "the two chief Nāgas":
these are Ananta and Gulika. "Door-leaf" means consisting of a door-panel; the plural number is used because there are many doors.

"At the threshold" (*dehalyām*) means on the lower wooden plank of the door. "Of that" (*tasya*) refers to the trident (*śūla*). By this, the very door under discussion is being referred to. Therefore, the meaning is that on the upper wooden plank, which is designated by the word "lap" (*utsaṅga*), there is a trident. Regarding "on the side by oneself," it has been stated that this is the place for kings and others.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is implied that they abide in their own respective directions according to their portions. Regarding the term "lightning": she has the form of the thunderbolt weapon (*vajrāyudha*).

Furthermore, on the four pillars, there are those elements and so forth in due order; and these are experts in the principles of dramaturgy (*nāṭyatattva*). Therefore, it should be understood that they have met with the obstacles (*vighna*) by means of this method. By this, [it is shown that] they are the destroyers of supernatural attainments (*siddhi*).

It is indicated that [the enemy] must be weakened even by means of stratagems involving deception (*bhedākhyopāya*). "Established" (*pratiṣṭhita*) means always present in the center of the dwelling; thus, the presence of the poet is indicated. "Below" (*adhaḥ*) means that by this, the creation of obstacles such as digging tunnels is prevented.
He states that the principal characters must be protected separately, saying "the hero" (*nāyakam*).

The term "jester" (*vidūṣaka*) is used because he serves as a subordinate element to the comic and erotic sentiments (*hāsya-śṛṅgāra*). For this very reason, this indicates the performance of the *daśarūpaka* (the ten types of drama), since there is no jester in the *samavakāra* (a specific type of minor drama). [Regarding the word] "Hara":
Because it is the first among many forms; *daivata* is simply *devatā*. (87–98) p.
33) Brahmā resides at the joint of the head, and likewise Śaṅkara is in the second.
And Viṣṇu resides in the third, and Skanda indeed in the fourth. || 93 ||
And in the fifth [pillar], the great nāgas Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka—thus were the gods installed in Jarjara for the destruction of obstacles. (94)
Brahmā himself is established in the center of the stage;
for the sake of the sacrifice, the scattering of flowers is performed in the middle of the stage.
And those Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Pannagas who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) have been appointed to guard the area beneath the stage-platform.
Indra protects the hero, Sarasvatī the heroine, Oṃkāra the jester, and Hara the remaining constituent elements. (97)
He said, "Those very deities who have been appointed here for protection shall themselves become the presiding deities (adhidaiva)."
In the meantime, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was addressed by all the gods:
"Let these obstacles first be pacified by you with conciliatory words."
First, conciliation should be employed, and secondly, indeed, bribery;
after those two, sowing dissension, and then punishment is applied. (100)
Having heard the words of the gods, Brahmā spoke to the obstacles:
"Why have you risen up for the destruction of the dance? (101)
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Virūpākṣa then spoke these words with conciliation,
together with the hosts of Daityas and the Gaṇas of obstacles.
This *Nāṭyaveda* which has been created by the Blessed One through the will of the gods—this is a response made by you for our sake on behalf of the gods. (103)
34) Now, when the essence of drama (*nāṭyatattva*) was being destroyed, he begins the investigation of it with the words "In this [situation]...
First, the protection was provided by the principle that "an evil person accepts the assistance of one who is powerless. Thus ends the pair of statements mentioned.
(Said by all): This shows that the poet’s words are to be followed.

First, he clarifies the sequence indicated by the words regarding the employment of conciliation (*sāma*) and the other means—beginning with "First, conciliation" and so forth. "Then" means when all other means have failed. In that situation, once his intention is known, it is easy to provide a remedy.

With this intention, he says: "Of the gods. To further strengthen the meaning of "for the sake of the gods," he says: "by the will of the gods. "Refusal" means humiliation. "By you" means by one for whom this is improper. He expresses this very impropriety through the address "O Grandfather of the World. That same...
He demonstrates his status as the Grandfather with the words "Just as... He states that the gods and the Daityas are born from himself with the word "all.
(99–104) Regarding the word "speech" (*vacana*): this is easily resolved; he shows by means of the singular number that there is no great effort required here. Therefore...

Thus, he begins as if stating an established conclusion: "Enough with you" (*alaṃ vaḥ*). The meaning is that [this fear] is produced by mere delusion, like the terror of a snake grasped through false cognition. It is well known in the world that the Daityas perform inauspicious deeds;
let their activity consist in the arrangement of the stage (*kṛtaraṅgavibhāga*). For the gods, it is the opposite of that.
The purpose of the drama is not such that it would cause you distress. What then? He says:

in our drama, which is like a direct perception, it is to be demonstrated only this much—that for one who performs good deeds there is a good result, and for one who performs evil deeds there is an evil result. It is not about [the actual existence of] gods or demons therein.

There is a certain burden [to be addressed]. For this very reason, even that which is a correct means (*sadupāya*) for you regarding dharma and so forth has been shown precisely as having a virtuous maturation (*śubhavipāka*). Therefore, the inclusion of the term "virtuous" (*śubha*) is intended to demonstrate the laxity of one side and to establish a connection with the Daityas.

First, it was taken up: the *Nāṭya-veda* differentiates and determines that which is auspicious and inauspicious—consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—by way of their distinct fruits of pleasure and pain. Of what nature is it?
It is "dependent upon the sequence of the states of action. For example: action consists of merit, demerit, and so forth; merit is...

"Generosity" refers to bathing and so forth; "unrighteousness" refers to violence, theft, and so forth; "disposition" refers to one's internal intent, such as the intention regarding self-interest or the interest of others arising from attachment to women and the like; "lineage" refers to family descent, such as being born in Āryāvarta or belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste and so forth. It is these factors that it requires as auxiliary conditions.

This is what is meant: it is not taught here that "in this place, at this time, one who acquires merit or demerit through such an action becomes a partaker of such a result. The word *vikalpaka* contains two causative suffixes (*ṇic*). (105–106)
(35) Therefore, O Grandfather of the World, you should not act in this manner;
for just as the gods, so too the Daityas have all emerged from you. || 104 ||
Having heard the words of the obstacles, Brahmā spoke these words:
"Enough of your anger, O Daityas; cast off your despondency, O sinless ones. (105)
I have composed the Nāṭya-veda, which distinguishes between the auspicious and inauspicious for you and the gods, and which takes into account the sequence of the manifestation of karma.
In this matter, there is no absolute experience for you or for the gods;
rather, it is the performance of this entire triple world, which is a representation of its various states of being.

But even so, one might ask: "Why has this been applied to our backs? To this he replies: "Not exclusively" (*naikāntataḥ*). The intended meaning is as follows: this was not applied to your backs by anyone; rather, it is the external manifestation of gods and asuras according to their actual state.
"Here" refers to the *Nāṭya-veda*. It is not that gods and asuras are exclusively represented [in this manner]; indeed, they are not represented at all.
In some manner;

for instance: there is no cognition of them as being real; nor by way of similarity, as in the case of twins; nor by way of error, as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell preceded by the memory of silver; nor by way of superimposition.

It is like the form of false cognition that follows immediately after the sublation by right cognition; it is not [the object] through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it, as in the case of a *vāhīka* being determined as a "cow"; nor through its being imagined, as in the case of the moon [imagined] in a face; nor through its being a representation of it, as in the case of a painting or a statue;
nor through its imitating it, as in the case of the eloquent exposition of a teacher and disciple. Nor...

It is like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) through a creation occurring at that very moment; it is not like the magic of hand-dexterity and so forth, which consists of a semblance produced by logical reasoning. In all these positions, because the spectator would remain indifferent due to the lack of uniqueness [in the experience], the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) would be impossible; and because the poet's subject matter would be restricted to a fixed description.

For it would be impossible to avoid impropriety if the poetic work itself were not accomplished; furthermore, because it would entail being subject to worldly joy, envy, and anger— just like an ordinary couple— and because that [worldly state] is rooted in the perception of both [self and other], there would be no resting in the consciousness of that [state] within the primary vision, namely, the vision of the poet.

What then is this? He says: "Of the three worlds. This is what is meant: such [beings] as Rāma and others are never brought within the path of valid cognition when they are described by scripture; nevertheless, at that time, a specific cognition of them arises from a single great sentence, such as the *Rāmāyaṇa*.

Nevertheless, because the specific characteristics (*viśeṣas*) terminate in their own particular nature (*svālakṣaṇya*), which consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) as something currently existing,
and yet that "presentness" of theirs is not admitted [by you].

To that extent, there is the cognition of particularity. Even in poetic works, it is the heart alone (*hṛdayam eva*) where the commonality (*sādhāraṇībhāva*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth occurs; even there, it is merely a matter of description.

Although commonality is possible, nevertheless, because there is an absence of intense aesthetic relish (*rasa*)— as in the case of a mere statement such as "this happens to those who act thus"— the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) does not emerge [into full realization]. In poetry (*kāvyam*), however, which has for its body words and meanings made charming by *guṇas* and *alaṃkāras*, and which has extraordinary *rasa* as its life-breath...

Due to the power of sympathetic resonance (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*), the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) becomes as if submerged [in the object]; however, no cognition arises there that is like a direct perception (*pratyakṣasākṣātkāra*) of everything. In drama (*nāṭya*), on the other hand, [the spectator thinks], "Some real purpose of mine will be accomplished," and so forth.

Due to the absence of mental formations based on a false intention regarding reality, and due to the mental formation of the intention: "May I become a practitioner of supramundane vision and hearing, worthy of universal respect, whose essence is the joy common to all assemblies,
and who has transcended the mundane world through the relish of appropriate song and instrumental music," [he remains] unmindful of worldly concerns.
Having made his own heart like a stainless mirror through the state of imaginative identification (*bhāvatā*),
he experiences an immersion (*tanmayībhāva*) arising from joy, sorrow, and other emotions produced by observing the mimetic gestures (*abhinaya*) of the needle and so forth;
this occurs by virtue of the entry of another actor upon hearing the recitation (*pāṭhya*).

In the case of a determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*) concerning objects such as Rāma or Rāvaṇa— which is not touched by the specificities of place and time, and which is not the locus for reflections on whether it is known through right knowledge, false knowledge, doubt, or mere imagination— ...

The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding Rāma, whose form was described by him, which persists as a continuous accompaniment indicated by the impressions of experiencing beautiful objects, songs, musical instruments, and women that co-occur with those [descriptions]—
that very impression, through five or six days, will become his marvelous life-story.
One whose mind has entered the nature of the Self perceives the universe through the gateway of the Self; thus,
without reflecting on the specificities of space and time for each individual member of the assembly,

[he perceives] that which is offered by the injunction consisting of the optative suffix (*liṅ*)— namely, "this is what those who act in this way [should do]"— as being of the very same nature as consciousness.

Through the entry of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) resulting from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of delightful songs, musical instruments, and so forth— which are accompanied by the tasting of incomparable flavors that delight the specific consciousness and are dear to the vital breath— that [flavor] is fixed deep within the heart; therefore,
it does not suffer even the slightest fading, even by hundreds of attempts to erase it.

By virtue of having a mental state that is constantly woven with the desire to obtain this or that auspicious thing and the desire to avoid the inauspicious, one performs what is auspicious and abandons what is inauspicious. Now, because of the attainment of the knowledge of the means [thereto], this very recollection is a specific kind of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), which has "drama" (*nāṭya*) as its synonym; it is not "imitation" (*anukāra*).

One should not be deluded; for by this [act of] "cheek-biting" (bhagaṇḍa), there is an absence of the cognition that another prince or someone else has been imitated, because it is well known among neutral observers that such a cause results only in laughter. With this intention, the Sage will say:
"Laughter arises from the imitation of the movements of others" (Chapter 7, verse 10).

For those belonging to that [opposing] faction, however, that very [instruction] results in hatred, envy, and the persistence of [wrong views]. Indeed, it is through the perception of that [instruction] alone that the hearts of the Daityas are agitated, thinking, "We have become objects of ridicule in this way.
And those who fear being ridiculed turn away from it; they do not [turn away] by means of instruction.

(37) But even so, let there be no fixed imitation [of the original]. What else is there besides imitation? Nothing at all, except for the impossibility [of such imitation]. For "imitation" means the production of something similar. To what, then, would it refer? Not, first of all, to Rāma and the like.
Because that [actor] is not something to be imitated. By this, the imitation of the excitants (*vibhāva*) such as women and so forth is refuted.

It is not [the imitation] of mental states (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of grief, anger, and the like; for an actor does not produce grief in himself that is similar to Rāma’s, because such [grief] is entirely absent in him. Or, even if it were present, it would not constitute an imitation. Not...

Furthermore, there exists no other entity that could be similar to grief; yet it produces its own manifestations, but only those of the same class, not those merely resembling it. For what purpose would there be a similarity between a common form and anything else?
As for similarity with respect to all that exists within the three worlds, that cannot be established simultaneously through the nature of specific particulars.
Perhaps, in some cases, it might be imitated in a fixed sequence; however, if its nature were merely that of a universal (sāmānya), what would be the purpose of imitation?

Therefore, one should not fall into the error of thinking that drama (*nāṭya*) is an indefinite imitation. This same intention should be understood in our teacher’s *Kāvyakautuka*, and not that it is an indefinite imitation.

Therefore, drama is that which is to be made the object of a particular reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*). And so it is said: when the conceit of perceiving the specific actor—such as Caitra or Maitra—along with their particular place, time, and so forth, has ceased through the application of particular costumes and the like, perception cannot occur without the introduction of at least a trace of such particularity; thus [the drama] is established.

Because words such as "Rāma" are employed here, and because they denote a person whose life is worthy of veneration due to his well-known nature, the [mental] apprehension (*anuvyavasāya*)— which arises through the mere removal of doubt regarding the possibility [of such a person existing]— is like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it is permeated by pleasant songs and the like.

Because it is a locus of wonder (*camatkāra*), it possesses the fitness for entry into the heart; through the fourfold dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), there is the concealment of its own true nature by means of passion (*rasa*) and so forth; and through the assistance of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from the spectator's knowledge, which has entered into the midst of the aesthetic apparatus (*rañjaka-sāmagrī*), its own essential being remains concealed.
By the performer being observed, who is aided by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by previously occurring worldly perception, inference, and so forth;

who is assisted by the impressions of the knowledge of the sensitive spectator (*sahṛdaya*) and the actor (*naṭa*); and who is supported by the resonance with the heart (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*) and the process of identification (*tanmayībhavana*).

The subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that is produced consists of the manifestation of the bliss of one’s own consciousness, which is colored by the respective mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*) in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth;

for this very reason, it is manifold, possessing synonyms such as *rasanā* (tasting), *āsvādana* (savoring), *camatkāra* (wonder), *carvaṇa* (chewing), *nirveśa* (enjoyment), and *bhoga* (experience). From that...

Whatever object appears is *nāṭya* (the dramatic representation). And that [object] may be merely the form of cognition, a superimposed nature consisting of a universal (*sāmānya*), a form produced at that very moment, or whatever else it may be. There is no purpose here in writing about irrelevant matters, which would only serve to display one's familiarity with the doctrines of other philosophical systems.
By creating obstacles to the investigation of the subject at hand, we cause distress to those of refined sensibility (*sahṛdaya*).

Therefore, drama (*nāṭya*) consists of a representation that takes the form of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), which is the cognition of a conceptual construction colored by aesthetic emotion; this is because it is an object to be known through that very cognition. It is not, however, of the nature of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). If, on the other hand, it were so...

It is said that this is an imitation because it follows the primary worldly means of production; however, there is no fault in this, since when a real difference exists in fact, the application of words is beyond dispute. This point will be elaborated upon in its proper place, so let it rest for now.

In some places there is Dharma, in some places sport, in some places wealth, and in some places tranquility; in some places laughter, in some places battle, in some places desire, and in some places slaughter. (108)
Dharma is for those who practice dharma; desire is for those who indulge in desire;
restraint is for the ill-behaved; and the act of subduing is for the disciplined. 109.
It generates audacity in the weak-willed, enthusiasm in those who pride themselves on being heroes, awakening in the ignorant, and even erudition in the learned. (110)

Since this is not an imitation, the objection raised by some—that there is no object of imitation in any circumstance that is joined with song and instrumental music—is without foundation. For it has already been stated that songs and the like do not constitute objects of imitation. Furthermore, the refutation that was stated [previously]— [...the rest of the sentence is omitted as per instructions...]

The claim that singing and instrumental music are widely renowned in the world as being part of activities such as sitting, walking, bathing, sleeping, waking, and eating— this too is untenable; for in the world, there is no singing or the like in the form of *dhruva* or *tāla* during walking and so forth, except as a mere auspicious rite (*maṅgala*).
Furthermore, since it would follow that even singing, instrumental music, and so forth would be subject to the notion of being mere imitations, enough of this.

Now, one might raise the following objection: "If drama (*nāṭya*) consists in the representation of whatever things exist in the three worlds, then everything should be seen within a single dramatic work, and within a single act (*aṅka*) or the like. Anticipating and refuting this doubt:

He concludes that [the *Nāṭyaśāstra*] possesses a purpose by means of the eight verses beginning with "In some cases, dharma... and ending with "...this *nāṭya* will produce instruction for the world.
And this has been explained by some as distinct sentences for each verse. And that...

Since it would be afflicted by defects such as redundancy, the necessity of supplying missing words (*adhyāhāra*), and mutual incoherence (*parasparāsaṅgati*), this [interpretation] must be disregarded.

Therefore, the construction here is as follows: it is "endowed with" (*upasampanna*) and "pervaded on all sides" (*sarvato vyāpta*) by various kinds of entities (*bhāva*), namely the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), the determinants (*ālambanavibhāva*), and so forth. And of these...

Since entities and so forth possess a nature that is differentiated by variations in place, time, fundamental constitution (*prakṛti*), and state, they too consist of manifold states. For this very reason, it says "superior and inferior. The connection is as follows: such being the case, this will come to pass; at the [proper] time, it will produce repose and produce beneficial instruction.

He asks, "What are the various kinds of states (bhāvas)? and answers with the words beginning "In some cases, dharma," and so forth. According to their respective application, terms such as *dharma* and the rest indicate the permanent (*sthāyin*), transitory (*vyabhicārin*), and other [emotions].

Thus, *dharma* refers to purpose (*artha*) and enthusiasm (*utsāha*) and so on; *krīḍā* (play) refers to wonder (*vismaya*) and so on; *śama* (tranquility) refers to world-weariness (*nirveda*) and so on; and *hāsya* (laughter) refers to mirth (*hāsa*) and so on.

"Battle" refers to [the sentiment of] wrath (*raudra*) and so forth; "love" refers to [the sentiment of] passion (*rati*) and so forth; "slaughter" refers to anger, fear, disgust, sorrow, and so forth.

By these terms, the appropriate transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) and determinants (*vibhāva*) are included. By the word "in some cases," any one of the ten types of drama (*daśarūpaka*) is indicated. For example:

(39) The distinction residing in various dramatic forms such as the *nāṭaka* and so forth is likewise a division that characterizes a single [type of] drama, such as the *nāṭaka*. What is meant is this: a certain dramatic form has a particular attribute as its primary feature, for example—

It may be a *nāṭaka* or a *prakaraṇa*. Just as the *bhāṇa* is well known for having playfulness (*krīḍā*) as its primary element, the primacy of plot (*artha*) belongs specifically to the *prakaraṇa* and similar forms. Thus, everything should be followed according to the definitions of the ten types of drama (*daśarūpaka*). Likewise, in some *nāṭakas*, dharma is the primary element—as, for example, in...

In the *Chalitarāma*, there is Rāma’s horse sacrifice (*aśvamedhayāga*). In some cases, there is play (*krīḍā*), as in the *Svapnavāsavadattā*. In this manner, it should be followed elsewhere as well. Likewise, even in a single drama, in a certain part, there is dharma (*dharma*), as in the *Abhijñānaśākuntala*: "Perhaps... [and so on].
This [daughter] of the householder would be born from a field of a different caste (aṅka-1).
Thus, in each drama, in certain sections, there are indeed many auspicious instances such as games and so forth;
however, fearing excessive prolixity, we have not described them in detail.
One might object: "Should one not merely describe the states, locations, times, and specific dispositions appropriate to each character?
What is the purpose of resorting to [the mention of] Rāma, Rāvaṇa, and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Dharma" (dharmaḥ). The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
For it is because the dramatic performance (*nāṭya*), which consists of the act of representation (*prayoga*), must follow the conduct of the world (*lokavṛtta*) that I have [composed it thus].

For this reason—that "this has been done"—dharma is said to pertain to those who have engaged in it, such as Rāma, Yudhiṣṭhira, and others. "Nigraha" means execution. Discipline (*dama*) and tranquility (*śama*) are the application of action pertaining to those who are disciplined and have conquered their senses; for discipline is indeed the conquest of the senses. Thus...
In this context, "laughter" (*hāsa*) is described as having "the production of audacity in those who are timid and objects of ridicule" as its *vibhāva* (determinant cause).
This refers to that humorous object which generates audacity. As he will state later:
"By means of distorted dress, ornaments of others, audacity, and so forth" (A-6), etc. [The term] "awakening" (*vibodha*) is derived from the causative form of the root.

Form (*rūpa*). It is the state of being made known as belonging to those who are established as non-Buddhas, through the instruction of means (*upāya*) and the process of training (*vyutpādyatva*). [This refers to] the learned ones, such as Bhīṣma and others. Their learning consists in being trained in the means.
By this, there is the definition of memory (*smṛti*), intelligence (*mati*), and so forth. "Grace" (*vilāsa*) means play (*krīḍā*). "Stability" (*sthairya*) means...

"Consisting of resolve" means having the very nature of enthusiasm. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *eva* (only/precisely). The meaning is: "as being related precisely to that which is well-known for being afflicted by suffering. *Dhṛti* is fortitude. This is what is meant:
because this dramatic action follows the ways of the world, and in the world, the earth and other such things are not [mere] supports.
Because they are capable of being experienced, whatever is well-known in relation to objects such as dharma— such as Rāma and others—
is grasped through the medium of the principal characters by virtue of their utility for the mere word [of the drama].
Such a drama, when performed, [is experienced] by the spectators through suffering caused by illness and the like.
For those afflicted by fatigue born of the hardships of travel and the like, by grief caused by the death of kinsmen and the like,
and likewise for ascetics exhausted by the extreme weakness resulting from the constant performance of arduous penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*;

It produces repose for those whose hearts are not [otherwise] settled, it obstructs the spread of suffering, and for those whose suffering has been countered, it is the cause of joy, fortitude (*dhṛti*), and so forth, as appropriate. For example:
fortitude for one afflicted by grief, play for one afflicted by disease, and pleasure for one afflicted by fatigue. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*)...
It should be understood that these include the awakening of the intellect of ascetics and so forth;
as well as the playfulness of lords and the steadfastness of one afflicted by suffering. (p. 40)
Wealth is the sustenance for those who live by wealth; it is the stability for those whose minds are distressed. 111.
This drama, endowed with various states and consisting of diverse internal conditions, has been composed by me as an imitation of worldly conduct. (112)
It is based on the actions of superior, inferior, and middling men;
it generates beneficial instruction and produces steadfastness, play, pleasure, and so forth. (113)
Thus, among the sentiments, the emotions, and all ritual actions,
drama shall become the source of all instruction in the world.
For those afflicted by suffering, those afflicted by fatigue, and those ascetics afflicted by grief,
this drama shall at the proper time become a source of rest.
It is not merely this much; rather, even at a later time, it produces a happiness that ripens as its result born from instruction.

Thus, for those who are suffering, the purpose is the attainment of happiness at a later time through the bestowal of the happiness that pacifies that suffering. As for those who are not suffering—such as princes and others whose lives consist primarily of happiness—for them...

This drama is for the purpose of instruction regarding the category of means such as dharma within worldly conduct. By the word "world" (*loka*), [it refers to] worldly conduct that is righteous, conducive to fame, conducive to long life, beneficial, and an enhancer of the intellect. (p. 41)
This drama will bring about instruction for the world. || 115 ||
There is no such knowledge, no such craft, no such science, no such art, no such yoga, and no such action that is not seen in this drama. (116)
Now, does it not provide instruction like that of a teacher? No, he says; rather, it increases one's intelligence.
The meaning is that it bestows such a capacity for self-insight (*pratibhā*). Nor is that cognition faulty;
thus he says it is "beneficial" (*hitam*), because it generates beneficial insight. He states the reason for this: because it is not devoid of *dharma*.

By the word *yaśas* (fame), that which produces worldly renown—namely, an extraordinary deed—is meant, such as Rāma’s piercing of the seven *sāla* trees. That which is conducive to such [deeds] is *yaśasya*. Practices that are causes for the increase of life-span are *āyus*;
that which is conducive to them is *āyuṣya*. In this same way, [it applies to] those who are suffering and those who are not suffering.

And it has been stated that this [treatise] is to be accepted. Suffering is either physical or mental. Physical suffering, moreover, is seen to be caused by fate, caused by oneself, or caused by another with the aim of a visible result; such is the entire range of those who suffer. This is the purpose of employing the specific distinctions in the phrase "of those afflicted by suffering," and so forth.

Some, however, explain "dharma for those engaged in dharma" and so forth as referring to the audience (*sāmājika*), with the intent that it be worthy of resonance in their hearts. Others, through methods of explanation such as eliding the vowel *a* (i.e., reading *adharmapravṛttānām*), interpret "those engaged in non-dharma" and so forth as being the opposite.

They explain [the text] with the intention that it is intended as an instruction. However, both of these views are incorrect, as they fall into faults such as tautology. For instance, the passage beginning with "This dharma leads to fame" is redundant. Furthermore, by this [text], instruction has not been given regarding the primary principle alone, nor merely regarding the means to the goal of human life.
He shows that this applies even to the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*) and so forth by saying "not that" (*na tat*). Regarding the phrase "in this":

when a drama (*nāṭya*) consisting of a description of the entities existing within the seven continents is being watched, whatever is not seen—that is, does not come within the range of the heart—such knowledge and so forth do not exist; this is the sense of the ellipsis. [The word] "knowledge" (*jñāna*)...
The *pādeya* consists of self-knowledge and so forth.

For example, in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "Those who delight in the Self, whose pleasure is fixed in unwavering *samādhi*... (1.23), and so on. *Śilpa* refers to the composition of garlands, paintings, books, and the like.
As in the verse beginning, "Just as with flowers and sprouts that are wound, strung, woven, gathered, or spread out," and so forth;
[the term] *vidyā* refers to the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) and the like.
Therefore, you should not harbor resentment toward the immortals;
this will be a dance that imitates the seven continents.
"That by which there is imitation— that which has been performed by me— is this very *nāṭya*.
The imitation of gods, asuras, kings, and householders in this world is designated as *nāṭya*."
And it should be understood that the drama of the Brahman-sages reveals their life-histories. || 118 ||
This very nature of the world, endowed with pleasure and pain, when combined with the gestures of the limbs and other elements, is designated as "drama" (nāṭya). || 119 ||

As in [the verse]: "Just as for a king who has provided for his governance through both tranquility and exertion" (*Bālarāmāyaṇa* 1.24), and so forth. *Kalā* refers to arts such as singing and instrumental music;
as in [the verse]: "Just as individual manifestation [is revealed] by the element of seasoning" (*Nāgānanda* 1.14), and so forth.
Yoga is the joining together of those very qualities beginning with knowledge and ending with power (*kalā*), through their own internal divisions and mutual subdivisions. For example:
"Act as the preceptor in the performance of the dance of the peacock, which suspects the presence of clouds."
The resonance of the drum swells intensely, filled with the sound of the flute;

and this [flute], following the *gamakas* of the lute through its rhythmic tempo (*laya*), draws forth the *mūrcchanā* that captivates the ear with the beautiful, modulated intervals of the hexatonic scale (*ṣāḍava*). (Bhejjala)
In passages such as *rādhāvipralambha*, the application of instrumental music and song has been performed there.
As for their mutual [application], for example:
"With the tips of her breasts slightly clouded, possessing a soft luster pale like the petals of the *lavalī* flower" (*Vikramorvaśīya* 5.8).
In such passages as these, there is indeed the application of the science of medicine to an element of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
"Action" (*karman*) refers to activities such as combat or wrestling. For example:
"...of him who stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, brandishing his sword, and casting three glances..."

"By gliding along the sequence of the tips of their feathers from the edge of the arrow, it was not at all perceived that they had departed from the target of Umādhava’s bow as it formed a circle; it is truly marvelous, truly marvelous, that all the enemies of the Lord of the Gods were struck down simultaneously! Thus [it is said].
43) Having thus stated that [the work] possesses a purpose, he returns to the subject at hand—the ancient account—saying: "Therefore, not here.
"That" means "for that reason. Here, in this drama, one should not harbor resentment toward the immortals; for even they are not present there [in the original story].

He says this very thing: "For an action (theatrical performance) consisting of an imitation of the seven continents is seen on the stage; yet there is no actual existence of oceans, islands, and so forth there"—this is the intended meaning (vv.
116–117). Anticipating the objection, "For what purpose are these names taken up?", he says: "Of the gods," and so forth.
Because these alone are the qualified persons (*adhikāripuruṣa*), and because it is impossible to demonstrate a state of being without a substratum (*nirādhāra*).

This has been stated previously. For this very reason, in cases where there is renown regarding those such as Bali and Prahlāda—who possess the qualities of natural nobility and the like without artifice—that [person] is also mentioned as the substratum. Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the Asuras": it is not only your enemies who are described here, but even the Brahman-sages. By this, our objection—"this is for the sake of the gods"—is refuted. Thus, both doubts are dispelled. He concludes with the essential meaning of this: "This which..."—namely, "this."

That which is denoted by the word "it" (yat) is the object of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that is equivalent to direct perception, because it is distinct from the conventional categories of truth and falsity well-known in the world. Drama (*nāṭya*) is an object being relished, which is perceived as belonging to oneself through its universality across all people. And that [object] consists of various forms of pleasure and pain.
It is accompanied by them, but it is not identical with them.
For instance, while joy (*rati*), laughter (*hāsa*), enthusiasm (*utsāha*), and wonder (*vismaya*) have the nature of pleasure (*sukha*),
[the aesthetic flavor] consists therein as a continuous connection with pleasure that persists over a long duration, having its life-force directed toward the object.

Due to an abundance of longing for that object and fear of misfortune, there is a permeation of pleasure by a portion of suffering; in the case of laughter accompanied by reflection, it takes the form of a brief suffering occurring momentarily within a continuity of happiness, resembling a flash of lightning;
and in the case of enthusiasm, it consists of a reflection upon the submergence into effort characterized by momentary suffering, [leading to] the future benefit of many people—

The nature of pleasure consists in the desire for a pleasure that will arise after a long duration through its causal efficacy. The nature of wonder consists in a pleasure equal to a sudden flash of lightning, being devoid of any subsequent mental connection.
However, anger, fear, grief, and disgust have the nature of suffering. In this regard:

Anger is characterized by the persistence of long-term suffering and is permeated by pleasure and pain due to the desire for the cultivation of absolute happiness found in sense objects; it is further defined by the persistence of immediate suffering that lacks such long-term continuity.
Fear is that which is permeated by a longing for the removal of that [suffering] and by the imagined anticipation of pleasure.
Sorrow, however, arises from the destruction of a desired object at both past and present times; it is entirely of the nature of suffering, being interwoven with the recollection of former happiness.
Aversion, which is permeated by a suspicious happiness that arises from being restrained from fleeing toward the objects of life that follow upon the production of pleasure,
is animated by the recollection of the entire accumulation of prior suffering and renders future suffering inconceivable.
Disgust (*nirveda*) has its source in abundant pleasure and pain. The same should be stated regarding the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, according to the view that pleasure and the rest are of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*), they do not possess that [objective] nature. Others, however, maintain that in this context their very essence must be understood as consisting in the experience of those [objects]. Thus are the worldly states whose nature is pleasure and pain.
The conceptualization of narratives from the Vedas, the sciences, and the histories constitutes [the category of] entities. (p. 44)
This dance shall become a means of diversion for the world.
"This drama will be a source of delight in the world, providing a means of inferring the meaning of what remains implicit in the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous.
In the meantime, the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke to all the gods:
Let the sacrifice be performed today according to the rules in the theater pavilion.
Let the sacrificial offering (bali) be prepared with gifts, oblations (homa), and mantras accompanied by medicinal herbs,
as well as with foods to be eaten, chewed, and drunk.
All those who have come to the world of mortals shall receive auspicious honor;
however, one should never engage in a performance without first honoring the Raṅga.

The meaning characterized by drama (*nāṭyalakṣaṇa*), which consists of a composite whole resembling that [original object] and permeated by its impressions (*saṃskāra*), follows the sequence of its very parts;
thus, the meaning characterized by drama consists precisely in following the forms of compassion, love, and so forth.
To explain how it becomes an object of cognition, he says: "consisting of gestures of the limbs and so forth" (*aṅgādi*). These are the gestures such as those of the body (*āṅgika*) and others;
they do not consist of signs, conventions, and the like.
Rather, they consist of worldly right and false cognitions that are equivalent to direct perception and immediate apprehension. Of that very [cognition]...

The *bhāvas* are those beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), which serve as the means for the perception of the synonymous relish (*āsvāda*) that is distinct from [the primary emotions] such as love (*rati*). For this very reason, because they cause [the emotion] to be brought face-to-face, they are designated by the term *abhinaya* (representation), which is not well-known in other worldly or scriptural contexts. Likewise, the *aṅgas* are those whose primary elements (*ādi*) are the branches (*śākhā*), dance (*nṛtta*), and song (*gīta*).

These are the *aṅgas* and so forth. Likewise, the *aṅgas*, the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*), and so on, are the excitants (*vibhāvas*) in the form of causes; the gestures (*abhinayas*) are the ensuants (*anubhāvas*). These are the causes for leading [the audience] toward the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), as he will state: "The production of rasa results from the conjunction of the excitants, ensuants, and transitory mental states" (Nāṭyaśāstra 6). [The work] is endowed with these. *Upa-*...

Having approached from here, it is reflected in the mirror of consciousness (*saṃvid-darpaṇa*). An object (*artha*) that has become thus is "the drama" (*nāṭya*), which is to be enacted (*naṭanīya*), to be danced (*nartanīya*), and likewise to be traversed with effort—that is, it must be entered into by the heart according to its true nature. Furthermore, it is the very essence of the lineage (*pāramparya*) of the actors (*naṭa*).
And conduct (*vṛtta*) consists of the tradition of the Dharma; and that is properly associated with pleasure and pain as its results, because those [results] arise subsequent to it. (p.
But he who arranges a performance without having first honored the stage—his knowledge shall be fruitless, and he shall go to the womb of an animal. || 123 ||
For this worship of the deities of the stage is equal to a sacrifice;
therefore, it should be performed with every effort by those who engage in dramatic performance.
Whether he be a dancer or even a lord of wealth, whoever does not perform worship himself, nor causes others to do so, incurs only decline. (125)
Whoever performs the worship according to the prescribed rules and as it has been seen [in the scriptures], shall obtain auspicious goals and go to the heavenly world. || 126 ||
Therefore, the result is the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. We shall explain this in detail later when defining the nature of existence.
(118–119) Thus, even when obstacles have been removed through conciliation, because divine injunctions are never in vain, [the process continues].

In order to demonstrate that the worship of the portions of deities previously assigned [to specific parts] must necessarily be performed because of their presence in those respective locations, he explains the statement "in this" by referring to the historical account, saying "within," meaning at that time; and he explains "according to rule" with the words "by the offering of oblations," and so forth. They are nourished at the conclusion of the oblation (*bali*).

*Bali* refers to that by which the deities are honored; it is a specific arrangement of rice grains and other materials of various colors. *Homa* refers to offerings such as sesame seeds and the like being cast into the fire. In both cases, the qualifying term is "mantra-herbs" (*mantrauṣadhī*):
the *mantras* are those to be mentioned below, and the *oṣadhis* (medicinal herbs) are *vacā*, *balā*, *ajamodā*, and so forth. There are also highly praised grains.

And: that which is hard and crisp, such as *śaṣkulī* (fried cakes) and *modaka* (sweetmeats), is called *bhojya* (food to be chewed). That which is to be swallowed is *bhakṣya* (food to be eaten), such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and rice-and-pulse (*kṛsara*). Drinks (*pāna*) include milk, grape juice, and so forth. The *bali* (offering) is the specific arrangement previously mentioned. Let these be prepared according to rule, joined with decorative patterns (*vicchitti*), for beauty is the primary concern.
Everything [is included] in the drama.
Now, as to the question, "What is the fruit for the gods in performing worship to the gods? he says: "Having gone to the world of mortals," and so forth.
The underlying meaning is that it is according to the principle: "Whatever a superior person practices... He says, "he should cause [it] to proceed."

Because he follows the conduct practiced by the gods; "in the world" is the ellipsis. (120–122) Now, one might ask: if the world were not to follow good conduct, what would happen? To this he says: "without honoring," etc. (p. 46).
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, together with the deities, exhorted me in this way: "Perform the worship of the arena."
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Origin of Drama," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
"Vain" means [it yields no fruit]. "Of him" refers to the teacher of drama (*nāṭyācārya*). He also states the transgression pertaining to the next world:
"and into the womb of an animal.
(123) Now, if there is a transgression for failing to worship, then what is the result of worshipping? Is it merely the cessation of that transgression? No; he says:
"—according to the prescribed rule. This means according to how it was ordained by the gods. To explain how this is known, he says: "as it has been seen";
the meaning is that this rule is one seen in the scriptures (*śāstra*). "Auspicious matters" refers to the attainment of wealth, honor, and renown in this world. (124–126)
Having thus addressed mortals, he returns to the subject at hand—the ancient tradition—by saying, "Having spoken thus.

Only the master of the art (nāṭyācārya) has authority over the sacrificial ground for the gods; only he obtains the fruit [of the performance]. By this, it is stated that the poet and the director of the spectacle possess the status of performers. That by which one is colored is the *raṅga*, namely, the drama (*nāṭya*).
Because it is the support for that [mandala], it is called the *maṇḍapa*; and because it is the presiding deity over that, the deities are also [included].
Thus, he provides the introduction to the second chapter on the *maṇḍapa*. May there be auspiciousness!
(127) [The one] who always offers praise at the lotus-feet of the Three-Eyed One, and who takes refuge in... [the text continues].
In this treatise on dramaturgy, made manifest through the state of his grace,
may the speech of Abhinavagupta shine forth in the hearts of those of great intelligence.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Origin of Drama," in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on Bharata’s *Nāṭyaśāstra*, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, the Great Śaiva.
p. 47) Śrīḥ.
Now begins the second chapter.
Having heard the words of Bharata, the sages then asked:
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the sacrifice that takes place in the theater."
Alternatively, how should the rituals performed therein, as well as the worship, be conducted by future men in that theater-hall? (2)
We worship the auspicious Śivā, who takes the form of water—the source, sustainer, seed, and creeper for the production of the drama of saṃsāra—and who is the beloved of her husband. 1.

In the preceding chapter, by virtue of the statement "according to reality" (1.5), the sage Bharata perceives that sacrifice and the like are internal [requirements] just like the recitation and other elements; thus, what need is there to mention that he would act through the determination of the ultimate truth? [The text reads: "he perceives through the determination of the ultimate truth. But in the second [chapter], how could there be a definition of the pavilion? For this very reason:
"Silence, song, and the stage—the summary" (6.10). He will explain the stage in its entirety later on.
Therefore, fearing that this might be so [or wondering how it could be], the sages questioned him.
Having thus conceived of the Supreme Self, the Sage spoke these words of Bharata, like the poet Brahmā to Śakra.

Like Bharata the director, like Kohala and others the masters of dramatic art, like the actors, like the Apsarases with their delicate accessories, like Svāti the player of the covered lute, and like Nārada the knower of song— thus was the pavilion well-guarded; the time of performance was like the festival of Indra, [and the performers were] those whose passion, hatred, and other afflictions were stilled.

The meaning is that the members [of the assembly] should ascertain the subject matter briefly explained in the preceding chapter, namely that the performance is preceded by the worship of the deity. (Regarding "yajanaṃ"): the connection is that this was explained in the concluded chapter as "perform the worship of the stage" (*raṅgapūjāṃ kuruṣva*). This concerns the sacrifice (*yajana*) directed toward the deities.

He shows this with the words "Or rather" (*atha vā*), intending to convey that although their question regarding the ritual action was forgotten because they thought there could be no completion of the pavilion without such action, it has now suddenly come back to mind.
This is for the purpose of setting aside the meaning of the previous question; therefore, [he speaks of] worship.
(48) Here, the very theater for drama is indeed the starting point of the application of drama;
therefore, you should first state its definition.
Having heard those words of the sages, Bharata said:
"Listen now to the characteristics and the worship of the theater hall."

The mental creation of the divine occurs in their homes and groves; whereas all human beings must bring about their states through effort, the ritual actions prescribed by the characteristics [of the person] must be performed by men with diligence. (All human states are to be accomplished according to their respective dispositions. 5.
Listen to how the theatrical pavilion (nāṭyamaṇḍapa) should be constructed,
and how its consecration and worship should be diligently performed.
The word *punar* means "again. *Kriyāḥ* refers to the procedures (*itikartavyatā*). *Lakṣaṇam* refers to the configuration, dimensions, and so forth.

Since instruction regarding things that have already passed would be useless, the phrase "by those yet to come" (*bhaviṣyadbhiḥ*) was stated. [The phrase] "by men" (*naraiḥ*) is used because the gods possess [their forms] through the mind (*manasā*). Now, one might ask: what is the function of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? There is no fault here, for a characteristic is so called because it is characterized (*lakṣyate*); thus, it is the configuration (*sanniveśa*).
Alternatively, the connection is as follows: "How is it that there is worship, characterized by ritual action, in that theater-hall which is to be used for the performance of future events? (1-2).
Having provided a resolution to the five previous questions, this other question [is now raised].

Anticipating this doubt, the sages speak again here, beginning with "ādi" (the origin). "Yoga" refers to the origin of the drama (*nāṭya*). By the word "tāvat" (first), it is stated that what was previously questioned is not being abandoned. The particle "eva" (only) follows immediately after the word "lakṣaṇa" (definition), because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is a subordinate part of that [definition], and because the sacrifice (*yajana*) occurs immediately after its completion. Regarding the phrase "of them": * *Nirṇayet* (he should determine): anticipating this doubt, the sages speak again. * *Iha ādir iti*: "Origin" (*ādi*) refers to the connection (*yoga*), that is, the production (*utpatti*) of the drama. * *Tāvat*: by this, it is stated that there is no abandonment of what was previously asked. * *Evakāraḥ*: the particle "eva" is placed immediately after the word "lakṣaṇa," because the procedure is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that [definition], and because the performance of the sacrifice follows immediately upon its accomplishment. * *Teṣām iti*: [referring to] "of them."

Otherwise, however, one should not speak at all for the reason already stated. By this verse, it is said that the knowledge of the characteristics and the worship is useful even for the gods, because even a mentally constructed emanation depends upon knowledge; for this very reason, "action" (*kriyā*) is not mentioned here. (3–4)

Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that [the ritual] action itself is not being described? To this he says: "Of the divine ones" (*divyānām*). The word "let it be heard" (*śrūyatām*) is understood to carry over.

Let the action (*kāryā kriyā*)—that is, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—of human beings be heard; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and worship (*pūjana*) are also included.
Why is it said in the scripture that this belongs to human beings alone? To this he says: "Of the divine ones," because they are [still] in the process of being created.

Even for karma, there is indeed the status of being an object (viṣayatva), wherein there are pleasure groves consisting of gardens, lakes, and sporting grounds, containing many highly diverse trees, creepers, and meadows, as well as flowers, fruits, and sprouts that grow according to the fixed sequence of births.
Having envisioned this theater hall here, the wise Viśvakarman designed its threefold arrangement according to the treatises.
The pavilion may be elongated, square, or triangular; their three measurements are the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
Their measurement is specified as being based on the hand and the cubit:
one hundred, eight, sixty-four, and thirty-two cubits respectively.

"What possibility is there for mental [offerings] in that house? Listen. Regarding "that": it refers to the manner in which the task must be performed by men with effort. Regarding "where": this refers to place and time. Regarding "the site" (*vāstu*): here, the measurement pertaining to the ground of the house is to be understood. It is stated that it is "described by the characteristics of worship" (5–6).

Regarding that, he asks what its characteristic is and says: "here, the theater hall. Here means in the dramatic arena (*nāṭyamaṇḍapa*). The word "and" (*ca*) implies its dimensions as well. It was designed by Viśvakarman. Was it by his own intellect? No; rather, it was according to the treatises (*śāstra*), having been deliberated upon in the theater hall. And he is capable of such deliberation.

Thus he says: "by the wise. He says that it is known. That treatise was composed, and since that too is rooted in another treatise, its beginninglessness through continuous succession (*pravāha*) is stated. He asks, "What is this threefold [nature]? and says: "and drawn out" (*vikṛṣṭa*). It is drawn out (*kṛṣṭa*) by division, meaning long, but not equally in the four directions. It has three corners; that which has three corners is "three-cornered" (*tryaśri*).

The suffix *ac* in the word *tadasm-in* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). Some maintain that these three alone are the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and so forth; others, however, say that since there is a triad for each [of the three], there are nine such divisions here. This latter view is the correct one. Thus he says: "Of those. That which constitutes being "eldest" and so forth is based on the measurement of the hand-staff (*hasta-daṇḍa*), and not based on their physical arrangement (*sanniveśa*). This is the meaning.

"One hundred and eight, sixty-four, and thirty-two"—thus some read with certainty. For them, there exists (also) a designation based on the hand-staff (*hasta-daṇḍa*). And all of this is stated merely as a possibility, not as a definitive enumeration; for there are not only this many divisions.
They are useful. Thus, eighteen varieties have been observed in the scripture.

Although they may not be useful when [the primary means] are otherwise available, they have nevertheless been specified so that the tradition (sampradāya) might not be interrupted, thinking that for some people there might be utility at some time. As it has been said: "When [the primary means] are not employed..."
Regarding the phrase "like a long sacrificial session" (*dīrghasatravat*):
one hundred and eight [days] is the superior [session], while sixty-four is the middling.
Likewise, the smallest hall is held to be thirty-two cubits [in length]. || 10 ||
