For the gods, it shall be the eldest; for kings, it shall be the middlemost;
but for the remaining constituent elements, the youngest is ordained. || 11 ||
Among all types of theaters, the middle one is considered the most excellent;
therein, both recited and sung performances will be most pleasant and easy to hear.
For all types of theaters, a threefold method is prescribed by practitioners:
the elongated, the square, and the triangular.
The smallest is recorded as triangular, the medium as square;
the largest is to be known as elongated by those who apply the Nāṭya-veda. And whatever measurement and characteristic has been specified by Viśvakarman—
And indeed, learn that very [teaching] concerning all the Prekṣā-halls. || 12 ||

An atom (aṇu), dust (rajas), a hair (vāla), a nit (likṣā), a louse-egg (yūkā), and likewise a barley-corn (yava); then a finger-breadth (aṅgula), a cubit (hasta), and a staff (daṇḍa) have thus been proclaimed. || 13 ||

He shows that this is applicable here with the words "one hundred and eight," and so forth. By the word "is desired," the intention is that [the number] remains even when there is a difference [in the types of characters]. Regarding the phrase "of the gods": in cases such as the *ḍima* and other genres where the hero and antagonist consist primarily of gods and asuras, the *ārabhaṭī* style predominates because of its utility for the extensive performance on the stage (*raṅgapīṭha*).

Furthermore, because activities such as circumambulation (*parikramaṇa*) are primarily concerned with musical instruments and the like, and because they involve the employment of higher and longer rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), the devotional state (*bhaktabhāva*) would be impossible [in a smaller space]; therefore, the meaning is that the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be one hundred and eight cubits in size. As for that which...

He explains that the "spectators" (*prekṣaka*) intended here are the gods and others, and not the persons being acted upon (*prayojya*), because the former have a fixed number. Although our own intention regarding this has appeared in works such as the *Daśarūpaka*, it has not entered the path of [the reader's] memory; it shall be demonstrated immediately thereafter. (10–11)
The term "measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) that has been specified; the singular number is used here to denote the class (*jāti*).
Eight *aṇu*s are said to be a *rajas*, and eight of those are called a *vāla*.
Eight hairs make one *likṣā*, and eight *likṣās* make one *yūkā*.
Eight lice are known as one barley-corn (yava), and eight barley-corns likewise constitute one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
Twenty-four such finger-breadths are said to be one cubit (hasta). || 15 ||
The staff is specified as being four cubits in measure;
by this very measure, I shall declare their determination.

He states what the measures are with the words "the atom, the mote," and so forth. He states their definitions with the words "eight atoms," and so forth. That from which perceptibility begins is the *aṇu* (atom).
An *aṇu* is a well-known transformation of an atom; or rather, it is simply an *aṇu* produced by two *dvyaṇukas* or two *paramāṇus*.

[They] are endowed with magnitude (*mahattva*). However, let there be atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*) in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) produced from two atoms. What contradiction is there here? Enough of this digression. "By this very [statement]" refers to what was stated in the passage beginning with "But for the gods... The term *maṇḍapāḥ*—for example, the measurement of the eldest is approximately [the same as] the *ḍma*. As he will state:
It should be understood as being characterized by thunderclaps, the falling of meteors, and eclipses of the moon and sun,
as well as by combat, wrestling, assault, and tumultuous conflict.
"The *ḍima* is crowded with gods, lords of serpents, *rākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, and *piśācas*;
it abounds in sixteen leading characters and is endowed with the *sāttvatī* and *ārabhaṭī* styles" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 18).
Likewise, he will later describe the intermediate length for dramas (*nāṭaka*) and the like, which are primarily intended for performance by kings: [text follows].
It should be understood as being associated with thunderclaps, the falling of meteors, and eclipses of the moon and sun,
as well as with those arising from combat, wrestling, and violent assault.
"The conduct of kings," as stated in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (18), and so forth.
The remaining types of characters (*prakṛti*), however, appear in the *bhāṇa*, the *prahasana*, and other such genres. As he will state later:
"The *bhāṇa* should be understood as having various bases, yet it is to be carried by a single [actor]" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 18).
"Likewise, by the Blessed One, by ascetics, by brahmins, and by others as well" (Nāṭyaśāstra 18), and so forth.

In such a performance where *prakṛti* (the fundamental nature) is predominant, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be of the smallest measurement. Among these pavilions, that which is the definitive conclusion is common to all; [this applies] in the middle pavilion.
For the performance of a *nāṭaka* or a *bhāṇa*, and for the smaller *ḍima* form as well,
one should construct that pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with sixty-four cubits in length.
And for mortals here, it would be thirty-two [yojanas] in width. || 17 ||

From this point forward, the theater stage (nāṭyamaṇḍapa) should not be constructed by the builders, because the performance of drama would otherwise fall into a state of indistinctness there. || 18 ||
But in a remote pavilion, the recitation must be performed with a raised voice;
because it cannot escape [the confines], it will very much fall into discordant tones.

"I shall speak"—this is the intended meaning: since there is a lack of facility for the performance of dramas and the like during the month of Jyeṣṭha, the middle [month] alone is appropriate; that indeed is the settled conclusion.
Furthermore, although the nature of characters such as gods, kings, and commoners is manifold...

"Wherein certainty is led toward through the application of dramatic representation"—this is what he demonstrates with the passage beginning "sixty-four hands," and so forth. The meaning is that if this pavilion exists—or if it does not exist—before or behind the performer, one is not fit for the performance (*karaṇa*). Regarding the word "by the performers" (*kartṛbhiḥ*): what [is meant]?

The meaning is: "by causing them to undergo fruitless exertion. Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): it means in that which exceeds the [proper] measure and in that which is extremely deficient in measure. Regarding the word "drama" (nāṭya): this is to show the various sub-divisions within the entire category. It is so called because drama (nāṭya) becomes manifest from it.
This should be understood with reference to the collective whole (*samudāya*). He demonstrates this very point by saying "the pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*). "Length" refers to its extension;

"width" refers to its breadth on both sides. By the phrase "of mortals," the intention is that since the pavilion is constructed for mortals, what purpose is served [by it] other than through its very function? He states this very point: "Beyond this, not so. From this...
The meaning is: because there exists such a thing as the "middle" (madhyama) for this reason. Regarding the word "above" (ūrdhvam):

it should be understood that the superiority of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists in its being neither less nor more [than the others]. Regarding the word "to be performed" (*kartavya*): excellence (*prakarpa*) is that which is superior;
that which transcends it is "distant" (*viprakṛṣṭa*). What is the measure of application? And in that case, regarding that eldest (*jyeṣṭha*).

It will be shown that "recitation is considered the primary body of drama" (Nāṭyaśāstra 14.2). Its quality of causing distress through its specific discordance would reach those standing nearby. The reason for this is that the tone, when uttered loudly and produced with extreme effort, results in a *kāku* (a modulated or affected intonation).
Wherein there is a division in the sky; likewise, that state which resides in the mouth of one situated at a distance, endowed with various visions.
Because of its excellence, that [abode] would attain a supreme state of invisibility. || 20 ||
Therefore, among all types of theaters, the middle one is desired, so that whatever is to be recited and sung may be heard most clearly therein. (21)
Toward the audience, it would become discordant, devoid of sound, and inaudible.
The reason for this is its nature of non-emission (*aniḥsaraṇadharmatvāt*). "Emission" (*saraṇa*) in an uninterrupted space means the commencement of a second sound;
the meaning is that this property does not exist [in the sound] because there is no diffusion of another sound. Likewise, in the case of something extremely minute...

In the pavilion, because the sound uttered with a high pitch has the nature of emerging from the mouth, it becomes sweet by way of resonance (*anuraṇana*), since no other [independent] sweet sound begins;
thus, the sweet tone would become such that it has perished [as a primary sound]. For resonance indeed belongs to the tone.

"We shall explain later, in the section on *geya*, that this consists in the perfection of the recitation (*pāṭhya-siddhi*). Because it shares the same security and success (*samāna-yogakṣema*) as that, the state of having a discordant tone (*visvaratva*) regarding the principal musical instrument is also implied by this. Thus he will conclude [the section] with the words 'and the *geya*.
The term *visvaratva* is a form derived from the root *svṛ*, meaning 'to sound' or 'to afflict. (17–19)

Having explained the destruction of the primary recitation and of the music, instrumental accompaniment, and so forth—which serve as its primary resonance—he now explains the category of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) as well, beginning with the words "And that which... The internal state (*bhāva*) residing in the mouth—that is, in the face—characterized by the *anubhāvas* such as the gaze, tears, perspiration, change of complexion, and so forth; likewise...

[This refers to] the crown, the head-dress, and so forth; by the word "and" (ca), the bodily [ornaments] are included. Because it is superior to the dwelling and because it is exceedingly vast, it may attain indistinctness. Likewise, there is the state of that which has a length (*dairghya*) that is advanced (*pragata*), drawn out (*kṛṣṭa*), or extended (*karṣaṇa*); then, for the reason of its smallness (*kanīyastva*), [it reaches] the highest...
One should attain a second state of unmanifestness produced by extreme proximity; for the first was said to be produced by extreme distance.
Thus, this should be explained with reference to both pavilions (*maṇḍapa*). Otherwise, the concluding statement, "therefore, the middle one is desired," would not be consistent. Thus he says:

"Of the theaters," and so forth. "Central" (madhyama) means that which exists in the middle. That is desired because, among all the forms [of performance], that recitation (*pāṭhya*) related to them which is primary, as well as the song (*gīta*)—which consists of the subtle form that colors the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—and, by the word "and" (*ca*), the instrumental music (*ātodya*), are most worthy of being heard.
It occurs. By the second *ca*, the meaning is that another type of performance (*abhinaya*) also becomes more visible. (20–21) p.
54) (A threefold rule is prescribed for all theaters.)
It should be drawn by practitioners as elongated, square, or even triangular.
The smallest [theater] is known to be triangular, the middle-sized square,
and the largest, which should be understood as elongated, by those who employ it for dramatic performance.
The mental creation of the gods is found in their houses and groves.
For all human beings indeed bring about their states through the application of effort. || 22 ||
Therefore, a human being should not compete with things created by the gods;
rather, I shall now fully describe the characteristics of a human dwelling.
First, the initiator should examine the divisions of the ground;
thereafter, with a desire for auspiciousness, he should begin the construction according to the prescribed measurements of the site.

Now, if such is the sequence of performance, then the procedure should be stated as relying solely on the hands. Even that [hand-based procedure] is not helpful where it is incomplete; in such cases, it must rely on the staff being played. If it is argued that this is said with the intention of considering divine nature or the spectators, even then, what is the point of this slight difference?
The following verse will be composed to refute the doubt as to how this is possible according to logic;
therefore, one should not suspect a redundancy with the preceding verse, because that [preceding] verse introduces the matter from a different perspective.
He states that verse, beginning with "Of the gods," and so forth. This is due to the abundance of *sattva* in their respective minds, which is produced by that [purity].

The activity characterized by the withdrawal of the senses is exceedingly pervasive even in the vast and extensive groves; what need is there to mention the matter of the pavilions? For this very reason, the plural form "in houses" (gṛheṣu) was employed. By that, the meaning is that those pavilions were mentioned in comparison with them. But the mind of passionate human beings is not like this.

Regarding this, he says: "By those created by the gods," etc. Since it is so, therefore I shall correctly proclaim the characteristics of a human dwelling alone. The word *tat* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.

(22–23) He explains what was meant by "correctly" with the words beginning "of the ground," etc. "Vibhāga" means the distinction [of the site] in terms of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted. "Vāstu" refers to...
One should begin by characterizing [the earth] as "grasping" and "valid cognition"; the word "to perform" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
That which is even, stable, firm, black, or white—[such is the earth].
The performers should construct the dance pavilion on that very ground. || 25 ||
Having first performed the purification, one should plow it up with a plough;
one should clear away bones, stakes, potsherds, as well as grasses and shrubs. (26)
Having purified the earth, one should then specify the measurement:
[the asterisms] Trīṇyuttarāṇi, Saumya, Viśākhā, and Revatī.
The asterisms Hasta, Tiṣya, and Anurādhā are praised for the work of laying the foundation;
one should stretch out the white thread during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism. (27)
The wise should prepare a thread made of cotton, or even of balbaja grass, or of muñja grass, or of bark, provided that it has no breakage.

He states that division with the words "level," and so forth. "Level" means even by nature, neither too low nor too high. "Firm" means having a non-shifting nature. "Hard" means not saline (anūṣara). "Black and white"—the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "or. Others, however, say it refers to being mixed. "To be made" means fit for the act of making. To the question "How?", he says "First," and so forth.

"Purification" (*śodhana*) refers to the removal of impure gravel and other debris located on the surface. Thereafter, one should clear away clods of earth, stones, and so forth using a plow. This very point is stated by the verse beginning with "bones" (*asthi*).
Having thus ascertained the purification of the ground both externally and internally, he states what is to be done immediately thereafter:

Regarding the phrase "having purified": he asks, "How is the measurement specified? and answers with the word "puṣpa" (flower). First, the whiteness of the thread is achieved through dyeing with flour-paste and so forth; the intended meaning is that a measuring line made of leather must not be used. For the master—the discerning patron—and for the performer—the director of the drama—it must be done with great care.

"Grasping the rope" means it must be held without being cut. And such [a state] should be applied with effort in both ways—through attentiveness and through the absence of support from a pillar or the like. "Constantly" means not only during this initial grasping, but also for the sake of fixing it upon another pillar that may appear later.
The meaning is: "in the measuring of the ground area and so forth. "Measuring with effort" refers to this exertion for the purpose of avoiding defects such as deficiency or excess.
If the cord is cut in half, the death of the master is certain;
if the rope is cut into three parts, the provocation of the kingdom is ordained.
If it is cut into four parts, the destruction of the practitioner is said to occur;
or even if it slips from the hand, some diminution of merit will take place. (30)
Therefore, one should always strive diligently to grasp the rope, and one must also take great care in the measurement of the theater hall. (31)
When the hour is favorable and the lunar day and the auspicious moment (karana) are propitious,
one should gratify the Brahmins and then have them proclaim an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Then, having offered the water of pacification (śāntitoya), one should extend the cord;
having made it sixty-four cubits long, one should then divide it into two parts.
Of that [area] which has been divided into two, one should arrange the *raṅgaśīrṣa* (stage-front) by dividing the rear portion equally into two halves. || 34 ||
Thus, there is no redundancy. A *muhūrta* is one beginning with Brāhma; a *tithi* is one beginning with Nandā; a *karaṇa* is one free from Viṣṭi and so forth (24–32).
He states what is to be done by means of stretching out the cord, beginning with "sixty-four," and so on.
Taking a site measuring sixty-four cubits in length and thirty-two cubits in width, one should lay a cord across the middle of its width. The front portion is the section for the spectators;
the rear portion is the section for the performers. Therein, that which will be behind the performer [is the stage].

That itself is the back [wall]. One should draw a line across its middle for the width. Thus, there are two sections of sixteen cubits each. Of these, the rear section of sixteen cubits is the dressing room (*nepathyagṛha*).
One should also divide the front section into two parts; the part situated at the back by half [of that].

The stage-front (*raṅgaśira*) shall be divided into eight cubits (*hasta*), serving as the space for the actors entering the performance. For the main stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*) of the theater (*nāṭyamaṇḍapa*) is situated like one lying on one's back;
its front is eight cubits. Behind that, however, the dressing room (*nepathyagṛha*) shall be sixteen cubits in length.

It is thus; however, in width, it is exactly thirty-two cubits. Furthermore, one should designate the dressing room (*naipathya*) and so forth in the western section, and then the *nepathyagṛha* (dressing chamber).
Having divided the portions according to the rule, as they truly are, and in due order. || 35 ||
And under an auspicious conjunction of stars, the erection of the pavilion should take place,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs, dundubhi drums, mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and other instruments.
Indeed, the installation must be performed with all musical instruments being played;
however, those who are undesirable, as well as heretics and those belonging to other stages of life (āśramas), should be excluded.
And for those men who are clad in saffron robes or are physically impaired,
an offering (bali) consisting of various kinds of food should be made at night.
Endowed with fragrances, flowers, and fruits, it extends throughout the ten directions;
in the east it is joined with white food, and in the south with blue food.
The offering (bali) in the west is yellow, and in the north it is red;
in whichever direction a deity is assigned, the offering should be of the corresponding color.
Such an offering, accompanied by mantras, should be given there;
and for the installation ceremony, rice-pudding with ghee should be given to the Brahmins.

And that is grasped there. Thus he says: "and in the western [part]. In that regard, some say the *raṅgapīṭha* (stage-platform) is sixteen [cubits] in width and eight cubits in length; others, however, reverse this very [measurement]. The essential point is that, in any case, the extension of the *aṅgapīṭha* must also be prescribed. As it will be said: "the stage..."

"Bharata should be drawn away" (Nāṭyaśāstra 12.20), and so forth. (33–35) Having thus stated the rule for the measurement, he describes the procedure for the construction consisting of the laying of bricks, beginning with "under an auspicious conjunction of stars," etc. An offering (*bali*) should be made in the ten directions—namely, the horizontal, upward, and downward directions.

Having said this, with the intention that the ritual procedure for the bali offering in the four directions must be performed exactly as stated and not otherwise, he describes the pervasive rite beginning with the words "of whatever kind" (yādṛśam). Therefore, [he says] regarding the southeast (āgneye):
Likewise, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered to the king, and rice with jaggery to the officiants;
furthermore, the wise should perform the installation under the constellation Mūla.
Having performed the installation in this manner during a favorable hour, on an auspicious lunar day, and under a good karana, one should then proceed with the work of plastering the walls.
Once the rite for the foundation has been completed,
the installation of the pillars shall then take place on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and with a propitious conjunction and division.
The erection of the pillars should be performed by a well-disciplined preceptor who has fasted for three nights, under either the asterism Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa.
The installation of the pillars should be performed at the auspicious time of sunrise;
on the first Brahmin pillar, [an offering] prepared with ghee and mustard seeds should be made.

The entire ritual procedure should be performed with white items, and one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) alone. Then, upon the pillar of the Kṣatriya, [one should place] cloth, garlands, and ointments.
Everything should be given in red, and molasses with rice (guḍaudana) should be offered to the twice-born;
this rite is to be performed at the Vaiśya-stambha in the northwestern direction.
All that has been offered should be given to the twice-born as ghee-rice;
and the rite for the pillar of the Śūdra should be performed properly, relying on the previously mentioned [directions] and the north.

The phrase "of red color" and so forth is to be inferred. The mantras are those which will be mentioned in the ritual procedure for the worship of Varuṇa. These should be employed in conjunction with the praise of the action and the [appropriate] context; for there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that one performs an action as it is remembered by means of a mantra. Others, however, say that the offering of oblations (*balikarma*) should be performed using only Vedic mantras addressed to that deity.
Others say it refers to their specific marks (*talliṅga*). The word "and" (*ca*) is displaced;
its meaning is that the satiation of Brāhmaṇas occurs not only at the commencement of the measurement, but also at the installation (*sthāpana*).
(36–43) Having thus performed the ritual for measurement, the ritual for installation, and the ritual for the walls, the ritual for the pillars (*stambha*) should be carried out.
He demonstrates this with the phrase "the work of the wall. "Sthāpana" means erecting. First, however, is the southeast corner (āgneya-koṇa). Its [characteristics are indicated] by its qualifiers...
One should diligently prepare a meal of *kṛsara* that is mostly blue for the twice-born;
and at the previously mentioned pillar of Brāhmaṇas, there should be white garlands and unguents.
One should place gold at the base as an ornament for the ear,
and copper should be provided below on the pillar designated for a Kṣatriya.
At the base of the Vaiśya pillar, one should cause silver to be given;
at the base of the Śūdra pillar, however, one should give iron alone.
Indeed, gold should be deposited at the bases of all the pillars amidst the sounding of auspicious and meritorious hymns and the shouts of "Victory! (53).
The installation of the pillars should be performed, preceded by offerings of flower garlands, along with abundant gifts of jewels, gifts of cows, and gifts of garments. (54)
Having gratified the Brahmins, he should then raise the pillars—those that are immovable, unshakable, and likewise firm. (55)
These are indeed declared to be the faults when a pillar rises up improperly;
lack of rain is said to result from its swaying, and fear of death from its tilting.

The injunction regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is to be inferred from the restatement (*anuvāda*). "In all cases, [the offering is] milk-rice (*pāyasa*)"—this is understood from the context of "to the twice-born. It should be understood that the food for everyone, in accordance with the injunction, is of a white color and so forth. "And then" (*tataśca*): the meaning is "ending with those" (*tadanta*). (44–54)
"Immovable" (acala) means that which is not described by the mind's shifting into another location.

"Unshakable" (akampya) means that in that very place, there is no loosening of the position. "Irreversible" (avalita) means that which does not need to be turned back by means of circular movements and the like.
They are called *doṣas* because they indicate faults and because they cause harm. He describes those faults, beginning with "lack of rain" and so forth: (55–57) p.
60) "In the case of trembling, however, there arises terrible fear from a foreign army."
But one should raise up the pillar Śiva, which is free from these defects.
At the Brahmastambha pavitrarite, a cow should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
for the remaining [rites], a meal should be provided for the performers during the installation ceremony.
That [food] should be given, purified by mantras, by the wise dance-instructor;
he should also feed the domestic priest and the king with honeyed milk-rice (madhupāyasa). || 59 ||
Likewise, [he should offer] all the performers as well as *kṛsarā* mixed with abundant salt;
having thus performed the entire rite, with all musical instruments being played, || 60 ||
Having consecrated them according to the rule and erected the pillars while remaining pure,
[he should do so] just as the immovable mountain Meru and the mighty Himavat stand firm.
"Be as immovable as you are, bringing victory to the lord of men;
likewise, [support] the pillar, the door, the wall, and the dressing room. (62)
Thus should the one who knows [the ritual] raise it by means of the rite prescribed by rule.
Beside the stage-platform, however, a *mattavāraṇī* (elephant-enclosure) should be constructed.

"It should be given"—by the force of the word "to a twice-born," it is understood that it should be given [to him]. Regarding the phrase "having consecrated," he states the mantra indicated [therein]:

"As follows. Experts in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) maintain that this [mantra] should be recited with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) at the beginning and the word of salutation (*namaḥ*) in the middle. "Become immovable" (*acalo bhava*)—this is a prescriptive injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), not a restatement (*anuvāda*).

"There shall be victory for you"—in this [expression], there is no tautology. Thus, one should effect the adaptation (*ūha*) by treating the wall as feminine and the house as neuter. Regarding the word "sides" (*pārśva*): because no specific distinction is mentioned and because of the dual number in the phrase "those two are equal" (*nā.
śā. 2.65*), it is understood from the gender and the dual case-ending that the reference is to the two future sides. (58–63)

Four pillars are erected outside the pavilion, having been brought out from the pavilion-site; thus, there are two pillars at the limit of the wall-opening. Beyond that, with respect to the pillars situated eight cubits apart from the wall, [there are likewise] those eight cubits apart—
(61) Equipped with four pillars and equal in measure to the stage-platform,
the *mattavāraṇī* should be constructed with a height of one and a half cubits.
The performance hall (raṅgamaṇḍapa) should be made equal to those two in height.
Upon it, one should likewise place garlands, incense, perfumes, and garments.
Offerings of various colors should be given, as well as a bali-oblation dear to the spirits (bhūtas);
furthermore, iron should be placed by the skilled at the base of the pillars.
At the meal, rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara) should be given as food for the Brāhmaṇas;
thus, preceded by these prescribed rites, the Mattavāraṇī festival should be performed.
Then the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha) should be constructed according to the rites prescribed by rule;
the stage-front (raṅgaśīrṣa), moreover, should be made provided with six wooden beams (ṣaḍdāruka).
"The two pillars" means that the *mattavāraṇī* is eight cubits in width and perfectly square;

however, according to those who maintain that "the length is the measurement," in their view, the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*) becomes eight cubits in depth and sixteen cubits in width, thus resulting in an elongated form. According to others...

The measurement here is in cubits (*hasta*); that is, with respect to the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*), the height of the *mattavāraṇī* should be made one and a half cubits. The dual number in the word "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) is intended as an indicator; since its purpose has been fulfilled there, it is not required here. Of that very [height]...

The height of the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha) is equal to its width. Thus, it is stated that the stage-platform is one and a half cubits high in relation to the level of the ground at its base. Consequently, the stage-platform is not excessively difficult to see due to the light from the *mattavāraṇī* (the elephant-enclosure).
This is indicated by the singular number in the word *utsedhena*. Otherwise, it would have been stated as *utsedhābhyām* (by the two heights).

Garlands, incense, and so forth should be offered at the very time of the creation [of the image], because those presiding over it, such as the *bhūtas*, must be attended with effort due to their fierce nature. Thus he says: "with the observance of the prescribed rites."

By the word *puraskāra*, the ritual procedure as prescribed in the treatises on architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) is intended. (64–67) Regarding the construction of the stage (*raṅgapīṭha*), he first describes the head of the stage (*raṅgaśīrṣa*):
having fixed two pillars, eight cubits apart from each other, against the wall of the dressing room (*nepathyagṛha*).
Between those two [pillars], there are two pillars with a distance of four cubits measured from the mouths [of the beams] and so forth.
There are six wooden pieces: the lower wood and the upper wood for each of them. That which contains these six wooden pieces is called *ṣaḍdārūka*.
In this case, there should be two doorways for the dressing room;
furthermore, black earth should be diligently applied here for filling.
Having ploughed with the plough and cleared away the clods, grass,
and pebbles, one should diligently yoke two oxen of pure color to the plough.
In this matter, the makers should be men free from physical defects, and the clay must be carried in new baskets by those whose limbs are complete. (71)
The stage-front (raṅgaśīrṣa) should be constructed with such [materials] with great care;
it must not be made like the back of a tortoise, nor likewise like the back of a fish.
The painting surface is praised when it has the appearance of a polished mirror;
and here, jewels should be offered, with a diamond in the east by the wise. (73)
Lapis lazuli is on the right side, crystal likewise on the west;
coral is on the north, while gold should be in the center.

The suffix *kan* is applied to the word *saṃjñā*. By that, the state of being endowed with various arrangements is obtained. Here, two doors for the dressing room (*nepathyagṛha*) should be made: one to the south and the other to the north.
And those two doors are achieved by means of the *kūrparābhinati* (the elbow-bend). For those actors (*pātra*),...
The stage-front (raṅgaśīrṣa) should be constructed for the rest of those who come, for the protection of the stage, and for the beauty of the stage.
Others, however, say:
"In this context, the *ācchapātaka* is adorned with wooden beams on both sides, above and below, and is provided with two pillars."

Thus they speak of the "six pieces of wood. Others, however, maintain that the beams at the top of the pillars extend far out from the projecting timber; from there, the crossbeams, the rafters, and the floor-boards are said to emerge. In the space [above], the walls are explained as being supported by pillars, along with lions and other beasts of prey that follow after them.

The *niryūhas* extend from the ends of the *tulās*; they consist of panels and walls, while the *kuharas* take the form of mountain caves, city fortresses, groves, and deep ravines—this constitutes the "six-wooded" (*ṣaḍdāruka*) structure. Furthermore, in every case, there are two doors running north-south for the vessels.
Because they enter by circling to the right or to the left according to their different modes of movement, they are of pure color, white, capable of bearing the yoke, and well-tamed. (68–71) p.
Having thus established the head of the color, one should employ the work of woodcarving, joined with primary and secondary motifs and utilizing various artistic crafts. (75)
It was endowed with various pleasure groves, adorned by many wild beasts, and decorated all around with statues of women. || 76 ||
It was provided with turrets and inner chambers, featuring various constructed altars,
joined by diverse arrangements, and adorned with latticed windows of variegated design.
It was provided with excellent seats, filled with flocks of doves,
and further adorned with pillars set upon various mosaic floors.
Having thus performed the procedure for the wooden framework, one should apply the work of the walls, or [construct] pillars, or elephant-tooth brackets, or even windows. (79)
Regarding "the back of a tortoise": that which is depressed on all sides and circular in shape in the center is slow (*manda*).

That same [shape] being elongated in the center is the back of a fish (*matsyapṛṣṭha*). Neither of those two should be made here; rather, it should be made even and level. The jewels and their weapons should be [arranged] according to their respective colors as appropriate.

"Having done so" means having previously analyzed it with the intellect. He analyzes what was called "the work of wood" with the passage beginning with "endowed with [main] arches and counter-arches" and ending with "and adorned with pillars. *Kuharāṇi* refers to mountain thickets, groves, and forest-like dwellings. *Sālabhañjikāḥ* are wooden figures.

The natures [of the deities] are lovely. Where there are altars (*vedikā*) of various forms, square, and where there are variegated lattices (*jāla*) in the form of squares and octagons, as well as windows (*gavākṣa*) consisting of circular apertures; where there are pedestals (*pīṭha*) upon the pillars, and upon those, supporting scales (*tulā*).

*Kapotālī* refers to the row of *viṭaṅka* (ornamental niches). The diversity of the *kuṭṭima* (paved floor) arises from the distinction between the *raṅgaśiraḥ* (stage-front), the *raṅgapīṭha* (stage-platform), and the two types of *mattavāraṇī* (drinking galleries).
In every case, this indicates the appropriate timber; or alternatively, it refers to the distinctions of color, such as red, white, blue, yellow, and so forth.

Regarding this, some say that *āroha* (elevation) and *pratiroha* (counter-elevation) are useful for the logical reasoning (*tarka*) of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
(72–78) One should not create a central space that is pierced by a secondary door at each main door, nor should one place a *nāgadanta* (dental-mold ornament) [in such a way].

Some say that the elephant-head (*gajamukha*) located at the upper, lower, and middle portions of the pillar is for the purpose of supporting the figurines (*putrikā*). Some say there are two floors, consisting of the lower and upper parts of the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*).
The *mattavāraṇī* (the elephant-enclosure) is formed by the addition of a second wall on all sides, according to the measurement for exiting to the exterior.

One should not construct a corner that resembles a circumambulatory path (pradakṣiṇa), nor one with a facing door, nor one where the door is pierced through [the corner], even if it is a gatehouse (dvārikā) or a temple tower (devaprāsādāṭṭālikā). (p. 64)
The performance hall for the dance, shaped like a mountain cave, shall have two levels. || 80 ||
Free from drafts, sheltered from the wind, and possessing a steady sound;
therefore, the dance pavilion should be made windless by its builders. (81)
By means of which there will be a deep resonance for the *kutapa* drum;
having performed the rite for the wall-work, one should cause the plastering of the wall to be applied. 82.
Once the walls have been plastered and polished on all sides, the application of whitewash (sudhākarma) must be diligently performed upon them.
One should employ the art of painting on surfaces that are level and naturally beautiful;
in such paintings, both men and women are to be depicted. (84)
Creeper-bindings (latābandha) should be performed, as well as actions arising from one's own enjoyment;
in this manner, the stage (nāṭyaveśma) should be arranged by the performers. (85)

Others say it is the second stage (*bhūmi*). Still others say it is because of the placement within another pavilion above. Some say it is the "two-stage" (*advibhūmi*) level. But the teachers explain it as containing a distributive sense (*vīpsā*): since two by two stages are dug out as depressions and elevations, it is so called because of that sequence of depressions and elevations (*nimnonnata-krameṇa*).

From the vicinity of the stage platform up to the door, [the height] should be equal to the height of the stage platform. For in this way, there is no mutual obstruction for the audience. Furthermore, because it has the form of a mountain cave, there is stability of sound and so forth, as well as softness.
It should be provided with latticed windows fitted with water-drains (or lattice-panels).
A *kutapa* is a group consisting of storytellers, singers, and musicians. It is so called because it "heats" (*tapati*) or illumines that stage of dance (*kurnāṭyabhūmi*).
Others say it protects (*pāti*) the sound (*kutaṃ*). Its depth lies precisely in that sound.
From the whirling [of sounds] and from the completion of the undertaking of mutual echoes;
the plastering of walls, the application of shells, sand, and mother-of-pearl; or the arrangements of vine-bindings, such as the binding of trees and creepers.

Or, it refers to the various types of arrangements for wrapping musical instruments upon creepers such as the *mālatī*, as well as the specific varieties of *piṇḍībandha* (structural formations) to be described later. He concludes this with: "Thus, it is extended" (79–85).
Furthermore, I shall indeed explain again the characteristics of the square:
it must be made thirty-two cubits on all sides. (86)
The theater pavilion, situated on an auspicious site and according to the rules of dramaturgy, follows the same procedure, characteristics, and auspicious rites that were previously described. (87)
One should cause all those [lines] to be drawn even in a square that is extended;
having made the square equal and having divided it with a cord.
On the outside, a firm wall should be constructed all around using closely joined bricks;
therein, on the inside, [the pillars] should be placed upon the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha).

Although it is possible to infer that [the altar] is a perfect square for this very reason, [the author] begins again with the words "once more" (*punareva*) with the intention of explaining it for the sake of clarity. [An objection is raised: But since the measurements of the pillars, the divisions, and the arrangement of the stages were not mentioned regarding the extended [altar], how is that?
In response to the doubt as to how this should be understood, the answer is given again by way of repetition:

since we shall describe that characteristic which pertains to the square in relation to the jar (*ghaṭa*)—that is, in relation to its being drawn out (*vikṛṣṭa*)—therefore the characteristic of being drawn out is not incomplete. Likewise, that which belongs to it...
By the word "again" (*punaḥ*), he shows that the characteristic already stated must also be applied to the square (*caturaśra*).
By means of that, he applies there what is called the requirement for the extension (*atideśa*) of the [measurement] not yet arrived at. He states [the rule for] the square:
"on all sides" (*samantataḥ*); the meaning is: on all four ends, that is, in all four directions. And "having divided" (*pravibhajya*).
The meaning is "just as before. If one asks, "If there is a wall on the outside, what is it like on the inside? he says: "There, on the inside.
One should divide the field on all sides into eight parts, so that it becomes sixty-four squares, like a chessboard with four squares per side. Therein, in the central group of four squares—

The stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*) is eight cubits on all sides. On its western side, there remains a field that is twelve cubits from east to west and thirty-two cubits from south to north. (In this context, that which is occupied by the stage-platform is indeed exactly eight cubits. As for the remaining field...

From the center of that, one should construct the stage-head (*raṅgaśiraḥ*) in the form of six wooden beams (*ṣaḍdāruka*) on the western side, measuring exactly the same as the eastern part— four cubits in width and thirty-two cubits in length— by dividing the field into its constituent parts. Then, from there...

First, the dressing room (nepathyagṛha) is located in the west. This being the case, once the stage platform (raṅgapīṭha) has been marked out, ten pillars—excluding the six wooden pillars—are to be placed.
Among them, four are at the four corners. There, starting from the southeast pillar, there is an interval of four cubits.
There is one pillar in the southern direction; likewise, a second from the southwest pillar. (p. 66) Ten pillars are capable of supporting the pavilion by those who employ them.
And outside the pillars, there is also a pedestal in the form of a staircase.
The residence for the spectators should be constructed with bricks and wood,
rising from the ground to a height of one cubit.
Having surveyed the stage-platform, one should perform the ritual pertaining to the seat;
then, at a distance of six [units], one should again erect pillars in their respective directions.

Likewise, there are two pillars in the north as well. On the eastern side, there are two pillars at a distance of four cubits from the pair of pillars located in the northeast and southeast; thus, there are six.
These ten consist of the four situated in the corners and the aforementioned six. Outside are the seats for the assembly members, or they may be outside of all [the other structures].
Because the vision is obstructed by extreme proximity; for this very reason, he says that it is "proper" when observing the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*).
By this, the state of having two levels is indeed indicated.
He states the rule for the pillars in between: "six others," [located] to the south of the stage-platform.

Two pillars should be set up four cubits apart from each other, and two others eight cubits apart from one another. Then, from the pillar opposite the southeast pillar, one should place the next pillar to its east at an interval of four cubits;
this is the procedure for the southern pillars among those previously established.
There are three pillars in the interval of the southern wall; likewise on the northern side as well.

Regarding the phrase "above them": one should provide eight additional [pillars]. Therein, on the northern part of the southern wall, at a distance of four cubits from the previously installed pillar and the wall, one should first install a pillar.

Thus, on the southern side of the northern wall; then, following the two sections of the stage area, there are two [pillars] at a distance of four cubits from the eastern wall, and likewise two more at a distance of four cubits from those— making eight in total.

One should place upon the pillars a pedestal measuring eight cubits, featuring a face fashioned from lotuses and other such motifs. Above this perforated face, the pillars—which serve as supports for the scales—shall hold beams (tulās) measuring one cubit in length. Thus [the structure] rests upon the pillars.
The rule for the pillars is in a square.

Regarding that very [square], Śrī Śaṅkuka and others say that one should, by one's own intellect, apply it to triangles when it is extended. Others, however, say that the statement "eight pillars again" refers to those pertaining to the dressing room (nepathyagṛha).
The knower [of the ritual] should, according to the prescribed rule, firmly establish eight pillars for the support of the pavilion, and furthermore, he should arrange [a structure] above them. (93)
Then, a pedestal measuring eight cubits in size should be established;
having pierced the face [of the image] to a depth of eight cubits, one should then place it upon those pedestals.
But the author of the Vārttika says: "The inner dressing room, two pillars, and four stools...
[and] these four [others], thus ten are mentioned."
The distance between the wall and the bases of the pillars should be exactly eight cubits at the end.
Thus it is said: "Datta, Adya, Vāta, and Atyatha; these [pillars] may be of various kinds. Four are situated on the pedestal (pīṭha), and hereafter, there are two each in front and behind."
The intent of the scripture is that six others, along with the intervening spaces, should likewise be constructed.
Those two pairs located here at the back and the front of the *pīṭha*—
of these, the other eight that were specified should also be placed above.
When those [clouds] are lifted up, there would be light here on the surface of the entire ocean.
"A pedestal in the shape of a staircase should be fashioned here on all sides with colors, so that light... [may reach] the upper directions.
Furthermore, many other such doctrines have not been written down for fear of excessive length in this book.

"This is Candrasodara (and here Sāra)," say the teachers. Here, a threefold arrangement of the viewing pavilion (*prekṣāmaṇḍapa*) has been made: the lower ground, the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*), and the stage (*raṅga*). Among these, this specific procedure for the placement of pillars has been stated.
To explain: he speaks of the pillars on the lower level, saying "there, from the interior.
In terms of width, twelve cubits, and likewise in length, four... (cubits should be left as intervals). Twelve pillars are to be provided with respect to the two walls.
In that regard, pillars should be provided by those who know [the craft] for the support of the pavilion;
they are the sustainers of the *dhāraṇī*, and they are adorned with women from the *śāla* [caste]. (95)
Then, the dressing room (nepathyagṛha) should be constructed with great care;
there shall be a single door for entry into the stage (raṅgapīṭha). 96.
Furthermore, one should cause the entry of the people to take place by facing another direction;
however, the second door should indeed be made to face the stage.

The distance between the hands [of the pillars] is eight *hasta*s with respect to one another; their mutual interval should be made in such a way that there is no piercing of the door. Thus, there are ten [pillars] in five rows.
He states the rule for the placement on the ground outside this group of ten pillars: "Of the pillars..."

"And also externally," and so forth; this is to be explained as before. Now, he describes the placement of the pillars (*stambha-nyāsa*) upon the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*): "six others," and so forth. This means that above [the stage], in the western corner of the *nepathyagṛha* (dressing room) characterized by the face of the stage-platform. As for the back of the stage-platform:

"The second [door] there is the *raṅgaśiras*"—this is stated in the singular with respect to the stage (*rāśi*). Therefore, two doors alone should be made at the *raṅgaśiras* for the entrance of actors situated in the *nepathya*. By the word "and" (*ca*), the door for other entrances is also included. Thus, it is summarized that according to another opinion, three [doors] should be constructed.
By using the term "all," he demonstrates that there is neither deficiency nor excess here, and thus permits an increase in the number of pillars in the remote [section] (86–94).
Regarding the phrase "on the triangular stage-platform, however, in the middle of each stage": here, "stage" (*raṅga*) refers to its head. Behind that—

*Raṃ* ... *geyādivābhitaḥ* (? is a *karmapravacanīya* indicating exclusion (*varjana*). [It means] excluding the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*), [referring to] the interior pavilion. There, among the thirty-two cubits, there are pillars at each corner on the stage-platform; thus, there are four [pillars] with an interval of eight cubits. Immediately after that, there are two pillars.

These six [pillars] are eight cubits apart; from that, one should leave a space twelve cubits long, and within that, at the front of the courtyard (raṅgaśira), which is four cubits long and thirty-two cubits wide, two scales (tule) are to be provided. For each scale, excluding the four pillars that are eight cubits [apart], there are eight [pillars].

[They] come into being. For this very reason, one should provide a transverse [beam] of eight cubits even within the interval of four cubits, so that the painting becomes balanced. This is what is meant by "eight pillars," and so forth.
... [or] the *sirā* (ridge-pole) above, such as the *śāda-saubhuya* and others. That which is above the *raṅgapīṭha* (the stage-platform)...
The meaning is "having the form of a head. And thus: "In a remote pavilion, the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha) should be made eight cubits in measurement relative to [the size of] the pavilion. (p. 69)
It was square, level, and adorned with an altar-like ledge.
The *mattavāraṇī* (the elephant-enclosure) should be constructed as previously specified by the authoritative measures, provided with four pillars on the sides of the altar (*vedikā*). || 99 ||
One should cause the stage-front (raṅgaśīrṣa) to be made either elevated or level;
however, in a rectangular space it should be elevated, and likewise level in a square one. || 100 ||
In this manner, by this rule, the house shall be square.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the triangular house.
The performers should construct a triangular, three-cornered dance hall;
in its center, they should have a triangular stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha) made. || 102 ||
The door of that house should be made on that very same corner, and a second one should also be made behind the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha). || 103 ||

The elevated stage-front (*raṅgaśira*) will be described; there, by rule, eight pillars are to be placed. However, he shows that they must be placed firmly with the words "there, the pillars. Now, he states the procedure regarding the remaining parts of the hand: "the dressing room" (*nepathyagṛhaka*). By the expression "entry into the stage-platform" (*raṅgapīṭhapraveśana*), he says this:
First, according to the division of the enclosures (*kakṣyā*), there are two gates; thus, the word "gate" (*dvāra*) is used in the singular by way of a collective formation (*ajāta-ekavacana*).
And the word "one" (*eka*) is intended with reference to a group (*rāśi*). The reason for forming this group is the entry into the vessel as an offering.
And so he will state in the *Kakṣyādhyāya*:

"The placement of the [actor's] belongings is in those two [rooms] previously described by me at the door of the dressing room (nepathyagṛha)" (Nāṭyaśāstra 13.2). And the entrance for the people is through the third door of the dressing room, by which the troupe of actors enters bringing their wives; the other door faces toward [the stage].

One should make [the entrance] in the eastern direction for the purpose of the entry of the assembly members by way of the door and courtyard. Now, with respect to what is "facing" (ābhimukhya)? It has been stated that it is in relation to the courtyards (kakṣyā) alone that the directions such as "east" and so forth are designated.
And as he will say:

"From whichever side the entrance for the actors and the entrance for the stage manager (nepathyaka) are located, that direction should be considered as the East by the wise in the application of drama. (Nāṭyaśāstra 13.11). Thus, the theater building has four doors.
Whatever rule pertains to a square [mandala], whether it relies upon walls or pillars, all of that should be employed by practitioners even for a triangular one. (104)
In this manner, theaters should be constructed by the wise according to this rule;
furthermore, I shall explain their worship according to the prescribed ritual. (105)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Construction of the Maṇḍapa," in the Indian Nāṭyaśāstra.

Others, however, maintain that one should construct two other side-doors with the first [type of] door as the primary cause for the sake of providing light; thus they describe the theater as having six doors. Now, he explains the remaining points concerning the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*) and the stage-head (*raṅgaśiras*): "But eight cubits... [referring to] the platform (*vedikā*).
In a work endowed with beauty, the previous measurement applies; its height is one and a half cubits (*adhyardhahasta*).

"Elevated" means relative to the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*). Indicating this here by way of context, it should be understood that in a large-scale [theater], three pillars more than that same measure must be constructed. The interval [between them] is also shown right here. (95–101)
Now, he begins the definition of the triangle by means of an extended application (atideśa), saying:

"The triangle. Its definition is "the three-cornered" (*trikoṇa*). And for the sake of favoring both [the square and the circle], there are simply two measurements drawn out from the square. In the center, the triangular stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*) itself [is formed]; likewise, so too is the head of the stage (*raṅgaśiras*).

And the dressing room (*nepathyagṛha*). "By that very corner" means by the one situated toward the west (*vāruṇī*). The "door" is the entrance for the people. It should not be made in that same corner as the door. He indicates the connection [between these points] with the words "thus by this. By this method, many theater pavilions (*nāṭyamaṇḍapa*) are [constructed], but not according to the previously mentioned calculation of eighteen varieties.

"By the wise" means by those who know how to perform reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*). Regarding the word "again" (*punar*): although it has been stated that all [deities] bestow auspiciousness, the meaning of the word "again" is "nevertheless, I shall speak. For the procedure (*vidhāna*) was not mentioned therein; thus he says, "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*). "Of these" refers to the deities situated in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); by this, the ritual services (*upacāra*) have been mentioned. (102–105)
Thus ends the second chapter, on the Maṇḍapa, in the Abhinavabhāratī, a commentary on the Indian Nāṭyaśāstra, composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara Ācārya Abhinavagupta.
p.
71) Śrī! Now begins the third chapter.
Once an auspicious theater hall has been constructed, endowed with all the required characteristics,
cows should reside there for seven days together with twice-born brahmins engaged in the recitation of prayers.
Then, at the arrival of night, having sprinkled his limbs with water purified by mantras, he should consecrate the dwelling and likewise the stage-platform.
Having entered the appropriate place, the initiated teacher of dance, being self-controlled, pure, having fasted for three nights, and wearing unwashed garments; || 3 ||
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the source of all worlds, Bhava;
and likewise to Viṣṇu, the grandfather of the universe, as well as Indra and Guha.
Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī, Siddhi, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Smṛti;
Soma and Sūrya, the Maruts, the world-protectors, and likewise the two Aśvins.
Mitra, Agni, the divine castes, the Rudras, Kāla, as well as Kali,
Mṛtyu, Niyati, and likewise Kāladaṇḍa.
When those devoted to nourishment [attain] ...
that sovereign body of fire.

The logical connection is that once the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is completed, worship must necessarily be performed. In that regard, this is the sequence of the ritual procedure: for if it were otherwise, the description of the preliminary rites (pūrvaraṅga) would have to occur immediately after the introductory chapter (adhyāya). Therefore, [the worship] will be shown as a supplement to the construction of the pavilion, because it is an indispensable act of worship. [This is indicated by the phrase] "by those intent on recitation" (japyaparaiḥ).
This means: by those who recite the mantras that destroy demons (*rakṣoghna*). Regarding the word "thence" (*tataḥ*):
[he should worship] Viṣṇu’s weapon and Vāsuki, the king of serpents.
Vajras, oceans of lightning, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and sages.
The spirits, piśācas, yakṣas, and the great lords of the guhyakas;
the asuras, those who obstruct dance, and likewise other daityas and rākṣasas.
Likewise, he saw the Nāṭyakumāris and the Mahāgrāmaṇyas,
as well as Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and hosts of Bhūtas.
Having bowed to these and other celestial sages with palms joined in reverence,
and having invoked them as they occupy their respective places, he should then speak as follows.
"You must take us under your protection during the night, and you, along with your followers, must provide assistance in this drama. (11)
Having worshipped all [the deities] together in one place and having applied the *kutapa* [musical instrument],
one should perform worship for the Jarjara [deity] for the sake of success in the dance (*nāṭya*).
You are the weapon of Mahendra, the destroyer of all Dānavas,
created by all the gods, and the eradicator of all obstacles.

After seven days. "He should perform the consecration" (*adhivāsayet*): the deities enter and take up residence in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). The consecration of the house is the invitation of the presiding deities performed by the dance master (*nāṭyācārya*). The initiate (*dīkṣita*) is one who has taken the vow. The protagonist (*nāyaka*) is the dance master. Having paid homage and having invoked [the deities].
The connection is that he "should say. And since the remembrance of the Supreme Lord is appropriate first, [he says] "Mahādeva.
Mahādeva is Gaṇapati, the great leader. "And others" refers to those mentioned in the first chapter (1.10).

"In one place" means on a portion of ground prepared as a sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*). "Kutapa" refers to the various types of musical instruments (*caturvidhātodyabhāṇḍāni*). "In one place" [refers to where these are kept].

“Niveśanam” means the setting up of a dilapidated [shrine] for the purpose of worship. “Āryeṇa nivasanīyam” means it is to be attended upon; here the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
Proclaim the victory of the king and the defeat of his enemies;
likewise, proclaim the welfare of cows, Brahmins, and Śiva, as well as the flourishing of the drama.
Having done this according to the rule, one should attend upon [the deity] in the dance pavilion;
then, when the night has turned to dawn, one should commence the worship here.

The worship of the stage (raṅgapūjana) should be performed under the asterisms of Ārdrā, Maghā, Bharaṇī, or the three preceding them (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā), or under Āśleṣā or Mūla. || 16 ||
The preceptor, being disciplined, pure, and initiated, must perform the illumination of the arena and the worship of the deities. (17)
At the end of the day, during the fierce and terrible Muhūrta presided over by Yama,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules and then install the deities.
Red protective amulets, red thread, and red perfumes are to be worshipped;
likewise, red *sumanas* flowers and whatever fruit may be red [should be offered]. || 19 ||
With barley, white mustard seeds, parched grain, unbroken rice grains, powder of *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, and husked *priyaṅgu* seeds. || 20 ||

The asterism is Bharaṇī. The term "in the former ones" is a designation with reference to the asterisms; these are Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā. (Regarding "illumination": it is well known as *nīrājana*, which consists of touching [the object] with a flaming blade of *darbha* grass. Regarding "amulets" (*pratisarā*): they are fashioned from thread.

*Granthimantaḥ* refers to specific types of knots. All that has been mentioned above is placed upon the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*), and so forth. The word *sūtra* means [the thread] all around... [this entire remainder] is the placement (*niveśana*). This means the offering of the *arghya* at the time of invocation (*āvāhana*). Others, however, say that—

The term *niiveśanam* is derived from the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). This is an adjective qualifying the *maṇḍala*. Regarding the phrase "the *maṇḍala* with barley and so forth," *nāgapuṣpa* refers to the *nāgadanta* plant. (11-21) p.
One should prepare the abode of the deities endowed with these materials;
first, one should draw the maṇḍala in its proper place according to the prescribed rule.
A mandala of sixteen cubits should be made all around,
and one should construct doors here in the four directions according to the prescribed rule.
And in the middle of this, two lines—one horizontal and one vertical—should be drawn; within the divisions of their enclosures, one should install the deities.
One should place Brahmā seated upon a lotus in the center of that;
first, the Blessed Lord Śiva should be placed together with his hosts of spirits.
Nārāyaṇa, Mahendra, Skanda, Sūrya, the two Aśvins, and Śaśin, as well as Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Śraddhā, and Medhā, [are stationed] in the east. (25)
In the southeast, Vahni (Agni) should be established together with Svāhā;
likewise the Viśvedevas along with the Gandharvas, and the Rudras together with the hosts of serpents.
To the south, however, Yama and Mitra, along with their followers, should be established;
one should also establish the Pitṛs, Piśācas, Uragas, and Guhyakas.

It should be made such that it measures sixteen cubits. Therefore, it is stated that the mandala is four cubits on the surface of the stage-platform itself. Consequently, there was no lack of space for sixteen cubits [as asserted] by Śaṅku and others, due to the constraints of the seat, pillars, and so forth. Thus, it remains unmade.

The passage beginning with "on the stage-platform" (*raṅgapīṭhe*) and so forth has been introduced excessively and in vain. Regarding the two lines: as previously stated, one line runs transversely from south to north, and a second line on the back runs from east to west. Between these two lines are the enclosures (*kakṣyā*), which are the various locations; these have been conceived through their respective divisions. As for the word "of that" (*tasya*): [it refers to the aforementioned].
Regarding "of the maṇḍala": "seated upon a lotus" means that a lotus should be fashioned in the center. Regarding "at the beginning": by this [it is meant] at the initial location. (p.
In the southwest, one should establish the Rākṣasas and the Bhūtas;
in the west, the oceans and Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures.
Likewise, one should establish the seven winds in the northwestern direction;
right there, Garuḍa should also be established along with the birds.
Likewise, one should place the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) in the northern direction,
as well as the Mothers of Dance, the Yakṣas, and the Guhyakas.

In the same manner, one should station the lords of the Gaṇas, such as Nandin and others, as well as the hosts of Brahman-sages and spirits, in the north-eastern direction according to their respective portions.
On the pillar, however, one should place Sanatkumāra on the south, and Dakṣa likewise.
One should install the village headman at the northern pillar for the purpose of worship. || 32 ||
By this very procedure, according to the proper place and according to the rule,
one should install all the deities who are well-disposed.
Having duly installed the deities in their respective places,
one should then perform their worship according to what is appropriate for each.

In the northeast corner; and because the invocation was stated in the same manner during the first occasion, the phrase "seated upon a lotus" (padmopaviṣṭam) is to be connected with each direction. By that, it is said to be a mandala of nine lotuses.
White garlands and unguents should be given to the deities; red garlands and unguents to the Gandharvas, Agni, and Sūrya. (35)
Having offered perfume, garlands, and incense in due order and according to the rules, one should then perform the bali offering and worship according to the prescribed ritual.
One should worship Brahmā with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and Sarasvatī with milk-rice (pāyasa); then Śiva, Viṣṇu, Mahendra, and the other deities are to be worshipped with sweetmeats (modaka).
Agni, the consumer of oblations, is [satisfied] with rice cooked in ghee; Soma and Arka with rice mixed with jaggery; the Viśvedevas along with the Gandharvas and the sages with honeyed milk-rice.
Having worshipped Yama and Mitra with parched grain and sweetmeats,
one should satisfy the ancestors, the piśācas, and the serpents with clarified butter and milk.
One should worship the hosts of spirits with cooked rice, meat, wine, rum, and fruit liquors, as well as with chickpeas soaked in minced meat.
By this very procedure, Mattavāraṇī is to be worshipped;
the hosts of Rākṣasas are to be worshipped with raw and cooked meat.
One who knows the proper rites should honor the Dānavas with offerings of liquor and meat; he should honor the remaining hosts of gods with cakes, fried pastries, and cooked rice.

"In the southeast" means the *āgneya* pillar; "in the northeast" means the *aiśāna* pillar—this is the meaning. "Well-established" means they have been installed through meditative visualization (*dhyāna*). "According to what is appropriate" means according to the sequence of whatever ritual procedure for a particular deity is seen in their respective scriptures. (22–34)
Having honored the oceans and the rivers with offerings of fish and flour-based foods, one should also worship Varuṇa and give gifts of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa). (43)
He should also honor the sages with various roots and fruits,
as well as the winds and the birds with diverse kinds of food and edibles.
One should worship all those Mothers of the dance, as well as Dhanada along with his followers, with cakes mixed with parched grain and various kinds of foods and edibles.
In this manner, their bali offering should be performed, consisting of various kinds of food;
furthermore, the ritual of the bali offering shall be described again according to the rules of the mantra.
O God of gods, O highly fortunate one, O Grandfather of all the worlds,
please accept this entire offering from me, purified by mantras.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Gaṇeśa, Destroyer of Tripura!
O Lord, please accept this oblation (bali) offered by me, purified by mantras.
O Nārāyaṇa of immeasurable gait, O Padmanābha, best of gods!
O Lord, please accept this Bali, purified by mantras and offered by me. (49)
O Purandara, Lord of the Immortals, wielder of the thunderbolt, performer of a hundred sacrifices!
O God, let Bali be seized, preceded by the prescribed rites and mantras.
O Skanda, General of the Divine Army, Blessed One, beloved of Śaṅkara!
O Six-faced One, may this offering be accepted with a gracious mind. (51)
(“O Mahādeva, O Great Yogin, God of gods, Supreme among Suras! O Lord,
having accepted this offering, protect [us] from obstacles that arise at all times.”)
O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O Sarasvatī, beloved of Hari!
Accept this bali offering, O Mother, which has been presented by me with devotion. (52)
All the descendants of Pulastya, the lords of the Rākṣasas of great power, who have arisen from various signs, accept this offering from me. (53)
May Lakṣmī, Siddhi, Mati, Medhā, and all those goddesses who are honored by all the worlds, accept this oblation of mine, purified by mantras. (54)
O Knower of the power of all beings, O Life of the World, O Wind-god! O Lord, please accept this offering, purified by mantras, which has been prepared and presented by me.
O God-faced one, best of deities, smoke-bannered consumer of oblations!
O Lord, Bali is now prepared with devotion; please accept this offering. (56)
O Sun, most excellent among all planetary deities, mass of splendor!
O Lord, this offering is now presented by me with devotion; please accept it. (57)
O Soma, lord of all grahas, king of the twice-born, beloved of the world!
Accept this offering of mine, purified by mantras and now presented. (58)
All the great lords of the Gaṇas, led by Nandīśvara, were addressed: "Let Bali be accepted with devotion; I have now commanded it. (59)
Salutation to all the ancestors; may they accept this offering.
And salutation eternally to the spirits to whom this offering is dear.
O Kāmapāla, homage to you eternally, for whom this ritual has been performed.
May Nārada, Tumburu, and all the Gandharvas led by Viśvāvasu accept this offering presented by me. (61)
Yama and the blessed Lord Mitra, the two lords worshipped by the world,
may they accept this offering of mine accompanied by sacred mantras.
And salutations again and again to the serpents who have gone to the subterranean realm;
may they, being honored and destroyers of evil, grant success in the art of dance.
May the god Varuṇa, the lord of all waters, whose vehicle is a swan, being worshipped, be pleased along with the oceans, rivers, and streams.
O Vainateya, O great being, O Lord of all birds, O All-pervading One!
O God, let Bali, purified by mantras and offered by me, be accepted.
May the Lord of Wealth, the Master of Yakṣas, the Guardian of the World, the Sovereign of Riches—
along with the Guhyakas and the Yakṣas— accept my offering.
Salutation be to the Mothers of Dance, to Brāhmī and the others; salutations again and again! O fair-faced and gracious ones, may this offering be accepted today.
May Rudra accept all my offerings,
as well as the weapon of Viṣṇu which has been raised by me with devotion to Viṣṇu.
Likewise, let Kṛtānta and Kāla, the lords over the slaughter of all living beings, as well as Mṛtyu and Niyati, accept my offering. (69)
And whatever local deities reside within this intoxicated female elephant enclosure,
may they properly accept this my offering, purified by mantras. (70)
To the other gods and gandharvas who dwell throughout the ten directions—those of heaven, the atmosphere, and the earth—to them this offering is made. (71)
One should place a jar filled with water and adorned with a garland of flowers in the center of the arena, and one should cause gold to be offered there.
Having covered all the musical instruments with cloths,
one should worship them with perfumes, garlands, incense, and various kinds of food, both solid and soft.
Having thus worshipped all the deities in their proper order, one should proceed.
But one who is worn out by old age should be honored; therefore, he is worn out by obstacles.
On the head there should be a white cloth on the Raudra festival,
a blue one on the Viṣṇu festival, and a red one on the Skanda festival.
On the Mṛḍaparvan day, one seeking welfare should give a variegated garment;
likewise, incense, garlands, and ointments of similar quality should be offered.
One should cover all musical instruments with cloths and worship them with perfumes, garlands, incense, and various kinds of food and edibles.
Having performed this entire rite with perfumes, garlands,
and ointments, one should consecrate the *jarjara* (the ritual effigy) for the purpose of crushing obstacles.

Garlands and ointments; the meaning is that in both cases the offering consists primarily of liquor and the like. Here, the ritual application of the pitcher (*kumbha*) which has been worshipped and established will take place.
In this matter, for the sake of destroying obstacles, you were created by the gods headed by Pitāmaha—possessing great heroism, the essence of a diamond, and a massive body. (78)
May Brahmā, together with all the hosts of gods, protect your head;
may Hara protect the second joint, and Janārdana the third. (79)
May your fourth [son] and the fifth, the best of serpents, protect you always; and for the sake of the gods, may you become Śiva.
O destroyer of enemies, you were indeed born under the constellation Abhijit;
therefore, bring about both victory and prosperity for the king. (81)
Having thus worshipped the jarjara and offered all the sacrificial oblations (bali),
one should then perform the fire-offering (homa) preceded by mantra-invocations.
With flames from lamps and torches, one should perform the purification of the sacrificial fire itself, as well as the king and the dancers, thereby increasing their radiance. (83)
Having illuminated the king and likewise the dancers with musical instruments,
and having sprinkled them again with water purified by mantras, he should speak to them as follows.
"You are born into a noble family and are adorned with a multitude of virtues;
may that which is endowed with the qualities of your birth be yours forever. (85)
Having thus spoken these words for the welfare of the king, the wise one should then offer benedictions for the sake of attaining success in the application of dance.
May Sarasvatī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Hrī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Smṛti, and Mati—the gentle Mothers—protect you and grant you success. (87)
Having performed the fire oblation (homa) according to the rule, preceded by the offering and the mantra,
the dance master (nāṭyācārya) should then break the jar with great care. (88)
If the pot remains unbroken, there will be fear for the master from his enemies;
but if it is broken, the destruction of the master's enemies should be known to occur. || 89 ||
Then, once the jar has been broken, the dance master should diligently take up a blazing lamp and illuminate the entire stage.
With roars, bursts, leaps, and sprints, one should employ that blazing and noisy [performance] in the center of the arena. || 91 ||
One should cause battles to be enacted on the stage with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, as well as mṛdaṅgas and paṇavas, and all musical instruments resounding together.
In that regard, being cut, split, torn, and covered in blood;
being wounded, ablaze, or distressed—these are the signs of success.
A theater properly consecrated indeed brings prosperity to the master, as well as to the city, including its children and the elderly, and likewise to the countryside. 94.
Furthermore, if the stage is ill-constructed or poorly presided over by the deities, it will cause the destruction of the drama and bring misfortune upon the king. (95)
*Āhuti* is the act of offering (*āhavana*). Having offered the oblation, it is likewise a true *āhuti*. [With] "blazing... [he speaks].
He states the application of the jar: "one should break," etc.
Whoever abandons this rule and acts according to his own whims will quickly suffer decline and go to the womb of an animal. || 96 ||
For this worship of the deities of the arena is equal to a sacrifice;
indeed, one should not engage in a performance without having first worshipped the arena.
When honored, these [deities] honor in return; when respected, they show respect.
Therefore, with every effort, the worship of the stage (raṅga-pūjana) must be performed. 98.
Fire, even when fanned by a strong wind, does not burn as intensely as a wrongly applied practice burns in an instant when it is put into effect. (99)
The worship of the stage (raṅgapūjana) must be performed by a drama teacher who is learned in the treatises, disciplined, pure, initiated, and tranquil. (100)
But he who, with an anxious mind, offers the bali-oblation at a displaced location,
being like a priest devoid of mantra, must perform an expiation.
Thus, this procedure which has been observed for the worship of the deities of the stage should be performed by practitioners in a new theater as well as during a performance. (102)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Worship of the Deities of the Stage," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.

The phrase "with an agitated mind" indicates a state of lack of concentration. In the expression "in the new theater," it is stated that [the term] is merely a part of the word *maṇḍapa*. Regarding the phrase "and in the performance" (*prekṣāyām*), some connect it with "new" (*navāyām*);
by this, they mean that worship should be performed. Others, however, say that worship must be performed at all times at the commencement of the performance.
May there be auspiciousness. (35-102) ||
Thus, applying the third chapter to the locations of the knots,
I, Abhinavagupta, through my intellect, am nourished by the reality of the essence of Śiva.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Worship of the Deities of the Stage," in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Bhāratīyanāṭyaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Abhinavagupta.
p. 84) Śrīḥ! Now begins the fourth chapter.
Having performed worship in this manner, I spoke to the Grandfather: "Command me, O Lord; which brahminical rite should be employed?"
"He who constantly reveals this universe through his own playful manifestations—he is Śambhu in the form of the Wind, the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain King.
Thus [it is said]. This is stated with the intention expressed in the first chapter; for it is as follows:
"All those who have gone to the world of mortals shall receive auspicious worship.
Thus, worship is an indispensable duty. And therein—worship of the stage. And therein—
"Perform the worship of the stage"—thus he urged me.
Or rather, this was said "in accordance with such words. (The word "by me") means "by one who has been commanded by Śiva. In the middle, however—

Alternatively: "Whatever rites and whatever worship are prescribed therein, how should a man perform them in a theater? (2-2).
