Thus, in response to the sage’s question regarding how the worship was performed, this [section] follows as a contextual elaboration on the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) as far as they are applicable.

[This is] the *pūraka* [section]: because it is impossible for all the procedures—such as the divine theater, the distribution of food, and the raising of the plow—to occur with the totality of their essential nature. This [section], however, must be performed within the first chapter.
Regarding the word "quickly": by this it is stated that one should not delay after the worship with the performance.

"Prayoga" means that which is performed; it is one of the ten types of dramatic forms (*daśarūpaka*). Although it was stated that the prologue (*prastāvanā*) is composed of the *sampheṭa* and *vidrava* (1.58), nevertheless, because the performance was obstructed by obstacles, once the pacification of those obstacles and the worship of the presiding deities were performed in the theater (*nāṭyamaṇḍapa*), this final [act] constitutes the actual commencement.
The question was indeed appropriate;
85) thereupon I was told by the Blessed One: "Engage in the churning for the nectar."
This generates enthusiasm and likewise brings delight to the gods.
O learned one, this *samavakāra* which I previously composed— which accomplishes the goals of dharma, kāma, and artha— let its performance be enacted.
When that *samavakāra* was performed, all the gods and demons became joyful upon witnessing the unfolding of the action.

"What performance should be employed? To this he replies with two verses, beginning with "Then, [saying] 'I am... and "Employ... The meaning is: by means of training him in the re-examination of that performance for his own sons, who are like actors. [He is] the one who taught me the means for attaining dharma, kāma, and artha.

This performance, titled *Amṛtamanthana*, which is a type of drama (*rūpaka*) known as a *samavakāra*, has been composed by you within the very process of creating the *Daśarūpaka*—a work that is inseparable from the creation of the science of dramaturgy (*nāṭyaveda*). Furthermore, through this rehearsal, you have rendered it fit for direct perception and capable of being fully realized. It is that [performance].
The connection [between the verses] in the two verses beginning with "O learned one, let it be employed" is as follows:

the word *tu* (but/then) indicates a reason; because this [work] generates enthusiasm, consisting of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) which arises from the enthusiasm of the four types of heroes as their underlying stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). The word *tathā* (thus) refers to that.
In this manner, it produces for all the gods a pleasure characterized by relishing (*carvaṇā*), which takes the form of aesthetic savoring (*rasanā*).

The compound [“*utsāhajanana*”] means that of which enthusiasm is the producer. And by that mode of pleasure, there is the production of enthusiasm regarding the means to attain the three aims of life (*trivarga*). By this, both the dramatic (*dṛśya*) and the literary (*śravya*) [poetry] are implied.
It should also be composed here with the intention of conveying the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), as well as with the intention of slightly revealing the [underlying] words.
That in which the subject matter (*artha*) is "evenly scattered" (*samavakīryate*) is the *samavakāra*. And its essential characteristics (*saṅgati*) are:
it is based on the seeds of the gods and the asuras, and its hero is famous and noble. (18.63)

By this, [the fault of] *darśitatā* (being shown) is indicated; and by the rule "an *aṅka* should be made for another purpose" (18.69), [the fault of] *avakīrṇatā* (intermixture) is also indicated. Furthermore, this performance—because it abounds in pleasure—is for those who are prone to agitation regarding a subject of a single flavor, and who fear the effort required for a continuous connection [of plot], being like gods (*devatulya*).

By means of indicating grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two words of different genders in the phrase "the churning of nectar is a *samavakāra*," he states that [the object] is the domain of identification (*adhyavasāna*), which involves a two-step mediation through the conceptualization of direct perception—that "this very thing is that. Precisely for that reason... (Note: The ellipsis indicates a portion of the original text where the specific conclusion or further explanation is omitted.)
Poets refer to the two plays as *Vikramorvaśīya* and *Svapnavāsavadatta*. (1–4) p.
86) Then, after some time, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] said to me:
Today we shall present a dramatic performance for the sake of the great-souled Three-eyed One.
Then, having gone together with the gods to the abode of the bull-bannered one and having worshipped Śiva, the Grandfather (Brahmā) subsequently spoke this: || 6 ||
O best of gods, you ought to grant your favor regarding this Samavakāra which has been composed by me, both in its hearing and its sight.
"Let us see," the Lord of Gods said to Druhiṇa.
Then the Blessed One said to me: "Be ready, O high-minded one. (8)
Then, on the slopes of the Himalayas, which were crowded with various mountains,
filled with many hosts of beings, and possessed of delightful caves and waterfalls— (9)
O best of the twice-born, the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) was performed there first;
likewise, the burning of Tripura, known as a *ḍima*, was then enacted.

Thus, seeing the conclusion of the historical narrative, he now connects this [verse] as an introduction to the performance of dance (*nṛtta*), which is the very life-force of all dramatic practice and the quintessence of the Kaiśikī style: "Of a certain... This refers to the duration of time required for instruction to be completed.

"By that much time having passed" means by that cause. By this, he shows that the performance of the drama should first be presented to one who knows it. Therefore, the explanation that the performance was shown to Brahmā by the power of that [time] is indeed incorrect; nor would one endeavor to present a subject matter already experienced to the Blessed One.

Otherwise, it would be inconsistent. Furthermore, by the phrase "we shall show," the poet’s own entry into the midst of that [scene] is indicated, which would suggest his role as an *utprekṣaka* (imaginative observer); enough of this.
By the word "mahātman" (great-souled one), he states that there is perfect propriety in his being the one who observes here. Regarding both hearing and seeing:

And thus he reflects. Likewise, it was stated by the word "causing to hear" (*śrāvayitavya*) that previously the investigator (*parīkṣaka*) should be made to hear by the poet (*kavi*). However, that the audience (*sāmājika*) should be made to hear is not particularly appropriate, because their engagement [in the investigation] would be impossible at that stage; and because if the goal were accomplished through mere hearing, the performance (*prayoga*) would be rendered futile. [This applies] to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

Because they are critics and because they are to be gratified, [the poet] offers them a great enjoyment consisting of the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through his superior knowledge. (5–9) p.
Then the hosts of spirits were delighted by the proclamation of their past deeds,
and Mahādeva, being well-pleased, spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
"O high-minded one, this drama has been perfectly created by you;
it brings fame, leads to auspiciousness, is meritorious, and increases the intellect. (12)
I too have remembered this dance, performed by me during the periods of twilight,
adorned with various *aṅgahāras* joined with diverse *karaṇas*.
In this context, he demonstrates that the sequence of performance is preceded by the *pūrvaraṅga* with the words beginning "the *pūrvaraṅga*," and so forth.

"This" refers to the *samavakāra*. It is also a *ḍima*, which primarily concerns the deeds of the Supreme Lord and is characterized by its connection to the burning of Tripura. By the word "performed" (*prayukta*), [it is indicated] that it was enacted by performers for the sake of pleasing the critics (*parīkṣaka*).

He states that something is to be employed; he makes manifest the satisfaction resulting from the fruit—saying "by me also this"—and by this he means the following: first, the sage Bharata, having observed the Bhagavat’s *nṛttakaiśikī*, composed something for the purpose of its performance.
Because there was no proper instruction regarding those two, they are not very well-integrated; for this very reason, he will say "properly" (samyak).

By using the word "remembered" (smṛtam), he shows that this [tradition] is beginningless. By the use of the plural number, he indicates its status as an object of reverence. Only the *aṅgahāra* produces the fruit of performance, which is dance (*nṛtta*); its constituent parts, however, are the *karaṇas* and so forth.

With the intention that there are thirty-two principal movements in the art of dance, he states the application of the qualifiers with the word "various" (*nānā*). He defines its specific function with the phrase "in the performance of the *pūrvaraṅga*. On the stage (*raṅga*), which is the locus of action, that initial *raṅga* (preliminary rite) which was performed by you as pure—that is, devoid of variety—is [now] performed by this [dance].
The variety mixed with dance is called *citra*. According to the sage Bharata, in its performance,

the ten dramatic elements (*daśāṅga*)— beginning with *pratyāhāra* and ending with *prarocanā*, including the nine female roles (*aṅganavaka*) occurring within the *yavanikā* (curtain)— are devoid of dance.
That which is employed merely as something to be done, yet not actually performed— such as the ten ornaments (aṅgadaśaka) that were intended for use—

is beneficial both in its visible and invisible aspects, possessing at least some degree of aesthetic charm (*rañjakatva*) therein. However, the intention here is that this [ornamentation], being mixed and variegated, properly bestows a fruit consisting of both visible and invisible results.

Regarding the great sentence (*mahāvākya*): "In this" means in the performance of the exalted preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) appropriate for the application you wish to employ. These gestures (*karaṇas*) and limb-movements (*aṅgahāras*) are employed therein; however, in a delicate preliminary rite, those performed by the Goddess (*Devī*) are not exalted.
(Regarding the *aṅgahāras*, p.
88: These must be correctly employed by you in this performance of the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*).
In the *vardhamānaka* compositions, in the songs, and in the *āsārita* melodies.
And you shall correctly represent the meanings within the great songs;
furthermore, this introductory ceremony (pūrvaraṅga) which has been performed by you is perfectly pure.
"And this [tantra], being mixed with these, shall be known as Citra.
Having heard the words of Maheśvara, Svayambhū replied: || 16 ||
"O best of gods, tell me of the application of the *aṅgahāras*.
Then the Lord of the World, having summoned Taṇḍu, spoke to him. (17)
"Tell Bharata indeed about the application of the *aṅgahāras*, as well as those *aṅgahāras* which were proclaimed by the high-souled Taṇḍu. (18)
I shall explain to you those [gestures] joined with the organs of action along with the exhalation (sarecaka);
they are known as Sthirahasta, Aṅgahāra, and likewise Paryastaka. || 19 ||

With this intention: "And as for the *Mahāgīta*, which is the beginningless form consisting of *bhītakas* and *vardhamānas*, you shall be able to represent its meaning through the proper sequence of *vardhamāna* and so forth, by employing the methods of *aṅgahāras* and *piṇḍībandhas* as appropriate; explain it."

Regarding the words "to Bharata": by this, the sage, considering himself a recipient of the Supreme Lord's grace, highly esteems himself, thinking: "The Lord has directed this very to me, saying, 'You shall be able to represent it [the drama] when directed by you'; yet he did not say so in the presence of the Chief [Sage]."

With the intention that a reply should be given, he shows that after hearing the words of Maheśvara, Svayambhū replied, saying "Having summoned Taṇḍu. In every reading, the word *taṇḍu* alone is appropriate, because of the observed etymological derivation of the word *tāṇḍava*. The words *taṇḍu* and *muni* are alternative names for those two.
Regarding the word "ya" (those): the Sage says this to Ātreya and the others—"the *karaṇas* along with the *sārecakas*.

Because they function as qualifiers, the *aṅgahāras* alone possess primacy; for that very reason, they are mentioned first. This is because they are the means (*upāya*). Among them, the definition of the *karaṇas* comes first.
Because they consist of an accumulation of those [atoms], (10-19) p.
"Just as one pierced by a needle, so too is one cast away."
Then the "thrown" (ākṣiptaka) is to be known, as well as the "struck" (udghaṭṭita), so it is remembered. || 20 ||
Viṣkambha is indeed proclaimed, as well as Aparājita;
Viṣkambhāpasṛta and likewise Mattākrīḍa. || 21 ||
The Svastika, the Recita, and the Pārśvasvastika;
the Vṛścikāpasṛta is proclaimed, and likewise another, the Bhramara. || 22 ||

The *mattaskhalitaka* (the stumbling gait of intoxication), the *madavilasita* (the playful gait of intoxication), the *gatimaṇḍalaka* (the circular gait), and likewise the *paricchinna* (the circumscribed gait) are to be known. || 23 ||
Then there may be the *parivṛttacita*, as well as the *vaiśākharecita*; furthermore, the *parāvṛtta* and the *alātaka* are to be understood in the same way. || 24 ||
Then the *pārśvaccheda* (side-cut) is proclaimed, as well as the *vidyudbhrānta* (lightning-twirl);
likewise there is the *ūrūdvṛtta* (thigh-rotation), and similarly the *ālīḍha* (left-leg-straddling). || 25 ||
Recita should also be understood as such, and likewise Acchurita is recorded;
furthermore, Ākṣiptarecita, and another called Sambhrānta. || 26 ||
Regarding that, he states the enumeration of the *aṅgahāras* with the passage beginning "sthirahasta" and ending with "these thirty-two.

The meaning is as follows: when the one hundred and eight *karaṇas* are known, through the application of the sixty-four *karaṇas*, there arises an uninterrupted movement of the limbs (*aṅgagati*)—that is, the manner of limb-movement.

Although the *aṅgahāras* are infinite, thirty-two have been specified by name because they are predominant due to their greater involvement in producing visible results; however, this is not an exhaustive enumeration.
An *aṅgahāra* is the manner of moving the limbs to reach a suitable location. And this belongs to Hara.
*Hāra* is a *prayoga*. A *hāra* that is accomplished through the *aṅgas* is an *aṅgahāra*. As he will say: "This [work] which is the life-story of Maheśvara" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.330).
The *apasarpa* and likewise the *ardhanikuṭṭaka* are to be known;
these thirty-two are proclaimed by name as the *aṅgahāras*. || 27 ||
I shall now explain their application based on the instruments, as well as how the movement of the hands and feet should be employed by practitioners. (28)
O twice-born ones, I shall indeed describe [the movements] in the *aṅgahāras* and in the *karaṇas*,
because the accomplishment of all *aṅgahāras* depends upon the *karaṇas*.
I shall now describe those [elements] by name as well as by their function:
the coordination of hands and feet constitutes the *karaṇa* of dance. (30)

Anticipating the objection that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of these [faculties] mentioned therein must be stated, he says: "But of these," and so forth. They can indeed be characterized only when the instruments (*karaṇa*) have been mentioned. Now, one might ask: will the mere sequential recitation of the instruments constitute their definition? No; he says: "the movement of the hands and feet," and so on.

Regarding the application of *aṅgahāras* that must be performed, I shall also describe the method of joining the limbs— such as the hands and feet— during the transition from one *karaṇa* to another *karaṇa* within that context; however, due to the word "ca" (and), I shall not describe it in certain instances.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating the *ūha* (adaptation). The word "vai" (*vai-śabda*) indicates the application of traditional authority (*āgama*). Regarding that which is to be stated concerning *aṅgahāras*, he asks what must first be defined and says: "of all" (*sarveṣām*). This refers to them by name as a mere enumeration (*uddeśa*), and not by way of definition (*lakṣaṇa*). In that regard, the general definition of both the *karaṇas* and the *aṅgahāras* [is as follows]:
He states [the means] for performing [this] with the words beginning "hand, foot," and so forth. *Kriyā* means action. Action of what? Of dance (*nṛtta*).

It is the action of the limbs—characterized by the hands—which consists of graceful movements. The meaning is that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that action which is distinct from actions directed toward objects to be rejected or accepted, and so on. Regarding the term *nṛtyasya*: the genitive case is used according to the principle of "treating as if it were the principal" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).
He states the essential nature of that action as "the conjunction of hands and feet"— that is,

the joining of the various primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅga) located in the anterior part of the body, characterized by the hands, with those located in the posterior part of the body, characterized by the feet, such as the sides, hips, thighs, shanks, and feet.

The meaning is that when there is an application of activity characterized by continuity and non-interruption, a single action consists in the performance of that [activity] until the attainment of another suitable location through the relinquishing of the connection with the previous location;
for in all cases, action terminates in a subsequent conjunction, and that [conjunction] is the desired subsequent conjunction.
There are two dance-movements (*nṛttakaraṇa*) that constitute the matrix of dance (*nṛttamātṛkā*). However, a full dance-step (*aṅgahāra*) consists of two, three, or four such matrices. (31)
With three [verses] there is a *kalāpaka*, and with four it becomes a *ṣaṇḍaka*;
with five there are the *karaṇas*, which is known as the *saṅghātaka*.
Aṅgahāras are proclaimed here as being joined with six, seven, eight, or likewise nine karaṇas. (33)

Since this is well-known in the world as having action as its limit, it is nothing new. The only thing additional here is what is called "possessing grace" (*savilāsatva*) through the entry of beauty. For this very reason, there is the qualification by the word *nṛtta* [in the compound] *nṛttakaraṇa*. However, the use of the word *karaṇa* is intended to refer to a single part, as in the case of [the name] Bhīmasena.
It is like the word *bhīma*.

Thus far, the general definition of a *karaṇa* has been given. Now, in order to compose the specific definition of an *aṅgahāra*, he provides the introductory foundation, stating: "two dance-*karaṇas*" and "the matrix of dance."

The *mātṛkā* is the source of origin for *nṛtta*, which consists of *aṅgahāras*. By the qualification "by the word *nṛtta*" [in the verse beginning] "those *sthānas*... (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.59), he shows its distinction from those *karaṇa-mātṛkās* that will be described; and [he specifies that this occurs] "without the employment of two *karaṇas*," meaning by means of two, three, or four.

There is no conceit regarding the dance itself. Beyond that, however, because of the conceit that "one is dancing," the two instruments are said to be the *nṛttamātṛkā*. Through this [definition], there is a collection of neither too little nor too much.
This is established by the definition of the *nṛttamātṛkā* and by the general definition of the *aṅgahāra*.
He permits the application of that which is useful for the *piṇḍībandha* (the structural binding), following the interval between the *aṅgahāras* produced by the two *karaṇas*, saying:

"Of these... He shall describe the *karaṇa*, which is the arrangement of hands and feet, as being connected specifically to the *aṅgahāras*. The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*).

[Objection: Should not the definitions of *sthānaka*, *cārī*, and so forth have been stated previously? [Response: Not so; for these are already known to the Sage through his knowledge of *nāṭya* alone. The *nṛtta-hastas* as well, being essentially *vartanā*, are indeed already known to him, since it has been stated: "this is *nṛtta*" (*idaṃ nṛttam*). Therefore, within the *āṅgika* [abhinaya]... (*Nāṭya-śāstra* 10).
Their [the hands and feet] will be described. However, it must be stated that they are indeed the instruments (*karaṇa*)... (they are what must be expressed here). (28, p.
92) Of these very [instruments], I shall explain the differentiation of hands and feet.
First, the palm-flower-folded [garment] is prepared, and the thighs are wrapped.
The *apaviddha*, the *samanakha*, the *līna*, the *svastikarecita*, the *maṇḍalasvastika*, and also the *nikuṭṭaka*. (35)
Likewise, the *ardhanikuṭṭa* and the *kaṭicchinna*, as well as the *ardharecitaka* and the *vakṣaḥsvastika*. (36)
The Unmatta, the Svastika, the Pṛṣṭhasvastika, the Diksvastika, the Alāta, and likewise the Kaṭīsama. (37)
Ākṣiptarecita, as well as Vikṣiptākṣiptaka;
Ardhasvastika has been taught, and likewise another, Añcita. || 38 ||
The *bhujaṅgatrāsita* has been described, as well as the *ūrdhvajānu*,
the *nikuñcita*, the *mattalli*, and indeed the *ardhamattalli*.
There may be the recakanikuṭṭa, as well as the pādāpaviddhaka;
likewise the valita, the ghūrṇita, and another, the lalita. (40)
Likewise, the *daṇḍapakṣa*, the *bhujaṅgatrasta-recita*, the *nūpura*, and the *vaiśākharecita* have been fully described. || 41 ||
The *bhramara*, the *catura*, the *bhujaṅgāñcita*, the *daṇḍarecitaka*, and likewise the *vṛścikakuṭṭita*. (42)
Likewise, the Kaṭibhrānta, the Latāvṛścika, the Chinnakaraṇa, and the Vṛścikarecita are declared to be Karaṇas. (43)

Regarding that, it was stated: "I shall explain them here according to their names and their functions. First, he speaks of them by name, beginning with "the cupped handful of flowers" (*talapuṣpapuṭa*), and so forth.
The scorpion, the striding, as well as the side-stamping, the forehead-mark, the traversing, the contracted, and the wheel-circle. (44)

The shoulder-circle (uromaṇḍala), the cast-off (ākṣipta), likewise the floor-play (talavilāsita), the bolt (argala), the scattered (vikṣipta), the turned-back (āvṛtta), and the swing-foot (dolapādaka). || 45 ||
The turned-back, the retreated, the side-step, the struck-down, the whirling lightning, the over-stepped, and the rolled-about; || 46 ||
The *gajakrīḍitaka* (elephant-play), likewise the *talasaṃsphoṭita* (slapping the palms), the *garuḍaplutaka* (Garuda-leap), and another called the *gaṇḍasūci* (cheek-needle). || 47 ||
The *parivṛtta*, the *samuddiṣṭa*, likewise the *pārśvajānu*, the *gṛdhrāvalīnaka*, the *sannata*, and also the *sūcī*. (48)
The *ardhasūcī* is declared as a *karaṇa*, as is the *sūcīviddha*;
likewise, the *apakrānta* and the *mayūralalita* have been proclaimed. (49)
The serpent-like, the staff-footed, and the deer-leap; the swaying, the hip-twist, the stumbling, and the elephant-trunk. (50)
The Prasarpitaka has been described, as well as the Siṃhavikrīḍita;
likewise the Siṃhākarṣita, the Udvṛtta, and the Upasṛta. || 51 ||
The *talasaṅghaṭṭita*, the *janita*, the *āvahitthaka*, the *niveśa*, the *melakākrīḍa*, and likewise the *urūdvṛtta*. (52)
The *madaskhalitaka*, the *viṣṇukrānta*, the *sambhrānta*, the *viṣkambha*, and also the *udghaṭṭita*. || 53 ||
The *vṛṣabhakrīḍita* (the bull’s play), the *lolita* (the swaying), and likewise another,
the *nāgāpasarpita* (the serpent’s glide), and similarly the *śakaṭāsya* (the cart-mouth). || 54 ||
Including the Gaṅgāvataraṇa, one hundred and eight have been mentioned;
indeed, these one hundred and eight instruments have been declared by me. (55)
In dance, combat, wrestling, as well as in the progression of movement and the execution of gaits,
I shall describe the various formations of martial movements.

In whatever [context] it may be applied, the teachers should employ it according to the requirements of the dramatic performance; generally, in the *karaṇa*, the left hand should be placed upon the chest.
The right hand should also follow the movement of the foot;
the movement of the hands and feet is joined with the hips, sides, and thighs. (58)
Understand that which is to be described concerning the chest, back, and abdomen, as well as the positions, the noble ones, and likewise the dance-hands. 59.

Anticipating the objection— "Since it has been stated that the limit is one hundred and eight [gestures], and since they are fixed as being applicable to the deployment of the *aṅgas* (limbs) with their respective disappearances (*pratyastamaya*), what is the purpose of this determination of number?"—
he says, beginning with "one hundred and eight," etc. [He explains] that dance which, in the context of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), functions as the actual substance.

It will be stated [later] that it is employed for covering the gaps occurring between different gestures (*abhinaya*), and so forth; likewise in dance, combat with weapons, and wrestling, as well as in the practice of various gaits. It is also employed for the sake of the excellence of limb-movement (*aṅgaprayoga*) in combat with weapons and the like, as well as in hand-to-hand fighting. [This is taught] separately in the chapter on Gait (*gatyadhyāya*). (Nāṭyaśāstra)

Furthermore, regarding the circumambulations (*parikrama*) that occur in the destinations (*gati*) to be described hereafter, their distinctness—due to the observation of separate ritual applications (*prayoga*) therein—is not irrelevant to the fact that there are one hundred and eight of them. We shall explain immediately below how this application (*viniyoga*) will occur. In this context, [the phrase] "one hundred and eight," and so forth...
Some do not recite this verse; others [recite] even more than that:
"The movement of the hands and feet, together with the hips, sides, and thighs."
Thus they recite this verse (34-58): "That should be known as the *mātṛkā*; through union with it, the instrument (*karaṇa*) comes into being. (p. 95)
Wherein the hips are level with the ears, as are the elbows, shoulders, and head. || 60 ||
With the chest well-elevated, that is indeed called *sauṣṭhava*;
with a cluster of flowers at the left side, the foot moves with its sole facing forward. || 61 ||

In this regard, he states the instrument (*karaṇa*) in its form as a great universal (*mahāsāmānya*): "Those which are the positions" (*sthānāni*). Here, the instrument is that which accomplishes two things: remaining stationary (*avasthāna*) and movement (*gati*). Among these, for remaining stationary, the *sthānaka* (standing postures) are employed; for movement, however, they are the *cārīs* (walking postures). Furthermore, for movement in the front part of the body, there are the *nṛttahastas* (dancing hand gestures) and glances (*dṛṣṭis*); for remaining stationary, there are the *patākā* and other [hand gestures].

This is subsumed by the word "ca" (and). Therefore, although there is an infinity of instruments (*karaṇa*) because movement and stillness are combined, nevertheless, this much alone has been stated because of its utility for the *aṅgahāra* [gestures]; such is the purport of the verse.
(1) *Talapuṣpapuṭa*. Regarding this, he states the characteristics according to the order of enumeration, beginning with "on the left" (*vāme*) and so forth:
"That which is called 'serpent-headed' (*sarpaśiras*) has its fingers placed without any interval."

The second [hand] is the *puṣpapuṭa*, which is placed alongside the side. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.150) In the movement of the foot on its forepart (*agratalasañcara*), the heel should be raised, the thumb extended, and all the fingers bent. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.273)
"The waist becomes bent, and the side likewise is bent;
similarly, the shoulder is drawn back, and the side is known to be slightly inclined. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.235).
The application of these [characteristics] is now described.
In that dance (*nṛtta*), it begins with both feet flat on the ground and the two hands first [extended], abounding everywhere like a creeper (*tā-latā*).

Thus the construction here is as follows: the *cārī* (step) has been executed by means of the action of unwinding (*udveṣṭita*), simultaneous with the throwing out of both arms; then, simultaneously with the action of winding (*apaveṣṭita*), having formed a *sūcī* (needle-step) with the second foot, one likewise forms a *svastika* with both feet and both hands.

"One should perform [it]" means: when there is a *svastika* on the back—that is, on the rear—and likewise a *svastika* on the right side with the left foot, and having turned away by means of the three-fold twisting (*trikavalanā*), it is called *pṛṣṭhasvastika*. Its application is precisely in the context already mentioned. Others, however, [apply] both hands to the region of the back.
Those desiring the *svastika* [mudrā] state that its application is used in the movement (*parikrama*) within the context of combat. (76) (17) *Dik-svastika*:
When that very *karaṇa* called *svastika*, which was previously described by the verse beginning with "with both hands... (*hastābhyām atha...*), is employed—
By means of the syllable *ca*, [the limbs] are placed at the sides, the front, and the back, facing the four directions with unbroken body;
for this very reason, it is called "body-joined" (*aṅgaśliṣṭa*). At that time, it is the "directional svastika" (*diksvastika*).
By specifying this in the center, he authorizes such an application for all the ritual procedures (*karaṇas*). And its application occurs during the transitions (*parivartas*) of the song.
As he will say: "When, under the influence of song, the body turns again and again" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.306), and so forth.
(77) (18) *Alāta* (the fire-brand).
When the foot is extended behind and covered by the bent [other] leg, with the heel falling toward the side, that is proclaimed as the *alātā* (firebrand) posture. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.41, p.
The *pārśvamudvāhita* is a *karaṇa* in which the hips are level;
the left hand should be at the heart, while the right is thrown out and extended (*akṣiptarecita*). || 80 ||
One should cause it to emerge from the shoulder; and one forms that *nṛttahasta* (or *nitambahasta*) with the right [hand]. That is—
"Having lifted the contracted foot, one should place it level with the knee or the breast; the second step is likewise raised above—this is proclaimed as *ūrdhvajānu*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.33).
Furthermore, from the placement of the *cārī*, the feet also receive designations such as *alātā* and so forth; this applies everywhere in the same manner.

"The two hips (*nitamba*) are said to emerge from the *bāhuśīrṣa*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 8.196). The application (*yojanā*) is as follows: while performing the *alātā* step with the right foot, one should form the hip with the right hand and execute a square (*caturaśra*) movement; then, with the left foot, one should perform the *ūrdhvajānu* [step], and subsequently with the left limb as well.

Thus, these too are called *alātacārī* because they are performed twice; this is the name of the movement itself. Its application is in the context of graceful dancing (*lalitanṛtta*), as for example in [the phrase] "devaṃ haṃ uṇavaśamiṃ" and so forth. (78) (19) *Kaṭīsama*.

By the phrase "having withdrawn immediately after the *svastika*," the performance of the *ācaryā* (the movement) that was implied by that [withdrawal], as well as the *apakrāntā* (the receding) *ācaryā*, is indicated. By the word "and" (*ca*), the two hands are determined to be in the *svastika* position. Then, one hand is placed at the navel in the *khaṭaka* gesture; likewise the other.

An *ardhacandra* [gesture] is at the hip. That same [leg] is bent to one side while the other is extended by the second limb. Having lifted and drawn back a contracted foot, one should place it with the arch raised; joined with the *jaṅghā-svastika*, that is known as the *ākṣiptā*. (Nāṭya Śāstra 10.37)
When the ring finger and the little finger are raised up like a discus, this same *kapittha* [mudrā] is then called *khaṭakāmukha*.
That [mudrā] in which the fingers, together with the thumb, are bent like a bow... (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.61)
That is the *ardhacandra* (Nāṭya Śāstra 9.43).
It should be known that the chest is raised upward (*udvāhita*) (Nāṭya Śāstra 9.231), and the sides likewise are raised. And here, the Vaiṣṇava standing posture (*sthānaka*) is level with the hips.
It is obtained from the *tattva-bandha*. When it is both *recita* and *apaviddha*, that is *ākṣiptarecita*.
The scattered [movement] of the hands and feet, and again their throwing forward. || 81 ||
O twice-born ones, that instrument should be known as the *vikṣiptākṣiptaka*;
having placed the feet in the *svastika* position and making the right hand like an elephant's trunk (82).
The distance between the two feet should be two tālas and one half-tāla;
one [foot] should be positioned evenly, while the other is triangular and situated on the side.
"With the shanks slightly bent and the limbs held with grace—this is indeed the Vaiṣṇava posture, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity here. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.52–53).
This [posture] should be employed by the *sūtradhāra* at the time of consecrating the *jarjarā*. (79)
(20) *Ākṣiptarecita*:

In the field of the heart, whichever hand is the left or the right is cast out (*kṣipta*) all around—upward and on both sides—by means of the *vyāvartita* movement; it is then *recita*, consisting of a swift whirling like the wings of a swan. (Nāṭya Śāstra 9.12)

193) Then, one [foot] is drawn up (*ākṣipta*), brought down toward the region of one's own chest with the face turned downward, bent (*añcita*), extended (*recita*), and cast aside (*apaviddha*). Because it has been withdrawn from the field of the limbs, this is the *ākṣiptarecita* gesture (*karaṇa*).
Here, the two feet take the form of the *añcita* and *sūcī* according to the application.
This [term] is employed when the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) consisting of mutual rejection and acceptance (*tyāga-upādāna-paraspara*) is to be indicated.
For example: "Ho there! Cisuṇa, bring this... bring that... and so forth. (80) (21) *Vikṣiptākṣiptaka* (The Scattered and the Gathered).
At the time of performing the *vyāvartana* (turning away) with one hand, there is a displacement (*vikṣepa*) characterized by the outward stepping out of the foot;

meanwhile, the second hand remains square (*caturaśra*). Then, by means of the *parivartita* movement, the projection of that hand and foot constitutes the displacement of the second [hand]. Its application occurs when the meaning of the sentence primarily concerns going and returning.
Some say that [this applies] as in the examples "āvarta," "ujaṃta," "puṇaṃ," "raga," "idam," and so forth.

However, the teachers (upādhyāyas) say: the application of these *karaṇas*—which have as their primary focus those hand-gestures (*abhinaya-hasta*) that will be described later—is in the enactment of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and not in the case of those whose primary focus is merely the movement of the fingers (*vartanā*).
Or, for one whose primary focus is exclusively on the dance-hands (*nṛttahasta*),
one should likewise indicate the left half-svastika position at the location of the chest (p. 108).
But when that very same hand is turned away and then turned around, [it is called *vyāvṛttaparivṛtta*]. || 83 ||
When the nose-tip is bent, that is declared the añcita (bent) posture;
having lifted the foot, one should rotate the thigh into a triangular shape. || 84 ||
From the rotation of the hips and knees, the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* (the "terrified serpent") posture arises;
having lifted the bent foot, one should place the knee level with the breast. (85)

However, the application [of this] is primarily in dance (*nṛtta*); others, however, apply it occasionally for the preservation of the integrity of the limbs. Its application occurs as appropriate during the intervals between other modes of representation (*abhinaya*), in movement and pacing, in the joining of different tempos (*tāla*), in combat, wrestling, *cārī* movements, postures (*sthānaka*), or in general transition; and this should be followed in all cases.
(22) The Half-Svastika: When one *latāhasta* is raised and swayed from side to side,
while the other hand, a *tripatāka*, is placed at the ear, it is proclaimed as the *karihasta*.
When extended horizontally and positioned at the sides, they are called *latā*.
Some read this as *kaṭihasta*; the commentary on that explains it as the *ardhacandra* hand placed upon the hip.
The *pakṣapradyotaka*, *vañcitaka*, and the *khaṭakāsyaka* on the left [are also mentioned]. (Nāṭya Śāstra 9.61)
The *ardhasvastika* arises from the application of the *svastika* with the feet alone. This *karaṇa* is indeed devoid of the *abhinaya-hasta*.
(23) *Añcita*:
when that very same [hand] which was called the *karihasta* in the *ardhasvastika-karaṇa* is performed with the *vyāvartita* movement.

The *añcita* [gesture] is so called because it resembles the bending and stretching of the essence [of the eyebrow], shaped like a young sprout on the field of the nose. Its employment occurs when the meaning of the sentence is primarily characterized by an intense curiosity directed toward an object situated in front of oneself.
For example: *eva-uvemmakuhe-uko*. (83)
(109) It is proclaimed that the hands, under the influence of the *prayoga*, have the knees raised (*ūrdhvajānu*);
having placed the foot in the *vṛścika* posture, one should contract the hand against the side. || 86 ||
The right [hand] at the tip of the nose should be known as being slightly bent;
[this is performed] with the left and right feet moving in a circling approach.
The hands are offered with the *mattalli* gesture, both twisted and cast aside;
the feet are in the *skhalita* and *apasṛta* positions, and the left hand is in the *recita* position. (88)

(24) *Bhujaṅgatrāsita* (The Serpent-Frightened). Because dance is established as beginningless, this *karaṇa* is of the form described: it is the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* *karaṇa*, characterized by the contraction of movement like one possessed by the fear of a serpent seen nearby. As for the two hands:

The *vyāvartita* and *parivartita* [hand gestures] occur according to the feet. In sequence, one is the *dolāhasta* (Nāṭya Śāstra 9.148) and the other is the *khaṭakāsya*; this is the *karaṇa*. Due to its similarity to this, however, the *bhujaṅgatrāsitā* foot-step (Nāṭya Śāstra 10.42) will be described. In this manner, that which is named "equal to the *karaṇa*" should be stated for all foot-steps (*cārīs*). (84)

(25) *Ūrdhvajānu*: When the heel is raised and the toes are likewise contracted, and the middle part [of the foot] is also contracted, that foot is called *parikuñcita* (fully contracted). (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 9.277)

The *ūrdhvajānu* (upward-knee) position shall be as follows: at the same time that [the other leg] is bent, that very hand—with fingers like young shoots or curved—is placed facing upward upon the knee of the bent breast. In this case, however, the other hand is in the *khaṭakāmukha* (sword-pointing) position against the chest. (85)
(26) *Nikuñcita*:

That foot which is described in the *karaṇa* called *vṛścika* as "the foot with the back arched" (*pṛṣṭhāñcita*) (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.108) is here referred to by the word *vṛścika*. Having thus extended the foot backward, [one performs this posture].

One hand should be curved at the region of the head and side, while the second should follow the region of the tip of the nose and be curved at the chest. Others, however, say that one [hand] at the tip of the nose is *patāka* and the other is *sūcyāsya*.
And this occurs in the representation of the primary meaning of a sentence—such as a deliberation, a resolve, or the like—directed toward ascending into the sky;
for example, in the case of Hanumān: "Here I am, swiftly ascending the path of the sky; what delay is there? (p.
The left hand should rest on the hip; this is known as *ardhamattalli*.
The right hand is extended (*recita*) and the left foot is stamped down (*nikuṭṭita*). (89)

The swing (dolā) indeed occurs on the left; it is performed with the extended and the struck (recitanikuṭṭita). The hands, in the khaṭakāmukha position, should be placed facing forward upon the surface of the navel.
(27) Mattallī:
The *cārī* shall likewise be of this same form (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 10.28). It is characterized by the two feet as they approach [the ground] while reeling; and the reeling is—

The second foot performs the *gulpha-svastika-upasarpaṇa* (the swastika-like movement of the ankles while approaching). Simultaneously with that, the two hands perform the *nitamba-udveṣṭita* (the hip-whirling movement). At the time of that approach, the *apaviddha* and *upaveṣṭita* (the cast-off and the encircling) movements are performed.
Thus it is done with the second limb. The plural number indicates that this is repeated again and again.

It indicates the *kriyā* (action). It is called *mattalli* because it extends (*tanoti*) intoxication (*mada*); it is the instrument through the application of repetition for one whose passion is intense. There is a diversion within those three *mattallis*. Its employment concerns subjects such as *mattaśekhara* and others. (28) *Ardhamattalli*.

The *recita* with the swan-wing (*haṃsapakṣa*) movement is a rapid rotation; the *skhalita* (stumbling) is the second [movement], occurring six times at the waist, reaching near the foot. This application concerns the domain of youthful intoxication.
(88) (29) The *recita-nikuṭṭita*.
"Savya" here refers to the right foot itself. "Nikuṭṭita" means by the action of striking upward;
having stood with the tip of the forefoot, the heel is dropped to the ground—that is the *udghaṭṭita*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.248)
When those two flags (patākās), being loosened and released, hang down laxly in the performance (*karaṇa*),
that is designated as the *dolā* (swing).
Through its association with the feminine gender, the *dolā* refers to the swaying of the hand by means of its movement back and forth.
It indicates:
(89) p. 111) When the two feet have moved away after being pierced by a needle, it is the *pādāpaviddhaka* [gesture].
The hand would be cast off, and likewise the foot would become like a needle.
Likewise, that which is opened and turned is called *valita*;
in this [gesture], the right hand is rotated and whirled, while the left is swung.
When the foot is drawn back from the *svastika* position, that is the *ghūrṇita* (whirling) *karaṇa*;
the left hand should be in the *karihasta* position and the right hand *vivartita* (revolved). || 93 ||

(30) *Pādāpaviddhaka*: With the two feet turned away from the navel-region, one should pierce the second foot with the foot called *sūcī*; that same *sūcī* foot should then be performed in conjunction with the *apakrānta* movement. The same should be done for the second [foot] as well.
When the heel is raised and the foot is positioned on the tip of the big toe, it is the *sūcīpāda* (needle-foot).
(Nāṭyaśāstra 9.279) Having performed a turning with the two thighs, it is the *apakrāntā* (stepping-out) from the foot. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.31)

This *karaṇa* is that in which one foot is cast aside and moved away; it is called *valita*. As for the hands, they are "serpent-heads" (*sarpaśirasa*), according to the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (9.191); this refers to the *sūcīmukha* hand. That—

One should withdraw from the field of the body; simultaneously, the needle-foot (sūcīpāda) also withdraws. Then, having performed the *bhramarikā* step and having executed the *atikrāntakrama*, one should rotate the triple-joint (*trika*).

From the whirling of the second foot with the sole [of the foot], it is known as *bhramarī* (the bee-step). (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.45) This very same [movement], through the twisting of the three [parts of the body], is called *valita* (twisted) and *ghūrṇita* (whirled).
When, having turned upward from the lateral field and rotated face-downward, it is whirled due to the state of being a swinging hand. (92) (p.
When the foot is repeatedly pressed down, that should be known as *lalita* by the wise;
having then raised the knee, one should place the vine (*latā*) upon it. (94)
That is called the *daṇḍapakṣa* movement by those who know the art of dance, wherein both arms are made to perform the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* and the *recita* gestures. (95)
With the two hands positioned on the left side, having made the *trika* well-flexed upon a bed of serpents, the two hands perform the *latārecita* gesture. 96.
(33) Lalita:
"The vine-hand (*latāhasta*) is raised high and sways from side to side; such is this left [hand]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.199)
Having performed various southern movements many times, the two buttocks emerge from the shoulder-heads;
likewise, the two sides emerge from the region of the hair and rise up at the flanks. (Nāṭya Śāstra 9.196)
"The two hair-binding gestures (*keśabandha*) are to be understood [as follows]" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 9.197).

Thus, the movement is performed through the application of such dance-hand gestures (*nṛttahasta*). From the word "and" (*ca*), at the conclusion of the movement, there is another [gesture], the *tripatāka*, at the ear (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 9.199); this is the *karihasta*. Furthermore, the foot is stamped (*nikuṭṭita*) in accordance with the hand.
Furthermore, by another limb: "that" refers here to the subject of graceful dancing. For this very reason, it is the *karaṇa* named *lalita* (34), which has the *daṇḍapakṣa* [as its characteristic].
Having lifted the bent foot so that the knee is level with the breast—this is the *ūrdhvajānucārī* (the movement where the knee is raised). (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.33)

Having formed the *latāhasta* (creeper-hand) according to the rule "extending them sideways" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 9.198), one should place one *latāhasta* over the knee; then, with the second limb in the same manner, because the two arms are positioned like a staff on one side, this is the *daṇḍapakṣa* (staff-wing) *karaṇa*. (94)

(35) *Bhujaṅgatrastarecita*. The word "that" (*tat*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. Having performed it according to the rule: "Having lifted the bent foot, one should rotate the thigh in a triangular manner" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 10.42).
Both *haṃsapakṣa* hands, moving rapidly (*drutabhrama*), should be led into the left field;
likewise, the foot and the anklet should be placed in the *nūpura* gesture.
The hands and feet are extended, and the hips and neck are also extended. || 97 ||
By means of the Vaiśākha stance, this becomes the Vaiśākha-recited;
the foot is cast in the svastika position, and likewise the two hands are twisted outward.
That is to be known as the *bhramaraka* due to the turning of the three [parts of the body];
the left hand should be bent (*añcita*), while the right is indeed *catura*. (99)
(36) *Nūpura*: Having bent the foot backward, one should quickly strike it down upon the ground with the sole facing forward; this is the *cārī* known as *nūpurapādikā*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.35)
Having performed the *trikavalana* with that *bhramarikā* dance-step (*cārī*), one then performs the *nūpurapādikā* step;
with the hand on the same side as the foot upon which one steps, [the arm] is extended (*recita*), while the second hand is in the *latāhasta* position. (96)
(37) *Vaiśākharecita*:

"The two *recita* dance-hands (*nṛttahasta*) are the *haṃsapakṣa* [hands] moving rapidly in a circular motion. Following that [description], the *recita* performed by the feet, neck, and hips should be understood. As stated by Rāhulaka:
One should know that *recita* consists of separate circular movements (*bhramaṇa*) performed at the neck, the hands, the waist, and the feet.
There should be an interval of three *tālas* and a half-*tāla* between the two feet.
One should fashion the seated thighs at three tālas and half a tāla.
The two feet are positioned in a triangle;
this is the vaiśākha stance. This technique is used for riding.
(97) (38) The *bhramaraka* [stance].
By this foot, the *ākṣiptā* movement is indicated:
"Having lifted and cast aside the bent foot, one should place it down extended;
when joined with the *jaṅghā-svastika*, that is known as *ākṣiptā*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.37)

When the right foot is stamped, it is proclaimed as the *catura* [step]. When the right foot is in the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* position and the hand is extended (*recita*), [it is likewise so designated]. (100)
The left hand, known as *latā*, should be curved like a serpent;
meanwhile, the hands and feet are cast out in all directions like a staff. (101)
The construction is as follows: immediately after the *svastika*, having extended the foot and simultaneously unwinding one hand so that the index finger and the others face outward (*nā. śā.
9.216*), one performs a triple twisting; then, with the second limb, one does exactly the same. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that this occurs immediately after that twisting.

The *svastika* itself is the foot. Here, the use of both the singular and dual numbers is indicated as being interchangeable. Alternatively, by the word "twisted" (*udveṣṭita*), the two prominent dance-hands (*nṛttahasta*) are implied:
"Having made the hands with their tips twisted like sprouting leaves..."
"The two [hands] should be extended upwards, tossed, and made prominent" (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.208).
Thus, having performed the movement simultaneously, the body is manifested through the rotation of the *pādasvastika*.
The suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of a name. This should be employed in the context of an upward, whirling motion. (98)
(39) *Catura* (the graceful):
"It is called *añcita* when the fingers are slightly bent" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 9.91).
In this [gesture], three fingers are extended, and likewise, the little finger is turned upward.
"Among those, the thumb is likewise; that hand is known as *catura*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.93).

By the word "only" (*eva*), it is indicated that [the space] from the chest region is sufficient for both [hands]. By the word "but" (*tu*), it is suggested that there is merely an excess in the arrangement. Regarding the term *kuṭṭita*:

"Standing on the tips of the soles of the feet, the heels are cast down upon the ground" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 9.266)—this is the form known as *udghaṭitāṅga*. It is used by the *vidūṣaka* at the beginning of an indicative gesture (*sūcī*) accompanied by astonishment, such as in the verse:
"Sānur, O excellent Khaṇḍadāsa... (99).
(40) *Bhujaṅgāñcitaka*:
"The foot is bent" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 10.42), and so forth; this is the foot from the *bhujaṅgatrāsitā* movement.
"The two *haṃsapakṣa* [hands] rotate rapidly" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 9.193); thus, the right [hand] is *recita*. "Extended sideways" (*Nāṭyaśāstra*...); thus [the left].
(Śā. 9-198) The left hand is the *latā* (creeper) dance-hand. (100) p. 115) When it is bent, that *karaṇa* should be known as *daṇḍakarecita*.
Then, having placed both feet in the vṛścika (scorpion) position, they were both stamped down.
The two hands should be positioned as such; that is to be known as the *vṛścikakuṭṭita*.
Having formed the *sūcī* [hand], one should place the right foot in the *apaviddha* position.
When the hip is bent, that is called *kaṭibhrānta*. The foot is drawn back with the toes curved upward and the sole turned up. (104)

(41) Daṇḍakarecita: By the throwing of the hands like a staff and by their extension, the "staff-wings" (*daṇḍapakṣau*) are indicated; by the throwing of the feet, however, the *cārī* known as "staff-feet" (*daṇḍapādā*) is formed.

The hands formed into swan-wings, rotated and turned back, with the arms likewise extended, are known as the *daṇḍapakṣa* (staff-wing) gesture. Having placed the foot upon the anklet, one should extend it forward. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.202)

"Quickly executed with a piercing action, that is known as *daṇḍapādā*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.44). This is a technique (*karaṇa*) whose object is joy; others say its application is in matters of arrogance. (101) (42) *vṛścikakuṭṭita*.

Having placed one foot with its sole turned upward and marked by a scorpion, with the calf drawn back, one should alternately strike both hands, like tender sprouts, against the head of one's own arm.
This [mudrā] is employed when the subject matter of the sentence primarily concerns wonder, the desire to travel through the sky, and so forth. As for example:
In such passages as *paḍividhāriaṃ uvakkhaṃhiā*, etc.
(102), there is the *kaṭibhrānta* [movement]:
having lifted the bent foot, one should extend it upward from the knee.
"By means of the foremost yoga, she is proclaimed as the needle (sūcī). (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.34, p.
116) And the left hand, called the creeper (latā), becomes the scorpion (vṛścika).
The *alapa* is at the region of the hips; the *chinnā* is at the hips by turns. 105.
By means of the Vaiśākha stance here, that severed Karaṇa is formed;
having placed the feet in Vṛścika and both hands in the Svastika position.
With the arms extended and the hands separated, one performs the *vṛścikarecita* (scorpion-recoiled) gesture;
likewise, the hands are bent at the upper arms and the foot is bent at the back.

Having quickly moved the left foot aside, one should place the right foot [in its position]. Simultaneously, by means of the process of turning the back, one should extend the waist. Or, by means of the *bhramarikā* movement (Nāṭya Śāstra 10.45), during the time of the rotation of the waist, both hands also [move] according to the requirements of their application.
The performance of turning away and turning around consists of standing in a square formation at the end of a *yojana*.
In the matter of completing the rhythmic pauses (*yati*) during his movement and progression, the application involves forms such as the palm-tree shape (*tālākāra*) and so forth.
(103) (44) *Latāvṛścika* (the "Creeper-Scorpion").
With the first half [of the verse], one performs the *vṛścika* posture with the left foot on the ground; this is its application during a descent from the sky. (104) (45) It is severed.
Gradually, through the lowering and raising of the two heels (*pārṣṇi*),

when there is a "cutting of the waist" (*kaṭiccheda*), the lowering and raising of the heels occur alternately; and in that very same manner, it takes place within the region of the sides of the waist.
The *alapa* gesture is characterized by fingers that curl like lotus petals upon the palm (*nā. śā. 9-91*). It is performed with both hands moving slightly back and forth in alternation.
According to the rule, "with the *vaiśākha* stance, there are three *tālas* and a half-*tāla*" (*nā. śā. 10-61*).

And by the definition "departing," it is then associated with the severing of the waist; its application is in matters such as the cutting off [of limbs], the resetting of joints, and the breaking of the *tāla* rhythm. (105) (46) *Vṛścikarecita*.
Those same two [hands], ending at the wrists, are the *svastika* (crossed) position.
When they are scattered apart, bent, like the wings of a swan, and moving rapidly, this is to be employed for the act of traveling through the air.

(47) *Vṛścika* (the scorpion):

The dual and singular numbers indicate that the [movement of] the body is not avoided. By bending the hand toward the shoulder, the application of the *karahasta* (elephant-trunk) gesture is indicated.
The *latāhasta* hand is raised, swaying from side to side;

(Nāṭya Śāstra 9.199) The state of having the back deeply arched is invariably concomitant with the performance of the *vṛścika* posture in all cases.
This should be understood in the context of the *vṛścika* (scorpion) applications. This *karaṇa* is the "scorpion" because its foot occupies the position of a scorpion's tail;

thus, the foot characterized by this [movement] is the *vṛścika*. Its application occurs in the movement through the air (*ākāśagati*) and in relation to subjects such as Airāvaṇa. For example: "He descends, creating the illusion of white clouds."
"This is the beloved of Abhramu, the son of Ravāda"—
thus it was revealed.
Then, having extended the right foot five *tālas* within the circle (*maṇḍala*), [he performed the dance].
One should assume the *ālīḍha* stance (*nā. śā.* 10-67).
By means of the gesture (*karaṇa*) consisting of the winding of the index finger and the others of one hand downward in a scattered manner (*nā. śā.* 9-216), [the first hand] is directed downwards.
The second [hand], by means of the gesture consisting of the turning back of the index finger and the others, is directed upwards; according to the sequence of the field, one [hand] is palm-upward.

The *haṃsapakṣa* (swan-wing), characterized by rapid whirling, is the *recaka* (exhalation). The other [movement] is downward-facing; thus, there is a unification of upward and downward. One should effect a union with the back part of that very foot by means of the big toe of the other [foot], characterized as a *tilaka* because it serves as the cause for the act of applying a *tilaka*; this procedure is employed for the purpose of attaining the state of a Vidyādhara. (110)

Having raised the bent foot, one should extend it forward;

Having performed that *cācarī*, one should place the foot being lowered in a bent position; then, having taken up the bent [foot] from behind, one should extend it through the sequence of movements at the end of the action. The *khaṭakāmukha* [hand-gesture] is placed on the chest. Its application is again with another limb; its application is in a forceful gait. (111) p.

This should be employed in the performance of the Deity who is filled with intense bliss (*nirbharānanda*), as for example in *dehasubhā-i-uṃ makarakali-aṇukāpālavidve-icalaṇaṃ dhi-ā-iṃ* and so forth. (112) (53) The Circle of the Discus (*cakramaṇḍala*).

The *aṅkitā* is a *cārī* performed at the beginning [of a sequence]. That *cārī* in which one foot moves on its sole either in front or behind, while the second foot remains stationary and rubs against it, is indeed the *aṅkitā*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.23)
This pertains to the matter of the hurried gait (*uddhata-parikrama*) and its refinement (*pariṣkaraṇa*). (113) (54) The circle of the chest (*ura-maṇḍala*):
having formed an inner circle with the foot dragged along the ground.
"Having moved another [hand] away again, that is known as *sthitāvarta*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.15).

the foot with its toes and sole pointing upward is extended sideways and upward. (116)
In the *talavilāsita* gesture, one should form the two hands with their palms slightly curved;

Its form is projected in the shape of a svastika. One [arm] should be coiled upward and the second coiled downward; when rotated at the region of the chest, they are known as the *ura-maṇḍalin* gestures. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.204) (114)

having raised the bent foot and drawn it back. Thus, by means of the *ākṣipta* foot-step and a slight bending of the side, [the hand] becomes square (*caturaśra*).
"The throwing of the *khaṭakāmukhī* [hand]" refers to the *ākṣiptakaraṇa* (the gesture of throwing) pertaining to the movements of the *vidūṣaka*.
(115) (56) *Talavilasita*: With that same foot raised, it should be performed with the sole either slightly arched (*añcita*) or joined together (*śliṣṭa*).

From the dual number, there is an application either alternately with the second limb or through repetition. When the two hands, in the form of banners (*patāka*), are mutually joined, and where there is a graceful joining (*śleṣaṇa*) in a distant space—the sky—of the soles of the feet and the palms of the hands, that is *talavilasita*. It is designated by the term *pādoddhāra*.
In matters concerning the stage manager (*sūtradhāra*) and others, the masters of drama (*nāṭyācārya*) apply [the following]:
(116) (57) *Argala*. When there is a bending of the little toe of the second foot, the leg—being called *sārdhāntālāhvajaṅgha*—is extended.

And his hand follows right after it, while that bolt remains ahead.
With hands and feet scattered about, whether behind or to the side. || 118 ||

The throwing of hands and feet; this refers to the indication of a haughty gait, circumambulation, and so forth. (118) (59) The *āvarta*:
the left foot is extended and then drawn back again.

"The left [hand] moves toward the right in the *cāṣagati* (the gait of a blue jay). (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.18). Where there is a slight turning (*āvartanam*) of the hand and foot, that is this *āvartakarana* (turning gesture).
This is to be employed when approaching the hero on occasions such as Sāgarikā’s binding with a noose.

One should then cause the hands, feet, and the triple-joint (*trika*) to be thrown back (*ākṣipta*) and turned over (*vivartayet*). || 121 ||

One should rotate [the hands]. When the two *haṃsapakṣa* hands are released and rotate rapidly, it is called *vivṛtta* due to the application of the turning of the three joints (*trikavivartana*). Its application is in the performance of a haughty gait. (121) (62) *Vinivṛtta*.

One should perform the withdrawal through the process of reversal (*pratyāvartana*). The extension of the limbs forward occurs alternately according to the application of the feet; or rather, "application" (*prayoga*) refers to movement, walking, combat, and so forth. The middle finger [is placed] on the forehead like a *tilaka*. By striking the earth with his foot, he performs the dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) of Maheśvara paralyzing [the enemy]; some say that here the "scorpion" (*vṛścika*) refers to the foot. Starting from the root of the thigh on the back, one should rotate it like a wheel; then, having performed the *āviddha* (twisted) movement skillfully by whirling it in a circular path (*maṇḍala-gati*) so that it touches the region of the practitioner's head from all sides, one should extend it. One should draw it forth extensively, moving it successively in all directions. That is the *pada*.
Like lightning, because of its whirling motion, it is called *vidyud-bhrānta* (lightning-whirl), pertaining to a high-paced movement such as circumambulation.
124) When it is drawn in circular patterns on all sides, that is termed *vidyud-bhrānta*.

Because of its engagement in this specific action, a change of bodily posture (*aṅgaparyāya*) is obtained here. And the application of this [dance] is appropriate only to a subject corresponding to its name.

Because the term *saṃśleṣita* (joined) is used for the hands, this is called *talasaṃsphoṭita*. Its application is specifically within that context, as in the passage beginning with "From the palm [comes] the Goddess, very pleasant and auspicious for people," and so forth.

Having performed a turning with the thighs, one should lift up the bent foot.
"One should cast this aside at the side; thus is the *apakrānta* sequence performed. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.31).
Having thus performed the *apakrānta* sequence, and having formed the *ūruvalitabaddhā* *cārī* by joining the shanks of each other, one should then form the *svastika* with the two thighs.

Having placed the foot in the *vṛścika* position, having made the two hands into *recita* *haṃsapakṣa* gestures moving rapidly, [one places] the foot...

From the whirling of the second foot, with the palm [of the hand], it becomes the *bhramarī* [mudrā]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.45) (140) p. 129) When both hands are likewise extended, that is declared to be the *sarpita*.
Having placed the foot in the *nūpura* position, one should extend the leg in the *daṇḍapāda* posture.
That which quickly pierces [the opponent] is called *daṇḍapāda*;
having performed the *atikrāntakrama* step, one should leap up and strike down.

(81) *Sarpita*: When, in a standing position, the heel is on the ground and the forepart of the foot is raised, and all the toes are bent, that foot is called *añcita* (bent). (Nāṭya Śāstra 9.275)

Having bent the foot and stepped back, the noble one has fled from the vicinity of the second foot; at that very same moment, the head moves to its side. Likewise, the hand on that side is extended (*recita*).
This is the procedure for the second hand and foot; the head likewise remains on that side. And for this very reason—
It is *parivāhita*. As he will say:
"When the head is turned sideways in turn, it is *parivāhita*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 8.27).
And this is understood from the authority of the *Māna* [treatise] to refer to the case of approaching without fault while using the feet. (141)
(82) Daṇḍapāda: Having bent the foot backward, one should quickly strike the ground with the sole of the foot; this is the *nūpurapādikā* carriage (*cārī*). (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.35)

Immediately following this, having performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the staff-step (*daṇḍapāda*) and so forth, one should extend the staff-step; that is known as the *kṣiprāpaviddha* maneuver. As it is said [in the Nāṭyaśāstra 10.44]:
"One should place the foot together with the staff, with the hand moving swiftly. Thus, it should be performed in conjunction with this very [maneuver].
This refers to the subject matter of haughty strides and the like.
(142) (83) The *hariṇapluta* [step]:
such indeed shall be the *hariṇaplutā* *cārī* (Nāṭya Śāstra 10.43). Now, of that—
The entry into the *karaṇas* was already explained previously (during the commentary on the *bhujaṅgatrāsita-karaṇa*). (143) p.
130) When the three [joints] are turned back, that is called *tatpreṅkholita*.
The two arms are extended upwards, and the hands have their fingers directed forward.
Likewise, the bound movement (baddhācārī) occurs in the nitamba posture;
having performed the sequence of the swing’s feet, both hands follow accordingly. (146)
Whether recited rapidly or even with faltering execution, the hand gesture (karaṇa) may become distorted:
one hand remains at the chest, while the other has its palm turned upward.

(84) *Preṅkholitaka*: One should swing the contracted foot from side to side (*dolā*) [Nāṭyaśāstra 10.36]. Having performed this, one should leap with the second [foot] and execute the *bhramarikā* [turn] [Nāṭyaśāstra 10.45]. (144)

(85) For the hips: the fingers are directed forward. Then, having brought the two *patāka* hands to the region of the head by means of the *vyāvartita* movement, and having moved the arms outwards in the upward space by means of the *parivartita* movement, [the hands are positioned] as before.
In that region, while looking at one another, one should place the two flags (patākās).

Then, with both hands having fingers directed toward the body, following that [movement], one should perform the *recita* and *ghūrṇita* gestures, characterized by the *nitamba-nṛtta-hasta*. This constitutes the state of having fingers facing the face (*mukhābhimukhāṅgulitvam*).
It is illuminated by three particles. [The two exits] from the arms and the head (*bāhuśīrṣa*) [are described in Nāṭyaśāstra 9.196].
Through the *nimeṣa* (or *aveśa*), due to that connection, it is accompanied by the instruments (*karaṇa*). (145) (86) This is the *skhalita* (stumbling).

Simultaneously with the going and coming of the swing’s feet, the two arms, characterized by [the movement of] swan wings, are engaged in going and coming; furthermore, this is done with the other limb. (146) p.
The añcita and caraṇa hands should be employed in the *karihastaka* gesture;
one hand should be *recita*, while the other is called *latā*. (148)

The two feet, with their soles extended forward, constitute the *prasarpitaka* movement; then, placing the first foot forward and moving the second with a swift step, [one performs the *alāta*]. || 149 ||
In the Siṃhavikrīḍita [mudrā], both hands are also known to follow the feet;
likewise, one foot is extended backward while the two hands are contracted. 150.

(87) *Karihastaka*: With the action of twisting upward (*prodveṣṭana*), the other hand is placed at the ear; the *tripatāka* hand is likewise directed toward that same side, and the foot is bent simultaneously with that upward-twisting motion and should be moved forward. This is performed with the *karihasta*.
This [gesture] is similar to the *nṛttahasta*; this is its name.
(The *latāhasta* is raised, swaying from side to side;
the other [hand], the *tripatāka*, is at the ear; [this is] the *karihasta*). Nāṭyaśāstra 9.199. (147)
(88) *Prasarpitaka*: The *haṃsapakṣa* [hand] moving rapidly is called *recita*. Another is the dance-hand (*nṛttahasta*) known as *latā*.
In the *recita* hand, the foot facing the direction [of movement] moves very slowly, rubbing against the ground between the feet.
This is the application regarding the movement of the *khecarī* [the sky-farer] (148) (89). The *siṃhavikrīḍita* [lion’s play]:
having swiftly cast forward the *alātā* foot-step, the hand follows in accordance with that very [movement]. (Nāṭyaśāstra)
(10-41) One should likewise perform the second *cakra* in this manner;
because it resembles the lion’s paw-strike (*siṃhakaraghāta*), it is the *Siṃhavikrīḍita*, pertaining to the domain of the fierce gait (*raudragati*).
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, the two [mudrās] known as Siṃhākarṣita should be performed in the same manner:
with the hand drawn back, the body drawn back, and the feet drawn back. (151)
This "upturned body" (udvṛttagātra) is known as the *udvṛtta* technique;
one foot is thrown forward (*ākṣipta*), and both hands follow that very foot. (152)
The body should be bent in that manner and likewise drawn forward;
having performed the sequence of the swing's feet, the hands are placed upon the soles. 153.

(90) *Siṃhākarṣita*: One foot is in the *vṛścika* (scorpion) position; the right and left hands are both bent and joined in the *svastika* with the palms like the buds of a lotus (*padmakośa*) and the thumbs tucked in (*ūrṇanābha*). When the second foot is likewise in the *vṛścika* position, then those two [hands]—

Having withdrawn [the hands] by means of the *kriyāvartana* movement, [placing] the hands once again in that very same manner for the purpose of the mimetic representation (*abhinaya*) of a lion and so forth, it is the *siṃhākarṣitaka*;
(150) (91) it is the *udvṛtta*.
Wherein the hands and feet are thrown out, extended, and brought [together], how is there a throwing of the entire body? He says:
having performed it joined with the *udvṛtta* movement, one should throw down the foot after having drawn it back, twisted it, and leaped up.
"But when the second [hand] is turned back, it is *udvṛttā*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.39). For this very reason, the *karaṇa* is called *udvṛta*. (151) (92) *Upasṛtaka*.
"Just as the Great Goddess requested," [it is said].
133) One should always move the left hand, with the palms joined together.
One hand is placed upon the chest, and the second hangs down. || 154 ||
The feet should be positioned on the tips of the toes in the *janita* posture;
having performed the *janita* posture, the two hands have their fingers directed forward. (155)
When the two hands fall slowly, that should be known as *avahitthaka*; the hands should be placed upon the chest, and the chest itself should be slightly hollowed out. (156)

(93) *Talasaṃghaṭṭita*: "The bent [hands] from side to side" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 10.36). Performing the *dolāpādā* foot-step, at that same time, the two hands are such that their palms are properly struck against one another.
Having placed both hands in the Vaiṣṇava position (*vaiṣṇava-sthānaka*) according to the rule "two palms...

(*tālau*, Nāṭyaśāstra 10.52), one should keep the right hand at the hip and perform a *recaka* (a downward sweeping motion) with the second [left] hand, characterized by a rapid rotation like the wing of a swan. This is employed when the meaning of the sentence is primarily characterized by compassion. *dhāṇavagalachipha...* (Aṅka).
*Dhi-a-caṇāri*, etc.
(153) (94). It is produced. With fists and hands upon the chest; hanging down, it is called *latā* (the creeper). This is the time for the commencement of other actions.

Thus, through the application of generating that particular configuration, brought about by the power of the appropriate *cārīs*, [the posture] *avahitthaka* is produced (*janitācārī*). In this *nāṭyaśāstra* (10.95),
the *muṣṭihasta* hand is placed at the chest, while the other hand moves forward.
"And the foot with the sole moving" (Nāṭya Śāstra 10.25). Thus,

having performed the *cārī* step, and likewise having placed both hands upon the regions of the forehead and the chest with the fingers directed forward in the manner of the *arālālapallava* gesture, [one should proceed] slowly.

Having performed the *udveṣṭita* (twisting) movement in sequence by placing the hands on the sides in a downward and upward order, one should again perform the *apaveṣṭita* (untwisting) and *parivartita* (turning) movements so that the *ārāla* and *lāpallava* hand gestures are brought face-to-face at the region of the chest.
This is its application when the intended meaning of the sentence is primarily to be concealed. Thus ends the section on the sequence of *avahittha* (concealment).
Namely: ai-tha-ga-aṃ ga-ika-ri tha-vi-phā-sa-ha-sa-śva-khe i-aṃ ba-i-saṃ pa-ri-hi.
The stationing within the maṇḍala, as well as the settling and the execution,
should consist of leaping up and falling down with both feet moving on the ground. (157)
That which is bent, curved, and characterized by the playful union of the limbs is indeed the *melakākrīḍita*.
One should place the hand, having performed the *āvṛtta* movement, bent upon the back of the thigh. (158)
The calves should be bent and likewise raised; the thighs should be turned upward.
The hands should be made to hang down, and the head should be tilted back. 159.
Others, however, say: "Having placed the hands in the *śukatuṇḍa* position, bent toward the chest, and slowly turned downward, this is the *avahittha*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.156)
They say this refers to the domain of weakness resulting from anxiety:
(155) (96) [the posture] with the body settled, the back stiffened, the shoulders drooping, and the chest uplifted.
The chest is arched.

(Nāṭya Śāstra 9-226) With the feet positioned four *tālas* apart within the *aindra* mandala, one should employ this [stance] in contexts such as mounting an elephant. Because it is used for marching without resting, it is called *niveśa*. (156)

(97) *Elakākrīḍita* (the goat’s play): at the time of falling, there is a bending of the limbs, followed by a twisting; thus, this *cārī* shall indeed be of a single form. This pertains to the movement and sphere of those of inferior nature. (157)
(98) *Ūrūdvṛtta* (the upturned thighs): When the heel of the foot moving on the ground is turned outward, and the shank is likewise bent and upturned, it is called *ūrūdvṛtta*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.22)
Together with this noble lady, by means of the *vyāvartitakaraṇa* gesture, one should cast the curved *khaṭaka* hand toward the thighs and the back;
this gesture pertains to subjects such as affectionate anger, jealousy, and supplication.
O twice-born ones, in the *madaskhalitaka* [dance], the feet are turned and whirled;
the foot extended forward is bent and directed upward toward the sky. (160)
When both hands are extended outward, that is called Viṣṇukrānta. Having rotated the hand, one should indeed contract it against the back of the thigh. || 161 ||
The thigh is likewise pierced; that is the *sambhrānta* movement. The hand is cast aside with the needle gesture, and the foot is likewise trampled (*nikuṭṭita*). || 162 ||
In the Viṣkambha and Karaṇa [mudrās], the left hand should rest upon the chest;
the feet should be thrust outward, and the palms of the hands should be joined together.

(99) *Madaskhalitaka* (The Stumble of Intoxication): The two arms swing; the head turns from side to side in alternation; the feet, having been turned and cast aside, and then lowered immediately after, move away in a *svastika* position in alternation. This pertains to the subject of intoxication by wine. (159)
(100) Viṣṇukrānta:
Herein lies such a stride of Viṣṇu; its application is restricted solely to those respective subjects. (160) (101) Sambhrānta: Confusion.
When the *āryā* posture has been assumed, the thigh is likewise [bent];

with the foot at the front of the *svastika*, it is both bent and extended. When one falls [sideways] while thus bent and cast aside, that is known as the *āviddhā* (the "cast-aside" posture). (Nāṭya Śāstra 10.38)
And at the time of practicing that movement, one should place the *alapallava* hand upon the back of the thigh by means of the *vyāvartita-parivartita* maneuver;
this pertains to the context of hurried circumambulation. (161) (102) The *viṣkambha*.

The left hand is pierced by the right hand with its needle-like tip (*sūcīmukha*), preceded by the departure [of the hand] from the *nṛttahasta* form. That same foot is *nikuṭṭita*. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that this is done with the second limb as well. By the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*), he says this again:
When the *udghaṭṭita* [mudrā] is performed, the wise should always bend the side;
having first employed the *alātaka*, one should indeed release both hands. (164)
In the *vṛṣabhakrīḍita* [mudrā], the hands are always contracted and bent;
the hands are *recita* and *avañcita*, and the head is shaken and turned. (165)

The foot characterized by the *sūcī* (needle) posture is [placed] behind, while the other is *nikuṭṭita* (stamped), and the remaining one is *alapaṅlava* (slightly bent). When this is performed again, it is called the *viṣkambha* (expansion) *karaṇa*, due to the expansion resulting from the obstruction of movement. (162)

(103) *Udghaṭṭita*: Having stood with the tips of the soles [of the feet] and the heels on the ground—thus [is defined] the foot (*nā. śā. 9-266*). With this [foot], the two hands are prepared to strike one another; furthermore, in the second foot, it is *udghaṭṭita*.

And in the same manner, there is the bending of the sides alternately; this pertains to the subject of joy (*pramoda*). (163) (104) *Vṛṣabhakrīḍita*: performing the *alātacārī* (as described in Nāṭyaśāstra 10.41), one should make the two hands *recita*; then they become *kuñcita*.
Having turned back the hands, one should then make the two arms, shaped like tender sprouts, bent and controlled;
thus, through the application of the two "gateways" (*aṅgadvāra*) of the bull, it is the *vṛṣabhakrīḍita* (the Bull’s Play). (164) (105) *Lolita*.

In the Vaiṣṇava posture, one should first perform the *recita* gesture, which has the swift, humming form of a swan’s wing; with both hands bent at the chest in the shape of a tender sprout, the head should be shaken, and it should be moved all around, turned toward both sides, and lowered. (165)
When [the feet] are on both sides, it is called *lolita*; when the feet are drawn back in a *svastika* and the head is turned around, it is [also so called]. (166)
The two hands should likewise be extended like a crawling serpent;
with the limbs settled, one should extend the foot, moving it with the palms.
Having raised the chest and assumed the "cart-mouth" (śakaṭāsya) posture,
