one should employ the two feet with their palms facing upward and the fingers extended, while the hands are in the tripatāka gesture with the faces turned downward.
(106) *Nāgāpasarpitam* (The Serpent’s Gliding). When the gait proceeds by turns toward the side, moving in a curved manner, it is called *nāgāpasarpitam*.
This pertains to the domain of youthful intoxication. (166)

(107) *Śakaṭāsya* (the cart-mouth posture): That by which the limbs are settled and made level is [the *śakaṭāsya*]. With the feet placed together at the knees, the foot—bent at the ankle in front, but not the knee itself—is to be extended so as to move at a distance of one and a half *tālas*.

Even with that [first hand] accompanied by it, the second hand is a *khaṭaka* on the chest; such indeed will be this *cārī* (*Nāṭya Śāstra* 10.16). By this arrangement, there is the sitting and throwing of a cart.
Its application is in subjects such as the play of children and in genres such as the *bhāṇikā*. (167)

(108) Gaṅgāvataraṇa. Regarding this, some say that by the phrase "with the surface of the fingers pointing upward," the standing position on the ground with the feet level and slightly raised is described.
And this is incorrect because it is not the meaning of the word. Therefore, the foot is not bent (*añcita*). Others, however, say:

"In this sequence, movement on the surface [of the stage] is the 'scorpion-foot' (*vṛścikapāda*). Still others, however, [say that] because of the letter *ca*, the change in sequence, and the downward bending of the foot, the *tripatāka* hands, and the head, one first lifts the foot by means of that.
Having stood still and placed the foot upward with the hands in the *patākā* (banner) position,

moving that foot gradually on its toes is called the *vṛścikapāda* (scorpion-foot). Others, however, due to the sequence being broken by the word "and" (*ca*) and because of the downward inclination of the head and the two *tripatākā* hands at that time, consider this to be the first lifting of the foot.
(138) "The two hands [at the sides] and the head bowed down— this is the descent of the Gaṅgā.
Whatever postures and whatever noble exertions have been described," (169)
This, however, shall be the movement of the feet for these [hands],
as well as those dance-hands (nṛttahasta) which have been described for the performance of dance.
The application of these [hand gestures] is briefly explained with respect to the instruments [of performance]:
generally, when an instrument is to be played, the left hand should be placed upon the chest. (171)
The foot and the following right hand should likewise be moved;
and those which have been described as *cārīs* as well as *nṛttahastas* should be employed in the same manner. (172)
That is to be known as the *mātṛkā*, and from its divisions come the instruments;
indeed, these one hundred and eight instruments have been declared by me. (173)
Hereafter, I shall explain the various formations of the *aṅgahāras*:
having extended and raised both hands, one should perform the *samapāda* stance. (174)

Having stood with one foot raised and placed above it, with two hands in the *tripatāka* gesture, one should gradually bend and lower that foot; in accordance with that, one should likewise bend the *tripatāka* hand. In the same manner, one should gradually [bend] the head. In this very way, preceded by the extension of the feet as in the *trivikrama* posture, [one performs the dance] of the goddess Gaṅgā.
The subject matter of this treatise is indicated by its very name, *Avataraṇa*. The word *iti* marks the conclusion.
(Thus ends the exposition of the one hundred and eight *karaṇas*). [Now follows] the definition of *aṅgahāra*.

Since the *talapuṣpapuṭa* was previously explained, it has been indicated that in all cases the procedure begins with an emphasis on the execution (*vartanā*); now he states the actual application. Concluding what has been said, he promises to define the *anaṅgahāras*, which follow in due order, according to their enumeration.

Regarding the passage beginning with "one hundred and eight" (*aṣṭottaraśatam*): because one hundred and eight instruments have been declared, for that reason, a superior and distinguished *aṅgahāra* is conceived—that by which they are differentiated from one another.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "I shall describe the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) among those very *aṅgahāras*. The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacanam*).
Having executed the *vyaṃsitāpasṛta* movement, one should extend the left hand upward;
then one should perform the *pratyālīḍha* stance and likewise the *nikuṭṭaka*. || 175 ||
Then one should perform ūrūdvṛtta, followed by ākṣipta and svastika; then nitamba, karihasta, and kaṭicchinna in their proper sequence. (176)
(1) *Sthirahasta* (the steady hand).
Therein, he defines *sthirahasta* according to the order of enumeration, beginning with "having extended" and ending with "beloved of Hara.
In that context, "having extended and raised the two hands" refers to what was previously defined as the *tripatākāñjali* held at the chest.
This is characterized by the determination of the initial procedure for the means (*karaṇa*) known as *līna* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.66).
And this has been stated by us in the very definition of that [means], while explaining the purpose of the term *patāka*.
For, through this [procedure], this and that means is indeed applied from the beginning of the *yoga*.

If it occurs through the application of *vartanā* and *cārī* appropriate to the hands, feet, and other limbs engaged in the act of seizing, then by that very means it becomes uninterrupted and auspicious.
Due to its continuity, like a firebrand wheel (*alātacakra*), it is to be synthesized by a single cognition; such is the firm hand (*sthirahasta*).
The connection is that [this] is called "nāmāṅgahāra. Thus, the phrase "in accordance with the yoga" is to be connected to all the *aṅgahāras*.
Others, however, explain it as: "This [is performed] for the pleasure of the Blessed One, even from the perspective of yoga, that is, meditative absorption (*samādhi*)."
"Samapāda" refers to the technique where the feet are joined together with the nails aligned. Regarding the feet being "joined with the nails aligned," [the *Nāṭyaveda-vyañjita* states]:
"The *ālīḍha* stance is that in which the two hands are extended toward the chest."
"When the two hands are scattered upward and downward, that is the *vyaṃsita* movement" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.108).

Having performed this defined movement, one should place both hands which were previously withdrawn and scattered in the upward position, and by means of the turning of the *ālīḍha* stance (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 10.70), assume the *pratyālīḍha* stance.

Then, when the hands are contracted [as described in] *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.69, "nikuṭṭite nikuṭṭitau," that is the ninth *karaṇa*. Following that, the *āvṛttakaraṇa* of the hand upon the back of the thigh [as described in] *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.159 is the ninety-eighth.
Then, the *svastika* performed with both hands and then with both feet [as described in] *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.75 is the fifteenth. After that...
Including "the hand and foot are drawn back" (*ākṣiptaṃ hastapādam*), there are fifty-five [varieties].
On page 140:
"This *sthirahasta* is an *aṅgahāra*, beloved by Hara."
The two [hands] are struck with palm-flowers, and the *vartita* [hand] is accompanied by the *sanikuṭṭaka*. || 177 ||
Then, having performed the *pratyālīḍha* and likewise the *nikuṭṭaka*,
[one performs] the *ūrūdvṛtta*, the *ākṣipta*, the *uraḥmaṇḍala*,
the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*. (178)
"The two arms are extended upward and the hands have their fingers facing forward" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.146)—this is the *nitambagati* (hip-movement). Then follows the *karihasta* (elephant-hand gesture):
"The left hand is placed upon the chest with its palm turned upward" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.148).
Thus ends the eighty-seventh [chapter]. Then, "the waist is severed by turns, [and] the arm [is severed] at the head" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.72)—this is the eleventh.
In this manner, through the correct application of the collection of instruments (*karaṇagrāma*), one accomplishes the *aṅgahāra* known as *sthirahasta*.

Therefore, in this context— meaning in all *aṅgahāras*— the masters of dramatic art (*nāṭyācāryas*) maintain that the entire collection of constituent parts of the *karaṇas*, that is, the whole range of *karaṇas*, should be employed facing the four directions. However, the Sage [Bharata], considering that [view] to be improper for both the future and the past, [states it] in the nineteenth [chapter].

In the *Aṅgahāra* called *Parivṛttakaracita* (*Nāṭya Śāstra* 4.219), he will state: "The rule for turning the face away shall likewise occur again. This is because such a statement would be logically inconsistent within the context of the rules for *Aṅgahāras*. Therefore, we shall explain this only among the *Āṅgika* [expressions].
For one who is defining the nature of the *Udveṣṭitakaraṇa*, the application of these [rules] serves only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). In practice...

And this [movement] is not deficient in its respective sentence-meaning, according to the degree of distance. We shall explain this further in the context of the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite), as stated in the passage beginning with "in battle and in wrestling" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.56). In such instances, these [movements] are sometimes employed specifically according to the subject matter. Thus, one who possesses a steady hand...
Since it is not observed that there is no completion [of the movement], the effort expended in its description is not in vain. (176) *Paryastaka*:
"The hollowed palms of flowers," and so forth. Some [commentators] explain that from "extending [the limbs]" up to "one should then perform the *pratyālīḍha*" [is one section].

In all *aṅgahāras*, they first apply the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) with the intention of asking, "How is the application for the initial connection of the limbs (*prathamāṅgasangatikaraṇa*)? Others, however, say that the common [procedures] appropriate for each individual *aṅgahāra* should be inferred by oneself. What is the loss of what has been heard (*śrutahāni*)?

Others say it is the *guṇa* [mudrā]. In that regard, first is the *puṣpapuṭa* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.61). Having rotated [the hands], the one called *śukatuṇḍa* is on the back of the thigh, and the left hand is at the chest (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.64).
Thus is *apaviddha*; when the wrists are bent, it is *vartita* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.62); and when they are *nikuṭṭita*, as stated [in Nāṭya Śāstra 4.69], page 141.
This is indeed the *paryastaka* limb-movement (*aṅgahāra*) originating from Hara;
it is performed by executing the *alapallava*, the *sūcī*, and the *vikṣipta*. (179)
Then one should perform the *āvartita*, and likewise the *nikuṭṭaka*;
as well as the *ūrūdvṛtta*, the *ākṣipta*, and the *uraḥmaṇḍala*. (180)
The *karihasta*, the *kaṭicchinna*, and this *sūcividdha* [are performed];
likewise, the *apaviddha* and the *sūcividdha* are both *karaṇas*. (181)

The *nikuṭṭaka* is the *karamāvṛttakaraṇa* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.159), which is the *ūrūdvṛtta*. Then there is the *ākṣipta*, according to "the hand and foot are thrown out" (4.116). The *uraḥmaṇḍala* is according to "the [hands] have moved away from the *svastika*" (4.115). Then the *nitambakaraṇa* is according to "the two arms have emerged upwards" (4.146).

Immediately following, "the left [hand] is placed on the chest" (4-148) constitutes the *karihasta* [gesture]. Then, "alternately" (4-72) constitutes the *kaṭicchinnam*. By means of these ten *karaṇas*, the *paryastaka* [posture] is formed. (178) (3) This is the *sūcīviddha*.

And the *arghapallavasūcī*. According to the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.138), "the *alapadma* [hand] in the region of the head and the *sūcī* foot" refers to the seventy-seventh *karaṇa* called *ardhasūcī*, characterized by the *alapallava* [hand]:
"The hand and foot are cast out (*vikṣipta*) either behind or to the side."

"One path" (*ekamārgam*) is explained [in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.119] as "disturbed. Regarding the fifty-ninth [technique], called *āvarta*: having extended the foot known as the *āvarta* and then bent it, one should rotate it forward in conjunction with the body.

"Subject to application" (*prayogavaśaga*)—this is what is expressed by the word *āvartita*. Therefore, the six movements beginning with *nikuṭṭaka* are performed just like the *aṅgahāras*, as in the case of the *sthirahasta* [posture]. (180)
(4) *Apaviddha*:
[The mudrā] beginning with the words "apavidhantu" and so forth;
having rotated it, one should strike it upon the back of the thigh known as the "parrot-beak."
"And the left hand, though resting on the chest, is cast aside" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.64, p.
One should rotate the spine with the hand turned back.
The two hands are at the level of the navel-circle, and likewise, they are cut off at the waist. || 182 ||
This is to be known as the *apaviddha-aṅgahāra* by performers;
having performed the *nūpura-karaṇa*, one should again perform the *vikṣiptālātaka*. (183)
One should again perform the *ākṣiptaka*, as well as the *uromaṇḍalaka*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*. (184)
"When one foot is pierced by the toe of the other foot, while the hands remain at the waist and chest, that is *sūcīviddha*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.139).
Having thus performed these two *karaṇas*, [one proceeds] with the *udveṣṭita* movement and the *baddhā* *cārī*.
Having formed a triple fold and characterized it with the *ūrormaṇḍala* hand, one should then perform the *uraḥmaṇḍala* gesture; from that, one should execute the *kaṭicchinna*.
When the feet are drawn back in a swastika formation, they constitute the *apaviddha* steps.
"The two hands are the chest-circle; that indeed is the chest-circle" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.115).

"By the performers" refers to those who are skilled in performance. By this, he says that the movement of the limbs cannot be correctly understood by the learned on their own. When, among these instruments...

Furthermore, that application which is accompanied by the actions of the middle, the turning, the head, the eyebrows, the eyes, and so forth, as well as its constituent parts (*aṃśa*), can be personally accepted by one who knows the reality of its essential nature (*svarūpa-tattva*). But for another person, even if it is described, it cannot be performed, nor can it be defined; it is like the rhythm of song and instrumental music.

And its application varies according to the difference in the meaning of the sentences; furthermore, there is an infinity of such applications. For even a well-trained author of grammatical rules cannot provide a definition for every single word of all sentences. Even if one were to inform another that "this [rule] should be applied after this," some form of personal application would still be required in the *saṃhitā*.

It should be performed. It was stated that the rules of restraint will be explained later; therefore, let it suffice to say that the determination of locations such as the mandala and so forth, which has been made here by some, is entirely useless. (182) (5) The Ākṣiptaka.
The *karaṇa* [known as] *nūpura* and so forth is as follows: having performed the *trika* with beautiful curvature (*suvalita*), the two hands are in the *latārecita* position (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.97).
Furthermore, in the foot-movement (*pādakaraṇa*) called *nūpura*, the hand and foot are in the *vikṣipta* position (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.119). Thus, it is the *vikṣipta*.
(143) This *aṅgahāra* should be known by performers as the *ākṣiptaka*.
In it, the hand is *udveṣṭita-apaviddha* and the foot is *nikuṭṭita*. || 185 ||
Then, by that same yoga, on the left side, the two hands should form the circle of the chest (uro-maṇḍalaka) and the hip (nitamba) in the "elephant-trunk" (kari-hastaka) gesture. 186.
In the *udghaṭṭita* dance, one should always perform the *sakati-cchinna* movement;
the hands are alternately rotated and the feet are likewise stamped. (187)
"Having placed the left foot upon the right shoulder and the right hand [upon the left], one should perform the sequence of the raised knee; this is known as the *alātaka*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.78).
Regarding those instances where there is a repetition, some say that in each case there is a double application.
The five *karaṇas* beginning with *ākṣipta*, as taught in the second *Aṅgahāra*:
"the *udghaṭṭita*,
and the *udveṣṭita* and *apaviddha*"— by this first verse, the application of two limbs in alternation is [described].
He states the *nikuṭṭaka* movement: "When the two hands are *nikuṭṭita*... (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.69).
The four movements beginning with *uraḥmaṇḍalaka* are exactly like those in the second *aṅgahāra*. (186) (7) *Viṣkambha*.

"Twisted alternately" (*paryāyodveṣṭitau*): by this half-verse, he states that the *nikuṭṭita* movement is performed with the first two circles (*maṇḍala*), just as in the preceding *aṅgahāra*. "Curved" (*kuñcitau*): this refers to the connection with both hands and feet.
Thus, there is an alternation of the two limbs for the *kuñcita* and *añcita* movements.
The state of being employed has been described:
"Having made the foot like a scorpion's tail, one should contract the hand at the side;
likewise, the right [hand] should be contracted at the tip of the nose" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.87).

Having formed the *svastika* with the two feet and the *karihasta* with the right [hand], one should likewise place the left [hand] at the region of the chest in the *ardhasvastika* position. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.83).
Immediately after this:
"But when that same hand is turned away and rotated, and bent toward the tip of the nose, then it is *añcita*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.83).
By this half-verse, he describes the tenth *karaṇa*, the *ardhanikuṭṭaka*.

Having formed the hand in the *caturaśra* (square) position, one should likewise perform the *kuñcita* (contracted), *avañcita* (extended), and *ūrūdvṛtta* (thigh-rotated) movements, as well as the *nikuṭṭaka* (stamping) with the foot. || 188 ||
Furthermore, the hand should be made to appear as if terrified by a serpent, then again as if writhing,
and the three [fingers] should be separated by means of the *bhramaraka* gesture.
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* are proclaimed as being in the *viṣkambha* position;
likewise, one should indeed cast out and toss up the staff-like foot and the hand. (190)
One should cause the left hand, together with the foot, to move in a deceptive manner; two *nikuṭṭaka* movements should be performed, and the *maṇḍala* gesture should be cast forward upon the chest.
In the Aparājita [mudrā], one should perform the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna*;
likewise, having performed the *kuṭṭita* movement, one should then perform the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*.
"The hand is placed upon the top of the other arm with its fingers directed forward,
joined by the half-curved [gesture]" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.70).
For in that case, the second hand is square-shaped like a *khaṭaka* and facing forward.
"Raising the contracted foot and turning the thigh into a triangle, with the hip and knee turned, it becomes the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.84).
The *bhujaṅgatrāsita* is of four kinds. By the use of the particle *eva* here, [the author] indicates the application of the hands, which was not explicitly stated.

And with the hand twisted [in the *udveṣṭita* gesture], simultaneously with that, one should perform the *chinna-trika* by means of the thirty-eighth *karaṇa*, the *bhramaraka*, all around; this is done through the application of both limbs. It is called "cut" (*chinna*) because of the twisting of the middle of the hips—for thus it is said:
The *svastika* foot is cast out and the two hands are likewise extended;
this is due to the bending of the triple-joint (*trika*). Thus is the *bhramaraka*. Then follow the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna*, just as in the previous *aṅgahāra*. (189)
(8) Aparājita:
"The staff-foot" and so forth.
Having placed the foot in the *nūpura* position, one should extend the leg like a staff.
And [the position] called *kṣiprāviddhakara* is the *daṇḍapāda* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.143, p.
With the hand in the *recita* gesture, one should indicate the *patāka* hand.
One should employ the ākṣiptaka movement, and likewise the urormaṇḍalaka.
The *latā* [gesture] is called *sakaṭicchinna*; it occurs when the *viṣkambha* is drawn back.
Having performed the *trika* with a beautiful twist, one likewise performs the *nūpura* gesture. (194)
Having performed the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* on the right side, as well as the *vaiśākharecita*, then the *ākṣiptaka*, and likewise the *paricchinna*. (195)
One should perform the *bāhyabhramaraka*, as well as the *ūromaṇḍala*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*. (196)

What was defined there has been demonstrated here by breaking it down through the passage beginning with "having scattered" (*vikṣipya*), and so forth. The *ālīḍha* stance is that which is described [in the *Nāṭyaśāstra*] at 4.109; the *vyaṃsita* is that which was mentioned among the first *aṅgahāras*.
By the words "the left hand," and so forth, he describes the eighty-eighth *karaṇa*, the *prasarpita*.
"One is the *recita* hand, and another is the one called *latā*;

[then there is] *prasarpitaka*. Thus, according to the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.149), there are two types of *nikuṭṭaka*: namely, *nikuṭṭa* and *ardhanikuṭṭa* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.69–70), when they are *nikuṭṭita*."

Regarding "the two hands": it means that the hand is placed upon the shoulder of the bent arm. "In the circle on the chest" means when the *maṇḍala* gesture is performed upon the chest (*ura-maṇḍala*). The four gestures beginning with *ākṣipta* and ending with *kaṭicchinna* are exactly like the second *aṅgahāra*.
(9) *Viṣkambhāpasṛta* (the withdrawn step).
Regarding *kuṭṭita* and so forth: both *nikuṭṭaka* and *ardhanikuṭṭaka* are included under the general term *kuṭṭita*. [This is explained in] *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.84: "The foot is bent... and so on.

The twenty-fourth [meter] is *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. By means of the half-verse beginning with "tene" and so forth, [the author] shows the thirty-fifth [meter] (*nā. śā.* 4.96). Having performed the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*, where both [feet] are *recita*.

"The two hands situated on the left side [form] the *bhujaṅgatrasta* [hand-posture]" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.96). Its application occurs through a rotation of the limbs; this he indicates by the mention of the *patāka* [hand]. The triad beginning with the *ākṣiptaka* is exactly like the previous *aṅgahāra*. Only here, in the *kaṭicchinna* *karaṇa* (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.71)...
By way of its variations, this single *latāhasta* becomes the *mattākrīḍa*, a *aṅgahāra* indeed beloved by Hara.
Having performed the recitation, one should likewise form the hand and foot gestures as well as the scorpion gesture. || 197 ||
Again, by that very same yoga, one should apply the scorpion posture, as well as the *nikuṭṭaka*, performed alternately on the left and the right in succession. (198)
The *sakaticheda* known as *latā* occurs in the *svastikarecita*;
having formed a *svastika* on the side, one should then perform the *nikuṭṭaka*.
Indeed, this same procedure should be followed for the second side as well;
then, having rotated the hand, one should strike it down upon the back of the thigh.
Then one should perform the ūrūdvṛtta, and again the ākṣipta;
likewise the nitamba, the karihasta, and the kaṭicchinna. (201)
This is proclaimed as the *pārśvasvastika* (side-cross) *aṅgahāra*. Having performed the *vṛścika* posture and likewise the hand gesture known as *latā*, [one proceeds]. (202)
One should again contract that very same hand at the tip of the nose;
having made that same [hand] encircled, one should rotate the hips. || 203 ||
The *karihasta* (elephant-hand) and *kaṭicchinna* (waist-cut) positions should be employed in the *vṛścikāpasṛta* (scorpion-receding);
likewise, one should perform the *nūpurapāda* (anklet-foot) and the *ākṣiptaka* (thrown-out). || 204 ||
Having fashioned the three [parts] well-rounded,
one should likewise make them well-defined and provide a needle-foot.
Likewise, the nitamba, the karihasta, and the uromaṇḍalaka. || 205 ||
Then, with the waist severed, that indeed is designated as the *bhramara*;
having performed the *mattallikaraṇa* and having rotated the right hand.
In the region of the cheek, however, it should be properly contracted, cast aside, and swift, combined with the clapping of the palm. 207.
The *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand) and the *kaṭicchinna* (waist-broken) gestures should be employed in the *mattaskhalitaka* (intoxicated-stumbling) gait,
using swinging hands that move about and feet drawn back in the *svastika* position.
With hands that are bent, rotated, and likewise struck together at the palms,
one should perform the *nikuṭṭita* and similarly the *ūrudvṛtta*.
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* gestures should be employed when there is playful movement out of intoxication;
having assumed the *maṇḍala* stance, the two hands should likewise be made *recita*.
With the foot extended, there should be the *mattallikaraṇa*;
likewise, there are the *ākṣiptakaraṇa* and the *uromaṇḍala*. || 211 ||
Likewise, there should be the "waist-cut" (kaṭicchinna) in the circle of movement;
then one should employ the "equal-footed" (samapāda), and immediately after that, the "completely cut" (paricchinna).
With the foot cast aside, there is likewise the *bāhyabhramaraka*;
with the left needle-step, there is the *atikrānta*, as well as the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. (213)
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* are prescribed for the *paricchinna*;
however, when [the hands] have slipped, the two hands should be placed above the head in the *svastika* position. (214)
Then, having bent the left hand and the body, one should exhale;
then, having raised the body and elevated it there, one should exhale again.
Having formed the hands known as *latā*, one should employ the *vṛścika* [mudrā], as well as the *recita*, the *karihasta*, and the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. || 216 ||
One should employ the ākṣiptaka and the svastika-pāda;
furthermore, the procedure for the parāṅmukha [turn] should be performed here in exactly the same manner.
"The left hand is called *latā*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.105), thus it is the *latāvṛścika* [hand-gesture]. "One hand is placed upon the chest" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.148).
"The *recita* [step] is the *unmattakaraṇa*" [mode of movement]. "With the foot bent (*añcita*), the two [hands] are in the *recita* [position]" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.74).
"One hand placed on the chest" is the *karihasta* [gesture]; "the foot bent" (*kuñcita-pāda*)— as stated in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.84)—
is the *karihasta* performed with a hip-cut (*kaṭicchinna*) and a whirling-turn (*parivṛtta-karecita*).
For when the two hands are cast off along with the body, they are uttered [as mantras]. || 218 ||
Again, raising the body with that same side, one should perform the *recaka* (exhalation);
likewise, one should perform the *nūpurapāda* and the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*.
The recited maṇḍala should be contracted at the head of the arms;
likewise, there are the raised thighs, the cast [thighs], and the chest-maṇḍala.
One should perform the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* gestures in the *vaiśākha* posture;
having first performed the *janita*, one should extend one foot.
The arms are extended upward; the hands and feet are cast out. This is the *ākṣiptaka* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.116).

Regarding the phrase "the foot is in the *svastika*," since this very [movement] extends as far as the *pādasvastika*, it indicates the *cārī* while describing the formation of the hips: "the two arms are extended upward" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.146).

Regarding the term *parāṅmukha*: among the *aṅgahāras*, the Sage, providing a general rule, says this: in all *aṅgahāras*, one should perform the movements (*karaṇas*) excluding the final pair of movements;
having employed those in the four directions, one should conclude facing forward with the final pair of movements.
(10) *Vaiśākharecita*. Regarding the term *recitau*: by this verse, he states that the *vaiśākharecita* is to be performed in sequence with two limbs.
"The *recita* of the hand and the foot," and so forth (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.98), refers to the *vaiśākharecita* *karaṇa*.
Having formed the *trika* well-rounded, with the hands in the *latā-recita* position and the foot likewise in the *nūpura* position—
this is the *nūpura-ūrdhva-pāda*. [It is performed] by lifting the bent foot, as stated in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.84).

"Bhujaṅgatrāsita" is the unmattakaraṇa (the mad gesture), characterized by a *recita* movement. Regarding the phrase "with the foot bent (*añcita*), the two [hands] are *recita*," it refers to the *maṇḍala* (the circular formation)—specifically the *maṇḍalasvastika*:
having formed the hands into a *svastika*, with palms facing upward and level, and directed forward.
By means of the maṇḍala posture; thus (Nā. Śā. 4.68, p.
150), one should likewise perform the *ālātaka* [fire-brand] movement, but rotate the triad.
And one should press the bent left hand against the region of the cheek. || 222 ||
Likewise, when the waist is severed, one should employ the *parāvṛtta* [turning] movement;
having performed the *svastika* formation, the two hands are then again extended outwards (*vyaṃsita*). || 223 ||

By the term *bāhuśīrṣa*, he refers to the *nikuṭṭita* gesture, as stated [in the Nāṭyaśāstra]: "When the two hands are *nikuṭṭita*" (Nā. Śā. 4.69). The collection of gestures beginning with *ūrūdvṛtta* is like the *aṅgahāra* described in sequence. (11) *Parāvṛtta*.
Regarding the phrase "the first" (*ādya*): "One hand is placed on the chest and the second is hanging down;
the foot is positioned on the tip of the palm [of the first hand]—this is the *janita*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.155). Thus, the word "first" (*ādya*)...
He states that this [karaṇa] is to be employed with the right limb: "One should extend one foot"—thus he describes the *śakaṭāsya* (cart-mouth) karaṇa:
"Seated, having extended the foot, moving the sole."

Having raised the chest and formed the "cart-mouth" (*śakaṭāsya*) posture, one should place the foot like a firebrand (*alāta*) and extend the right hand; performing this sequence with the knee raised is the *alātaka* posture. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.168, 4.78)

Thus ends the *alāta*. As for the *bhramaraka*, it is said: "One should rotate the triple-joint (*trika*). Furthermore: "The foot is drawn back into a *svastika*, the hands are likewise rotated inward, and this is due to the flexion of the *trika*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.99).
By this half-verse beginning with "the left hand bent," he specifies that the *karihasta* gesture should be struck against the region of the cheek (*gaṇḍadeśa*).
The left hand is placed upon the chest, while the other [right] hand has its palm turned upward.
Having performed the añcita foot, the *karihastaka* should be employed. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.148) "Alternately" (*paryāyaśas*) means with a broken waist. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.71, p.
One should employ the *alātaka* (firebrand) movement with the knees raised and tucked;
likewise, the *ardhasūcī*, the *vikṣipta*, and the *udvṛtta-ākṣiptaka*. || 224 ||
In the *aṅgahāra* known as *alātaka*, one should perform the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinnaka* gestures;
having bent the hands toward the chest, one should then raise the knees upward. || 225 ||
(12) Alātaka:
"Svastika," and so forth. According to the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.68), "the two svastikas" constitute the *svastika* [hand-gesture].
By the dual number in "and the two *vyaṃsita*s," he indicates the double employment of the *vyaṃsita* gesture, separated by the *svastika*.

Where one stands in the *ālīḍha* posture with both hands extended at the chest, one hand upward and the other downward, it is called *vyaṃsita* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.109). Having placed the foot in the *alāta* position, one should extend the right hand.
"One should perform the *ūrdhvajānu* sequence; this is the *alātaka* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.78).
Raising the bent foot, one should place the knee level with the breast;
the two hands are under the control of the performance in the *ūrdhvajānu* [posture] (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.86)."
Having made the foot like a scorpion, one should contract the hand at the side;
and the right [hand] at the tip of the nose—this is *nikuñcita*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.87) *Alapadma* is in the region of the head, and the right foot is like a needle. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.138)
The Half-Needle (ardhasūcī): When the hands and feet are cast out to the side or even behind, moving along a single path, that is the Vikṣipta [step]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.119)
"With upthrown hands, with upthrown feet, with the body twisted upward—this is the *udvṛttakaraṇa*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.152).
"Where the hands and feet are thrown out with speed, that is the *ākṣipta* [movement]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.116).
Thus is the *ākṣipta*.

"The left hand is placed on the chest with its palm turned upward, while the other [right hand] is bent; and the foot is likewise bent"—this is the *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand) (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.148). Alternately, it is called *kaṭicchinnā* (the hip-severed) (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.72), which is the *kaṭicchinnā* [mudrā].
Having performed the *ākṣiptasvastika*, one should rotate the three [limbs];
the two hands form the *uraḥmaṇḍalaka* [mudrā], and the hips form the *karihastaka*. (226)
Likewise, the *kaṭicchinna* (waist-cut) and *pārśvaccheda* (side-cut) are prescribed;
one should apply the *sūcī* (needle-step) with the left foot and the *vidyudbhrānta* (lightning-turn) with the right.
Furthermore, with the right [hand] there is the needle, and with the left, the whirling lightning;
likewise, there is the severed and the one that has overstepped on the left.
(13) *Pārśvaccheda* (The Side-Cut).
"Having cut," and so forth. By this, he describes the forty-second technique, the *Vṛścikakuṭṭita*.
Having placed the foot like a scorpion, both [feet] are then cut (*nikuṭṭita*).

The two hands are to be positioned [as described]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.103) "The foot is bent" refers to Ūrdhvajānu (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.86); "the hand and foot are thrown forward" refers to Ākṣiptaka (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.116);
and "with both hands and both feet" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.75).
The Svastika. Regarding the formation of the *uro-maṇḍalaka* through the two hands:
"When the feet have moved away from the *svastika*, there is the *āviddha* step; at that time, the two hands form the *uro-maṇḍalaka*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.115).
The triad beginning with *nitamba* is as before. (14) *Vidyudbhrānta*.

Regarding the phrase "the needle" (*sūcī*) and so forth, he describes the formation of the half-needle hand (*ardhasūcīkaraṇa*) to be employed on the left side of the body: "the *alapadma* [hand] is at the region of the head."
(NAŚĀ 4.138) The *vidyudbhrānta* movement with the right [hand]:
one should extend the foot, which is turned backward and rubbed against the head;
it is the *vidyudbhrānta*, pierced in all directions like a mandala. (NAŚĀ 4.126)
To the south of this [is the next]. Again, these same two [positions] with the limbs reversed. Thus it says, "again to the south.
"Paricchinnam" means the instrument (karaṇa) is cut;
as for the two shoots (pallavau), they are cut at the region of the hips, which is the hip in its various aspects.
By means of the Vaiśākha stance (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.106,
it is known as the *latā* [gesture], the *sakatichinna*, and the *vidyudbhrānta*.
Having performed the *nūpurapāda* posture, with the right and left [legs] hanging down. || 229 ||
Then, with those two hands at the sides, one should perform the *vikṣipta*;
likewise, with those same two, the *sūcī*, and one should rotate the *trika*. || 230 ||
In the *udvṛttaka* [mudrā], one should always perform the *latākhya* [hand gesture] with the hips turned;
the hands should be in *ālīḍha* and *vyasita* positions, and one should strike at the head of the arm. (231)
Having performed the *atikrāntakrama* (the crossing-step), one should extend [the hands] forward;
the two hands, under the influence of the *prayoga*, are in the *atikrānta* position. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.127) This, with the left limb, is called *latā*; thus it is the *latāvṛścika*.

The left hand is called *latā* (the creeper), with the foot bent backward and the fingers curved upward with their palms facing up; this is the *latāvṛścika* (creeper-scorpion). The *kaṭicchinna* (waist-broken) is as described before.
(15) *Udvṛttaka*: Having performed the *nūpurapāda* [step],
having made the triple-folded (*trika*) well-turned, and having formed the two hands in the *latārecitaka* [mudrā].

"And likewise, one should place the anklet on the foot in the *nupūra* [movement]. By using the dual number for "hands" (*karau*) and by mentioning them alternately as "right and left," it indicates simultaneity;
thus, the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* (the thirty-second) and the *bhujaṅgāñcita* (the fortieth) [are described].
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Gṛdhrāvalīnaka," demonstrates the seventy-fourth *karaṇa*:
"The right foot is in the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* position, the right hand is *recita*,
and the left hand is called *latā*" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.101).

"With the foot extended behind, the knee slightly bent, and the two arms stretched out—that is the *gṛdhrāvalīnaka* posture" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.135). For this very reason, he concludes with these two *karaṇas* immediately followed by the *vikṣipta*. Thus, the *vikṣipta*.

Regarding the phrase "and the hands and feet" (*hastapādaṃ ca*) [Nā. Śā. 4.119], he states in the concluding summary that this also occurs through the sequence of the limbs of desire: "Immediately after those two, the *sūcī*.
The left foot should be in the *nūpura* position and the right in the *alāta*;
with that very [stance], one should perform the *ākṣiptaka*, while the two hands are in the *uro-maṇḍala* position.
One should employ the *karihasta* hand-gesture in the *kaṭicchinna* (waist-cut) posture during the *ālīḍha* stance;
having made the hand *recita* (extended), one should bend the side and extend it.
Again, by that very same yoga, one should exhale the measure of the body; the exhalation (recaka) is to be performed upon the circle of the chest.

Because the application [of the yoga] is perceived through that sequence of limbs, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is raised for the sake of joining them. (By means of the triple rotation and the bound *āryā*, the *nitamba* is the instrument;
then, by "the foot bent backwards" and so forth, the forty-fourth [instrument], the *latāvṛścika*; then the *kaṭicchinnam*).
(16) Ālīḍha.
Regarding "ālīḍha":
the ālīḍha stance is that in which the two hands are extended toward the chest.
"Upward and downward, and scattered—this is *vyaṃsitam*" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.109);

thus he demonstrates *vyaṃsitam*. "With the head of the arm"—this is the ninth *karaṇa*, *nikuṭṭaka*. "When the two hands are *nikuṭṭita* to the left, [with] the anklet [on the thirty-sixth]" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.69); this is the *nikuṭṭitaka* *karaṇa*.

Then, having made the *alāta* foot, one should perform the *vyamsita* [step] (*alātakam*) (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.78). "By that very [hand]" means by the right [hand]. "With the hand and foot thrown forward" refers to the *ākṣipta* [movement] (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.116). The three *karaṇas*, beginning with *uraḥmaṇḍala*, are as before.

(17) *Recita*. "The hand is *recita*. By this verse, he includes all *karaṇas* that possess the *recana* (extension) of the hands. And so he will conclude later with the words, "the *recita* *karaṇa*. For the singular number is used here in the sense of a class (*jāti*).

One might perform something; for there is a performance called *recita* which is expressed by this term. By the word "kārya" (to be performed), it indicates that the composition of those various *karaṇas*—joined as limbs through one's own intellect and as if they were one's own effects—is indeed a marvelous (*citram*) task. For this very reason, this *aṅgahāra* is a mixture of diverse varieties.
And so it is heard elsewhere:
"When an *aṅgahāra* is performed, however, one should execute the 'waist-cut' (*kaṭicchinna*)."
Having placed the foot in the *nūpura* position, one should then rotate the triple-joint (*trika*).

"By means of twenty-five diverse *mātṛkās*, Maheśvara produced various [movements], just as one produces the path of song (*geyamārga*) with seven notes, having performed the *recita* and *aṅgahāra*. Thus, regarding "the *svastika* and the *recita-viddha*" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.67), there is the *svastika-recita*. The hand is thrown out (*apaviddha*) by means of the *sūcī* [finger].
(Nāṭya Śāstra 4.72) and so forth constitute the *ardharecita* [gesture].

"The chest is in the *svastika* position, and the *unmatta* [hand]—these are the first twelve," and "the left hand should be at the heart" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.80) constitute the *ākṣiptarecita*. "The foot is stumbling and withdrawn"—this is the *ardhamattalli* (Nāṭya Śāstra).
4-89) *recakanikuṭṭakaṃ* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4-90),
having performed *bhujaṅgatrāsita*, where both [feet] are *recita*;
these three beginning with that are *bhujaṅgatrastarecita* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4-96) and *nūpura* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4-97).
And the Vaiśākharecita (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.98);
"the foot is in the bhujaṅgatrāsita [position] and the right hand is recited" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.101)— these two *karaṇas*, namely the Bhujaṅgāñcitaka and the Daṇḍarecitaka (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.102).

*Vṛścikarecita* is defined as "having made the foot like a scorpion and the hands in the *svastika* [position]," and so forth (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.107). *Vyaṃsita* is defined as "wherein there is the *ālīḍha* stance," and so forth (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.109). *Ākṣipta* consists of the two [movements] beginning with "the hand and foot," and so forth (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.122). *Vivṛtta* and *vinivṛtta* are defined in *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.123.

"The hand and foot are drawn back and the *trika* is turned" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.128)—this is the *vivartitaka*. "The foot is extended behind," and so forth (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.131)—this is the *garuḍaplutaka*.
"Having placed the foot like a scorpion, and likewise the hands are *recita*" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.141).

Thus ends the Mayūralalita; and the Prasarpitaka (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.142). "The sequence of the swing-step should be performed" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.147), and so forth, is the Skhalita. "But one is the Recita" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.149) is the Prasarpitaka. "The sequence of the swing-step" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.154) is the Talasaṅghaṭṭita.

One should employ the pair beginning with *alātakam* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.165), as well as *vṛṣabhakrīḍitakam* and *lolitam* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.166). In this manner, the twenty-five *karaṇas* should be applied with variety,
following the sequence of four, six, and so forth.
With the hand turned away, one should rotate the very same triad; having made the left hand *ālātaka*, one should apply the *sūcī* right there. || 236 ||
One should always perform the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* gestures when executing the *ācchurita*;
likewise, the feet are extended in the *svastika* position and the hands are extended in the *svastika* position.
Having thus effected the separation by that same procedure,
one should again perform the upward lifting using the very same *recaka* breathings.
Due to its repetitive nature, it continues until it is completed in the four directions; for it is said:

"The *aṅgahāra* consists of two, three, or even four *mātṛkās*" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.31). Then, by that same yoga, one bends the limbs with this [phrase], moving in a circular pattern through variety in the middle.
He states that this succession of instrumental actions is to be employed when there is an interval:
"When [the dancer] has both arms hanging down and the body is bent, that which is cast inward should be known as the *cakramaṇḍala*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.114)
The word *ānamya* and so forth contains the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). The application [of the movement] should be performed as follows:
first, the *vīro-maṇḍala* and the *kaṭicchinna*;
(18) then the *ācchurita*.

"An anklet," and so forth. By the phrase "one should rotate the measured *trika* [triangle] as an anklet," the *bhramaraka* (swarming bee) step is implied—the *svastika* foot... and the turning of the *trika*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.99).
Regarding "by the *vyaṃsita*," *vyaṃsita* refers to that stance (*sthānaka*) which is the *ālīḍha*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.109).

Then the *alātaka*: "having made the *alāta* [the *caraṇa*]" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.78). By the word "only" (*eva*) in "only the *trika*," it is indicated that "the buttocks and the two arms are extended upwards" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.146).
Following that, there are two *karaṇas* as before.

(19) *Ākṣiptarecita* [is defined as]: "the two *recita* [hands] in the *svastika* [position]," and so forth. In whatever *karaṇa* there is a combination of *recita* and *svastika* for either the hands or the feet, that very thing is permitted here as well by means of its separate designation. *Recita*.

Indeed, by this very [method], these *karaṇas* are formed: the *svastikarecita*, the *svastikau recitāv iddhau* (as described in Nāṭyaśāstra 4.76–77), the *pṛṣṭhasvastika* and *diksvastika* with arms cast out and drawn in (*vikṣiptākṣiptabāhubhyām*), and so forth;
the *kaṭīsama* and *svastikāpasṛta* foot (as described in Nāṭyaśāstra 4.79); and the *bhūrṇita*.
(157) Furthermore, there are indeed the *udvṛtta*, the *ākṣiptaka*, the *uromaṇḍala*,
the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*. || 239 ||
For this method of the *karaṇas* is traditionally taught as being performed with the limbs cast out and bent;
having executed the *vikṣipta-karaṇa*, the hands and feet follow the movement of the face.
The right hand is rotated and whirled, while the left is swung;
the foot is drawn back in the *svastika* position. (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.93). Thus is the *bhramaraka*; [also] the *ākṣipta-svastika-pāda* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.99); and the *vṛścikarecita*.
"Making the feet scissor-like (*vṛścika*) and [forming] the *svastika*," thus [it is said in] the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.107). This is the *pārśvanikuṭṭaka*.

"The two hands, however, are in the *svastika* position at the side," thus [it is said in] the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.110). This is the *uraḥmaṇḍalaka*. "With the *svastika* [hands] drawn back," thus [it is said in] the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.115). This is the *sannata*. "Having leaped, the two feet should be placed in front in the *svastika* position," thus [it is said in the *Nāṭyaśāstra*].

"Like a lion drawing [its prey]" (*siṃhākarṣitaka*) according to *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.136; "with the back extended" (*pṛṣṭhaprasārita*) according to *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.151; "the *nāgāpasarpita*" according to *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.167, which states: "the feet are drawn back in the *svastika*. However, because there is no *recana* (extension/bending) in the *vakṣaḥ-svastika* and other such movements, they are not included here. Others, however, maintain that even in those cases, it occurs through the sequence of the rotation of the limbs.
Those who desire the *recita* [movement] also include that;

likewise, having performed the *hastapādasvastika* and the *tadrecita* with variety according to that very same method, the raising of the hand and foot must be done with the limbs remaining unbroken. By this, wherever—

Wherever this [description] exists, it indicates that particular instrument (*karaṇa*). For example: "Having placed the staff-wing (*daṇḍapakṣa*) with the knees raised, one should then place a creeper (*latā*) upon it" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.95); "having made a forehead-mark (*lalāṭatilaka*), a scorpion (*vṛścika*), and a foot" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.111); "the *talavilāsita* is a foot with the fingers pointing upward" (Nāṭyaśāstra).
*Niśumbhita*:
the foot is bent backward and the chest is raised;
the hand should be placed on the forehead mark (*tilaka*). Thus [it is said in] *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.125.
"Whirling like lightning with the foot turned back"—this is the *gajakrīḍita* (elephant-play) [according to Nāṭyaśāstra 4.126];

"the left hand bent at the ear"—this is the *karṇa* [gesture] [according to Nāṭyaśāstra 4.129]; "the two arms extended upward"—this is the *nitamba* [gesture] [according to Nāṭyaśāstra 4.146]; "the foot extended upward"—this is the *viṣṇukrānta* [gesture].
Accompanied by the left index finger, one should wave the left hand.
In the region of the chest, there should be the left [breast], as well as the three-fold curling mark.
The *nūpurākṣiptaka*, the *ardhasvastika*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *uromaṇḍalaka*. || 242 ||

When [the dancer] is bewildered, the performers of the dance should execute the "severed waist" (kaṭicchinna), having performed the "withdrawn step" (apakrāntakrama) and the "deceived hand" (vyaṃsitahasta). || 243 ||

From that, "udvṛtta" refers to the *ūrūdvṛtta* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.159). Since this is seen among the *samākṣipta* movements, one should rotate the movement and perform that specific motion. "The hand and foot are thrown out" (*ākṣipta*) refers to the *ākṣipta* movement (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.116). "The feet are drawn away in a *svastika*" refers to the *ūromaṇḍala* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.115).
And because of the word "and" (ca), as well as due to association (sāhacarya), some maintain that even [the term] *kaṭicchinnam* is intended at the end.
(20) *Sambhrānta* (the bewildered):
"The scattered," and so forth. "With hands and feet scattered" (*nā. śā. 4-119*) refers to the *vikṣipta* (scattered).
"Hands and feet following the face" indicates the *añcita* (bent), as well as the *gaṇḍasūcī* and *gaṅgāvatara*.
When that same hand is turned away and turned around so as to be oblique toward the tip of the nose— according to the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.83)—
it is called *gaṇḍasūcī*, "the cheek-pointing," as described in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (4.132) as "the side raised like a needle."
"The foot with its palm facing upward, the two hands bent downward like the triple-bannered gesture (*tripatākā*)—this is the *Gaṅgāvataraṇa* [mudrā]" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.169).
By the phrase "accompanied by the left *sūcī*," he indicates the *ardhasūcī* and the *daṇḍapāda*. [Then there is] the *alapaḍma*.
"In the region of the head" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.138)—this refers to the half-sūcī.
Having placed the foot in the *nūpura* position, one should extend the leg in the *daṇḍapāda* [position].
"With the hand quickly thrust forward" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.143)—this refers to the *daṇḍapāda*.
One should likewise perform the *udveṣṭita*, the *ardhasūcī*,
the *vikṣipta*, the *sakaṭicchanna*, as well as the *udvṛtta* and the *ākṣiptaka*. (244)
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* gestures should be performed during the *apasarpaṇa*;
having executed the *nūpurapāda*, one should then strike the *drugha* step.
And this is performed with the left side of the body. "Savya" refers to the right chest, because of the utility of the left side. By this, he indicates the *catura* (fourfold) movement:
"The left hand should be bent (*añcita*), and the right should indeed be *catura*."
"The right foot is stamped; that is proclaimed as *catura*. (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.100).

"The *trika* is turned" refers to the *bhramaraka*; "the *ākṣipta* [is performed] with the *svastika*" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.99); "having made the *trika* well-turned" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.97) refers to the *nūpura*. The hand and foot are also *ākṣipta*.

Thus it is introduced. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.116) Having formed the *svastika* foot-position and placing the right hand on the hip, one likewise places the left hand at the chest; this is the *ardhasvastika*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.82)
The *ityardhasvastika* [is as follows]. The four [positions] beginning with *nitamba* are as before. (242) (21) *Apasarpita*. *Apakrānta*, etc. *Apakrānta*—
"Having rotated the foot across the thigh, one should place it in the *apakrānta* step;
the two hands, under the control of the application, are in the *apakrānta* [position]. (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.140).
"The *vyaṃsita*" is the *ālīḍha* stance where the two hands are at the chest. Therefore...

By the use of the particle *eva*, he indicates that one should grasp only the action of the hand from the "twisted" (*vyaṃsita*) hand-posture. The singular number is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). He points out the "unwound" (*udveṣṭita*) hand-posture of the elephant-hand (*karihasta*) with the verse: "The left hand is placed on the chest, while the other has its palm turned upward and unwound" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.148). [This is] the *alapadma* [hand-posture].

The *ardhasūcī* (half-sūcī) is defined as "the foot like a needle at the region of the head" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.138). The *vikṣipta* (scattered) is defined as "the hands and feet scattered" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.119). The *kaṭicchinnā* (waist-broken) is defined as "alternately [broken] at the waist" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.71). Here, the term *udvṛtta* refers to the *urūdvṛtta* (thigh-turned), as stated in *Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.159. As before, [this applies] at the end.
(Three) modes of action. (244) Now, the *ardhasūcī*:
one should cause the two hands and the triple-joint (*trika*) to follow the foot and rotate.
Having contracted the hands and feet, one should again form the circle of hair on the chest.
The *karihasta*, the *kaṭicchinna*, and the *kārya* [are used] in the *ardhanikuṭṭaka*;
these thirty-two *aṅgahāras* have been proclaimed, O best of the twice-born. (247)
(22) *Ardhanikuṭṭaka*:

"Having performed the *nūpurapāda*," and so forth. Having made the three [parts] well-turned—this is the *nūpurapāda* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.97). With the words "having quickly drawn back," etc., he describes the *vivṛtta* movement.

"O twice-born ones, in the *vivṛtta* karaṇa, the hands and feet are thrown out (*ākṣipta*), the *trika* is turned (*vivartita*), and likewise the two hands are extended (*recita*). Thus (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.122). By the word "having contracted" (*nikuṭya*), he refers to those *karaṇas* in which the hands and feet are contracted (*nikuṭṭita*).

The *nikuṭṭita*, *ardhanikuṭṭaka*, and so forth; the triad beginning with *ura-maṇḍalaka* is like the previous *aṅgahāras*. Regarding those which are *aṅgahāras*, their counter-performance (*pratikaraṇa*) is of the same magnitude as the original; its execution is possible through the sequence of *vartanā* (turning) for as long as it takes to complete the *kalās* (temporal units). Among those, which...

The six, twelve, twenty-four, and so forth, which consist of the *karaṇas*, when combined with one or two practiced [units], are to be understood by means of the triangular measure (*tryaśra*). This is because it is possible to insert them into the middle of one or two [units] through the application of *tāla* and *kalā*. And these sixteen are present here.

As before, those consisting of eight, sixteen, and so forth— whether practiced with one or two [beats], or perhaps slightly more— are to be understood as pertaining to the square *tāla* (caturaśratāla). It should be considered that even if one of these sixteen is occasionally deficient, it can still be rectified through the performance of another.
Among those, the *apaviddha*, *udghaṭṭita*, *viṣkambha*, *tadapasṛta*, *svastikarecita*, *vṛścikāpasṛta*,
*mattaskhalita*, *gatimaṇḍala*, *parivṛttakarecita*, *parāvṛttaka*, *alātaka*,
*udvṛttaka*, *recita*, *ākṣiptarecita*, *sambhrānta*, and *ardhanikuṭṭaka* are the sixteen *tryaśratāla* (triangular rhythmic patterns). Of these:
There are as many [performances] as there are square-based [theatrical spaces]. In that regard,

some maintain that because they are performed within the thirty-two forms— consisting of the sixteen intermediate subdivisions of the two-fold primary divisions of the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary ritual), beginning with *utthāpana* and ending with *prarocanā*, all of which take place outside the curtain— the total number is thirty-two.

However, some say: for each performance of four dancers there are four [movements], and since the *piṇḍī*, *recaka*, *nyāsa*, and *apanyāsa* occur four times each, there are thirty-two. We shall clarify this in the explanation of the *pūrvaraṅga* (Nāṭya Śāstra 5); so, enough of this.
(161) Furthermore, learn from me as I describe the four *recakas*:
the first is the *pādarecaka* (foot-extension), and the second is the *kaṭirecaka* (hip-extension). || 248 ||
The third is the hand-releasing [movement], while the fourth is the throat-releasing;
that which is called *recita* is designated for separation and for turning.
Recaka (the exhalation) consists of lifting up, moving apart, and also shifting;
it involves moving from one side to another with faltering and wavering steps.
Others, however, maintain that for *gītakas*—whether based on *aṅgas*, *vastus*, or both—the *vastu* is threefold;
there are nine *vardhamāna* causes, four *āsāritas*, and one type of *pāṇika*. It is because of such variety in the *brahmagītis* that thirty-two [types] have been proclaimed.

Therefore, they say that even in the *aṅgahāra* [of the performance], it lasts for only that long due to its application. Others, however, say that because it was spoken by the Supreme Lord, it is a cause for the attainment of all fruits, as is appropriate.
Having kept this in mind, he concludes again: "These thirty-two... (247).

Now he describes the *recakas* (exhalations), beginning with "the foot-recaka": it consists of the movement of the feet alone—not the heels or the soles—but the bending, lowering, raising, and swinging of them inward and outward, as well as the movement of the tips of the big toes. The movement of the hands alone is like that of two swan-wings, performed alternately.

[This refers to] rapid whirling; the neck being bent back (recita), as well as shaking and turning; and from whirling in all directions, one should know [the posture] called *recitāṅgaka*. By the mention of these specific numbers, [the author] demonstrates that these are to be employed separately by one standing in positions such as *vaiśākha* or *maṇḍala*, using the *vaiśākharecita* [movement].

He shows that these are included within the *karaṇas*; furthermore, they are mentioned even though they are contained within the *aṅgahāras* of the *karaṇas*, for the purpose of demonstrating that they have a distinct, unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
And their employment occurs in a performance where soft singing and instrumental music are predominant.
Tumburu said this:

"The wise know the *recakas* through the *aṅgahāras* and the operations (*karaṇas*) at the beginning, middle, and end. Here too, it is evident that this is the opinion of the Sage, since he points out [the *recakas*] here and there with the word "together" (*saha*), stating, "I shall explain the *sarecakas*" (*Nāṭyaśāstra*).

4-19) Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: do the *karaṇas*, *aṅgahāras*, and *recakas* serve merely to produce variety within the *pūrvaraṅga* itself? We say: no; we do not maintain that here [their function is limited to that].
The *pādarecaka* is said to consist of various movements of the foot,
as well as the upward turning of the triple-joint (*trika*) and the bending of the waist.
Likewise, *apasarpaṇa* (stepping aside) is called *kaṭirecaka*;
[the others are] *udvartana*, *parikṣepa*, *vikṣepa*, and *parivartana*.
The spreading of the hand is called *hastarecaka*;
likewise, there are *udvāhana* (lifting), *sannamana* (lowering), and *pārśvasannati* (inclining to the side).
The wise should also recognize the whirling of the neck as a *recaka*.
Having seen Śaṅkara dancing with *recakas* and *aṅgahāras*, [the gods were amazed]. (249)
And Pārvatī was dancing with graceful movements,
accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, paṭahas, bhāṇḍas, ḍiṇḍimas, and gomukhas.
How, then? Also by way of pleasing the deities. And that too is merely for the sake of variety.

With the intention that [this is achieved] through the means of producing the *piṇḍībandha*—which serves as a representation of the banners of those respective deities—the sage Bharata spoke of a former tradition (*purākalpa*) in four verses in order to introduce the *piṇḍībandha*:

By the words "with recakas and aṅgahāras," and so forth; here there are four *ca*s (conjunctions). Among them, one indicates a cause (*hetu*) and the others indicate conjunction (*samuccaya*). The connection is as follows:
because [the sacrifice] was characterized by mṛdaṅgas and other instruments struck by the Pramathas, who were overwhelmed by intense joy, at the sacrifice of Dakṣa.

When [the enemy] was slain, she danced out of the power of her great joy; the construction "nṛtyantīṃ nṛtyantīm" (dancing while dancing) is formed according to the rule *dhātusambandhe pratyayāḥ* (suffixes are used when there is a connection between verbal roots). Otherwise, one would have to say "nṛttavantam" (one who has already danced), and so forth. At the time of twilight, which is the end of the day, that is, at a moment of expansion through delight—and for that very reason, being meritorious in nature—she dances constantly, intensely, and exceedingly.
For that reason: having seen Śaṅkara dancing with graceful movements (*aṅgahāra*) and *recaka* gestures, yet not in a delicate manner;

and having seen the Blessed Lady dancing according to the true nature of the matter (*arthatattva*), employing only delicate techniques. "From that very [source]" means from those very [elements]; namely, the *aṅgahāras* and the *recakas*.
Having seen those group-formations (*piṇḍībandha*) caused by that [deity], Nandin, as well as Bhadramukha, Vīrabhadra,
and other such hosts of deities headed by Nandin and Bhadra, gave them the name *piṇḍībandha*.
And because of the similarity of their forms, they performed this practice of *piṇḍībandha* according to its defining characteristics.

"Up to the limit of the characteristics. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of "limit. The meaning is that, having observed the perfection of specific forms as being inseparable from the performance of the *aṅgahāras*, they correctly applied [the movements] and established the characteristics. Because of the two being performers, [it results in] a delicate meter—
When the sacrifice of Dakṣa had been destroyed, at the time of twilight, Maheśvara [was accompanied] by the sounding of paṇavas, darduras, and all kinds of musical instruments. (251)
They danced with various gestures of the limbs, following the rhythms and beats;
then, having seen the formations of the dance groups, the Gaṇas headed by Nandin and Bhadra [approached].
They gave names to these lumps according to their characteristics:
the lump of Īśvara is Īśvarī, and that of Nandin is Paṭṭasī.

By the simultaneous performance of the two dances, he indicates the accomplishment of the *piṇḍībandha* formation: "the hosts headed by Nandibhadra. By this, he also states that there may be four or more performers—namely, the group called Nandibhadra.
The *mṛdaṅga* drum occupies the position fixed for Nandikeśvara; the *muraja* and the *bherī* [drums occupy their respective places].
The *maharṣaka*, *bhaṅga*, and *mardala* are filled with fragments of bell-metal; the *ḍiṇḍima* is a *karaṭikā*;

the *gomukha* is a *dhaṅgī* (or *ḍhaṅgī*); the *paṭaha* is joined with internal strings (*antarīyukta*) or joined with stretched strings (*tatantrīyukta*); the *paṇava*, *dardura*, and the support for the great *ghaṭikā*—all these are varieties of drums covered with leather. *Laya*...
It consists of the fast, medium, and slow tempos; its foundation is the *tāla*.

Furthermore, it consists of the essence of the various musical elements (*dhātu*)—such as specific flutelike sounds regulated by particular types of increasing songs—and the nature of the dry performance consisting of all types of percussion instruments (*avanaddha-vādya*) established upon a fixed rhythm (*laya*).

And in drama, it is through a change [of state] according to the transformation of the mental states to be employed; having effected a connection with its power—that is, its capacity—and being followed by that [power], it should be understood in both ways through the principle of *tantra* (concise expression), namely, as "having been followed" (*anusṛtam*) and as "being followed" (*anugamyamānaḥ*). This [actor] follows the power of the tempo (*laya*) and the rhythm (*tāla*), because he conforms to the power of the tempo and the rhythm.
Regarding the phrase "wherein":

[an objection is raised]—but surely tempo (*laya*) and so forth follow the limbs only in *nāṭya* (dramatic performance), not in *nṛtta* (pure dance); for *nāṭya* has a distinct division within the *āṅgika* (gestural) category.
It is replied: here, the purpose of employing the *vardhamāna* and other rhythmic patterns is to achieve the attainment of specific transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

And regarding the performance of dance with its accessories, there is freedom of choice concerning the status of the subordinate and the principal elements. When the song and so forth are primary, then the bodily movements (aṅga) must conform to them.
It is with this very intention that he will say:
"One should employ the *cārī* in accordance with that movement which follows the instrumental music" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.281).
However, when the dance is given primacy as a means of producing invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*), then it [the *cārī*] should be performed in accordance with that.
There is the recourse to *gītaka* and other such forms. As he will state with reference to them:
"One *gītaka*, such as the *madraka* and others among songs, is to be employed;
or else, the *vardhamāna* is used here, wherein the *tāṇḍava* is appropriate" (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.13).

By this fourth quarter [of the verse], the predominance of *tāṇḍava* and its utility for the *gītaka* and so forth are stated; yet there is no difference from *nāṭya*. For in *nāṭya*, both the bodily gesture (*aṅga*) and the song (*gītaka*) are established; likewise, [it includes] the hands, feet, *cārīs*, *maṇḍalas*, and so on.

Whatever is useful as a constituent element (*aṅga*) therein is necessarily fixed by its own nature or by the arrangement of tempo (*laya*) and so forth, because it is employed according to the specific sentiment (*rasa*), and not otherwise. This should be understood to apply likewise to the singing of the *dhruvā* and other such elements.
For that very *dhruvā* is sometimes employed with a quick tempo (*druta*) and sometimes with a slow tempo (*vilambita*); thus both [tempos] occur [in certain instances]. In that case as well—

And song is the application of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) [which is the tantra]. But here, both song and its constituent parts (*aṅga*) are self-established. For indeed, whatever specific nature of tempo, time-measure, and pitch has been defined for each does not deviate, just like mantras and so forth; nor is it like the Vedas [in this regard].

The relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is established through their mutual application. For instance, in the case of the *aṅgahāra* [dance movement] defined as "thrown away" (*apaviddha*) and "quick" (*druta*) (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.207), even in the *gītaka* and other such forms, the tempo (*laya*) and other elements occurring within the stream of the flow are not performed otherwise. Therefore, this [work] restricts the general principle that "the qualities (*guṇas*) follow the principal (*pradhāna*). However...

Even when two factors are established independently, the relationship of constituent and constituted (*aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva*) consists merely in this: that whatever is fit to be combined with another is applied to it.
This is like the case of two kings who possess pride and indignation arising from the onset of a conflict with an enemy; for this very reason, it is "applied."
Thus it has been said; by that very statement, performing [the rite] in such a manner is indicated.

In that context, since the drums and other musical instruments were set in motion by the Pramathas when Dakṣa’s sacrifice was destroyed, the dance follows that [music]. During the twilight hours, which consist of the outpouring of the bliss that is the heart's essence—
O Blessed One, since dance is primary, there is the engagement of instrumental music and so forth;
it is for this very reason that the meaning has been stated generally by means of the third case ending denoting a characteristic (itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa).
And the mention of these two occasions is precisely for this purpose; for when something is a defining characteristic, it is observed to be exactly thus.
For instance—just as in the case of *ḍombikā* and similar forms, song itself at that time serves another purpose, while dance and so forth function as subordinate to it;
for even there, the movements of the feet and other limbs are performed with delicate members.
Furthermore, in some cases, such as in *prasthāna* and the like, there is a predominance of either the vocal elements (*varṇa*) or the bodily gestures (*aṅga*).
In some cases, there is a predominance of the subject matter expressed through song, as in the *Tripuradāha-ḍima* and similar works (in the category of *śilpaka*, etc.);

in other cases, there is a predominance of instrumental music, as in the *bhāṇaka* and similar works, involving the performance of broken (*bhagna*) or irregular (*khaṇḍa*) time-measures (*tāla*); and in some cases, there is a predominance of dance (*nṛtta*), as for example...
Following the performance of the *ḍombikā* and other dances, at the occasion of the *huḍukka* drum,
there should be a *piṇḍī* for Caṇḍikā, likewise borne by a lion.
The Tārkṣyapiṇḍī belongs to Viṣṇu, and the Padmapiṇḍī belongs to Svayambhū.
The *piṇḍī* of Śakra is Airāvatī; the *piṇḍī* of Mānmatha is Jhaṣapiṇḍī; the *piṇḍī* of Kumāra is Śikhipiṇḍī; and the *piṇḍī* of Śrī is Rūpapiṇḍī. (255)
The *dhārāpiṇḍī* belongs to the Gaṅgā; the *pāśapiṇḍī* belongs to Yama;
the *nadīpiṇḍī* belongs to Varuṇa; and the *yākṣī* belongs to Kubera. (256)

For this very reason, it is well known there by the local vernacular as the *cillimārga*. Indeed, this is the *cārīmārga* because of the predominance of its constituent parts (*aṅga*). Even therein, due to its variety, singing, instrumental music, and so forth, also attain predominance from time to time. Furthermore, among instrumental music itself, there is predominance through the distinction between wind instruments (*suṣira*) and percussion (*āvanaddha*), and so on.
This should be analyzed according to its application; enough with further elaboration.

In this regard, these structural arrangements (*piṇḍībandha*) are divided into many types based on the distinctions of the foundation (*ādhāra*), the limbs (*aṅga*), the application (*prayoga*), and the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). Among these, the ground (*bhūmi*) consists of seven divisions each, due to the distinction between the two types of space (*ākāśa*).

Thus, there are seven varieties of substrates (*ādhāra*). There are also seven varieties of limbs (*aṅga*), namely: the two hands, the two feet, the two eyes, and the head; these together amount to forty-nine. Whether the performer be one or many, that performance—whether symmetrical (*samaprayoga*) or asymmetrical (*viṣamaprayoga*)—is accomplished through the *aṅgahāra* by means of this fourfold division.
By multiplying forty-nine by eight, there are three hundred and ninety-two *piṇḍībandhas* belonging to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarāḥ*).
At the time of twilight at the end of the night of cosmic dissolution, the multitude [of deities] [occupies] the courtyard of the limbs within the arena of the true void.
"Having attained a state variegated by the manifold movements and postures of extended limbs,
and weaving a diverse creation both in the sky and within Your own body, O Blessed One, You alone, the Architect of the Three Worlds and the Universal Form, expand forth. Thus [it is said].

And by this method, even the mere application of the *karaṇa*— by way of indicating the respective portions (*bhāga*) and so forth that possess the nature of the various deities within the *piṇḍībandhas*— becomes a source of joy. Thus, therein, with reference to the principal deity...

He demonstrates the arrangements of the *piṇḍī* (the ritual altar) with five verses beginning with "Of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*). Because the Blessed One alone is the primary object to be propitiated, the *piṇṇī* arrangement takes the form of a *śivaliṅga*, corresponding exactly to His unmanifest, undifferentiated nature which is denoted by the word "Lord" (*īśvara*).
The ball of *hal* belongs to Bala, while the ball of *sarpa* belongs to the serpents; the great ball of Gāṇeśvarī is the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. (257)
Raudrī, belonging to the enemy of Andhaka (Śiva), has the form and configuration of a trident;
likewise, it should be understood for the other deities as well, in their respective order. (258)

A *piṇḍī* is a collection of the foundational parts (*ādhārāṅga*) and so forth. It is called a *piṇḍībandha* because it is thus bound—that is, it is introduced into the intellect—or because it is formed as a physical body within space and the like; it is a specific configuration.
The term *piṇḍī* is used here to denote a part of that whole. Alternatively, it refers specifically to those [parts] characterized by such a *piṇḍī*.

Furthermore, that by which one is bound together is the *piṇḍībandha*, such as the *karaṇas* and *aṅgahāras*. And at the conclusion, there will be a *piṇḍībandha* of the Blessed One himself in his manifest form.
Following the Supreme Lord, there will be [the description] of the principal [deity], who establishes the characteristics of the *piṇḍībandha*.
Of Nandin; the *paṭṭasa* is a specific type of weapon shaped like a trident in both cases.

After that, [the seat] of the Blessed Lady: it is a lion and it is her vehicle, thus "of him" (i.e., of the lion). By virtue of being stepped upon. Or, the lion is the pedestal (*liṅga*) of the earth. This shows its resemblance to that form. After that, [the seats] of Viṣṇu and Brahmā.

*Airāvatī* is shaped like an elephant; *Rūpapiṇḍī* is shaped like a lotus (*padmā*). Furthermore, when *Dhārāpiṇḍī* is applied repeatedly, it becomes a river-mass (*nadīpiṇḍī*). *Yākṣī* is the weapon of Vaiśravaṇa and is shaped like a mallet (*mudgara*).
Having thus explained those to be established, he shows them elsewhere as well with the words "in this way" (*evam*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in others":
In the third chapter, they were described as objects of worship; it was with that very intention that the phrase "in due order" was stated.

They consist of the worship of the banner (*dhvaja*), the oblation (*āhuti*), the weapons (*āyudha*), and the specific mounts (*vāhana*). By the expression "possessing signs" (*sacihnakāḥ*), they are also characterized by certain forms that indicate [their respective] rituals and so forth.

This is what is meant: whatever deity is mentioned, she must subsequently be propitiated with dance. In the midst of that, a performance of bodily movements (*aṅgaprayoga*) imitating her weapons, vehicles, actions, and states must be performed. For this very reason, in the verse beginning with "standing on the tips of her feet" (*pādāgrasthitayā*), [this is implied].

The propitiation of the Bhagavatī is accomplished through the action of forming a cup with the palms and flowers (*talapuṣpapuṭakaraṇa*), which indicates a specific distinction. By the gesture of placing the hand upon the forehead (*tilake ca karaḥ sthāpya*)—this being the sixty-fourth *karaṇa*—the Bhagavān is propitiated. Furthermore, by the phrase "when the two hands are struck together" (*nikuṭṭitau yadā hastau*)—this being the ninth *karaṇa*—the form of a trident (*triśūlākṛti*) is produced.
Perfection of the body: indicating the movement in the form of Tārkṣya by means of the Garuḍa-leap; the continuous stream by means of the descent of the Gaṅgā; the gliding away of the nāgas (p.
The *piṇḍībandhas* should be employed as banners, clearly marked with signs;
likewise, there are *recakas*, *aṅgahāras*, and *piṇḍībandhas*. (251)

The *bhogapiṇḍī*: by extending and raising both hands with the *aṅgahāra* (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.174), there is the accomplishment of the *piṇḍīs* such as the *ākā(dhā)rīya*, the terrestrial trident (*bhaumatriśūla*), and the *śivaliṅga*. Through the *recita* and the *ākṣiptarecita*, there is the accomplishment of all the aforementioned varieties of movements (*cāra*) and supports (*cādhāra*), which are infinite in their divisions. Likewise...
And it is stated in the *Nandimat*:
"The *aṅgahāra* called *recita* is indeed twofold; by it the deities are entirely satisfied, therefore one should employ it in the *tāṇḍava*."
In this manner, other points should also be inferred; however, they have not been written down in their entirety due to lack of utility.
Only a general direction has been indicated for the purpose of preserving the tradition from decline.
He concludes this with the words "the exhalations" (*recakāḥ*), by means of the mention of the *piṇḍībandha*.

The collection of *karaṇas* such as *śikhipiṇḍi*, *mayūralalita*, and others consists of skillful means (*upāya*). For this very reason, even when a *karaṇa* is performed alone, its application serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) by pleasing the deity; just as that [application] occurs for the *viṣṇukrānta* and the *cakramaṇḍala*, which indicate the playful sports (*krīḍā*) of Viṣṇu.

By the word "eva" (only/itself), there is a connection with the formation of *piṇḍībandhas* as being inseparable from the application of *aṅgahāras*. Thus, *aṅgahāras* themselves are *piṇḍībandhas*, as well as other *piṇḍībandhas*; this is a summary of the *kevalakaraṇas*.
By the word "ca" (and), it is indicated that when both *karaṇas* serve as the means for the accomplishment of a *piṇḍībandha*, [the former term applies].

He states the permission for the performance of even that which is a constructed *aṅgahāra* consisting of a collection of movements: it is for this very purpose that the definition of the *nṛttamātṛkā* and the general definition of the *aṅgahāras* were composed. (248–259)

Regarding the word "having created" (*sṛṣṭvā*): One might object that this contradicts the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that dance (*nṛtta*) is performed during the junctions of the day (*sandhyā-kāla*). This is not so;

for although the positions (*sthānaka*), foot-movements (*cārī*), dances, hand-gestures (*hasta*), facial expressions (*bhūta*), and movements of the eyes (*tārā-karma*)—like the castes (*varṇa*)—are beginningless by way of their continuous flow, they were [nonetheless] brought forth by the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Self, through His particular excellence of beauty.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction in saying that the re-manifestation [of the world] is like that of the Vedas; for even though the letters of the Vedas are beginningless and eternal,
their arrangement is based on a sequence manifested through the successful impact of the respective places and articulators (sthāna-karaṇa) in each individual living being.

It is created; yet it is eternal through a continuous stream (*pravāha*) that is of the same nature as each preceding composition. Likewise, dance is also [eternal in this sense], so there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Regarding the word "given" (*dattā*): one who grants independence (*svātantrya*) to that [dance] regarding what is produced by his own intellect, in that [act of granting].

He shows that what has been introduced with variety does not contradict what has been seen; therefore, in this case, the predominance of beauty alone is superior.
