Thus, it should be understood that as long as the observed object (*lakṣya*) is not discordant, [the use of] the non-present tense (*anadyatana*) is not improper. "To the Sage" (*munaye*) means to one who is skilled in the processes of inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*) and so forth.
Having created them, they were then given by the Blessed One to the Sage during the *tāṇḍava* dance;
and by him, in turn, they were properly handed over along with the musical instruments (*gānabhāṇḍa*). || 260 ||
For this reason, since wealth has been bestowed, the performance consisting of dance is executed with perfect variety.

"Perfectly" (*samyak*) means that which proceeds (*samyañci*) in accordance with the proper rhythm (*tāla*) and harmony; thus, it refers to the song (*gīta*) that has become perfect. "Bhāṇḍa" refers to one who speaks or produces sound.
Or, by means of this etymology stated in the *Puṣkarādhyāya*—namely, "that which is to be performed" (*bhaḍitavyam*)—it is called *tāṇḍava*.

Here, that song and instrumental music are properly refined and follow its [the dance's] lead; being primarily characterized by dance, it is accompanied by song and instrumental music. For this very reason, this belongs to Taṇḍu, and is thus *Tāṇḍava*.

Thus it is recorded by the grammarians. (260) Here, the sage Bharata himself raises a doubt held by others: "And how could there be acting for those sages who, being ignorant, were themselves unacquainted with acting and the like?"

Furthermore, if the *gīta* and *āsārita* were already mentioned [in the previous context], the statement "when the *gīta* and *āsārita* have been stated" would be redundant. Therefore, it is the Sage himself who raises this doubt; or rather, in order to reveal this as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the phrase "the sages said" was interpolated in the middle by those of delicate intellect.

In this regard, the following doubt arises: Is dance distinct from drama, or is it non-distinct? Even if it were distinct, would it have a purpose or no purpose? It cannot be distinct, because there is no difference between them in terms of the movement of limbs, dancing, and singing, given that the application of dramatic gesture (abhinaya) consists of these very elements.

There is indeed a perception of that which is yet to come (*bhāvya*) when the object is being led forward, whether it pertains to the meaning of a sentence or the meaning of a dramatic performance; furthermore, no internal distinction exists between these within the *Daśarūpaka*.
This is so even in the case of a single character who must convey [the emotion] regarding a beloved friend or similar person, even though they are not present.

The employment of speech and response directed toward that [unseen person] occurs in drama as well; it is found in the *ākāśabhāṣita* (speech to the air) and in the *bhāṇa* type of play. As Rāhula said:
"Even though he is out of sight, a noble woman should speak of her beloved as if he were present before her."
"And the friend [is also used]; this is the dramatic convention (nāṭyadharma) declared by Bharata as a pair.

Likewise, regarding the *bhāṇa*: "Or that which is performed by a single person (*ekāki*) should be employed in a work possessing many limbs (*anekāṅga*); for the Sage will say that it should be 'performed by one' (*ekahārya*), like a *bhāṇaka*. The author of the *Vārttika* has also stated:
(169) When the performance follows the expressed meaning and the object to be conveyed is the same through the movements of the limbs,
what difference exists between dance (*nṛtta*) and drama (*nāṭya*)?

To this it is replied: If it is argued that drama does not exist because of the absence of direct perception (*sākṣādbuddhi*), that is incorrect. For there occurs the possibility of cognition such as: "This woman, intent on praising the virtues of her beloved, dances; the *khaṇḍitā* woman dances; the *kalahāntaritā* woman dances. As it has been said:
That very woman who was so passionately devoted to her beloved when he spoke words praising his such virtues— she alone should be imitated here in the presence of her friend.
By this, it has been shown that those things to be understood through enthusiasm (*utsāha*) possess the quality of being imitable (*anukāryatva*).
Now, as for the claim that there is no difference from drama (*nāṭya*) because of the observation of the representation of the forms being sung—that is not the case.
For it has already been stated that a mere distinction in sub-varieties, which serves as the basis for differentiation, is possible everywhere. Not so.

This is the point of distinction: because that [expression] exists even in drama (*nāṭya*). And it will be stated in the section on the rules for the characteristics of physical acting (*śārīrābhinaya*) regarding the limbs and sub-limbs: "In the *dhruvā* songs, acting is performed by means of joy, sorrow, anger, and so forth."
"And that which is performed as drama (*nāṭyāyita*) should be known as being conjoined with the aesthetic flavor (*bhāva-rasa*) [of the emotion]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 22.47).

Furthermore, in that context, the embellishing elements (*uparañjaka*)—namely song, dramatic performance, and the theatrical form (*rūpaka*)—are manifest through both speech and gesture (*abhinaya*), and their application is universal.

If it is argued that *dombikā*, *prasthāna*, *śidrakabhāṇaka*, *bhāṇikā*, *rāgakāvya*, and so forth, are distinct from drama (*nāṭya*) because they are not included within the definitions of the ten types of dramatic forms (*daśarūpaka*), then that is an absolute error; for even though *toṭaka*, *prakaraṇikā*, *rāsaka*, and others are not included therein, they nonetheless possess the nature of drama.

But Kohala says that because the solution is the same, even verbal representation (vācika-abhinaya) exists in certain cases, such as in seated recitation (*āsīna-pāṭhya*) and so forth; for example, in [the passage] beginning with "aho gāṇagāṇabullibhāṇa. However, the artificial (āhārya) representation is primarily established as one [type], and even in the *bhāṇa* and other forms, it does not change from moment to moment.

Even the *sāttvika* [abhinaya] was indeed accepted by Kohala and others, as they recorded such statements as "abhinaya is distinct from *sattva*. However, the *āṅgika* [abhinaya] alone is [the primary subject]. Just as there is a lack of mutual connection between the sentences of *astrī*, *ḍombiaka*, *kaṣidga*, and *kāna*, so it is even in the *samavakāra*.

If it is argued that in the case of the *aṅgas*, the connection occurs with a meaning where the female is not predominant, here too the same applies. Since the praise of the deity and the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) based on the male-female state are followed throughout, and since that alone is predominant, he will say: "That which is produced by the basis of the praise of the deity and which rests upon the male-female state."

For this very reason, it is promised in the *Cūḍāmaṇiḍombikā*: "O friend, vomit the essence of the drops; here is the speech that is not to be measured. [The text continues: "Therefore, the connoisseurs remember it as the *Vadhūcūḍāmaṇi*. Consequently, dance (*nṛtta*) is not distinct from drama (*nāṭya*)."
Because it is endowed with the tallakṣaṇa characteristics, the performance of dance that was created is known as tāṇḍava. (p. 170)
The sages said:
When gestures were performed by those who know them for the purpose of acquiring objects, [it was done] thus. (261)

This is what he says: "When for the sake of attaining [the meaning]. Because, for the purpose of attaining the meanings—the meanings of poetry—and for the sake of accepting them through the cognition of direct perception, the performers who know that have executed the physical and other forms of dramatic representation (abhinaya). Therefore, for that reason, this dance (nṛtta) was performed.
The meaning is that it is designated by the term *nṛtta* (dance), and not by the term *nāṭya* (drama) itself. Or, let it be distinct;

even so, what nature or characteristic does it require and admit within its own essence? Is it worldly (*laukikatva*) or transcendent (*lokottaratva*)? If it were worldly, it would be equivalent to objects such as a jar, being a mere imitation thereof.

Or it may take the form of a reflection and so forth; even in those cases, it consists essentially of the shadow of drama (*nāṭya*). For these—such as painted figures, puppets, and the like—are outpourings of parts of drama itself, conceived by authors through a wealth of cognition that approximates direct perception, extending to the conclusion of the narrative. Thus, in its transcendental nature, however...
That is merely a sub-division of drama itself;

moreover, even such a work is not purposeless, for it would serve as an illustration of those [emotions and states] (*bhāva*). This is unproven, because instruction regarding the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) is observed in narrative poems (*ākhyāyikā*) such as the *Rāghavavijaya*.
But in the case of the *ḍombikā*, it is precisely because of the instruction on the supreme secret of concealed passion (*pracchannarāga*) belonging to Kāma himself.

This is because, by the statement "that which is adherence to the left" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 22.199), concealed passion is declared in the context of general dramatic representation to be the very essence and totality of the god Manmatha.

Even in works such as the *Bhāṇa*, *Preraṇabhāṇa*, and *Bhāṇikā*, where there is a description of lions, boars, bears, buffaloes, and so forth, one observes that the instruction given pertains solely to human goals (*puruṣārtha*) through such means as *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth), and *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration).
Thus, there is no difference [between these genres] even on account of a difference in purpose. As it has been said:

Regarding the phrase "when for the sake of attainment": when, for the sake of attaining objects— that is, purposes such as *dharma* and so forth— poets who know those [objects] have composed works such as *rāgakāvya* (lyrical poetry) to be performed as an enactment (*abhinaya*),
why is this not *nṛtta* (pure dance), and why is *nāṭya* (dramatic performance) not *nṛtta*?

For even that [action] consists of the movement of the limbs. And when the object is the same, what distinct nature (*svabhāva*) could it require as a differentiator? The meaning is that such a distinct nature does not exist. Or, as the *Vārttika* states:
"In this way, there is instruction by means of subordinate sentences regarding those things to be seen with passion."
The description of the lion and so forth is concluded by means of an arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration by a general principle) in some instances. Thus [it is said].
Therefore, because there is no difference between its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and its purpose (*prayojana*), dance (*nṛtta*) is not distinct from drama (*nāṭya*).

Now, it may be argued that the performance of *rāga*-poems and the like (such as the *Rāghavavijaya*) is indeed drama, because of their connection with dramatic representation (*abhinaya*). As for that which is devoid of dramatic representation and so forth, being merely...

Our dance will consist of the turning of the body, the rolling of the eyes, the raising of the eyebrows, the movement of the pupils, the shifting of the feet, the trembling, the quivering of the hips, the casting of glances, and so forth— in which there is not even the slightest suspicion of *nāṭya* (dramatic representation). Is it not so?
What is the purpose of observing that? Has it not been stated regarding its utility for drama:
"Its branches, its dance, and likewise its sprout—these are the elements of dramatic representation" (Nāṭyaśāstra 8.15)?

He refutes this with the words, "When for the sake of attainment. Here, drama (*nāṭya*) is defined by the characteristic stated in *Nāṭyaśāstra* 1.119: "This which is the nature of the world... In that context, the utility of the dramatic representations (*abhinaya*) consists in the attainment of being directed toward the meaning already expressed. However, for dance (*nṛtta*) of the aforementioned form, there is no such purpose whatsoever.
If it is argued that its utility lies in its capacity as an embellishment (*uparañjakatā*), like song or instrumental music, then regarding song first:
"That which cannot be expressed by poetry should be accomplished through song.
This follows the principle: "Those things which one would not express by means of words—[one should express them] by those very meanings of the words," and so forth.

It serves a purpose by indicating the innate disposition (*prakṛti*), mental state (*citta*), activity (*vṛtti*), narrative content (*kathā*), and situation (*avasthā*) [of the character]. For the singer as well, it serves to stimulate the rhythmic tempo (*tāla*) through its similarity to the song. However, among these, dance (*nṛtta*) requires a specific inherent nature (*svabhāva*) for its performer; it has been stated that it is of no use in matters such as combat, wrestling, movement, or circumambulation.

In that regard as well, what kind of nature does it depend upon—mundane or supramundane? If it is mundane, its inclusion within the worldly dharma (*lokadharmin*) follows from its being something to be employed; furthermore, its very limbs will be defined through the sequence of the *cārī*, the *maṇḍala*, and so forth. Even if, however, it is supramundane, it is nonetheless established. One should perform it in an upward direction.
In this way, according to the principle of the classification of objects to be represented by the four types of hand-gestures (*catura-hasta*),
there is further superiority through the inclusion of beautiful and captivating elements; and when there is an entry into dramatic convention (*nāṭya-dharmin*),
there is once again a state of superiority over ordinary drama (*nāṭya*).

Now it is argued: "This [is done] for the sake of establishing the variety of the performance of the *pūrvaraṅga*. Even in that case, [it would have to be] either together with the *brahmagīti* employed in the *pūrvaraṅga*, or by way of a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) between them.
Of these, in the first position there would be an inconsistency; but in the latter position—
How is there an absence of the *āhitāṅgika* hand-gestures (*hastacaryā*) and so forth?
This has been stated:
"And you shall correctly represent the meanings even in the *Mahāgītas*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.15).

Here he says: "When for the sake of attaining the meaning. This means for the sake of attaining—that is, for the sake of bringing face-to-face—the meanings expressed by the words of the song. If this enactment intended as dance (*nṛtta*) has been prescribed, then why, when the status of being an enactment (*abhinaya*) is equal, is this considered dance and not drama (*nāṭya*)? To explain:
When the dramatic representation of the meaning of a song is to be performed,

what other natural state (*svabhāva*) does it require besides the physical gestures (*āṅgika*), hand movements (*hastaka*), and other forms of acting? The meaning is that it requires nothing else at all.
(172) Why has this dance been performed? To what nature does it refer?
It is neither connected with the meaning of the song, nor does it bring that meaning to realization. (262)
"Why was this dance performed amidst these songs and melodic expansions?
(Bharata: "To this it is replied: indeed, dance does not depend upon any particular purpose. (263)

Now it is said: its utility does not lie in the mimetic representation (*abhinaya*) of objects such as songs (*gītaka*). Rather, its utility in songs and the like is otherwise. To this he replies: "It is neither connected with the meaning of the song, nor is it an evoker (*bhāvaka*) of that meaning. Here, the meanings of the song are those things that constitute it, such as the *vastu*, the *aṅgas*, and so forth. In those [meanings], it is not...

The meaning is that although it is connected within that [group], it is not included among them. For if its inclusion in the middle were from the very beginning as a constituent part (*aṅga*), then even if it were something else, it would still be useful for that purpose because it would be a constituent of its commencement; however, this has neither been accepted nor is it logical.
Because dance is of the same nature as song, which has a companion.
Now, one might object: "Just as musical instruments such as wind instruments, though connected to its [the dancer's] limbs, are useful therein, so too will this [dance] be.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Nor is there any purpose... [The word *artha*] is sought as the primary element in the song and so forth.

The meaning is that it is being defined; [this refers to] the essential nature, the state of being a word, and so forth. Even for that, this does not become its producer (*bhāvaka*) or its bringer-attainment (*prāpaka*).
This is what is meant: because in the portion consisting of the vowel, it possesses the quality of being a vowel by virtue of being attached [to it] in the form of a reflection.

The utility of the hollowed instrument (suṣira) is praised in its aspect of song consisting of the essence of musical notes, by virtue of providing the proper pitch and leading to the ultimate realization of those notes. As for the percussion instrument (avanaddha), although it serves the purpose of conveying the meaning through the rhythmic placement of steps (padapāta) by being a means to achieve similarity with that [vocal melody], it is nonetheless non-different from drama (nāṭya) because its form is that of dramatic representation (abhinaya).
It has been said, "it might be so.

Now it is argued: as for that dance (*nṛtta*) which consists of the execution of *recaka* movements and bodily gestures (*aṅgahāra*), no meaning whatsoever is expressed by it; rather, it is like [the effect of] specific mantras.

And likewise, the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is achieved through specific meditations (*bhāvanāviśeṣa*). This has been declared in the mantras indicative of particular deities and in their songs, as well as in the *āsārita* songs. Regarding the *āsārita* songs—numbering twenty-seven—which consist of the *bhāva*, the *ārambha*, the *gītāṅga*, and the *vastu*: [The text continues: "In the *āsārita* songs... [and so forth].
In the four [categories] beginning with *vardhamāna*—and by the word "and" (*ca*), including *pāṇikāya*—this dance consisting of *aṅgahāras* and comprising thirty-two varieties is not connected;
if there were such a connection, it would now be nothing at all. Thus, in the separate treatises on dance (*nṛttakāvya*) and so forth...
It is precisely the nature of drama (*nāṭya*). Even in terms of utility for drama, the application of *nṛtta*, rhythm (*tāla*), song (*gīta*), and so forth, would also be difficult to establish;
such is the summary of the threefold prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
To refute this, he says in the three verses beginning with "In this regard, it is said" (*atrocyate*). Regarding this prima facie argument, it is stated:
The word "answer" (*pratyuttara*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In that regard, it was stated [on p.
173] that because drama (*nāṭya*) and the like consist of the movement of limbs, dance, and song, there is no distinction [between them].
Because of [the existence of] dancing in erotic poetry and the like, this reason is clearly inconclusive even with respect to worldly dance. However,

in the case of worldly movements of the limbs accompanied by the definitions of drama (*nāṭya*) and so forth— whether being recited or performed— how could it be that the collection of words is not performed as its meaning is being enacted?

It is not followed up; nor is it brought to a state of being fit for direct realization. The theory of reaching [the object] is unestablished, because even in the world, we observe that [an object] is conveyed by speech and so forth, which follows upon the movement of the limbs and minor members [of the body], and because of the absence of mental joy [in such cases].

This is because one clearly perceives that [the song] possesses the quality of being an auxiliary (*sāttvika-aṅga*) to the emotion, due to the state of identification (*tanmayībhāva*) established through the correspondence between the words and their referents.
Furthermore, the other position—that it applies equally to dance (*nṛtta*) as well—is likewise correct; for instance, in the case of *ḍombikā* and other such dance-poems.

In the case of the employment of phonemes and so forth that have fallen away from their proper color (varṇa), there is no question of abhinaya at all; what, then, is there to be deliberated upon therein? It will be determined that even that which is merely the nature of dance (*nṛtta*) is such because of the delicacy of the essential meaning residing in the cultivated meaning of the poetic content (*kāvyārtha*).
Let this matter rest for now.

However, immediately following that, at the occasion of the performance of the *kalā* involving the circumambulation of the stream (*dhārāparikrama*), when the song beginning with "pā-āla alosasāhiṇihujayajaya lacchimaccamali-ā" is sung, whose speech does it take the form of? If...
At that time, when a worldly *ḍombikā*— a dancing girl who has come to perform— speaks such worldly words concerning the nature of things, she expresses,
through her own sequential and unified utterances as a singer and so forth, a meaning that is equivalent to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).
And we have stated that the definition of drama (*nāṭya*) is its being an effect within the scope of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that is equivalent to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).
Therefore, just as someone [induces] someone else [to experience an emotion] through a sequence such as singing under the pretext of something else...

Either by means of manifesting a concrete object or by entering into the listener's will, it produces an extraordinary degree of attraction in someone’s mind. Even when dancing or singing, it should be understood in the same way as in the case of the *ḍombikā* and similar forms. In expressions such as "the mocking *ḍombī*" (*viḍambiḍombī*), that very same *ḍombikā* is present in the speech itself.

Having previously served as a minister with the intent of pleasing the king through songs, dances, or other musical performances consisting of words that expressed what was gratifying to the lord of men, she now— having failed to obtain such an opportunity for secret amorous play in the midst of it— has once again become like this.

She might describe someone as being such-and-such, a thief or a lover; or someone else there as being such-and-such; or a certain mature female messenger as being such-and-such—and so forth—thereby stating a means of acquiring wealth through the favor of that prince, who is suitable for entering the heart of the prince, while presenting that very prince as an external object, or in that same manner.

Another activity directed toward wealth is also described; the performance of the *ḍombikā* is summarized in the *Guṇamālā* with the verse beginning, "I shall take [her] as half of Śiva’s portion, for she is my ill-fortune," and so forth. Therein, that dancing *ḍombikā*, surrounded by many clever male attendants (*ceṭaka*) skilled in highly pleasing songs and the like, [addresses] you...

Thinking, "I have thus praised her," she, having transmitted her own words through the mouth of the singer standing among them, dances in her ordinary form, matching the rhythm (*laya*) and tempo (*tāla*) of the drama being sung by him;
and as for the meaning of the words being sung by him—
174) In order to demonstrate the penetration into the hearts of those who are to be won over, such as kings and others,
[the author] shows that [the aesthetic emotion] possesses the same status as the movements of the hands, eyebrows, horripilation, and changes in the eyes found in worldly transactions.
This also implies the arising of facial expressions and so forth.

Thus, having primarily effected delight through song and having demonstrated the subsidiary functions that serve it as well as the primary function itself, she again captures his heart through dance; this is *nṛtta*.
She leads that which was sung as the primary state into a subordinate state; consequently,
disregarding its dramatic representation, she performs bodily gestures whose emotional states are distracted by the very emotions being expressed in the song.
In cases such as the embrace of a lover in a state of *laya* (absorption),

since this much portion consists of worldly experience, what room is there for the suspicion of a relationship between an instigator and one instigated? Or, of which spectator could such a thing be suspected?
The intended purpose is instruction. Furthermore, after that, just as she [the teacher] employed song, dance, and so forth, the dancer does not employ anything similar;

for the *ḍombikā* does not demonstrate [it] as if it were a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), because there is no concealment of her own essential nature by means of the dancer's external accoutrements (*āhārya*) and the like. For that very reason, it is not...
She demonstrates the *ḍombikā* as if it were a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). However, she likewise displays dance (*nṛtta*) together with dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) and alone;

thus, regarding its status as a constituent of drama (*nāṭyāṅga*), it consists merely in the display of what is seen therein, such as the *patākā* hand-gesture and so forth. Therefore, drama is the embellisher (*saṃskāraka*) of dance, and thus receives the designation of "limb" (*aṅga*) and so on.
Thus it is spoken by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
Even this conventional usage—that dance (*nṛtta*) is like the life-force or the reflection of the prologue (*prastāvanā*) of drama (*nāṭya*)—is likewise derived from that [metaphorical basis].
For here, even the name "drama" does not apply, since in the *urdhva* and other [forms], there is an absence of the breaking of the four-square symmetry (*cāturaśrya-bhaṅga*).
Because that state [of being a real object] and so forth is impossible; for if it were a form of drama (*nāṭyarūpatva*),

there would necessarily have to be a restriction of language toward the actor and a restriction of meter, ornament, and so forth, which are useful for the fulfillment of the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) that is like a direct perception (*sākṣātkārakalpa*).

The employment of that [element], such as the portions of the *jāti* (verse-types) and so forth belonging to the *āhāryaviśeṣa*, as well as the *parikrama* (circumambulation) and other such actions, would not be appropriate for this [type of drama] alone;

yet it is not the case that it does not exist [there]. Furthermore, even the *ākāśabhāṣita* (speech directed to empty space), which is associated with the possibility of the fundamental *pāṭhya* (recited text), may occur. [Examples include] the *pādatāḍitaka* and other such elements found in the *bhāṇa* type of dramatic composition.

In this case, however, nothing at all has been stated by anyone from the very outset. As for what was said regarding the singing in the passage beginning with "Aho gāṇa" (Oh, the singing!), namely that it is the woman herself who is to be imitated here—that too has been refuted by this [explanation], because the true nature of the dancer is not being concealed; for the conventional usage is that "this woman, separated by a quarrel" or "this broken-hearted woman, is dancing."
It is figurative; for that dance follows the songs and instrumental music contained within the *rūpaka* (dramatic work) sung for its sake, but it is not primary.
This is because [the dancer] adopts such appropriate attire as having long locks of hair, wearing a braid, and not wearing auspicious bracelets.

Because of its deficiency. Furthermore, the suspicion raised regarding "theatricality" (*nāṭyāyitatva*) is a delusion in an inappropriate place; for it is precisely that which is being sung which is enacted by the actors, since otherwise an inconsistency would arise.
Rather, it is according to the specific tempo (*laya*), rhythm (*tāla*), and so forth, that the enactment capable of indicating the particular meaning [of the song] is performed.

In accordance with the dominant sentiments (rasas), such as the *sāttvika* and others, the performance is rendered suitable through the fulfillment of appropriate meanings by means of *dhruvā* singing. Indeed, these subtle varieties—beginning with the "sprout" (*pallava*) and ending with the "germinating sprout" (*nivṛtty-aṅkura*)—are intended for the purpose of dramatic representation (*nāṭya*). And this [is to be applied] only within its own proper domain.

We shall elaborate [on this]. Thus, there is no suspicion whatsoever of its being a mere dramatic performance (*nāṭyāyita*) here, because the fundamental element of *abhinaya* (acting) itself is absent.
When that [acting] is present, as for example: "Release me, O Valavai! O Aia! O Irao! O Guhaṃsaṇa! O Liṇaa! O Agnicciṅja! and so forth.
However, dance was introduced so as to produce beauty;
for generally, dance is desired by all people according to their very nature. (264)

The direct perception of fainting and so forth, as well as the falling of limbs from the bed and the like, might also occur in a dramatic poem (*nṛttakāvya*), as in the passage beginning with *hośaṃ daṇaṣaka hamahumā-iṣaka*.
However, it has been stated more than once that this is not the case here. By this, the difference in purpose is also refuted; for indeed—
The performance of a dance is undertaken with the intention that "the audience may be pleased" or "may attain proficiency";
however, the success of that [intention] may occur as an incidental consequence (*nāntarīyaka*).
For, like the performance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice or the removal of a musical discord, it is indeed directed toward a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*).

The application [of this principle] is as follows: although the worldly engagement of a *ḍombikā* or similar performer is for the purpose of pleasing a prince or other spectators based on what has been seen, nowadays both of these are absent. The engagement or the act of inciting a dancer results solely in the fruit of propitiating a deity. As it is said therein:
"By whatever *lāsya* dance this deity is constantly pleased;
by whatever *tāṇḍava* [is performed], Śiva, together with his retinue and Soma, [is pleased]. Thus it is said.

And at the root, just as in the case of a cook and others, the pleasure to be accomplished is produced by the association with a particular object situated within the midst of real entities such as form, taste, and so forth;
this is the case for the manifestation of another extraordinary form belonging specifically to the description of the *ḍombikā*.

And that one experiences the intention of linguistic derivation—what kind of possibility is this even in the case of song? But in drama, that [intention] alone is primary, because it was established from the very beginning by the sage Bharata and others in that very manner. Otherwise, however, there would be a lack of completion in the life [of the art].

This teaching of the fourfold set beginning with Dharma—which reveals the extreme wickedness of human nature—is like the instruction of ancient legends; for it proceeds from the root [of the tradition] through the reciters of the books, since the intention therein is solely for the sake of proficiency [in those recitations]. Thus, there is a difference in the result.

Furthermore, another distinction in their characteristics will be explained later during the occasion of commenting on the text that serves as the reason for refuting the suspicion that [nṛtta] is of the nature of *nāṭya*.
Therefore, because there is no difference between the definition and the purpose of *nāṭya*, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus he says: "Nṛtta is the agent..."
The *Nāṭya-veda*, when being sought as a certain object and being attained as a direct realization,

does not depend on anything else by which there would be a difference in its definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Likewise, no object for the sake of the audience depends on any one of the means— such as dharma and so forth— to be communicated, by which there would also be a difference in its purpose (*prayojana*).
Therefore, for this reason, this dance (*nṛtta*) was set in motion; it is designated by the very term "dance" (*nṛtta*) and not as "dramatic performance" (*nāṭya*).
For there is not even a single purely dramatic element, such as the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite) and so forth. Or rather, the reading is: "by this much [it is established] following that."

The passage beginning with "for the sake of attainment" (*prāptyartham*) has already been answered. Now, one might ask: "Granted that dance (*nṛtta*) is of such a nature, how is it of use in drama (*nāṭya*)? To this it is replied: "How, then, is song (*gītaka*) of use?
And considering it to be auspicious, this dance is prescribed for occasions such as weddings, births, arrivals, festivals, and other times of prosperity. (265)
And this dance was introduced as a means of diversion;
and because of its rejection, it was subsequently adopted by the hosts of spirits.
It has been said: "Those things which one should not speak with words," and "that which is not expressed through poetry.
Let there be for the *dhruvā* merely the recitation itself; enough with the exertion involved in the expansion of musical performance consisting of the application of phonemes and poetic ornaments.

But was it not stated previously that the needle-like [element], which is charming because it enters the heart itself, serves as the gateway for the entry into the heart of the grand display of the plot— the characters of which, such as Rāma and Rāvaṇa, consist of both refined and vulgar aspects? In that case, is it not that very [element] which constitutes the dance?
Its utility in drama lies in its internal application to movements such as turning and revolving;

for specifically, without it, drama—which is otherwise like a firebrand’s circle—would not even be graspable by the intellect. Therefore, it serves as the thread that strings together the rubies of pure abhinaya.

Because it shares the same nature as dance (*nṛtta*)—consisting of movements such as *valana* (turning) and so forth—and because it is proximate to it, drama (*nāṭya*) pervades internal elements such as song (*gīta*).

This is what [the author] states: "But it shall produce beauty. Dance (*nṛtta*) is that which has been set in motion, which is excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*), uninterrupted (*atruṭita*), and skillful (*dakṣiṇa*) in its *varṇanā*, *vilāsa*, *valana*, and so forth, as previously described regarding the limbs of the body and the body itself.

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: "the dance (*nṛtta*), which consists of graceful gestures (*vilāsa*), movements (*ceṣṭā*), and postures (*avasthāna*), and which is composed of those very elements, should produce excellence (*śobhā*)—that is, fitness for delight—and an attendant wonder (*camatkāra*) inseparable from that excellence, pre-eminently (*prakarṣeṇa*), by way of its distinction from singing (*gāna*) and so forth; thus the dance was initiated. This is stated with respect to the cause (*hetu*).
The indicator (liṅga).

Now, an objection is raised: "But isn't it the case that even food and other such things possess the quality of being an attractor (*rañjakatva*)? Should not those too be included here? He dispels this doubt midway with the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*).

In matters such as marriage, childbirth, and processions, it is by nature desired and cherished by everyone in the world to dance with their own bodies as the self, within those very natures that are regarded as the self. Indeed, every person dances by nature at their own preferred events like marriages; even he who plays the instrument while dancing does so likewise.
Even by a fool, it is considered auspicious: marriage, which is the bringing home of the bride; the entire festival preceding that;

the birth of a son, which is the act of procreation; then the arrival of the son-in-law together with his bride at the house of the parents-in-law everywhere, which is the *āvāha*; and the festivities of kings, such as the performance of state affairs and so forth.
"Prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is the attainment of one's desires, the arising of what is longed for.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the text refers to] the attainment of auspicious things not even desired, and so forth. Through this, the connection with the three verses beginning with *vinodanam* is established. And this should also be applied to the *Kaiśikī* style (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 1.42).
This has been shown here.

To provide a resolution to the question of what nature it depends upon, he says: "And for this very reason. And for this reason, the dance was set in motion; it was applied and performed according to its characteristics during the *pūrvaraṅga* at the commencement.
The connection [is as follows]. The word "eva" (only/indeed) indicates the reason:
those [movements] which are employed in song and so forth, and which correctly demarcate the divisions of the dance, [are the *mārga*]. (p. 177)
And the god also spoke to Taṇḍu, preceded by a dance.
Because they were rejected— since the *jjhaṇṭumā* and other such dry syllables were rejected by the gods and set in motion by hosts of spirits, Daityas, and the like—
we accept this [Vedic recitation] along with its musical instruments, as it has been sung forth. (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.35)
Thus it will be stated.
Therefore, because such songs as the *madraka* and others lack the representation of dramatic objects at their beginning, they are devoid of *abhinaya* (gesticulation).

The divisions (*vibhāga*) of the pure dramatic limb (*nāṭyāṅga*), which bring about its division, are employed at the beginning without being suspected [of being improper]. This is what is meant: in the introductory sections (*upohana*) of songs, the dance (*nṛtta*) should be performed in this purely pure manner. As he will say:
"In that context, the entry of the dancer must be performed by means of the entire array of her ornaments,

consisting of throwing and counter-throwing" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.300). Consequently, it is established that there is no entrance [into the performance] during the intervals between the components of the song.
Furthermore, the introductory sections (*āvāpa*) and the exits (*niṣkrāma*) of what is to be deliberated upon certainly do not possess the status of being limbs (*aṅga*) of the song.

Although it is stated regarding the great songs (*mahāgīta*) that "one should [express] the meanings of the verses" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.15), and it will be said later that "thereafter one should perform the representation" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.290), thus implying that this [representation] occurs first, nevertheless, even there, it is not primary.

It has been stated that the purpose [of the arts] is representation as established in drama (*nāṭya*). Furthermore, such a formulation is used because they are observed to be members of drama insofar as they are capable of being represented. Moreover, just as in worldly narratives, they serve merely to direct the attention toward the limbs of the body, such as gestures and behavior.

One's own meaning is represented according to what is to be expressed; for in that case, the purpose of representation is not the production of a state resembling direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), but merely the induction of absorption (*laya*) and so forth into that [state]. Likewise here too, there would be merely conformity to that meaning, which amounts to nothing more than the communication to another.

...he says that even though it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) occurring at the very beginning, it is employed as something distinct from the time [of the main performance], consisting mostly of *ḍombikā* as suggested by its being traditionally sung first in the world, and containing abundant words of praise; thus he states this refutation of a specific type of song (*gītiviśeṣa*). This was not [stated] by Bharata-muni.

In some places it is indicated. Others, however, maintain that at the end of the song, only the *cchandakas* and so forth are to be employed; these are the *pratikṣepas*, which serve as the basis for the variety of dances (*nṛttavaicitrya*) and involve the rejection of limbs according to one's preference. And the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)...

The term "prayukta" (employed) is used for the purpose of including [the states] such as *āsārita* within the formal arrangement (*vyavasthā*), and the word "satī" (being) is to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). Furthermore, the opinion of the Sage (*muni*) supports these two points.
Let this dance be performed by resorting to the application of song;
for generally, the ritual of the *tāṇḍava* should be based upon the praise of the deity. (268)

Thus, the status of dance as a constituent element (*nāṭyāṅga*) of drama, as well as its utility like that of song and other elements, has been established. Now, demonstrating that the subject matter— such as poetry characterized by dominant musical moods (*rāga*) and the like— is itself a constituent of drama, he speaks in the manner of an ancient legend (*purākalpa*) to further support the case for dance:
"By the Lord," and so forth. The particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only). [It means] by the Lord alone, by Maheśvara alone.
Taṇḍu was addressed with excellence and great respect, preceded by satisfaction. To the question "What? he says: "That which is sung is *gīta*, [meaning] poetry (*kāvya*).
Relying upon that which is the preeminent union with it—characterized by the penetration of its meaning—and not [relying on] mere shadow.

Having pervaded all around, the dance— such as the *tāṇḍava* and so forth— which, though its nature is sound, consists of the movement of limbs through states such as aesthetic absorption (*sāmarasya*) and dissolution (*laya*),
is integrated with the phonemes, ornaments, tempo (*laya*), word-meanings, and sentence-meanings contained within the dramatic forms being sung.
Let that [performance] be set in motion. As it was said by Kohala:
"In ancient times, Nārada, moist with devotion, sang the 'Destruction of Tripura' while Śambhu was dancing at twilight;
his mind was then entirely absorbed in that song."
Delighted, he performed a dramatic gesture and then spoke to Taṇḍu:
"O child, apply this Tāṇḍava dance through dramatic expression and performance."

By the word "atha" (now/then), it is indicated that this [music] is not merely pure [sound], nor is it merely the act of singing; rather, it is connected solely with the playing of musical instruments (*bhāṇḍavādya*), and even follows the words that serve as the basis for the song. Furthermore, its conformity [to those words] arises from following their meaning.

Now, one might ask: "What is the cause for the application of the term *tāṇḍava*? Anticipating this, he says: "Generally speaking" (*prāyeṇa*). By the term *tāṇḍava*, all dance (*nṛtta*) is meant; the word *lāsya* applies [to it] by proximity according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*).
In that context, it is prescribed: "In this [work], the dance is enjoined," thus it is a *vidhi*. That which is being enjoined is poetry (*kāvyam*), which always [contains] praise (*stutim*).

And he resorts to it as being worthy of description; therefore, that poetry has the heroic sentiment (*dharmavīra*) as its primary element. Although other sentiments (*rasa*) are also present there, in drama (*nāṭya*), it is the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). "Performance" (*prayoga*) means that which is employed;
he shows that [drama] in which the poetry is delicate, smooth, and continuous. This is the origin of the erotic sentiment.

Its existence is found herein. It arises from the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment in its full form; for the mental states of love exist within it. This is characterized by a smooth application of the *śṛṅgāra* sentiment, whether in its complete or incomplete manifestation. And although it will be stated later that there is no *rasa* other than in drama (*nāṭya*), nevertheless—
Since poetry is indeed the outflow of drama, there is an entry into aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). And by this, drama is a constituent part of the aesthetic flavor of dance.
By the use of the word "mostly," even things such as flattery toward a king are included.
By the word "and" (*ca*), [other types] such as the smooth mixed with the vehement, and the vehement mixed with the smooth, are also included.

By the phrase "it will be included," all that is to be characterized is indicated by this [definition]. For instance, in the *ḍombikās*, which proceed primarily with flatteries addressed to a king, the style is exclusively delicate (*sukumāra*).

The form is pure. Among the *bhāṇakas*, the description of the exploits of Nṛsiṃha and others is indeed *uddhata* (exalted). Furthermore, when even that which is *masṛṇa* (soft) enters into the *uddhata*, it is entirely appropriate. Here too, there is a distinction based on brevity and extensiveness (*pūrvaḥ prasthānaprabandhaḥ*; *uttaraḥ ṣidgakabhedaḥ*). But in the *uddhata* [style]...
The *bhāṇikā* is a sub-variety [of the *prahasana*] due to its smooth and subtle entry [into the plot]. Other forms as well— such as the *preraṇa*,
*rāmākrīḍa*, *karāsaka*, *hallīsaka*, and so forth— which are distinguished by the variety of their brevity or length, should be understood as being included within this very category.
This has been stated by the ancients:
"That performance in which the mind of the audience is captivated by expressions pregnant with concealed passion is considered *masṛṇa-ḍombikā*."
Since it employs descriptions of [deities] such as Nṛsiṃha and Sūkara,
the Bhāṇa should be performed by a female dancer (naṭakī) with exaggerated movements of the limbs.
Having made the gait of elephants and other animals equal, as well as their movement while traveling, that departure which is slightly impelled and very smooth is called *prasthāna*.
When a bold conduct toward the husband is described in the presence of a female friend,
yet is occasionally softened— a rogue’s behavior— that is indeed *ṣidgaka*.
Where there is play such as wrestling like that of children, or games involving boars and lions,
or play performed with banners and the like, that is considered *bhāṇikā*.
A *preraṇa*, however, consists primarily of humor and is accompanied by riddles;
while a *rāmākrīḍa* is said to be joined with descriptions of the seasons.
That dance performed by a circle [of performers] is known as the Hallīsaka;
in it, there should be one leader, just as Hari is for the cowherd women.

"The *rāsaka* involves many female dancers, is endowed with various rhythms (*tāla*) and tempos (*laya*), and ranges from thirty-two pairs up to sixty-four; it is characterized by both smooth (*masṛṇa*) and vigorous (*uddhata*) movements," and so forth.
These compositions consist essentially of dance (*nṛtta*); they are not distinct from dramas (*nāṭaka*) and the like, which consist essentially of dramatic representation (*nāṭya*).

The *Rāghavavijaya*, including the slaying of Mārīca and other episodes, is a work of poetic sentiment (*rāgakāvya*). Due to fear of excessive length and because it is not particularly useful, this has not been written down in its entirety as far as possible; however, whatever is useful, we shall describe in due course.
This, then, is the manner of objection regarding the words; however, in that regard, some raise the fault of mutual inconsistency (*asaṅgati*).

And the performance of the *tāṇḍava* enacted by Taṇḍu—which is characterized by delicate execution and arises from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*)—is the ritual procedure [to be described]. (269)

That [melody] is indeed established by the same rules as those for the *pūrva* and so forth. However, when this very method is composed according to the rules of *kalā*, it brings forth varieties of *rāgakāvya* (lyrical poetry), such as the *Rāghavavijaya* and the *Mārīcavadha*. As it has been said by Kohala:
(Through the application of different pauses and also through various sentiments,) how is it that poetry,
which is well-executed with manifold flavors, is thus remembered?

Furthermore, since the musical mode (*rāga*) is subordinate as the support for the song (*gīti*), it is the song itself that holds primacy; thus, unlike in drama, there is no inversion of the *rāga* or the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) due to an inversion of the poetic meaning.
For instance, in the *Rāghavavijaya*, the work is sustained by the *ṭhakkara-rāga* alone, despite its subject matter requiring diverse descriptions.

The slaying of Mārīca was performed with the Kakubha grāmarāga alone; for this very reason, these are called *rāgakāvyas*. Since *rāga* consists of song, it is the melody itself, and the poem is that which serves as its substratum. Thus, this dance also proceeded from the Blessed One himself in seven distinct modes. To illustrate: there is pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*).

It consists of the recaka limb-movements (*aṅgahāra*); then it becomes intent upon the representation (*abhinaya*) of songs and so forth; and even beyond that, it follows merely the act of singing as well as the rhythm of the musical instruments (*vādya-tāla*). [It involves] the swinging of the arms, trembling of the chest, the bending and raising of the sides of the body, the movement of the feet, and the quivering and shaking of the eyebrows.
It consists merely of the movement of the limbs, such as the contraction of the thighs and the shifting of the feet. As it was stated by Taṇḍu:
"Then, properly equipped with the musical instruments for singing, the performance of dance [should be undertaken]," and so forth. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.260)
For here, the etymological derivation is stated as "song" (*gīti*) being "singing" (*gāna*).

Furthermore, it is fourfold, following the meaning of poetry which is divided into four types—exalted (*uddhata*), delicate (*sukumāra*), and their combinations. Among these, the first type [is used] in worldly independent dance (*svatantranṛtta*) or for propitiating deities and the like.

Secondly, it was stated previously that the entire universe, including the *tāṇḍava* and other dances, is pervaded by this [Nāṭya] as the object of the remaining dance within the rules for the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*):
"O Bharata, indeed, explain to me the application of the *aṅgahāras*" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.18).
The Blessed One taught the *aṅgahāras* along with their applications there by means of Taṇḍu.
In that very context, such *aṅgahāras* were taught to me; thus they were demonstrated by the Sage together with *recakas* and *piṇḍībandhas*. The *karaṇas* as well—
Having demonstrated the nature of dance as a secondary consequence arising from the refutation of objections suspected due to its utility, [the author now asks:
"But what kind of performance (prayoga), O limb (aṅga), is it?
Having reached the *vardhamānaka* [meter], I shall explain its characteristics, for it attains an increase of *kalās* through the augmentation of syllables. (270)
Having stated that [this] is taught among the *hāras*, he speaks in order to follow up on the subject at hand: "of that *tāṇḍava* which has been employed.

Therein, it was said that there is the employment of *aṅgahāras* because they are appropriate for the *pūrvaraṅga*. And in that context, it was previously stated that the *vardhamānaka* tempo alone is suitable for the application of *tāṇḍava*, according to [the rule]:
"In that [performance], *tāṇḍava* is joined where it is appropriate" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 5.13). Thus, it is the *vardhamānaka* tempo that is fit for the connection with *tāṇḍava*.

One takes up the *vardhamāna* [rhythm]. Immediately thereafter, however, the rule concerning the subject matter of song (*gītaka*) and so forth will be stated. The reference "of that" (*tasya*) is a retrospective pointer intended to connect with a term separated by an interval; it dispels the suspicion that the taking up mentioned immediately before might refer to *tāṇḍava* (the male dance), since it is prompted by the *taṇḍu* [measure]. It is called a "rule" (*vidhi*) because one acts according to it.

The *vidhi* is the body (*gātra*). Having observed that, this performance (*kriyā-prayoga*) itself is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because it serves to differentiate [it] from other things. The connection [of the sentence] is: "In that regard, I shall describe the definition consisting of action (*kriyā-ātmaka-lakṣaṇa*). (269) [Objection:

But was not that action already mentioned as pertaining to the instruments (*karaṇa*) and the *aṅgahāras*? [Response: True; however, it was not mentioned as being mixed with song (*gīta*) and rhythm (*tāla*).
But here, having reached the *tāla* called *vardhamāna* and having employed it as a means for achieving rhythmic balance (*sāmyāpādana*),
[one worships] the Lord, the Master praised by the gods, who is denoted by the word *vardhamāna* because he is the substratum for the measurement and singing of that [rhythm]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 31.98)

Having encountered this collection of sentences beginning with "iti" and taking them as the basis for representation, and having encountered the specific song implied by them, and relying upon the regulation of speed, pitch, and so forth within the movements of bending and turning of the limbs, I shall speak.
The connection [is as follows]: it means that he will describe the *tāṇḍava* dance as it has arisen through its connection with the *vardhamāna* song, rhythm (*tāla*), and gesture (*abhinaya*).
In this regard, there is a restatement of the definition of the *vardhamāna* [song] according to what is to come (*bhaviṣyal-lakṣaṇānuvādena*) [Nāṭyaśāstra 1.31].

To describe the application of the *tāṇḍava*, he first states its form with the words beginning "of the *kalās*": the *kaniṣṭha-sāritaka* consists of seventeen *kalās*. That same [form], with double the tempo (*laya*), is the *layāntara*. The *madhyama* consists of thirty-three *kalās*, and the *jyeṣṭha* consists of sixty-five *kalās*. Thus, by way of the *kalās* and their tempos, as well as by way of their number—
There is an increase (*vṛddhi*). By that very increase, the increase of the number of feet (*padavṛddhi*) in the *hīyamāna* [section] is implied. As he will state:

"But there are four groups in the *yugma*, in the *oja*, and so forth" (Nāṭyaśāstra 32.97). Here, however, the syllables and their increase follow precisely the *kalā*s, as does the increase of the dancers; for in the first *sārita* dance, there is indeed only one [dancer].
The *prayoktrī* [is applied] in the sequence beginning with "two in the second" and so forth. Therefore, because of its connection with growth (*vṛddhi*), it is called *vardhamānaka*;

the suffix *-kan* is used here as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, there will be a sequence of ten repetitions of the *kaṇḍikās*. Also, whatever variation there may be in the performance (*prayoga*) according to the specific arrangement of syllables, by that sequence as well [the term is applied].

There is an increase in the *kalās* and so forth; therefore, the intended meaning here is that the performance of the *aṅgahāras* and the complete procedure for the formation of the *piṇḍībandhas* reach perfect accomplishment. (270) p.
It is called *vardhamānaka* because it increases from the base (*laya*).
O best of the twice-born, having performed the arrangement of the *kutapa* sections in the proper manner, [one should proceed]. (271)

Having thus explained the application of the *tāṇḍava* by restating its characteristics, he states the ritual action prescribed by rule, preceded by a formal proposition, beginning with the words "having performed" (*kṛtvā*), and so forth. It will be stated in the section on the rules for the *pūrvaraṅga*:
"The performance of the *āsārita* should take place for the purpose of distinguishing the divisions of the musical measures (*kalā*)."
"And from the chanting of the deities, the rule for song is likewise to be known" (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.21).
Therein, with the first half [of the verse], he describes the application of the *ārāsa* and *rāsita* melodies using dry syllables (*śuṣkākṣara*). And so he will state:
"But these [are used] in the outer song (*bahirgīta*), while those performed behind the curtain (*antaryavanikā*)... (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.11).

With the second half-verse, beginning with the words "by the sound of external song," he describes the application of the *āsārita* accompanied by meaningful phrases. And it is said in that very same place:
"Then, one should have them performed here joined with all the *kutapas*."
Having indeed drawn aside the curtain, [he performed] the various acts of dance and recitation.
"Of the songs, such as the Madrakā and others" (Nāṭya Śāstra 5.12), and so forth.

At that occasion, this application of dance occurs; he indicates that very occasion with the half-verse beginning "having performed" (*kṛtvā*). *Kutapa* refers to the fourfold musical instruments—so called because they produce sound (*śabda*) from the *kuta* [or *kutapa*, a woolen blanket]—as well as the group of those who play them. Of that...

Specific placement (*viśeṣeṇa nyāsa*) means systematic arrangement. In this context, specific placement refers to the appropriate application of notes, tempo, rhythm, and rhythmic units (*kalā*). This very [process], beginning with *pratyāhāra* and ending with the performance of the *āsārita*, constitutes the complete *vinyāsa*. Through the action of the *āsārita*, it applies to the percussion instrument and its performer.

It has been stated that the *prastāva* is performed in this manner for the *kalāpātaprayoga* which is about to be executed. And that complete arrangement (*vinyāsa*) is shown by the word "properly" (*yathāvat*). If the reading is *anupūrvaśas*, it indicates the collection of constituent parts (*aṅgajāta*) beginning with the introduction (*pratyāhārāvataraṇa*). By this, the following is meant:

When the inner curtain has fallen, [there occurs] that which consists of the introduction to the performance of musical instruments— the life-breath of the application of dry words— and which yields visible results,
as well as the scriptural result of pacifying obstacles through the satisfaction of the Daityas and others.

This is the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*) regarding the set of constituent parts (*aṅgakalāpa*) when they are employed. The phrase "the performance of the *āsārita*" contains meaningful words; the sense is "that which [is performed]. By the plural number in "by the performers" (*prayoktṛbhiḥ*), he indicates the accompaniment of other musical instruments.
He demonstrates the sequence of the performance with the words beginning "In that regard, however" (*tatra tu*). The *upohana* consists of dry syllables (*śuṣkākṣara*).

In the *kaniṣṭhāsārita*, there are five *kalās*. That limb (*aṅga*) in which the notes (*svaras*), along with their durations (*padakāla*) and tempos (*tālas*), are presented both in brief and in detail is so described. Singing (*gāna*) refers to the wind instrument (*suṣirātodya*), because it is sung from the notes of the registers (*sthānasvara*); thus they are called "notes" (*svarāṇi*) and "with sound" (*sādinādi*).
Thereafter, the performers should employ the *āsārita* technique;
in that context, having performed the *upohana* accompanied by the singing of the strings. (272)
The entrance of the dancer should be performed accompanied by musical instruments;
however, in the case of the *jāti* known as *viśuddhakaraṇā*, one should employ instrumental music [alone]. (273)
One should employ the *cārī* of that [foot] with a movement following the instrumental music;
here, by means of the *vaiśākha* stance, there is the *sarvarecakacāriṇī*.
Having taken up a handful of flowers, she should enter the performance pavilion;
then, having cast down the handful of flowers and circumambulated the stage-altar, [she should proceed]. (275)

By this, the two types of instruments covered with leather (ghanāvanaddha) are excluded here. At the conclusion of the *upohana*, the entry of the dancer occurs. Therein, the musical instrument (*bhāṇḍavādya*) is a drum (*puṣkaravādya*), and that belongs to the class of pure instrumental techniques (*viśuddhakaraṇajāti*).
And that [technique] is observed among middle-aged women. Thence—
Thus, here the suspicion that [the Lord] is a mere imitator or a direct experiencer is refuted.
For instance, if the Supreme Lord were subject to being impelled like Rāma and others, it would follow that he belongs to the same class of minds as the primary *prakṛti* and so forth.
In that regard—
the single syllable in the Pure [Vidyā] shall be the musical instrument for all paths:
*ddhaṃ dhāṃ kho kho ṇā ṇādi*, which constitutes the prescribed mantra.
"She is to be known as pure; for women of middle [status], the birth is equal" (Nāṭyaśāstra 34.136–138).

"Pure" (*viśuddha*) refers to that which is denoted by a single syllable. "Instrument" (*karaṇa*) refers to a *aṅgahāra*. In the initial state, this very phoneme is used in such expressions as *tattat rundahi rundahi* and so forth. The movement (*gati*) that follows such instrumental music is characterized as *cārī*.

The connection [is as follows]: by the statement "one should employ the instrumental *aṅgahāras*," the subordinate application of the *bhāṇḍavādya* (percussive instruments) is primarily indicated. As it has been stated by Bhaṭṭatōṭa: "the employment of this alternating instrument.
Immediately after that, he describes the performance: "with the *vaiśākha* stance," and so forth.
By this, he defines the *vaiśākha-recita* gesture: "The hands and feet are extended (*recita*), and the hips and neck are extended" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.97).
(274) Regarding the phrase "holding a handful of flowers": by the word "releasing," the formation of a hollowed cup of flowers with the palms is indicated.
The meaning is that one should demonstrate the throwing of flowers (*puṣpākṣepa*) by way of the sequence of bodily movements (*aṅgaprakrama*).
Having prostrated before the deities, one should then perform the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*).
Where there is singing accompanied by dramatic performance, one should not employ instrumental music there. || 276 ||
In the performance of the *aṅgahāras*, however, the *bhāṇḍa* musical instruments are prescribed;
[the music] should be even, harmonious, well-divided, clear, and produced by pure strokes. (277)

Others, however, say that there is an immediate offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and liberation (*mokṣa*): the circumambulation on all sides of the performance platform (*raṅgapīṭha*), the act of embracing [the deity] right in the midst of the previously worshipped deities, and the gesture of prostration (*praṇāmābhinaya*); these two are indicated by the word "and" (*ca*) as occurring at the same time.

The phrase "one should perform" (*cācaret*) is to be disregarded; rather, it refers to "thereafter, the enactment" (*tato'bhinayam*), based on its temporal priority. This is intended to demonstrate that through the excellence of devotion and the contemplation of that meaning, there is a distinctness of object. For the enactment (*abhinaya*) concerning the meaning of the words and the meaning of the sentence of the *āsārita* verse brings them toward oneself by directing them into one's own being. It is not, however, [merely a physical imitation].
To the audience:
the particle *yatra* has the sense of "because" (*yataḥ*). Therefore, because it is sung—that is, the sentence being sung—should be enacted and directed toward oneself. And that singing...

The characteristics of color, ornament, and mark, as well as the facing [of the instruments] and the symmetry of the limbs, should be understood accordingly. For that reason, because of its primary importance, one should not employ the *avanaddha* instrument—which serves as a covering—at that time;
one should not apply it independently nor bring it in with excessive force. And by means of the repetition [in the word] "wherever" (*yatra*), the technical definition [is established].
He states [this] as being universal.

(276) He states the remaining application by way of restatement: "In the case of the employment of an *aṅgahāra*. The word "tu" has the sense of "eva"; thus, it means "in the employment of an *aṅgahāra* that is purely [such], devoid of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*)."

When dance is predominant, the instrumental music follows it; specifically, with regard to the application of the *antara*, that [music] is prescribed—that is, it is performed and maintained. For this very reason, because there is no further material [to take up], one should again join that same substance with dance once more. (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.284)

Thus, regarding that which is to be described— the summoning of the dancer and the subsequent *āsārita* song— it has been shown that there is a sequential application of the instrumental music, the sung melody, and the dance, each in turn being predominant, which constitutes pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*).
It has been stated that "the playing of musical instruments (bhāṇḍavādya) is prescribed. He shows what that is like by saying "equal" (sama).

It consists of the eightfold equality of syllables, limbs, time-measures (tāla), tempo (laya), pauses (yati), hand-grasping (pāṇigraha), and structural placement (nyāsa), as well as the equality of time and place;
this harmony will be explained in the chapter on the drum (puṣkara-adhyāya). Among those, that which is produced by time-measures (tāla) is sixfold, and [that which is produced by] hands is twofold.

[The quality] is produced by the place of articulation and the location of the high pitch (svara). Through connection with that, the sound possesses a state of being well-colored (*samaraktabhāva*), which is its pleasing essential nature (*hṛdyasvarūpatā*). And that [pleasing nature] arises from the application of three kinds of polishing (*mārjanā*), such as that of a peacock feather (*māyūrī*) and so forth. Because it is properly polished by that, it is "colored" (*rakta*) and distinct. And immediately after striking [the instrument], through the application of pressure (*pīḍita-yoga*)...
In the *tāṇḍava*, musicians skilled in instrumental music should employ instruments that capture the movements of the dance limbs and manifest the sense of rhythmic interruption (*viccheda*).
Having performed with song and instrumental music, the dancer should then exit from there. || 278 ||
By this very same procedure, others enter separately;
then other women, in due order, form the *piṇḍīs*.

"Consisting of identical syllables" (*samānākṣara*) means that where the repetition of the phonemes beginning with *ka* is clearly manifest. "Born from the striking" (*prahārajā*) means they are situated at the end of the syllables, at the conclusion of the pure or purified forms;
or alternatively, they are situated on one or another path, such as the path of *āliptikā* and so forth, wherein the dance consists of *aṅgahāras*.

The instruments are like its limbs; or rather, it takes up—that is, accepts through convention—the limbs of song, such as the *mukha* (introduction) and so forth, and this [acceptance] is "equal" (*sama*), the meaning of which has already been explained.
Therefore, the sense is this: it causes the musical instrument—which is the agent of the act of dancing—to take up [the performance].

"Dance" (*nṛtta*) is so called because it applies its own limbs as if they were dancing, through the employment of various artistic variations; it is described thus because, as soon as it is heard, it forcibly makes the limbs dance as if with grace. For example:
And regarding the phrase "taken by hundreds of those who cut through the thick, sharp, and dense [obstacles] with the hands of the *karta*, *kakataka*, *nakra*, and *kunda*":
that musical instrument of this kind which will be described in the chapter on the *puṣkara* drums should be employed here at this juncture for the *tāṇḍava*.
Indeed, a verse of this very nature will appear in the chapter on the *puṣkara* drums (Nāṭya Śāstra 34.172). Therein:

In this context, there are two types of injunctions and restatements (*vidhi* and *anuvāda*) that must be reversed. The *tāṇḍava* was mentioned previously; therein it was stated that such instrumental music (*vādya*) should be performed.
Thus, with the word "having employed" (*prayujya*), he concludes the performance of the first *āsārita* by means of this half-verse. Of these...

And at the beginning of the application, he provides a technical definition (paribhāṣā) in three verses, starting with "By this very [means]" and ending with "endowed with the instrument. Regarding the term *gāna*: it is that which is sung (*gīyate*) and is thus called song (*gīta*). When song and instrumental music are present as the primary elements, the dancer employs dance; likewise, through the movement of the notes, there is a predominance of dance.

Then, having employed song and instrumental music appropriate to the occasion and having made them conform to herself, the dancer—though not like in actual drama where the self is concealed by assuming the actual form of Rāma and others—should exit and withdraw; however, she should not depart entirely, because it will be stated later [Nāṭya Śāstra 4.286]: "Two means 'a second'. The others...
Do they enter simultaneously? No; he says "separately," meaning one by one in succession.
Now, raising the doubt as to how many other [channels] there are that enter by this very method, he says "and others.
When the four [channels], beginning with the *kaniṣṭhā*, have been drawn in (āsārita) in sequence, [they enter] according to their respective order.
Those other [compositions] which they bind in ways different from the four types of *piṇḍībandha* that will be described hereafter are called "others" (*aparāḥ*).
By this, it is implied that there are exactly four [types]. The word "a *piṇḍī*" (*piṇḍīm*) is used in the singular to denote the class (*jāti*). (279) p.
The overturning should be performed until the *piṇḍī* is tied;
once the *piṇḍī* has been tied, all those women should then depart.
In this context, the instrumentalists should perform music during the *piṇḍībandhas*, accompanied by the execution of various musical sequences according to the measure of the *paryastaka*.
Having thus explained the distinctness of the entry (*praveśapṛthaktva*), he states another definition: "as long as it is *paryastaka*.

The reading is "as long as the *piṇḍī* is not bound. Here, the words "tāvat" and "yāvat" are out of their usual order. As long as the *paryastaka*—the performance characterized by the *kevalāsārita* and *abhīhitaka*—is to be performed, so long [the following applies].

The *piṇḍī* is bound; until then, the binding of the *piṇḍī* should not be performed, but it must be done immediately thereafter—this is the meaning. It is avoided by the dancer who has already entered. According to the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), that performance in which there is a single, solid, and continuous movement of the limbs is called *paryastaka* in the terminology of the dance masters (*nṛttācārya*).

It is well known as the *paryastaka*. The *paryastaka* is a bodily procedure devoid of dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*). Furthermore, it should not be performed during the *piṇḍibandha*; rather, the meaning is that it should be performed immediately after that. As for what has been stated by some—that it is for the sake of training the dancer who entered first and so forth—that is entirely inconsistent and should be disregarded.

It is established as a convention that until the dance suitable for the *piṇḍībandha* (the formal structural arrangement) commences, the *āsārita* performance should be enacted by the dancer alone, having dismissed the other dancers who have already entered.

He states another technical definition: "having formed a cluster" (*piṇḍī baddhvā*). Having performed the dance application (*nṛttaprayoga*) of that *āsārita*, all of them should exit—that is, they should withdraw.

For this very reason, the poetic masters such as Śrīrāṇaka and others, who depend upon this very position, employ the practice of the "four withdrawals" (*caturapasāraka*) in works such as the *ḍombikā*. (280)

He states another definition: "In the *piṇḍībandhas*," and so forth. To the same extent that there is the application of the *paryastaka* and *āsārita* in the performance of *abhinaya*, to that same extent there is also the application of *aṅgahāras* useful for the *piṇḍībandhas*, which fall within that [same category]. However, it is diverse, manifold, and of various kinds.

And when the musical performance (*vādyavidhi*) is employed in vain (*mogha*), it is endowed with those *karaṇas* and *kriyās* which are to be pierced (*vedhya*) by the Blessed Lady, as will be described hereafter. Where there is a *kalā* of two measures (*dvimātrā*), that is the *citramārga*; the term *ogha* is obtained from the word itself, for it is precisely therein that the *ogha* is observed. (281)

Thus, having established this sixfold technical terminology— namely, separate entry (*pṛthakpraveśa*), the performance of a solo dance (*ekākiny-abhinaya-prayoga*), the performance of group movements (*sambhūya-aṅgahāra-prayoga*), the subsequent exit (*apasāra*), the duration of time (*tāvatkālatā*), and the variety of dance and instrumental music (*nṛtta-vādya-vaicitrya*)— [the author proceeds] to the second [chapter].
There, the bringing down [of the deity] should again be performed exactly as before;
thereafter, one should employ the singing of the *āsārita* once more. (282)
The dancer should also enter according to the very same procedure as before,
and she should perform the meaning of the song of the second *sārita*.
Furthermore, one should demonstrate that very same subject matter through dance as well;
then, when the *āsārita* is completed, the dancer shall exit from there. || 284 ||
The others enter as before; indeed, the same procedure applies.
Thus, at every step, this rule for the āsārita must be performed.
He describes the application of the *āsārita* for another tempo (*laya*) with the words: "In that case, the *upavahana*.

He first provides this technical definition: "Where" refers to where the *kaniṣṭhāsārita* was previously employed. "More" (*bhūyas*) means more frequently, that is, for six beats (*ṣaṭkala*). "More" implies, due to the increase in tempo, that it is somehow somewhat greater.

"By the very same [method] as before," refers to the passage beginning with "In that case, however, there is the *upohana*. Because of the word "also" (*api*), what was indicated immediately after "and having bowed to the deity" is included: "or by means of a movement following the musical instruments," and so forth. Then, that second dancer [performs] the *gītaka*—the song related to a specific rhythm (*tāla*)—of the *āsārita*, as well as the sentence being sung.
One should enact its meaning. Furthermore, that very same subject matter, characterized by a *sārita* performed at another tempo (*laya*), constitutes the second [act].

By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that she was previously entered [into the performance] as well. And through dance—consisting solely of *aṅgahāras*—one should demonstrate the enactment by way of its similarity [to the original action].
Immediately after the performance of the *āsārita*, she too should withdraw along with her. (284) Now, he states the performance of the third and fourth *āsāritas* by way of extension: "as before.
This means separately. "The same" refers to that which was previously mentioned as having performed the *upohana*.
The meaning is that this has been stated by means of the six technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*).

Now, when only one *āsārita* is employed, he shows through an extended application (*atideśa*) that this is a sequence of diverse applications, beginning with the words "in this way" (*evam*) and so forth. The singular number is not restrictive; for when even a single *āsārita* is used...
Then he applies himself to those [arts] which are for the purpose of buffoonery and likewise for the purpose of singing. (p. 188)
One [finger] should be joined first, and likewise two for the second. || 286 ||
The first [piṇḍī] consists of three entities, the third consists of three, and the fourth consists of four;
thus, four rules for the piṇḍīs have been proclaimed. || 287 ||

The four *padas*—namely, *cheda*, *mukha*, *pratimukha*, and *saṃharaṇa* (Nāṭyaśāstra 31.80)—are its characteristics; based upon these, this fourfold *apasāra* application, like that of Vardhamāna, should be employed in the performance of instrumental music and vocal singing. As he will say: "In this manner..."
"The four components" (caturaṅgāni) refers to Nāṭyaśāstra 31.82. This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "one, however" (*ekā tu*, etc.).
"The subject matter" (*vastu*) is a component (*aṅga*). Regarding "one should employ" (*yuñjyāt*), the word "by means of dance" (*nṛttena*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
As for the fact that some here perform twice over that subject matter which consists of three *mātrās* and so forth, that is indeed incorrect. Others, however, [do this] thus at every step.
They have described this and the following half-verse as the concluding statement for the *vardhamāna* performance. Others, however, say: the *āsārita* is the place of manifestation for the *padas*;
the performance consists of ten repetitions of the *kaṇḍikās*. For instance: *viśālā saṅgatā sunandā*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "sumukhī," four sections will be explained (Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter 31, verses 120ff), consisting respectively of nine, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two *kalās*. Following Viśālā is Saṅgatā; following Anuviśālā is Sunandā; following Saṅgatā is Viśālā; following Viśālā is Sumukhī; and following Sunandā is Saṅgatā Viśālā—these constitute ten cycles (*parivartas*). Among these:

In the three sections beginning with *Viśāla*, the sections are connected to both [the preceding and following] as in the case of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣivat*); thus, through the double application of the seventeen-beat (*saptadaśakala*) measure, it occupies the position of the slow (*kaniṣṭha*) and intermediate (*layāntarita*) tempos. Thereafter, in the three sections beginning with *Sunanda*, it occupies the position of the thirty-three-beat (*trayastriṃśatkalā*) *madhyamāsārita*.
Then, in the four primary positions beginning with Sumukhī, there is the performance of the *jyeṣṭhāsārita* consisting of sixty-five *kalās*.

Thus, in the steps (*padāni*), positions (*sthānāni*), and variations of the *kaṇḍikā* and so forth of this *āsārita*, there is the dance practice involving four *apasārakas*. Regarding this, it is said: "Even one... (*ekā tv iti*). This refers to the position of the *vastvāsārita*. Thus...
