The intent of the third commentary is that this is the application (prayoga) and extension (atideśa) of the increasing number of *kaṇḍikās* (or their modification). As for the second commentary, however, nothing further has been stated there; therefore, it should simply be disregarded.
It has been stated that the methods of *piṇḍībandha* (group-formation) are to be employed in succession as they are introduced. To the question "Which are these?", he says:

"Of the *piṇḍīs*, etc. *Vidhayaḥ* means types or modes. Among those, one type consists of a form of *piṇḍībandha* that is pleasing due to its distinct internal features and is to be employed in a single [instance].
Because it lacks a specific name, it is expressed by a general term. Thus he says: "The structural integration (piṇḍībandha) [is so called] because of its state as a whole (piṇḍatva).
The *piṇḍī*, the *śṛṅkhalikā*, the *latābandha*, and then the *bhedyaka*.
The *piṇḍībandha* is so called because of its massiveness (*piṇḍatva*), while the *śṛṅkhalikā* is formed by a chain-like structure. (288)
The *latā* [hand] bound with fingers interlaced is known as the *bhedyaka* when accompanied by a dance;
the *piṇḍibandha* occurs at the little finger, while the *śṛṅkhalā* occurs within the interval of the *laya*.
In the middle [measure] there is the *latābandha*, and in the superior [measure] there is the *bhedyaka*;
likewise, there are various origins for the *piṇḍīs*, as well as the *yantra* and the *bhadrāsana*.

The *piṇḍībandha*, which consists of the mutual connection of dancers employed [in performance], is of two kinds: either of the same class (*sajātīya*), like a pair of lotuses bound by a single stalk; or of different classes (*vijātīya*), like a lotus whose stalk is grasped by the beaks of two swans. This latter type is designated by the term *gulma* or *śṛṅkhalikā*.

The *latābandha* (creeper-binding), however, which is performed by three dancers, attains a variety of forms like a net due to its capacity for greater diversity; as before, it consists of both similar and dissimilar elements. As for that performed by four dancers, since there are three forms within this great sentence (*mahāvākya*), it must be differentiated by those many modes; thus, from them—

And because it is not understood from the application of a single being, it is "divisible" (*bhedyaka*). The meaning is that it has entered into a single application as the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*). That, however, exists together with the three aforementioned dances (*nṛtta*).
(288) He clarifies its being employed by one and so forth with the words beginning "the *piṇḍībandha* is in the *kaniṣṭhā*," etc. Now, [one might ask]:

Anticipating the question of how these *piṇḍī*-bindings are accomplished, he demonstrates their accomplishment as produced by the distinctions of the supports (*ādhāra*) and so forth, beginning with the verse "The womb of the *piṇḍīs* is manifold. In that regard,
just as there is a connection (*anusandhi*) for the *putraka* and others whose limbs are separate, so too [is it here].

A *yantra* is the synthesis of the constituent parts that serve as supports, such as the earth, body, space, and so forth. It is mentioned first because it occurs most frequently. By this, the mixed varieties are subsumed.
Regarding the phrase "the auspicious one is clearly [the seat]," its seat or location is clearly upon the earth and so forth.
"From observation" (*darśanāt*) is a summary of a single division. By this, the division of the constituent parts of the substratum (*ādhārāṅga*) is shown.

However, the division of the performer and the performance was already shown previously and is also mentioned here as "the application of training" (*śikṣāyoga*). This refers to the practice of the variety of bodily movements (*aṅgavikṣepa*) within the specific instrumental gestures (*karaṇa*) and sequences of movements (*aṅgahāra*).

(190) Likewise, the application of the training must be practiced by those who practice it; O you whose wealth is austerity, the application should be performed in this manner during the *Vardhamāna* [recitation]. 291.

Thus, the distinction of the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) has been shown. It is precisely from this that we have drawn our support when explaining at length [the passage] beginning with "by means of *recakas* and *aṅgahāras*" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 4.249).
By the inclusion of the term "various" (*vividha*), he indicates the infinity of its divisions through the mixing of those [elements]. And that [has been explained] by us...

This has already been shown previously. (290) Now, one might wonder whether this entire method of constructing the *piṇḍī* is useful here or not; anticipating this doubt, he says: "And it should be employed in exactly that way. By all these aforementioned methods, the construction of the *piṇḍī*, *śṛṅkhalaka*, and so forth, is to be applied.

Thus far. Regarding this, some provide the following explanation: "The *yacchecchadya-karma* is a leather machine (*carmayantra*), while the *kāṣṭhamayī-prakṛti* is a throne (*bhadrāsana*). However, only those with refined aesthetic sensibility (*sahṛdaya*) can discern whether this is correct or incorrect.
Likewise, [this is understood] from observing the limbs of song, instrumental music, dance, the formation of groups (*piṇḍībandha*), and so forth.

It has also been indicated that *nṛtya* is not distinct from *nāṭya*. Furthermore, this method of structural composition (*piṇḍībandha*) is not absent from actual performance (*lakṣya*). It cannot be extracted like a great medicinal herb fallen amidst the two positions of mere dance (*kevalanṛttaka*), because it is unstable; however, it can be recovered through careful attention.
"It is indeed possible," so one should not resort to indolence in this matter. Otherwise, they state the performance as follows:
namely, in the passage "one, however, first," the first [singer] performs the *prathamāsārita*; then the second performs the *dvitīyāsārita*.
Simultaneously with that, the first performs only the *aṅgahāra*. Thus, the third [performs].
He enacts the meaning of the third *sārita*; then two [dancers] employ the *aṅgahāra*.

When the fourth performs the fourth enactment, three [dancers] delight with the *aṅgahāra*. Others, however, maintain that there is a coordination even in the application of the enactment. This includes the various types of group formations (*piṇḍībandha*) such as the *jāla-śṛṅkhalikā* and so forth.
And they desire [the dancers] to form various arrangements by binding each other’s arms.
Now, having reached the *vardhamānaka* [formation], he concludes the vow with the words beginning "evam" (thus), etc.
Having thus described the application of the *vardhamāna* primarily, [he now speaks of] the songs such as the *madraka*, etc. (Nāṭya-śāstra).

Regarding what will be stated in *Śā. 5-13*, he makes a formal declaration for the sake of its determination: "Of the *gītās*, etc. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that [the following] applies as a supplement to all [the preceding topics] and also implies a secondary connection (*anvācaya*). The definition of the *chandaka* and other elements to be employed up to the *āsārita* will be stated precisely as being supplementary to those [gītās]. For instance, in the *Tālādhyāya* (*Nā. 29.1–4*), it is said: "The *chandaka*, *chinnaka*, *kalopeta*, *dhruvaka*, *praveśaka*, *nirgamana*, *saṃkrama*, *samudga*, *dvikhaṇḍa*, *trikhaṇḍa*, *caturkhaṇḍa*, *pañcakhaṇḍa*, *ṣaṭkhaṇḍa*, *saptakhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭakhaṇḍa*, *navakhaṇḍa*, *daśakhaṇḍa*, *ekādaśakhaṇḍa*, *dvādaśakhaṇḍa*, *trayodaśakhaṇḍa*, *caturdaśakhaṇḍa*, *pañcadaśakhaṇḍa*, *ṣoḍaśakhaṇḍa*, *saptadaśakhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭādaśakhaṇḍa*, *ekonaviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *viṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *ekaviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *dvāviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *trayoviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *caturviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *pañcaviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *ṣaḍviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *saptaviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭāviṃśatikhaṇḍa*, *ekonatriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *triṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *ekatriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *dvātriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *trayastriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *catustriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *pañcatriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *ṣaṭtriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *saptatriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭātriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *ekonacatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *catvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *ekacatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *dvicatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *tricatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *catuścatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *pañcacatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *ṣaṭcatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *saptacatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭācatvāriṃśatkhaṇḍa*, *ekonapañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *pañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *ekapañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *dvipañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *tripañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *catuṣpañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *pañcapañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *ṣaṭpañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *saptapañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭapañcāśatkhaṇḍa*, *ekonapaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *ṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *ekaṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *dviṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *triṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *catuḥṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *pañcaṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *ṣaṭṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *saptaṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭaṣaṣṭikhaṇḍa*, *ekonasaptatikhaṇḍa*, *ekonāśītikhaṇḍa*, *aśītikhaṇḍa*, *ekāśītikhaṇḍa*, *dvyaśītikhaṇḍa*, *tryaśītikhaṇḍa*, *caturaśītikhaṇḍa*, *pañcāśītikhaṇḍa*, *ṣaḍaśītikhaṇḍa*, *saptāśītikhaṇḍa*, *aṣṭāśītikhaṇḍa*, *ekonana (Śā.
a-31) The application of the *vardhamānāsāritaka*, the *gītakapāṇilatānta*, and the *chandaka*, as well as the application of the four-line verses (*catuṣpadā*), will now be described.
(191) I shall further explain the rules for songs and meters— those which are based on subject matter and those which are composed according to their constituent parts. 292.
I shall describe their songs, as well as the application of dance and instrumental music;
therein, the entry of the female dancer should be performed with the full musical ensemble.

That which is produced by throwing and counter-throwing, refined by the removal of vessels, should first be performed as a dramatic representation; such is the *gītaka* (song) containing all thematic elements.
"In all [these] past [traditions], *chandas* is desired at the end;
then there is the four-limbed, the three-limbed, the nine-limbed, and likewise the couplet (*yugma*).
There is also the four-footed and the single-limbed," and so forth. Therefore, by virtue of its predominance—
In that context, there is a rule for the specific types of *gītaka* and so forth when they are employed [in a composition], but not when they are used independently.

Those *cchandaka*s are those in which the elements (*vastu-aṅga*) and so forth belonging to a *gītaka* are adopted according to one's own will, being employed without a fixed restriction of one, two, three, or more;
these are what nowadays exist in the form of dance rhythms (*nṛtta-tāla*).

The *ḍombikā*, *nartakī*, *ila*, *caraṇa*, and so forth are well known. [Regarding the word] "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*): for although the rule concerning the *vardhamāna* has been stated, more extensive material will now be explained.
In that regard, he begins to demonstrate the procedure for dance (*nṛtta*) based on songs (*gītaka*) and rhythmic cycles (*tāla*) with the words "those which... (*yāni*).

There are many *vastu* elements such as the *khaṇḍalaka* and others, while the *aṅga* elements are few. Among them, three *gītaka*s are based on the *vastu*: the *madraka*, the *parāntaka*, and the *prakarī*. The other four *aṅga*s are the *ullopyaka*, the *rocitaka*, the *oveṇaka*, and the *uttara*. He states their sequence in order:

Regarding the phrase "of them": I shall now describe the rules for their dance (*nṛtta*) and instrumental music (*vādya*). Among those, the *kṣepas* which occur at the beginning of the first *vastu*, and the *pratikṣepas* which occur at the beginnings of the second *vastu* and so forth—known as *pratyupohanās*—are, according to another school of thought, distinct from these and consist of remnants of song (*gītaśeṣa*) having a separate duration that is not included within [the *vastu*].

Having employed songs set to the lute (*tantrī*), the entry of the dancer should be performed accompanied by musical instruments (*bhāṇḍavādya*), primarily featuring the *puṣkara* drum as prescribed in the chapter on drums, being struck with fingers that move slowly and slightly. (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.20)

This is what is meant: having employed the *ākṣiptikā* and the *upohana* regarding the first subject matter, there is the entrance of the dancer (*nartakī*). Regarding the second and subsequent subjects, there is the *pratyupohana*. As for the construction of the words: having combined it with the stringed instrument and the song, it is performed during the *kṣepa* and *pratikṣepa*.
Furthermore, one should demonstrate that very same subject matter through dance as well;
the procedure for which was previously explained in the section on dance, gesture, and instrumental music. (295)
This [method] should also apply to the *vastukas* (lyrical themes) of songs during the performance of the *āsārita*.
Thus is recorded the rule for songs composed upon a *vastu*. || 296 ||
Listen also to the characteristics of songs composed with gestures;
for the very same rules that apply to the subject matter apply to dance, dramatic representation, and instrumental music as well.
One should likewise apply that same [rhythm] even to the chandakas bound to the limbs, as well as to instrumental music composed of long syllables and short syllables. (298)

One should apply the *sopohana* at the beginning of the section (*mukha*) in order to separate the syllables, whenever a limb [of the performance] returns again and again due to the requirements of the melody. (299)

Where there is completion, from such a descent, the effect—the manifestation of all vessels, musical instruments, and so forth—occurs. The meaning is that it occurs at the beginning of the first [act] and so on.
*Vastuka* means the very object itself. All of that should be enacted at the beginning and then joined with dance. (294)

He asks, "How so? and replies: "The rule which [applies]... The very same method that applies to the *āsārita* (the introductory dance) is the method here as well. Just as in the *āsāritas* there is a restriction regarding the number [of dancers], the performance of the dance proceeds with an increase in the number of female dancers; previously, however, the dramatic representation was performed by a single woman, and in the dance, there is the employment of musicians and the like. It is the same here too. Therefore...
One should understand that here the number of objects refers to the dancers.
Concluding this, he begins another topic: "In this way, for those based on the subject matter," and so forth.

One should apply [the rules] regarding musical instruments in the passage beginning with "for the purification of the instruments" and so forth. One should likewise apply them to the compositions based on the limbs [of dance]. Thus:
Even among all the remaining *bhūtas* and within the independent *chandakas*,

he demonstrates a distinction by saying "the instrumental" (*vādya*). Forms such as *dhiṃghiṃḍhan* and *tran*, though heavy, sometimes occur in great numbers when employed in *tāla* due to the swiftness of effort.
As in *yathotsāhacchaṭā* and so forth, [the sequence] is *tthītthītthītthan*, *dhṛt*, *datthakudahiṃ*; this constitutes one *kalā*. Therefore it is said:

"Even in a composition consisting of few syllables, there is the joining of the first [syllable] at the beginning of the *ardha* (half-measure) and so on, because of the emptiness of the first half-*kalā* and so forth. And likewise, in *cañcatpuṭa*, in the first *kalā*, [the syllables] are simply *t hiviṭā*.
p.
193) Among these, the first should be performed as a dramatic representation (abhineya), while the remainder should be joined with dance (nṛtta).
When, by the power of the song, a limb is repeated again and again, [it constitutes dance]. || 300 ||

To avoid that [fault], he says: for heavy syllables (*varṇa*), especially down to the atom (*aṇu*), that instrumental music (*tadvādya*) should be performed as preeminent through its three or four morae (*trimātra-caturmātratayā*).
This [rule applies] to the member called *mukha* or *upavahasa*, and even in the *vastunibandha* and the *upohana* members.

The method of instrumental music (*vādyavidhi*). However, because its constituent parts (*aṅga*) are few, it does not receive the designation of "limb" (*aṅganibandha*) there. Now, he says—since it applies as a supplement to everything—"when, by virtue of the song, it is a limb," and so forth. This refers to when the primary limbs (*mukhyāṅga*) recur again and again. How? In the case of the fourfold song (*gīti*).

"By the power (*vaśāt*) of the Māgadhī and other [dialects]" means by their efficacy. For it will be stated at the end of the *Dhruvādhyāya*: "The Māgadhī is declared to arise from the non-return of words" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 32.438), and so forth.

There is also a reading "by the power of the song" (*gītavaśāt*), which has the same meaning; that is, by the song (*gītim*) or that which is being sung (*gīyamānam*). In that context, "the rule" (*vidhim*) refers to this.
It will be stated in the chapter on *tāla*:
"The number of syllables is counted as two, or even as three" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 31.103).

Regarding the word "therein": it means in the turning back (*nivartana*). Regarding "the first": it refers to the first turn (*āvarta*). Regarding "the rest," and so forth: it refers to the other turns.

These are to be employed for pure dance (*śuddha-nṛtta*). Therefore, it is shown that dance occurs not only at the conclusion of the plot elements (*vastu*) and other components, but also occasionally during the intermediate transitions (*parivarta*). As for what was stated by Rāhulaka regarding the performance without repetition, that too should be understood as being of this very nature.

As for what some have imagined regarding the verse "jalaṇihiculu-i mā-imā" (*māna* being contained in a drop from the ocean), namely that it "unfolds" (*unmīlyate*) and so forth—that holds true in every case; let it be so for now.
(300) In that regard, he states the rule for the *vādya* (instrumental) performance: "By the power of the revolving song, the limb..."

When that which consists of the performance of *śākhācārī* occurs, then, as in dance where instrumental music is predominant, the diversity of the instrument should be displayed according to its possibility. Previously, indeed, that diversity was constrained by the meaning of the poetry; now, however, there is no such restriction for it. And thus, in the actual performance (*lakṣya*):

Considering that there is no contraction of the hands (*pātra*) and so forth in the *prāveśikī* [mudrā], the masters of song (*gītācārya*) speak of the employment of a triad. This will be examined later, so let it rest for now.
The *tāla* has three types of hand positions (*pāṇi*): *samapāṇi*, *uparipāṇi*, and *ardhapāṇi* (Nāṭya Śāstra 31–329).
Because it is manifested by that [melody], it is threefold: that which occurs together with song and dance, or that which occurs before them;
[this refers to] the meter (*chandas*) of syllables and words.
One should employ instrumental music there in conjunction with the three tempos (layas); the performers here must play the instrument in accordance with the tempo. || 301 ||
The *tata* [vowel] and the *anugata*, as well as the *ogha* accompanied by the *karaṇas*, should be applied firmly to the *tattva*; and in the middle, it should be *anugata*.
Furthermore, this procedure pertaining to the instruments should be applied repeatedly as a flood;
having reached the *chandogīta*, one should cause the limbs (*aṅga*) to revolve.

This rule must always be observed regarding dance, dramatic gesture, and instrumental music; for those [performances] that are based on a specific subject matter, the conclusion should occur at the end of them.
"However, when there is a reversal of the limbs (*aṅga*), the initial capture (*graha*) is considered [the standard].
*Sāmya* is the tempo (*laya*). The threefold division of *druta* and so forth is produced by the interval of *kalā* and time (*kāla*) (Nāṭyaśāstra 31–326).
And this threefold nature is also an indicator for the divisions of the paths of *yati* and so forth.
Now, raising the question of what kind of instrumental music (*vādya*) is used in the first *āvarta*, he says: "Just as the tempo (*laya*).

For in the first *āvarta*, the instrumental music must be performed strictly in accordance with the tempo—whether fast (*druta*) or otherwise—that is appropriate for the limbs (*aṅga*) due to the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of the meaning of the poetry. Others, however, without considering the words "just as" (*yathā*) and "thus" (*tathā*), [interpret this] merely as a supplement to the preceding section.

They bring out the meaning of the verse as follows: "Just as an instrumental performance is joined with the variety of triple tempo (*tripāṇi-laya*), so too must the tempo of the vocal parts and the song be maintained. And he shows, with the reason provided in the three-quarter verse, that this [tempo] must not be transgressed: (301) Furthermore, he demonstrates with the three-quarter verse that this must not be transgressed, providing the underlying reason:

"In this very manner" means: because this dance has the purpose of pleasing and is for the sake of praising the Lord, the Blessed Mahādeva, for that reason it is being raised up for the attainment of what is seen. This same rule applies to the *gītakāsāritas*, to those [remaining] (*taccheṣeṣu*), and to the *chandakas*. As for the *pāṇikā*:

Because her body is limited in size, she herself does not become the vessel for the *tāṇḍava* dance. For that [dance], being primarily *lāsya* within the delicate preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*), is determined precisely from the nature of *lāsya* itself as described for the sake of demonstrating skill in its performance; otherwise, if the *tāṇḍava* were intended for use in the preliminary ritual, there would be no mention of *lāsya* in that chapter.

What is the occasion [for this objection]? If it is argued that [the *daśāṅga*] is useless for the mere instrumental part (*vādyāṅgamātra*), then there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of applying the *daśāṅga* even to cases such as the employment [of instruments], and that will be refuted. If it is not employed in that [latter case], then [the following applies] on page 195:
In this same manner, this rule should be applied to songs and also to āsāritas;
for this [performance] based on the praise of the deity is delicate—understand it thus. (302)
Furthermore, that conversation between a man and a woman which arises from desire should be known as *sukumāra* (tender), for it originates from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*). || 303 ||

We do not consider these to be *geyapada*s; this will be explained in the chapter on *tāla*. However, since they are subordinate to the *gītaka* and other such forms, they are included within the *chanda* [section] and are therefore not mentioned here. Furthermore, the *gītaka* occurs even in the independent *āsārita*.
As for the application of the *tāṇḍava*, it is when this [performance] is structured by means of *piṇḍībandha*s.

At that time, the placement of each individual limb occurs separately for each of them; even when extended by analogy through the *tadotātideśa*, it is exactly the same. The performance begins with the entry of the dancer according to the division of the four primary limbs. It is precisely for this purpose that it was stated in the *Vardhamāna*:

Furthermore, there is the mention of the *āsārita* and *saṅkīrtana*. In the context of the *parapūrvaraṅga*, the inclusion of those [other elements] must be explained by means of the word "also" (*api*), starting from the statement:
"at the end of all songs," followed by:
"the four-footed, as well as the single-limbed... whether in pairs or according to their measure."

Having thus defined [the dance] as "abounding in erotic sentiment and possessing three tempos" (*Nāṭya Śāstra* 31.293), the *lāsya* with its ten components will be defined in the chapter on rhythm (*tāla*) in the thirty-first [chapter].
Furthermore, it will be explained that the *lāsya-gāna* is included within the four *caccatpuṭa* meters, and so forth.

Since the *catuṣpadā* composed by Viśākhila and others has been subsumed by the Sage [Bharata] within the *lasya-gāna*, it is shown that this *catuṣpadā* should be employed at the end of the *gītaka*s or at the end of the *pāṇika*.
With this intention, he introduces the subject, saying: "Learn the *sukumāra*. The word "tu" (but/however) [is used].

It should be considered from the perspective of the subsequent [stage], meaning "but it is delicate. For this very reason, he formulates the rule for coloring by means of his own faculty of reasoning and exclusion (*hāpoha*). In that regard as well, everything—such as "with the increase of the limbs, there is an increase of the dancer"—is to be inferred; such is the meaning. (302)

Now, one might ask: "What is that which is delicate? To this he says: "But [the love] of woman and man. One *tu* (but) has been understood from the preceding context; the second *tu* qualifies the "delicate" (*sukumāraka*). For that alone is delicate, and not that which consists of the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the comic (*hāsya*), and so forth. What is that? He says: it is the love (*kāma*) of woman and man—of the woman...
It is the desire of a person—whether of a man or of a woman.

Therefore, that speech which arises from the heart of a poet through the process of intention (*vivakṣā*) is "delicate" (*sukumāra*), being the very sentence that produces poetry (*kāvya*). For this reason alone, there exists a state of mutual causality.
For this very reason, he says: where there is the mere possibility of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) being mutually caused, there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
Therefore, even a composition consisting solely of that state [of mutual causality] is not contradictory to *ḍombikā* and other such works, as well as to the *vidūṣaka* and so forth.
Furthermore, one should understand that the composition must not lack the manifestation of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) at the beginning of the performance and so forth.
196) Regarding the Supreme Lord, in whichever particular state the dancers should employ their dance, [that state should be observed].
I shall explain all of that; listen to it from me, O twice-born ones. (304)
When the limbs and the subject matter have ceased, as well as when the colors have ceased,
and likewise in a place of exaltation, the knower of that [dance] should employ the dance.
Whatever is seen that pertains to the passion of a couple, there the dance should be performed, arising from the quality of the purpose of great joy. 306.

For while the Blessed Lady was performing asceticism, she became single-mindedly devoted to him; thus, in that state where there is merely the condition of passion (*kāma-avasthā*) consisting of mutual affection (*anu-bandha*), it is simply the erotic and the comic.
Beyond that, however, in the deeds of the Supreme Lord, such as the taking over of half his body and so forth, these [emotions] are indeed the erotic and the comic.
Because the delicate [sentiment] does not spread due to its having two branches, it remains even today only on one side.

Compassion (*karuṇa*) and the like are not possible in the Blessed One, nor are they appropriate there; thus, that [sentiment] is not delicate. As for the description of Sītā’s fainting and so forth in the *Rāghavavijaya* and other works, that is a frantic dance (*tāṇḍava*). And it is not...

In that regard, there is the application of dance (*nṛtta*) consisting of delicate bodily movements (*aṅgahāra*) fashioned by the *sītā* [tune]; however, according to the principle of contemplating the meaning of the song (*gīta*), whatever action belongs to the Furious (*raudra*) sentiment is also [included] under the Compassionate (*karuṇa*), and thus, by extension, there is the employment of such corresponding dramatic representation (*abhinaya*). Enough with this prolixity. (303)

He states the remainder of what was to be said: "In which [rāga], for which [mūrcchanā]," and so forth. Whatever poetry is delicate (*sukumāra*), the singing based upon it is likewise [delicate]. The dance (*nṛtta*) is also included therein. Regarding that, it has been stated: "For that very same subject matter... (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.295), and likewise: "When, by virtue of the song, the limb... (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.300).
299) Thus [it is said]. As for the application of dance (*nṛttayojana*), it is a rule preceded by a restatement of that [same principle].

(304) Regarding the phrase "but upon the cessation of the limbs and the substance": the particle *tu* is displaced in order and serves as an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). The cessation (*nivṛtti*) of the *varṇas*—namely, the *sthāyins* and so forth, which consist of the expansion of the performance of song (*gītakriyā*)—occurs, for example, in the *parāntaka* and other such forms. In the *pratiśākhā*, however...

As it will be stated: "And also the *pratiśākhā* and so forth"—therefore, a dance master who understands the distinctions between chapters, prosperity, locations, and emotional states (*bhāva*) should employ that dance which has been described as having such a variety of vocal and instrumental modes within the transformations of limbs, substances, colors, and syllables. (305)

Thereafter, he provides an illustration: "That which is seen," etc. That portion of poetry in which the amorous acts of a couple—a woman and a man—are heard as the subject matter (*vācya*), and furthermore, that which arises from qualities whose purpose is great joy (*praharṣa*); that quality which has joy as its aim.
Wherever the beloved is present, the sight of the time of menstruation and so forth,
as well as dance connected with the meaning of songs, is also desired there. (307)
A young woman who has been rejected, deceived, or separated by a quarrel should not employ dance upon that limb [of her body] where she feels such pain. || 308 ||
When engaged in conversation with her female friend, or when her beloved is not present, she should not perform the dance; nor should she do so for one whose beloved has gone abroad.
Attachment, speech, listening to the words of a female messenger (*dūtī*), and so forth, arise from that [love]; the dance produced by them and absorbed therein should be applied there.

This is to be understood as occurring among the stages of love (*kāmāvasthā*). By this, even within the *śṛṅgāra* [rasa], the dance pertaining to the woman prepared for a tryst (*vāsakasajjā*) and the woman going to meet her lover (*abhisārikā*) has been described. (306)

He speaks regarding the woman whose husband is under her own control: "where he is present. In whichever limb there is a connection with the meaning—that is, the expressed sense—of the poem being sung, and where, upon the presence of the beloved, there occurs the observation of the season such as spring, or of time such as the rising of the moon, there dance takes place. (307)
In order to demonstrate the fruit of this rule, he says: "She who is deceived," and so forth.
"When her beloved does not come to the appointed place because of some distraction, she is a *khaṇḍitā*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 22.209).
"She whose lover, having sent a messenger and even given a rendezvous,
does not arrive for some reason here, is indeed deceived. (Nāṭyaśāstra 22.210) "She whose lover, having departed due to a quarrel born of jealousy, does not return..."
She, having fallen under the power of remorse, is a *kalahāntaritā* (one separated by a quarrel).
(Nāṭyaśāstra 22.208) Regarding the word "aṅga": it refers to the section of the poem that serves as its basis. Anticipating the doubt, "Why does the dance not continue for this long?", he says:
"proceeding from her friend. Likewise, when the beloved is absent...

Even regarding the account (*vṛttānta*) consisting of conversations concerning him, reflections on the means for his reunion, and so forth—in that too, dancing is not to be employed. By this, the woman longing in separation (*virahotkaṇṭhitā*) is characterized. The woman prepared for the tryst (*vāsakasajjā*) is described in the same way when her beloved does not arrive; however, the distinction is that the woman whose love has been slighted (*khaṇḍitā*) is one who has discovered his infidelity. Or, it may refer to one whose beloved has gone abroad (*proṣitabhartṛkā*).

Even in states such as that of a woman whose husband is away, when one considers whether the beloved is absent, difficult to reach, or perhaps merely residing in the heart, then there is no dancing; for in those cases, the performance reaches its conclusion immediately after the preliminary actions (*karaṇa*).
"When the manifestation of the [proper] season and so forth occurs by means of a female messenger (*dūtī*),
and is connected with longing and anxiety, one should not employ dance therein. Rather, one should gradually apply whatever gesture (*aṅga*) the heroine might find pleasing."
From that time forward, one should apply the dance to the remaining limbs. || 310 ||
It should be understood in such a way that, because of its perishable nature, that very [state] must be resorted to therein;

it is not said to be "numbered as two" or "numbered as three. Although an illustrative example is obtained through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*) and the meaning has already been shown, it is not stated explicitly by its own name here, because dance is intended as the primary subject.

Regarding the phrase "in which limb" (*yasminnaṅge*) and "serenity" (*prasādam*): it refers to the state of having a clear heart, by whatever means a young woman might obtain it. This [instruction] should be understood as applying not only to the case of one whose passion has been interrupted, but rather to all cases. From that point onward, regarding the phrase "in the remaining limbs," the meaning is as follows: in this context, those pertaining to dramatic performance (*nāṭya*)—
The examples of drama provided by some should be considered inappropriate.

As for the claim that where heroines such as the *khaṇḍitā* (the neglected wife) and others are directly portrayed, dances consisting of movements like *valana* (turning) and *āvartana* (whirling) should not be employed—that argument has no basis whatsoever. For instance:
Through sighs of anxiety and weariness, through the simulation of a burning heart,
through conversations with her friends, and through observations of her own physical state;
By means of exhaustion, dejection, and the shedding of tears; by the expression of anger;
by being devoid of ornaments, by straightforwardness, and by weeping out of sorrow.

"The woman who has been slighted (*khaṇḍitā*), the deceived (*vipralabdhā*), she separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*), and likewise she whose husband is away (*proṣitanāthā*)— one should employ these emotional states (*bhāva*). Thus it will be stated in the section on general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*).
When one is despondent, fainted, terrified, afflicted by loathing or grief,
exhausted, asleep, bewildered, motionless, or likewise languid;

When she is intoxicated, negligent, or excessively drunk; when she is absorbed in thought, established in austerity, afflicted by disease, tormented by fever, distressed by fear, or overwhelmed by cold.
One should not perform gestures with the hands; rather, one should act based on the inner being (*sattva*).
Furthermore, whatever limb may be employed for the purpose of praising the deity— (Nāṭyaśāstra 9.176–178, p. 199).
One should not employ this [dance] with the Māheśvara gaits, which are characterized by the graceful movements of the limbs and are bold. || 311 ||
As for the song connected with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), which concerns men and women,
one should employ it with graceful bodily movements (aṅgahāra) performed by the goddesses.
I shall now fully explain the rules regarding the four-footed *narkuṭaka*, the *khañjaka*, and the *parigītaka*, as well as the procedure for the performance of musical instruments.
If there is a four-footed [meter] joined with the Khañjana and the Ṛkuṭa, and if there is a caesura at the end of each foot, there will be the acquisition of goods for that [person]. || 314 ||
Thus he will state regarding the *āṅgika* (bodily) expression.

Such being the case, there is no room here for the *hasta-abhinaya* (hand gestures) itself; so what occasion is there for the suspicion of its integration through movements such as *valana* (twisting) or *āvartana* (turning), such that a prohibition of them would need to be stated here? Nor is it the case here...

Let it suffice that the *nāṭya* has been introduced. Thus, at the conclusion of the *gītaka* and so forth, a *catuṣpadā* should be employed as a *pāṇikā* which adopts the singing of the *lāsya*. By this much, the *gītaka* and other elements are performed in their entirety.
It is for this very purpose [that one should visualize] Śaṅkara and Pārvatī dancing with a delicate performance.

Beginning from the opening verse (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.249), the very nature of dance has been demonstrated as having two branches. (310) Here, he explains the division of this twofold dance in three verses, starting with the words "based on the praise of the gods."
"Whose limb? refers to that belonging to Chandaka.
"By the arrogant ones" means by those primarily characterized by the *vidyud-bhrānta*, *garuṇḍa-plutaka*, and other [gaits]. The reason for this is that they were dispatched by Maheśvara.
"By the graceful ones" refers to that which is not connected with the second set of four gaits.
[The dance] begins with the hips [moving] like a cluster of *talapuṣpa* flowers. The reason for this is that they have been fashioned by the Goddess.

(312) Thus has the procedure for the dance (*nṛttavidhi*) been described in relation to the four-line verse (*catuṣpadā*) which incorporates singing with rhythmic movement (*salāsya*). Now, the procedure for the musicians (*bhāṇḍavidhi*) must be stated. In that regard, the *dhruvā* is performed with four lines; and those lines—

That which will be described by means of dry syllables such as *jhaṇṭum* (or *digla*, etc. is as follows: "That which is sung by singers seated on seats, accompanied by the singing of stringed instruments, is called *śuṣka* (dry) song-text. (Kāvyamīmāṃsā, Nāṭyaśāstra 18.185).
(200) That which is fixed, joined with meter, having equal feet and equal syllables—
in the conclusion of its feet, there shall be the grasping of the forefinger. || 315 ||
Having performed one round of both singing and instrumental accompaniment, he should again apply the return of the verses together with the musical instruments.

Thus [it is said], or [alternatively] by means of meaningful words (*sārthakapada*). In that case as well, the quarters (*pāda*) are formed either by syllables (*varṇavṛtta*) or by morae (*mātrāvṛtta*). These may be equal, half-equal, or unequal. And these are primarily joined with the *khañjana* and *ṛkuṭaka* meters; as will be stated in the chapter on *dhruva*, there are eight [of them].
Regarding the *narkuṭakas*, there are three types of *khañjaka* meters (*kāvyamīmāṃsāśāstra* 32.280;
301). Beginning with this, others have emerged from them, such as the *yugmaujas* and the *viṣama* [meters] (*nāṭyaśāstra* 32.308).

This concerns the introduction of musical instruments (*bhāṇḍavādya*). Regarding the four-line verse known as *narkuṭaka*: although it consists of four lines, because of its proximity [to the preceding], it is sung within the four-line [meter]; furthermore, the *trivṛttaka* mentioned in the chapter on *dhruvās*, or the *śuṣkagīta*, is likewise in that very same place. Thus, among these three types, there is the introduction of musical instruments.
I shall now describe the procedure for the *puṣkaravādya*.
A four-line *dhruvā* is performed according to either the *khañjakā* or *narkuṭaka* meter;
in this [performance], the singing is accompanied by the *śrīvaṃśa* [flute] for as long as the penultimate *kalā* of the first line lasts.
But that other unit of time (*kalā*) called *sannipāta*, which is defined by the sound produced by the joining of two hands,
should be the occasion for beginning the instrumental music (*bhāṇḍavādya*) at the time of singing it;
[this applies] to those [songs] whose nature consists of half-even and uneven meters.
The rule applies to a four-line stanza (*catuṣpadī*) composed of the *narkuṭaka*, *khañjaka*, and *jāti* meters.
However, regarding that which is composed of the *jāti* meters consisting of *varṇavṛtta* and *samavṛtta*, he states the rule as "that which is *dhruvā*" (*yā dhruvā*).
It is a four-line stanza with equal feet (*samapādā*). This is the meaning: that which is a four-line stanza is joined with a meter (*chandasā yuktā*). It is "joined" (*yuktā*).

"Joined with the *jāti*, *gati*, *varṇa*, and *vṛtta*" means it consists of a *samavṛtta* of that same *jāti*. When the first quarter (*pāda*) is completed, in the second quarter, one should employ a musical instrument such as a *bhāṇḍa* (drum), characterized by the forefinger (*pradeśinī*) or the index finger (*tarjanī*), beginning from three *kalās* (*trikalaprabhṛti*). In that case, it is done with a pair (*yugmena*).
When it consists of four feet—as will be stated [in the *Nāḍīśāstra*]: "Or, by measure, it is even or odd" (*nā.

śā.* 31.293)—and the path consists of three (or two) *kalās*, then the seventh *kalā* is in the second foot; because that exiting *kalā* is to be employed with the index finger (*tarjanī*), it is called the "index finger" (*tarjanī*). However, when measured in four *kalās*, it is the thirteenth.
But when the limbs and the subject matter have ceased, and when there is the cessation of other colors,
as well as during their presentation, one should employ musical instruments such as drums. (317)
Furthermore, whatever intermediate paths may be formed by the instruments of the strings and the voice,
the *sūcī* [movement] should be employed upon them along with the *bhāṇḍa* in the *tāṇḍava*.

The *tarjanī* [finger-mark] is for the *āvāpa* (insertion) time; however, when measured by a triangle, then the fifth [mātrā] is two *kalās*, with the *kaniṣṭhā* [finger-mark] for the exiting *kalā* and the *tarjanī* [for the insertion]. But in the four-*kalā* [measure], the ninth [mātrā] is the *āvāpa-kalā* [marked by] the *tarjanī*. This will be explained in the chapter on *tāla*, beginning with the words: "The exit of the *kaniṣṭhā* finger," and so forth.
The *niṣkrāma* [gesture] is performed with the index finger, as stated in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (31.41–42), and so forth. This has been stated concisely by the teacher Dattila:
"The wise know [the *niṣkrāma*] to proceed respectively from the first, second, middle, and final quarter-parts of the verse."
Joined with the little finger and the ring finger, it is formed by the middle finger and the index finger.
"It should be devoid of the middle of the odd [beats].

Thus, it is meant that the falling of the *kalā* in the second foot, which is to be employed by the index finger (*tarjanī*), involves the taking up of the musical instrument (*bhāṇḍagraha*) and the entry of the dancer (*nartakī*) characterized thereby. Others [say]:

Regarding the *ākāśagraha*, those who consider the *graha* to consist of the soundless portion (*niśśabdakalā*)— asserting that the *graha* occurs here precisely at the fall (*pāta*) which is characterized by the conjunction (*sannipāta*) accompanied by sound— describe the movement to the foot-part indicated by the word "forefinger" (*pradeśinī*) as being indeed with sound, up to the limit of the *pādagraha*.

Regarding the five "hand-falls" (*pāṇiprapāta*) which will be explained in the *Puṣkara-adhyāya*, the commentary states that among them, the fall of the index finger (*pradeśinī*) signifies the grasping of a vessel; this is the conjunction (*sannipāta*), which is a favor (*anugraha*). This is according to the context, as well as by the passage to be stated in the *Dhruva-adhyāya* beginning with "the four planets are fixed" (*caturgrahā dhruvāḥ*).
"Some are *sannipāta*-seizers, others are *kāśa*-seizers; some are *pradeśinī*-seizers, and likewise others are *samagraha*-seizers" (Nāṭyaśāstra 32.423).
According to this rule, those who know the subject matter have disregarded what is contradictory [to the definition]. (315)
Now, one might object: "In that case, the dancer has entered [the stage] from that point onward and performs the acting;

however, as for that first quarter or even the portion exceeding it, the dancer has not yet entered—what then is the status of that part? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having made one... [referring to] that pure division which was previously mentioned.
That song, which recounts the life-story of Maheśvara, should be performed with musical instruments by one who applies this [method]. (p. 202)
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva. || 319 ||
"It should be performed together" means that it is to be employed later; this is what is being stated.

The mention of "feet" (pāda) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). By this, it is meant that one must effect a cessation—that is, a turning back—from as much of the portion as was previously employed by the instrumentalist (*bhāṇḍavādya*) but not yet performed. This is what is stated.
It occurs.

(316) Now, here, under the guise of naming specific musical instruments and the like within this four-line verse, he shows the place for dancing: "But upon the completion of the bodily substance (*aṅgavastu*)," etc. The particle *tu* is displaced [from its usual position] and serves as an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). Or, it refers to a single limb (*aṅga*).

Or, regarding every object—whether it be a permanent entity devoid of a body, or a specific quality such as stability—one should apply, according to the logic of each branch (*pratiśākha-nyāya*), that transformation which consists of presentation (*upasthāpanā*) and so forth;
among those, one should employ with excellence a variety of musical instruments and vocalization endowed with manifold diversity. And by virtue of that, therein...
The meaning is that one should perform the application of dance movements and gestures (*nṛttāṅgahāra*).

(317) Now, the rule for the four-line *śuṣkākṣarā* must be stated; however, that [form] is employed first, because it was previously stated [in the rule] "when [the performers] have sat down on their seats. Therefore, in the case of *geya*—that is, in poetry intended to be sung—[this applies].

The phrase "understanding the *pada*" indicates that its nature is that of a foundational framework (*pīṭhabandha*). Likewise, in the case of other *ṣidgaka* songs, the [text] is not present before what is to be sung; therefore, it is not in the form of a *nākā*. For this very reason, in the *geya*, the term "*dhruvāgīte geyam*" (to be sung in the *dhruvā* song) has the same meaning as "*gātavyam*" (to be sung). He states that rule: "And those which are the intermediate paths. *Antara* means...
The means by which the mutual distinction [of notes] is sought is the *antaramārga*.

That tone (*svara*) is characterized as being both *saṃvādī* (consonant) and *anuvādī* (dissonant); and because it lacks predominance of meaning (*arthaprādhānyābhāva*), it is designated by that very [term].

For this very reason, he says: "by the action of the string (*tantrīkriyayā*) or by the action of speech (*vākkriyayā*). That very [action] is [so called] due to its lack of meaning (*nirarthakatayā*).
In these [performances], the application of the *bhāṇḍa* (the buffoon) occurs precisely because they are performed collectively.

For the *sūcī-abhinaya* (indicative acting) of a dancer consists merely of the movements of the limbs and *sāttvika* expressions, devoid of hand-gestures (*hastābhinaya*) that follow the poetic meaning of the dramatic elements (*lāsyāṅga*), due to her concealment [of the plot]. As he will say:

"When the meaning of the sentence is first joined with the components of the sentence-substance (*vākyavastu*), then follows the enactment through speech (*vāc*); this is what is to be understood here as the 'component' (*aṅga*). And this enactment, performed by means of the three types of *tāla*—namely, the measured tempo (*kṛtatā*) and so forth—used in the performance of singing, is still seen today.

In this way, the *vardhamānaka* performance or the *gītaka* performance becomes complete and endowed with its causal basis through the application of *chanda* and the application of *catuṣpada*. Therefore, following the introductory sequence of the *tālādhyāya*, [there follow] the *vardhamāna*, *āsāritaka*, *gītaka*, *chanda*, and *catuṣpada*.
The procedure for the lāsya and gāna included therein will be described in sequence.
203) Thus has this procedure been taught according to the performance of the tāṇḍava.
Furthermore, what else may be told regarding the rules of the science of drama?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Tāṇḍava," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
"There are three types of songs, such as the Madrakā and others" (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.13)—this verse will appear in the chapter on the *pūrvaraṅga*.
Its meaning has already been determined previously. Therefore, having considered this [verse] in light of that introductory passage (*apasāra*), this stated purpose must be carried out. (318)

Now, one might wonder whether the [performance] possesses fruit solely through the primary fruit belonging to the *pūrvaraṅga*, or whether there is also another fruit. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "(Of Maheśvara). By demonstrating that it possesses a separate fruit, he shows that this [work] is to be employed independently; thus he says: "of Maheśvara. [The word] "caritam" (deed).

The word "ceṣṭitam" [is used]. The term "prayojayet" is employed through *tantra* (economy of expression), applying the causative suffix (*ṇic*) both in its primary sense and in the sense of the causal agent. Consequently, the purification of sin for the patron who employs the performance, for the discerning audience who initiates it, and for the assembly of spectators, as well as the infinite fruit consisting of rebirth in the world of Śiva, belong to the dance.

It is not stated that there is a different purpose [for the four-line verse] other than the single purpose already observed. Furthermore, when used independently, the use of the *chandakas* and the four-line verse even in isolation is indeed permitted;
and as for their ancillaries, they are to be performed according to the sequence beginning with "becoming one who holds a handful of flowers" (*puṣpāñjalidharā bhūtvā*).

In the world, there is the application of syllables (*varṇas*). Following the rule "at the end of its quarter" (*tasyāḥ pādāvasāne tu*) and so forth, there is the procedure for the *dhārā*, *parikrama*, and other elements; according to the rule "when [it occurs] by the power of the song" (*yadā gītavaśāt*, Nāṭyaśāstra 4.300), there is the fourfold method of *apasāraka* and so forth, involving the doubling of meaning and the use of *guṇāla*, *kavāraṇaka*, *guñjikā*, and the like.

In the *ḍombikā* and other such forms, the teachers should gradually increase the number of dancers; and in accordance with the rhythm (*tāla*), following the rules for the combination of the three types of tempo (*tripāṇilaya*) and so forth, there should be the circumambulation of the stage (*dhārāparikrama*) and the like, characterized by a tempo embraced by the specific rhythmic flow (*layapariṣvaṅkitalayatālaparikrama*). (319)
All of this is for the purpose of pleasing the Lord;
thus, concluding with these words, he creates an opening for the next chapter with the passage beginning "In this way, this...
and so forth. "In this way" means by the method previously described. "From practice" (prayogataḥ) refers to the application (prayogam).
Apart from that which consists of drama (*nāṭya*), another rule or method distinct from it is observed; likewise, in the case of dramas and the like,

with respect to the refinement of the performance, a method such as acting is observed by virtue of the performer’s identification with the character— as is the case for the audience— but not [in the same way].
In this [work], there exists the nature of a drama that is both directly perceived and mentally constructed.

Due to the absence of the application of the fourfold dramatic representation (abhinaya) and because rasa and bhāva are not predominant, singing, instrumental music, and dance hold primacy at will, according to the tradition of the elder dancers. This is the case in poetry.
Because it depends upon a [real] object (*vastu*), it does not consist of the nature of a reflection that is the very life-breath of the prologue of a drama;

because it is threefold, it is impossible for it to attain reality in states such as intoxication or fainting; and because singing and so forth are invariably prompted by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), it exists primarily through the predominance of song and the like.
Because it is performed by one whose lineage is unbroken, and because its very nature as poetry is inseparable from being supported by song,

and because— despite the variety of methods in its progression, its structural composition, and its rhythmic arrangement— it ultimately rests solely upon dance, and furthermore, because the primary fruit belongs to the performer, the instigator, and the singer, drama (*nāṭya*) is distinct from that [poetry].
"The function of that [word] is differentiated"—this is the meaning of the word, according to the opinion of the Teacher (Upādhyāya).
Whether a limb such as the sentiment, the emotion, the gaze, the hand, the head, and so forth, be complete or incomplete—(p. 204) [it is so].

"How indeed can there be a distinction between *nāṭya* and *nṛtta* when their nature as imitation is equal?"—this is the *Harṣavārtika*. "Dance (*nṛtta*) is that which is performed by means of a few elements of drama (*nāṭya*), such as those suitable for training or those done at will; it is the fruit of practice"—this is Bhaṭṭa Yantra. "It is merely a convention, like the auspicious rites at weddings and so forth"—this is Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa.
The performance of *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava* is indeed a specific variety of drama (*nāṭya*), because it consists of the complete imitation [of real action].
For instance, upon the entrance of Aśvatthāman, there is the "needle-pierced" gesture (*sūcīviddha*) with the knees raised high (*ūrdhvajānu*), and so forth.
Purūravas performed the *alapallavasūcī*; Garuḍa, the *garuḍaplutaka*; Rāvaṇa, the *puṣkara* and *vaiśākharecitaka*;
Vatsarāja, the *agnisambhrama*; and Jaṭāyu, the *gṛdhrāvalīnaka* and *melakākrīḍita*—these were performed through various dramatic gestures (*citrābhinaya*) in his youth.

It is precisely the application of the instruments [of performance]. Since the elements such as the *padārtha* (the meaning of words) and so forth are also employed in drama (*nāṭya*), Master Kīrtidhara maintains that this is indeed drama itself. Furthermore, they state the meaning of the word [“drama”] in accordance with their own system; one should consider therein its propriety or impropriety.
Only experts truly know; enough with this prolixity.

By way of incidental discussion, or through the sequence of one topic leading to another, something else related to dance—well-known as being part of the present subject of drama—is [briefly] introduced.

With the intention of explaining [the term] "interrupter," he says: "nāṭya. Regarding the injunction—that is, the performance—of that very *nāṭya* which is the Veda; may there be auspiciousness! (320) May the mass of darkness be shattered by the rays from the three eyes fashioned from the sun, moon, and fire!
Abhinavagupta has clearly explained this *Tāṇḍava* [of the *Tantrāloka*].
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the performance of the *tāṇḍava*, in the *Abhinavabhārati*, a commentary on the *Nāṭyaśāstra*, composed by the great Śaiva teacher Abhinavagupta.
p. 205) Śrī! Now begins the fifth chapter.
Having heard Bharata’s words regarding the cause for the continuity of the drama, the sages, with delighted minds, spoke these words once again: || 1 ||
Just as there is this origin of drama and the production of the *jarjara* mask, so too is there the pacification of obstacles and the worship of the deities. (2)
All that has been heard by us has been grasped and comprehended; yet we wish to know it once more in its entirety and according to its true nature. (3)
O Brahman, you should explain that great splendor, which is endowed with all auspicious marks and serves as the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga), exactly as we understand it.
We bow to that Śāṅkarī, whose form is the sky, who acts as the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) for the production of the drama of saṃsāra by providing it with its stage space.

In order to establish the connection between the chapters, he begins with a narrative of the past (*purākalpa*), starting with the words "of Bharata. "The lineage of drama" (*nāṭyasantāna*) means the continuity of drama, which is its non-interruption through the removal of the apprehension of a break caused by the narration of mere dance (*nṛtta*). When drama was inquired about, by the power of fate, dance—which yields great fruit—was also understood through its distinction [from drama]. And from that knowledge...
That drama, divided [into its components], has also been well understood. And because that drama, being thus colored [by those components], captivates the heart, there is a state of delighted mind.
This depends upon perceiving the excellence of the disciple, which consists in the capacity for grasping, retaining, and so forth, the reality of one's own [teaching].
With the intention of encouraging the teacher, they say "so it is. This restates the purport of the four chapters, namely that the dance has entered into the very midst of the worship.
He also demonstrates the knowledge of reasoning, refutation, and so forth—by the words "having grasped," and by the word "and" (*ca*).
"Having retained it, it was firmly grasped and ascertained; 'in its entirety' means completely.
(p. 206) But having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata—
He spoke these words again regarding the preliminary ritual procedures.

O illustrious ones, understand from me as I speak the preliminary ritual (pūrvaraṅga), including the divisions of the feet (pādabhāga), the musical measures (kalā), and likewise the transitions (parivarta). || 6 ||
"According to reality" (*yathātattvam*) they say refers to adherence to the truth. "We wish to know the preliminary rite" (*pūrvaraṅga*) indicates the desire to know (*jijñāsā*).
"Explain it so that we may understand it as being endowed with all characteristics" shows the seeking of a teacher even regarding the manner of exposition. Great is your splendor...
That [inquiry] consists of knowledge. The address [“O best of the twice-born”] is for the purpose of encouraging the teacher.
As it is said: “When the preliminary rite has been performed, O best of the twice-born, this [inquiry] follows first therein” (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.10).
Thus, because it is to be employed preceded by the desire to know and the observation [of the world], the desire to know arises in that very manner.
"In this performance of the *pūrvaraṅga*, let it be properly employed by you" (Nāṭya Śāstra 4.14).

And: "This *pūrvaraṅga* must be performed by you in its pure form" (4.15). By these words expressing the Supreme Lord’s reverence, [the practice] is further confirmed as being most firmly established. Thus, the intended meaning is that it must necessarily be worshipped in that very manner (1.5).

The meaning of "gadata" is that you should first determine [the matter] by means of the mere word; for the true nature of the *āśrāvaṇa* and so forth will be properly established in the section on *geya* (Nāṭya Śāstra 29). The genitive case is used here in the sense of disregard:
"Disregarding what has been stated, understand it through your own intellect. Although I have [already] explained this here in due order...

This was not stated because the section on *geya* is also very far removed [from the current context]. Nevertheless, the sequence of meaning—according to the principle that "whatever has a connection with whatever"—must be observed, and not the literal verbal sequence; thus, having transferred this disregard for the order of utterance onto the speaker, it was so stated.
There, he first explains the term *pūrvaraṅga* through its etymological derivation, beginning with the words "parts of the feet" (*pādabhāgā*).

In this context, the *pūrvaraṅga* consists precisely of the external limbs [of the performance]. And these are songs (*gītaka*), namely the *utthāpana* and the *dhruvā* forms. That [performance] is characterized by the *dvikala* *cañcatpuṭa* and *cācapuṭa* rhythms, and is performed with a specific gait (*gatigata*). Thus it is.

The intended meaning is as follows: first, regarding the *pūrvaraṅga*. In that context, a *mātrā* is that which begins with the sixteenth part of a *mātrā*; it is a thing (*vastu*) begun by that [part]. Thus, what is sung in the compositions of *vastu* is accepted as being of such a duration. Furthermore, the parts consist of two *kalās*, four *kalās*, and the rhythmic patterns (*mārga*) such as *cañcatpuṭa* and others.
It occurs through attachment. Just as in the case of syllables such as *cañcatpuṭa* and others, they are attached to divisions such as *kalā*;
thus, the path of syllables is subsumed by the grasping of *kalās*.
In this way, everything—whether consisting of two or four *kalās* according to the syllables—is [subsumed].
(207) O best of the twice-born, because this performance is first employed on the stage, it is therefore to be known as the *pūrvaraṅga* (the preliminary rite). || 7 ||
Singing such as *gītakas* and *vardhamānas*, and that which is being sung, namely *geya*, is included under the term "form" (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, by the word "art" (*kalā*), the sevenfold rhythmic arts (*tālakalā*) beginning with *niṣkrāma* are expressed; through this, the entire path of rhythm (*tālamārga*), which consists of measurement (*māna*), is grasped. And there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) for words of identical form even when they have different meanings.

"Feet," and so forth. They are called "turns" (*parivarta*) because they revolve in this manner. By means of turns numbering two, three, and so on, the entire procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is encompassed. By the word "and" (*ca*), the mere stringing together [of notes] (*tantrī*) and so forth is included. By the particle "only" (*eva*), the performance alone is indicated. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the application of the relationship between primary and subordinate elements (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) is shown according to their respective requirements.

By the second *evakāra* (the particle "only"), its status as a constituent of drama (*nāṭyāṅgatā*) is indicated; and by the second *cakāra* (the particle "and"), recitation (*pāṭhya*) and so forth, as well as pure dance (*nṛtta*), are included. Thus, it is stated that the *pūrvaraṅga* is that which consists of song, rhythm, instrumental music, dance, and recitation—whether employed individually or collectively—as a constituent part of drama, because [it is performed] on the stage (*raṅga*) or in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
Whether it be in the foundational [text] or on the stage, it will exist as something present in the intellect; and indeed, it is appropriate that it be there first.

For, without the preliminary members such as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth, the assembly of factors for singing and the like would not be complete—how then could there be the performance of the drama? Indeed, a cloth cannot possibly be produced without threads, a shuttle, a loom, and so on.

[It is] to be performed. It will be stated later that even though it serves no purpose other than as a mere restriction—like eating while facing east—it is nevertheless [performed]. Therefore, because it is the "first" (*pūrva*) "stage" (*raṅga*), it is *pūrvaraṅga*. This is a compound formed according to the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), or else the inversion of word order follows the *rājadanta*-class (Pāṇini 2.2.31).

Śrī Harṣa, however, using the word *raṅga* to denote the triple symphony (*tauryatrika*), considered that very performance of the dramatic elements to be the *pūrvaraṅga*; thus, he understood the compound as "that which is both prior (*pūrva*) and a stage (*raṅga*). As he said:

"Those portions of the stage (*raṅga*) which have been seen for the sake of the dramatic states (*avasthā*) in the performance (*nāṭya*), and specifically that very first one in which [the preliminaries] are pure—that is the *pūrvaraṅga*," and so forth. However, the interpretation that it is "the front part of the stage" is incorrect; for this is not a single portion of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), nor is it...
Of drama (*nāṭya*). For this [drama] does not have the nature of an imitation consisting of an explanatory recitation of emotional states (*bhāva*);

rather, like grammar (*śikṣā*) and so forth, it is an ultimate reality that serves as an instrument for the perfection of performance, having an object such as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) which is comparable to eating and so forth. Here, dance (*nṛtta*) also enters as a cause of variety, being contained within the form of drama.

"Dance" (*nṛtta*) here refers to that which bears the burden of imitation according to the principle of dance indicated by its "sprout" (*aṅkura*); however, it is indeed real (*satya*), like the offering of incense, unguents, and so forth, having the fruit of pleasing the deity. Thus, the compound *pūrvo raṅge* is to be understood in this very way. (5–7)
Its constituent parts, however, should be performed in their proper order:
through the combination of strings and instruments, as well as through the application of vocal recitation (*pāṭhya*). (8)
Withdrawal, descent, and likewise the commencement;
the sounding, the hand of the mouth, and the rubbing. (9)

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the collection of limbs such as *pratyāhāra* constitutes the *pūrvaraṅga*? Then how can it be said that singing and so forth constitute the *pūrvaraṅga*? Anticipating this doubt, he states a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) consisting of seven and a half verses, beginning with "But its limbs... and ending with "...for they exist in the *pūrvaraṅga*. The word "of this" (*asya*) refers to the *pūrvaraṅga*.

In the *turha* [section]: the nine elements beginning with *pratyāhāra* and ending with *āsārita*, which are yet to be characterized, are to be performed behind the curtain (*antarjavanika*). Immediately thereafter, the ten elements beginning with *gītaka* and ending with *prarocanā* are to be performed outside the curtain; this is the meaning. And those elements, beginning with the performance of *gītaka* and ending with *prarocanā*, which are outside the curtain—

Since all ten of these are effects insofar as they are related to that which has been described as having the form of being characterized by the "quarter-parts" (*pādabhāga*) and so forth, the connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: therefore, the *pūrvaraṅga* is precisely the "quarter-parts" and so forth. For when there is a deficiency or excess among the constituent parts (*aṅga*), the majority [prevails].

The varieties of the *pūrvaraṅga* will be shown in the section on singing (*geya*) at [A-29]. However, those mentioned here would result only in confusion for those who are not familiar with the underlying principles of the system.
And it is said in the *Vārttika*: "The division of the stage (*raṅgabheda*) occurs in the group of six beginning with the *nāndī*, but not in the introduction (*avataraṇa*) of the *pratyāhāra*."

The former [elements] are the colored areas, the doors, and so forth; the latter are not begun with the quarter-parts of the feet and so on. True. However, here "color" (*raṅga*) does not refer to the state of being beautiful or a specific connection, but rather to mere existence. And it will be stated that this exists everywhere. Thus he says: "Because these..."
Since these occur during the *pūrvaraṅga*, they should be performed as its constituent parts.

In that context, the *yavanikā* (curtain) is situated between the stage (*raṅgapīṭha*) and its head (*tacchiraḥ*). By the performers, namely the actors (*naṭa*), who have entered within it—primarily, or alternatively, by the performers such as the lute-players (*vaiṇika*) and others—[the following is enacted].

The *prayojya* [elements] are withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth; however, the songs (*gītaka*), the *piṇḍī*, and the recitations (*pāṭhya*) are performed when the curtain has been removed. By the verse beginning with "of the songs" (*gītānām*), the performance of either a song (*gītaka*) or a *vardhamāna* is stated. Others, however, [cite]: "Now, moreover, in the appropriate place... (*atha api sthāne*, Nāṭyaśāstra 5.13).

Those who read "ato'pi" (for this reason also) admit that both [the deity and the song] are primary; however, that contradicts the final member of the compound. Furthermore, in the rule for the instruction, there will be only one subordinate element (*aṅga*), not two.
As it is said: "From the mention of the deities, the procedure for the song is likewise to be known" (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.21).
p.
209) Then the *saṅghoṭanā* should be performed, as well as the *mārgāsārita*;
likewise, the *jyeṣṭha*, *madhya*, and *kaniṣṭha* *āsāritas* [should be performed]. || 10 ||
These songs, however, which are sung outside, should be performed by the actors standing behind the inner curtain, accompanied by stringed instruments.
Then, having removed the curtain, one should have all the Kutapas joined together here,
along with the performances of dance and song.
One song from among the Madrakas and others should be employed;
furthermore, the Vardhamāna or the Tāṇḍava dance should be performed here as appropriate.
Then the raising [of the curtain] should be performed, as well as the change of scene;
likewise, the Nāndī, the Śuṣkāvakṛṣṭā, and the Raṅgadvāra.
Furthermore, the *cārī*, the *mahācārī*, the *trika*, and the *prarocanā* constitute the preliminary rites (*pūrvaraṅga*). (15)
O twice-born ones, these constituent parts are to be performed in the ritual of the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga);
I shall explain their characteristics in due order.

Some maintain that there is only one single limb (*aṅga*) which possesses both natures. By the word "also" (*api*), [the author] indicates that whatever [limbs] there may be; at the very occasion of the enumeration (*uddeśa*), he shows the application (*viniyoga*) of this limb to *nṛtta* by stating, "wherein there is *tāṇḍava*.
By this, he demonstrates that the limbs of *nāṭya* and so forth may even be devoid of *nṛtta*. Thus, at that very time...
And there is the conventional usage of the term "pure. As he will say: "It is pure, and yet it is variegated" (8.15).

Thus, even though the meaning is identical to the general definition of the *pūrvaraṅga*, he shows that this very enumeration applies to those constituent parts (*aṅga*) which are to be employed—by saying "these."
The meaning is that by means of this sequential exposition, these [elements] are indeed of such a number. Furthermore, the arrangement of the *kutapa* is known as *pratyāhāra*.
Thus has the descent been described, as well as the settling of the singers. || 17 ||

He begins to define these according to their enumeration with the words "of these": he states their order as follows—"but of the *kutapa*," etc. Between the dressing room (*nepathyagṛha*) and the door, the drummer (*mārdaṅgika*) faces east;
to his left are the player of the hand-drum (*pāṇavika*) and the player of the *dārdarika*; to the south of the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*), [the player of the *karaṭaka*] faces north.

The singer stands in front of him, facing south, while female singers stand to his north. To his left is the lute-player; elsewhere there are two flute-players. Thus, the diverse group—which protects the specific sounds (pāti kuṃ tapati) and bestows brilliance upon the stage of the drama—is described.
Nyāsa is the bringing together in one place of those who were scattered; it is the same as pratyāhāra (withdrawal).

Although the arrangement of the singers is indeed within the middle of the kutapa, with the male singers facing [the audience] and the female singers to the north of the stage, nevertheless, their entrance—
The name "separate limb" (*pṛthag-aṅga*) has been stated in order to demonstrate the inevitability of the *aṅganāgīta* within the group of those who cause delight. As it has been said:
"Even though a man sings, the procedure of singing is endowed with its defining characteristics."
"Even so, a performance devoid of women does not bring happiness" (Nāṭyaśāstra 33.5–7). As for the one who says:

"But as for the statement [in the future verse], 'by Nārada and other Gandharvas' (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.32), since the authorship of singing by males alone will be mentioned there, a separate introduction has been stated here [anticipating that objection]."

This [objection] has no force here; for by means of the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) compound "gandharvyaś ca gandharvāś ca" (female Gandharvas and male Gandharvas), the singing of women is also possible in this context. Thus, up to the point of the *avataraṇa*, there is in reality only one single *aṅga*.
For this very reason, a single performance is carried out in both cases. As he will state in the *Puṣkara-adhyāya* (Nāṭya Śāstra 34–...):
198) Beginning with "when the drummers and others are seated," [it says]: "First is the *trisāma*;
it is threefold, tripled in that same way, and likewise based on the *āḍita* [rhythm].
It consists of three beats (*trikalā*) and six beats (*ṣaṭkalā*), because of its being a *trisāma* among the *trisāma*s" (Kāśī-mu-nā-śā 33.209).

Endowed with the three *sāmans*, pierced by the syllables of the three *sāmans*, and possessed of heavy and light syllables—the letter *ya* and the letter *ma* shall each be multiplied by three. (Nāṭyaśāstra 34.159; Kāśīkhaṇḍa 33.210)
The commencement of the performance that is being sung is proclaimed as the *ārambha*; however, for the purpose of tuning the musical instruments, there should be the procedure of *āśrāvaṇā*. (18)
The hand is positioned at the mouth [of the instrument] for the purpose of distinguishing the playing technique;
however, the striking [of the strings] serves to produce strength in the strings. (19)

That which consists of three *sāmā*s is the *pratyāhāra*, up to the point of the "descended limit" (*avatīrṇakoṭi*). At the limit of descent, the *chandas* should be equal or the syllables should be equal; the instrumental music should follow the external song and be employed to produce curiosity and the like in women, children, fools, and others.

Others consider "niveśana" (settling) to refer to the placement of the notes (*sthāna*) and the tones (*svara*), and not to the act of sitting down here. Thus, the employment of the seven tones (*saptasvaraparigraha*)—beginning with the descent (*avataraṇa*) and the swift movement (*āśugati*)—is to be applied through the seven limbs consisting of the *jāti* forms and so forth, along with the pure (*śuddha*) sevenfold [scale], in the performance of the *śuddhasaptaka-gīti*. This is stated in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* regarding the rule for the *ghanatāla* (thick rhythm).

31) This will be examined in detail later. (16–17) But surely, as long as the commencement of the ritual actions such as the *parigīta* has not been performed, how can there even be the application of the three *sāmans*?
True. Let it be determined for what purpose this sequence of application exists here.

These constituent elements (*aṅga*) have, for the time being, only perceptible purposes. To explain: first, it must be understood that the form of the presentation of the embellishing group (*uparañjakavarga*) is intended; this is because song, as something to be sung, is primarily an embellishment, and because that [embellishment] is rooted in the bodily notes (*śārīrasvara*) which serve as its prototype (*bimba*).

The beginning, called *ālāpa*, consists of the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of that [sound]. Following that, there is the *hāśrāvaṇā*, which causes the contemplation—containing all musical instruments (*sarvātodya*) and primarily characterized by the rhythmic measure (*tāla*) known as *māna*—to be heard on all sides. After that, for the sake of contemplating the nature of the sound of the lute (*vaiṇava-svara*), which has become a reflected image (*pratibimba*):

Vaktrapāṇi consists of the coordination of the divisions of the *dakṣiṇā* and other modes of performance. It is called *vaktra* because it begins with the mouth (*vaktra*), due to the operation of the fingers of the hand. Regarding "the *dakṣiṇā* and so forth": these are the modes of performance known as *dakṣiṇā*, *vṛtti*, and *citra*. In these, the following is the rule: the principal [element] is the song, and both [elements] are instrumental music, respectively.
When song is predominant and instrumental music is subordinate, it is *dakṣiṇā*; when both song and instrumental music are predominant, it is *vṛtti*;

and when instrumental music is predominant and song is subordinate, it is *citrā*. Following that, there is *aparighaṭṭanā*, which consists of the coordination of dry (non-lyrical) applications occurring within the divisions of the *vṛtti*s; for the root *ghaṭṭ* means "to move."
From the text: "Dry application" (*śuṣkaprayoga*). It is said that "dry" (*śuṣka*) refers to "sung without [meaning]" (*nirgīta*) and "sung outside" (*bahirgīta*).

Among these, that which is sung devoid of words that convey meaning is "sung without [meaning]" (*nirgīta*). That which has become external to the meaningful words being sung is "sung outside" (*bahirgīta*).

That which is employed with dry, meaningless syllables such as *kaṃdu* and so forth is the meaning of "dry" (*śuṣka*). Subsequently, because one subsists on the playing of the lute (*vīṇā*), the connection of the covered instrument (*avanaddha-vādya*) is performed by means of the fivefold striking with both hands and so on; this is *saṅghoṭanā*. [The root] *ghuṭ*...

Regarding the transformation: for it will be stated in the Puṣkara-adhyāya—"First [the breath] emerges from the body, then it goes to the wooden [flute], and thereafter to that which is born of the lotus" (Nāṭyaśāstra 34.31). (18–19)
(Regarding the phrase "by means of *samapāṇi* and so forth": for it is traditionally taught that "the *yati*, *pāṇi*, and *laya* are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of *tāla*";
thus, *pāṇi* is a constituent part of *tāla*. And that is of three kinds. As it has been said:)
One should know the *samapāṇi*, as well as the *ardhapāṇi* and likewise the *uparipāṇi*,
which serve as the foundation for song and instrumental music.

That instrumental playing which is equal to the tempo (*laya*) is called *samapāṇi*. That which is drawn out by half [the duration] of the tempo is proclaimed as *ardhapāṇi*. That instrumental playing which is above the tempo is proclaimed as *pāṇi* (or *uparipāṇi*).
Likewise, for the purpose of distinguishing the hands, there should be the method of rhythmic clapping;
