through the combination of strings and instruments, it is intended as the *mārgāsārita*. (20)
The performance of the *āsārita* should take place for the purpose of distinguishing the clarity of the musical measures (*kalā*);
likewise, the procedure for song (*gīta-vidhi*) is to be understood from the recitation of the deities.

Regarding the term *sopari*: "If there is elision (*lopa*) for the sake of completing the metrical foot (*pāda-pūraṇa*)," this means that the elision of the *su*-suffix of the word *saḥ* occurs when, by means of such elision, the metrical foot is completed. As in the case of *prahārapañcaka*, which [is formed] by means of the *samapāṇi*, *ardhapāṇi*, *ardhārdhapāṇi*, *pārśvapāṇi*, and *pradeśinīpāṇi*.

The meaning is that there is a "fivefold stroke" (*prahāra-pañcaka*) by means of that union. Furthermore, one should effect the mutual blending of the sounds of the flute (*vaiṇava*) and the *pauṣkara* drum, which take the form of the original nature (*prakṛti*), its modifications (*vikṛti*), the measure (*meyamāna*), the follower (*anuhārin*), and the leader (*anuhartṛ*). This is the *mārgāsārita*. It is so called because it resides in its own path (*mārge*), characterized by the original nature and the rest.
In this context, "gocare" refers to that wherein there is the drawing out or movement on all sides of the form of the *vikāra* and other elements of the *puṣkara-vādya*.
Subsequently, when the nature of the object of cognition (*meyamāna*) is joined together, there is the introduction of the rhythmic structure (*tāla*) inherent in the musical material (*geyavastu*).
This concerns the *kalās*, the *āvāpas*, the *pātas*, and the *śamyā*s and so forth.

And this is the method for the *anusandhi* (connection). Thus, for the time being, the employment of the elements of the *antaryavanikā* (inner curtain) serves solely an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because without them, the performance itself would not be accomplished. And so it has been stated by the poet named Bhejjala in his own drama:
"In the performance of the dance of the peacock, suspecting a cloud," and so forth.

Thus, when a performance for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) has first been carried out, the rule for the external singing (*bahirgīta*) follows subsequently according to the members (*aṅga*) that have a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). And in accordance with that, those [members] are [performed] with specific instrumental rhythms (*dhātu*).
The procedure for the placement [of the performers] and the singing and instrumental music: therein, the performance of the *pratyāhāra* and *avataraṇa* is carried out with three *sāmans*.

This is because the *kutapa* rugs are arranged at the three directions of the stage platform (*raṅgapīṭha*). At the beginning, the rhythm (*tāla*) consists of three beats; however, there is one beat for the *śamyā*, and two beats for the *tālas*.
Furthermore, the *śamyā* is in two beats (*dvikalā*), while the *tāla* should be made in two beats (*dvikala*).
(Nāṭya Śāstra 29.95) Moreover, the *sannipāta* is in two beats; likewise, the *pitāputraka* preceded by six [beats] is in two beats.
(Nāṭya Śāstra 29.100) Similarly, in the beginning of the *cañcatpuṭa*, there is the application of *tāla*.
With the hands above the *śamyā*, there are two *tālas*; thus is one *kala*.

With the hands level, there are two *śamyās* and likewise two *tālas*. Again, with the hand lowered, there is a *śamyā* and two *tālas*, and the subsequent [measure] is exactly the same. (Nāṭyaśāstra 29.89)

"Likewise, there shall be the *cañcatpuṭa*; thus indeed is the *āśrāvaṇa* rhythm (*tāla*). (Nāṭyaśāstra 29.90). However, Śaṅkuka reads "and likewise the *uttara*" in place of [the reading] "and likewise the *uttara*," and he indicates that [the term] "of two beats" (*dvikala*) occurs in place of "of one beat" (*ekakala*).
From here on, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the rite of awakening (utthāpana),
because by means of this, the reciters of auspicious hymns (nāndīpāṭhakas) awaken the ritual application (prayoga) herein.
Therefore, it is traditionally taught that the raising [of the image] should take place on this very stage beforehand. || 22 ||

Some, based on the evidence that *āśravaṇā* was mentioned previously in the twenty-eighth chapter (verses 29–86) and that *ārambha* is recited here first, maintain that there is an option between them; thus, they propose both the practice of *nirgīta* following the contemplation of the nature of all musical instruments (*sarvātodyasvarūpānusandhinirgīta*) and the practice of *lāpaka* (*lāpakakriyā*). (Or perhaps: the practice of *nirgīta* and the procedure of *tāla*?)
Whatever arrangement of the *śamyā* and *tāla* occurs in the two-time Madraka dance,
all of that should be performed in the mouth of the Vaktrapāṇi, which is characterized by eight beats.
Below that, one should again perform the *pañcapāṇicatuṣṭaya*;
this *tāla* belongs to Vaktrapāṇi and is based on the *mukha* and *pratimukha*.
Some, however, maintain that it occurs at half a *vaktra* (or half a *pāṇi*); by them, neither the sequence of the subject matter (*vastukrama*) nor the term *vṛtti* [is accounted for].
*Carcita* is so called because of its being rubbed together like a *saṃpiṣṭaka* (a ground cake); thus it is the *parighaṭṭanatāla*. Regarding that:
"In the seven-limbed [tāla], there are twelve beats; in the twelve-limbed, there are ten.
Having first performed the *niṣkrāma*, one should employ three *śamyās*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 31.278).
Then there are three *tālas*, followed by a *śamyā* and a *tāla*;
thereafter, another *śamyā* and *tāla* should be performed, and finally, a *sannipāta*.
In the seven-limbed *oveṇaka*, this is considered to be the *sampiṣṭaka*.
"By the combination of two *śamyā* measures, there are ten *kalās* in the twelve-limbed [measure]. (Nāṭyaśāstra 31.280).
However, Śaṅkuka reads: "The *atitāla* here is like a baked brick" (Nāṭyaśāstra 29.112).
The wise should know that the *pakveṣṭaka* is another variety of the triangular *tāla*.
"Endowed with a prolated (*pluta*) mora at the end of the five-syllable mantra of the Guru" (Nāṭyaśāstra 31.21);
others, however, read:
"And at the end of the five-syllable mantra of the Guru, it is endowed with two prolated moras."
Likewise, there are two [cases]: the word *sampiṣṭa* (crushed), like the word *tuva*, denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*), as in the expression "like the head" (*śīrṣakavat*).
For indeed, its [meaning]...
And because the world-protectors circumambulate it in the four directions and offer salutations, it is therefore called "circumambulation" (parivartana). || 23 ||
And at that time, it has become an auxiliary (*aṅga*). The context (*prakaraṇa*) alone is the witness here for its application.
This [text] is recited between these two, like the *śīrṣaka* and the *ālāsārita*.
Is the meaning "of the baked brick likewise, with two *pluta*s of the *tāla*" etc. appropriate? No, it is not consistent.
"In the *saṅghoṭanā*, however, the *tāla* is like the head with five hands" (*Nāṭyaśāstra*, Kāśī ed., 29.142).
Regarding these two limbs as well, some desire a variation in sequence as before.
"And its *tāla* is proclaimed to be just like the *bālāsārita*" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 29.116).

Thus is the *tāla* for the *mārgāsārita*. Furthermore, the *abhisṛta* and *parisṛta* [varieties] should also be employed here within the midst of the *mārgāsārita*, or alternatively, in its place, according to one's choice. That which is called *līlākṛta* will be explained in the section on the rules for percussion instruments (*tāḍatodya*) in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (29.117); it is not included here. And regarding the three *āsāritas*:
This sequence of application will be explained in detail by [the author] himself in the chapter on *tāla* (Nāṭyaśāstra 31.146–173).
For this very reason, even in the *pratyāhāra* and other sections, the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) remains applicable by its mere existence during the *pūrvaraṅga*. And here:

The rules for dry syllables (*śuṣkākṣara*) and percussion instruments (*dhātuvādya*) will appear in the twenty-eighth chapter, and the rules for the *tata* and *todya* instruments in the third chapter on the drum (*puṣkara*) (Nāṭyaśāstra 34); therefore, they should be understood from those very sources. They have not been written here, however, for fear of prolixity.

And here, for the sake of variety, some maintain that even the *pravṛtti* such as "only what is appropriate" (*samucitamātra*) and so forth—which is suitable for the future form of the drama (*rūpaka*)—should also be recited. For if this were the case, the restriction [implied by the rule] "by those [styles] employed in the application of recitation" (*tathā pāṭhyayogakṛtaiḥ*, Nāṭyaśāstra 5.8) would not be overly narrow. And this is logical; for just as...

In delightful arrangements of beds provided with excellent furnishings, and even in the case of footstools, pillars, incense, garments, and so forth, there is a connection with various forms primarily suited to the pair of lovers, as well as in battle-appropriate armor, narrow passages, and the like.

Furthermore, the evocation of fear in timid people through the arrangement of forms such as Nṛsiṃha and Garuḍa will likewise occur in an exceedingly beautiful drama (*nāṭya*) upon the presentation of the group of embellishing elements (*uparañjakavarga*) and so forth;

this too must be performed precisely through the application of delicate singing, recitation, and acting (*gītapāṭhyābhinaya*) as described by him. And that [should take place] only when [the audience] has been cleared away.
On the curtain: for within the section on "Raising" (*utthāpanāṅga*), there is a performance consisting of a single beat (*ekakala*) accompanied by recitation (*pāṭhya*).
For he will say later, "because they raise [it]," and so forth; that is, because they raise up the performance previously executed on the stage, such as the withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the rest.

The meaning is that they clarify [the matter] through the recitation and dramatic performance (abhinaya) of the chapters that define the nature of the fruit; for this very purpose of providing scope for the recitation, there is here this specific mention of the praise of the deity, the song, and the particular fruit.
Otherwise, it would have been sufficient to state generally that "this is to be employed for the propitiation of the deity."
Because the application of specific instructions would be fruitless;
for [the mantra] is always employed in conjunction with words of benediction. (p. 215)
Therefore, it is designated by the name *nāndī* for the sake of gods, twice-born men, kings, and others.
Others, however, say that the application of that [melody] follows after each individual limb [of the song]. But it must be examined what exactly constitutes that "application.
Here, however, the meaning is "this. By the manner of saying "it is done," the singing of that [melody] is indicated, even when it is joined with words.

Since the *pāṭhya* (recitation), *yoga*, and other elements are objects of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth occurring behind the inner curtain (*antaryavanikā*), they are also described for the sake of the inner curtain. Thus, the nine constituent parts (*navāṅga*) have been stated.
Now, [the text continues] with the verse beginning: "Then, having indeed opened the curtain" (*nā. śā. 5.12*).
He defines, in their proper order, the ten ancillaries (aṅga) of the rules for singing that were previously mentioned, beginning with "from recitation" (kīrtanāt), and so forth.

"Recitation" (kīrtana) means praise. "From that" refers to the cause of the recited text. Following that is "satisfaction through dry syllables" (śuṣkākṣara-nirvṛti), which is one of the types of songs (gītaka) or the "increasing" (vardhamāna) form.
And in that regard, the *tāla* will be explained in the thirty-first chapter on *tāla*.

(21) As for the phrase "because": if the *pratyāhāra* and so forth were to be employed here, then this would be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *pūrvaraṅga*, since the sequence is already established. [The term] "reciters of the *nāndī*" refers to...

By means of the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*) indicated by that very [verse], the ancient poets used to write: "At the end of the *nāndī*, the stage-manager (*sūtradhāra*). And this [verse] is to be employed in performance day after day. Moreover, this [verse] is always of this very form.
While a variation in other recited parts, such as the introductory verses (*utthāpana*), is observed due to the requirements of the performance, this is not the case here.
The intention of the word "constant" (*nitya*) is that this applies to the recitation of the *nāndī*.

By the inclusion of the term "etcetera," [the audience] such as the patron of the performance (*prekṣāpati*) and others are meant. And this very *nāndī* will be designated as "proclamation" (*prarocanā*) in the definition of the components of the *bhāratī* style: "It is indeed victorious, prosperous, and auspicious" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 20.27).
By such statements as these, that which is *prarocanā* (the incitement to interest) here will occur there. In this context,
among the intervals following the offering of the *nāndī*, he counts as the fifth limb (*aṅga*) that which is to be employed in the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite) known as the *vardhamāna*.

Now, some say: "In this way, since the procedure for the *gītaka* occurs not only after the first act (*aṅga*) but also within other acts, and because it exists even in the *vardhamāna-prayoga* and the *citra*, the number does not remain fixed; thus, it does not fall upon the *pada* and is therefore not subject to further counting—so there is no fault. (24)

"However, it should be 'dried and drawn out' (śuṣkāvakṛṣṭā) here"; thus, "dried and drawn out" alone is prescribed. And here, that very [term] is characterized. The definition of the "drawn out" (avakṛṣṭā), however, should be understood by way of a restatement (anuvāda). Otherwise, that which is about to be stated...
(216) Since here the *dhruvā* has been extracted by means of dry syllables alone,
it is therefore called "extracted from dry [text]," revealing the worn-out verses. || 25 ||
Since the acting (abhinaya) is introduced here first, it should therefore be known as the "Entrance to the Stage" (raṅgadvāra), consisting of vocal and physical expression (vāgaṅgābhinaya). || 26 ||
"For when [the offering] is properly prepared and drawn out, the Nāgas indeed become pleased;

likewise, when it is dried and drawn out, the host of Pitṛs becomes pleased" (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.50)—this [statement] would then be rendered irrelevant. In that regard, the definition of "drawn out" (*avakṛṣṭā*) is as follows:
"Endowed with the *mukha* and *pratimukha*, the *avakṛṣṭā* is prescribed" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 32.12); such is the rule for the *tāla*.
And in other states (*anyabhāveṣu*), the *kṛṣṭā* is recited [in the context of the causes of substances] (*dravyahetuṣu*).
"Because it is joined with compassion, the *avakṛṣṭā* should therefore be [employed]" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 32.341).

Thus, the nature of the procedure for the recitation of the meaning of the sentence (vākyārtha-gāna), as well as the application of the *śamyā* and other elements, will be explained later in this [work]. When this [recitation] has been employed, following it comes the dramatic performance (*nāṭya*).
It should be performed in exactly this manner using dry syllables (*śuṣkākṣara*). In that regard, because of the commonality of being drawn out (*avakṛṣṭa*), it is treated separately.
[In the phrase] "by the successive steps" (*kramapātaiḥ*), that which shows the worn-out verses immediately follows;

[the phrase] "this is the dry-drawn" (*śuṣkāvakṛṣṭā*) means this [dhruvā] is drawn out in a dry manner. This is the *dhruvā* that is drawn out (*avakṛṣṭā*). It is "dry-drawn" because of that. He says: "For" (*hi*) means "because. "In this" (*atra*) refers to its being a subordinate member (*aṅgatāyām*). Of the drawn-out (*avakṛṣṭasya*).
[The verse] is endowed with all those characteristics, yet [it refers to a song] consisting solely of useless, dry syllables such as *jhaṃṭhu* and so forth.

Others, however, think that this verse will apply to the case where both qualities—being "dry" (*śuṣka*) and "extracted" (*apakṛṣṭa*)—are present in a single *dhruvā*, namely in the case of a *yuktā* that has been extracted (*apakṛṣṭā*). But the Upādhyāyas [hold a different view].

The fruit that is included within the "dried" (*śuṣkā*) and the "withdrawn" (*avakṛṣṭā*) will be explained later; however, here only the "dried" is characterized. By this definition, the "withdrawn" is also indicated here by the two words "this" (*iyam*) and "and" (*ca*). (25) p.

Because it involves the practice of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), it is celebrated as cārī; and because it involves the practice of the furious sentiment (raudra), it is likewise celebrated as mahācārī. || 27 ||
Where the Vidūṣaka, the Sūtradhāra, and likewise the Pāripārśvaka engage in conversation, that too is considered Trigata. || 28 ||
That which is an address by means of an established fact, based on the cause and reasoning of the poetic work through its introduction, is to be known as *prarocanā* (the incitement). 29.

"Abhinīyata" means "being enacted," which refers to a specific type of dramatic composition (*rūpaka*). It is introduced here in brief by way of defining its meaning, purpose, and so forth, through the medium of the recitation (*pāṭhya*). That wherein [the characters] are enacted and the performance (*abhinaya*) is carried out accordingly is like a gateway to the drama that is yet to come upon the stage.

In the general context of the "raising" (*utthāpana*) member [of the *prastāvanā*], drama (*nāṭya*) was raised; here, however, it is distinguished by being a specific type of dramatic work (*rūpaka*). (26) Regarding the phrase "of the erotic sentiment" (*śṛṅgārasya*): that in which the life-story of the Blessed One together with the Great Goddess is described, primarily characterized by the erotic sentiment, and in which poetry is likewise primarily devoted to its praise—that alone [is intended].

That [performance] in which [the dance] is demonstrated and employed through bodily movements (*aṅgahāra*), gaits (*cārī*), and so forth, is called *cārī*. That [performance] in which a poem— such as the *Tripuramardana* of the Blessed One— which is sung and abounds in the *raudra* (fierce) sentiment,
is described in the form of praise, is performed there with the very same *maṇḍala-aṅgahāras* suited to it and characterized by vigor.
"Mahācārī" means "Vidūṣaka. A Vidūṣaka is one of the two *pāripārśvika*s (attendants) who possesses the dress, speech, and conduct of a Vidūṣaka.
"Where" refers to in a drama such as the *Nāgānanda*, where a dialogue concerning the specific subject matter of the drama and so forth is about to occur.

It is mixed with humor (*hāsya*). Although this has already been mentioned, there is no redundancy because its specific details were intended to be explained through works such as the *Nāgānanda*. That very introduction to the drama (*kāvyopakṣepa*) is designated by the term "trigata" because it is dependent upon three [characters].
By means of that introduction to the drama acting as a cause, there is an address to the members of the audience regarding that subject.

The invitation (*nimantraṇa*) means it is characterized by the perfected state (*siddhi*) through the perfected one. Since from this indeed there will arise joy and proficiency for the seeker, therefore, "let this be observed"—this is the *prarocanā* (the inducement), because it serves as the cause for producing superior interest. And he says that activity will not occur merely from his word:
"Reasoning based on cause" (*hetuyukti*) means that its purpose is the brief statement of the reasoning—the connection or application—of the cause.

Thus, these ten external limbs of the curtain (*yavanikā*), though distinct, also have visible results; for instance, the singing of the *dhruvā* verses depends upon the *gītaka* and *vardhamāna* meters, which in turn serve as the basis for the dramatic performance (*nāṭya*).
Because the *prakṛti* must necessarily be addressed first in the intellect due to its being the basis of subsistence...
218) Hereafter, I shall indeed proclaim the ritual procedure for the *āśrāvaṇa*.
Likewise, [he explained] the correct cause for the origin of the external method of singing. || 30 ||
But when the sevenfold form, consisting of the variegated, the sacrificial fee, and the ritual action, has been set in motion—
along with the removal [of obstacles], the singing, the praise of the deity, and the rejoicing— (31)
Furthermore, whatever is undertaken from that point onward must first be established in the intellect within its general form.
Then, for the sake of observing right conduct, there is the salutation to the deity. After that, there is the supreme invocation for the purpose of bringing [the deity] face-to-face. And after that—

There is the stimulation of that which serves as a means for pacifying anticipated obstacles. Then, by way of ancient precedents (*purākalpa*), there must be an even more specific consideration of the application [of the means]. Furthermore, because the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and heroic (*vīra*) sentiments possess the excellence of being the most captivating and the highest human goals in all circumstances, they are introduced. And even that is for the sake of the delicate people who are to be instructed in the drama.

In this specific type of poetry characterized primarily by the laughter that delights all through the expression of spontaneous freedom (*svacchandatā*), there is a consideration of the subject matter you intend to express; furthermore, there is a determination of its purpose. Thus, for those composing a treatise (*śāstra*) or for worldly [composition], there is the adoption of an opening statement.

The investigation into the subject matter to be enacted, as well as everything from the commencement of the performance up to the *prarocanā* (the prologue) such as the *gītakapiṇḍī*, follows strictly worldly conventions. Here, one should not urge [the audience] toward the capacity or the definition of any particular dramatic element (*aṅga*), because this performance is intended for people of delicate sensibilities.

Therefore, this is not at all extraordinary. It should simply be understood that it is composed with such variety because the primary aim of drama is its artistic construction, and for the sake of attaining unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Enough of this prolixity. (27–29)
Is it not the case that this is so? Furthermore, regarding the nature of the sound of a song projected outward from the act of sounding and so forth—which is the referent (*padārtha*) here?
It refers to the action of the procedure of sounding. Thus, the meaning is: in the performance (*vidhi*) of those [acts] such as sounding and so forth.

I shall explain the ritual action consisting of performance and protection; the production [of the rite] through the prescription of the external song as a means of expression; and the cause and purpose for the application in the prescription of the external song itself. (30) He states this by way of a reference to a former age (*purākalpa*) in eleven verses beginning with "Citra": it is remembered as *bahirgīta*.
By this much [is explained] up to verse 5.41: the *vṛttimārgas*—namely *citrā* and the others—are characterized respectively by song, instrumental music, or both as predominant.

The term *citadakṣiṇasahitā vṛttiḥ* is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*). The *gītaka* pertaining to that [type of *vṛtti*], along with the *upohana*, *pratyupohana*, *vardhamāna*, and *nirgīta*, constitutes the *āśrāvaṇā* as well as the *ārambha*.
Together with what will be stated in the twenty-eighth [and twenty-ninth] chapters beginning with these words (Nā. Śā.
29.82), and celebrated by the praise of the deity which constitutes its expressed meaning (*vācya*), that [song] is prosperous and abundant.
When that has been set in motion and employed, that singing is being sung.
(219) By Nārada and other Gandharvas in the assembly hall, the gods and Dānavas were made to hear [the song] perfectly performed, accompanied by proper rhythm and tempo. || 32 ||
Having heard that pleasant song, which was celebrated as a hymn to the gods,
all the Daityas and Rākṣasas became agitated out of envy.
Having deliberated with one another, they stood there and spoke thus:
"We shall take up this song, together with its instrumental accompaniment. (34)
The gods are satisfied by the mere mention of their deeds;
we accept what is sung, and we are always pleased right here. (35)
There, those Daityas, being pleased, were performing [their rites] again and again;
then the gods, becoming enraged, addressed Nārada.
Even upon hearing that which produces happiness, the Daityas were agitated. Why? Out of envy (*mātsarya*). And why was that? It is said:

because it was being celebrated with praises such as "O, how delightful! and "Excellent! Excellent! by the gods. The particle *tu* has the sense of "also. By whom, then, was that [praise] instigated? He says: "By Nārada and others."
The meaning is "presided over by that. "That" refers to the seven forms (*saptarūpa*). (Nā. Śā. 31; Kā. Mā. Pu. 521).
*Laya* refers to the fast tempo (*druta*) and so forth. *Tālas* are characterized by the *śamyā* and other measures, being triangular, square, or mixed.
By the word "having deliberated," it is indicated that others should be satisfied with this [work]. Having established their position, they remained there.
He points out what is being expressed as indicated by the word [“amitrā”]: “you” (referring to the phrase *nirgītam*).

This refers to the musical instrument, specifically the lute (*vīṇā*) known as *śuṣka* which is played therein. Now, one might ask: what is the reason for mentioning that? He says: “we shall be pleased. Even in the absence of formal praise and recitation, [it is done] out of conceit.
The meaning is "by means of complete satisfaction. For a specific kind of joy produced by self-conceit is indeed observed, as for example when hearing that a king has arrived.
"Therein" refers to what has been explained. They "accomplish"; they say that accomplishment is success (*siddhi*).

(Regarding the phrase "produced by the basis of metallurgical/alchemical arts": *dhātavaḥ* refers to specific types of strings [or metallic elements] arising from the particular conjunction of fingers.)

The musical notes of the flute (*vaiṇavasvara*) are called *vistāra*, *vyañjana*, and *āviddhakaraṇa*; through the process of coloring (*rañjanā*), these four distinct [notes] of the invisible particularity are sequentially differentiated.
These Dānavas, together with the Rākṣasas, are delighted when there is no singing;
let this ritual practice perish—what do you think? (37)
Having heard the words of the gods, Nārada spoke these words: "Let this song, which was produced by relying upon alchemy, not perish. (38)

However, this song shall be devoid of vocal melody, yet it will be joined with instrumental introductions (upohana) and adorned with the playing of musical instruments (dhātuvādya), according to the rules of the seven musical notes (saptarūpa). || 39 ||
Bound by this song, the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas,
being gratified, shall cause neither agitation nor obstruction here.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this was sung internally out of rivalry with the Daityas;
it is remembered as "sung externally" (Bahirgīta) because of the great respect shown to the gods.

Then, wise men should employ [this] on a multi-toned lute (citravīṇā), endowed with heavy and light syllables according to the musical scales (dhātu), and joined with phonetic ornaments (varṇālaṅkāra). 42.

The alchemy of the elements (*dhātuvādya*) has sevenfold characteristics; its reliance upon that [system] is what constitutes "that which is made by means of it. What benefit is there in such an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) thing? It is not in the descriptions of praise regarding the unseen that there is a prescription; for indeed, by that [prescription] being employed at the beginning, middle, and end, [the purpose is achieved].

He also mentions other qualities, such as the charming gait and so forth, by means of providing an opportunity for the variety of lute-playing, with the words "accompanied by song" (*nirgītena*). The meaning is that they were "bound"— that is, won over— by his effortless, playful movement on foot, according to the maxim of nourishing a young monkey.

Having thus established the cause of its indestructibility, he defines the etymology of its name: "Thus" (*evam*) and "sung" (*gītam*) constitute the first part of the name. It is called "sung" because it was sung without meaning; however, that is traditionally remembered as having been sung by the Gandharvas externally. [The question] "Why? Out of rivalry with the Daityas" means: this acceptance was made by them out of rivalry with the Daityas; for that reason.

Now, one might ask: "If it has been accepted by them, then what of it? Why was this designation made? To this he says: "Of the gods" (*devānām*). This means: by means of that mental estimation (*mananam*) which has the gods as its object and is characterized by their numerical preponderance and excellence; with that as the purpose, we consider the gods to be superior in number to the Dānavas. And thus, this [designation] is not internal [to us].
The meaning is that they should understand it thus: "The external song is being sung by us. (31-41) p.
221) Since the songless is sung through the arrangement of phonemes, [it is called *nirgīta*].
And due to the envy of the gods, this was remembered as the "Bahirgīta. || 43 ||
That which has been declared by me as the Nirgīta, endowed with its seven forms,
and that which consists of the Utthāpana and so forth— the cause of that is now being stated.
When the ritual call (āśrāvaṇā) is properly performed, the Daityas are constantly satisfied;
and when the hand is placed at the mouth, the Dānavas are always satisfied.

One might ask: "Should this not be performed using only the seven *rūpas*? He says, "No"—namely, "by means of the *dhātus*. That which is to be performed is characterized by those *dhātus* of the aforementioned nature—such as striking with the palm of the hand and so forth—which are applied to a multi-colored lute (*vīṇā*) for the purpose of embellishing a dramatic performance (*nāṭya-uparañjana*). How? In the case of percussion instruments (*bhāṇḍavādya*), they serve the purpose of movement (*gati-artha*).
Those [syllables] which are heavy, such as *ghṛ*, *bhṛṅ*, and so forth, and those which are light, such as *maṭ*, *kaṭ*, and so forth— having combined these therein,

by this it is stated that they serve as coloring agents for the musical instruments and the like. Likewise, in the singing of the *dhruva* section, those vowels such as *sthāyin* and so forth, and those ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) such as *prasanna* and so forth, are properly combined therein.
Having established the connection, he demonstrates its function as an embellishment for singing. Now, the word "atha" (then/also) has the sense of "api" (also).
Alternatively, there is a reading: "prayojyaṃ kuśalair atha" (it should be employed by the skilled, or...).
Anticipating the objection—"But surely it already has the designation 'nirgīta'; what then is the reason for this [new] one?"—he says:

Regarding the term *nirgītam*: it means a word (*padam*) that conveys meaning. "Phonemes" (*varṇāḥ*) refers to those such as *jhaṃ*, *ṭuṃ*, and so forth, as well as the *sthāyī* (stable) and other [musical] elements. Anticipating the objection—"But since this is already included within *lakṣaṇā* (indication), how can it be considered external?"—the author says: "And because of their envy. For they were envious of it.

Out of sheer force, they manifested great respect; therefore, in order to capture his heart, this was spoken. And to show that this is not entirely without foundation, he indicates by the use of the particle *ca* that there is also a literal significance:
it is "sung outside" (*bahir-gītam*) of the meaningful words (*sārthakebhyaḥ padebhyaḥ*) being sung.

Having thus explained, in that same sequence, the cause of non-destruction and the basis for the application of designations, he makes his formal declaration with the words beginning "It has been sung" (*nirgītam*). "The *āśrāvaṇā* and so forth have been sung, endowed with the seven musical notes (*saptarūpa*).
This is the rule for the song (*gītaka*). "The remaining [parts], such as the *utthāpanā* and so forth, are the external elements of the curtain (*yavanikāṅga*). Of that—
The cause is the purpose. (42–44) p.
222) But when the friction was accomplished, the host of Rākṣasas was satisfied.
And the Guhyakas are also pleased by the act of fanning. || 46 ||
For when they have attained the path-asārita, the yakṣas indeed become joyful;
and when the gītakas are employed, the gods are constantly satisfied. (47)
When the *vardhamāna* [mudrā] is employed, Rudra, together with his followers, is pleased;
likewise, when the *utthāpana* [mudrā] is applied, Brahmā becomes gratified here in this world.
The world-protectors are pleased when the *parivartana* is performed;
furthermore, when the *nāndī* application is made, the Moon becomes delighted. (49)
For when the *yuktā* [offering] is drawn out, the Nāgas indeed become pleased;
likewise, when the *śuṣkā* is drawn out, the host of Pitṛs becomes pleased. (50)
When the *raṅgadvāra* (theatrical prologue) is employed, Viṣṇu becomes pleased here;
when the *jarjara* (the ritual invocation) is performed, the Vighnas and Vināyakas are satisfied. (51)

He demonstrates this with eight verses beginning with "In the *āśrāvaṇā*" and ending with "the host of spirits (*bhūtagaṇa*) would come to be. The practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the others are included within the *āśrāvaṇā* itself, because this [stage] serves as their limit. In some manuscripts—
O twice-born ones, when the descent is performed, the Yātudhānas together with the Pannagas are gratified by the withdrawal of the senses, and the Apsarases there are satisfied.

"The Gandharvas are also pleased when the performance has begun. Thus, a half-verse is seen [in the text]. It should be understood that the satisfaction resulting from the high regard for the acceptance of what is either spontaneous or intentionally composed pertains to a distinguished subject matter. Regarding the term *mārgāsāritam*: it is both the path (*mārga*) and the extended melody (*āsārita*).

*Mārgāsāritam* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). By the term *mārga*, a single part [of the performance] is designated as *mārgāsāritam*. By the word *āsārita*, two components—namely, *āsārita* and *it*—are expressed. Thus, every component is characterized.
By the word *āsārita*, the rule for *āsārita* is indicated; thus, by means of this collective copulative compound, both components are [designated].

This fruit has been described: "the gods" [is attained] by praising his (Rudra's) deeds; and this pair of fruits is optional, depending on the performance of either the *gītaka* or the *vardhamāna*. "Brahmā" [is attained] through the first creation, such as that of Brahmā.
Likewise, when the Āryā is employed here, Umā shall be pleased;
but when the Mahācāryā is employed, the host of spirits (bhūtagaṇa) shall be pleased. || 52 ||

This worship of the deities, beginning with the invocation (āśrāvaṇā) and ending with the dismissal (cāryanta), as well as the arrangement of the ritual limbs (aṅgavikalpana), has been described by me in the preliminary performance (pūrvaraṅga). || 53 ||
O best of the twice-born, whatever deity is pleased by whatever means, and whatever is dear to whose mind— that has been explained by me accordingly in the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga).

The activity therein pertains to the subject matter of drama (*nāṭya*). And that [activity] is here worshipped (or expressed) by means of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Regarding "the moon": this is because of the recitation in the *nāndī* [verse], "Victory to Soma" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 5.110). "The serpents" (*nāgāḥ*) refers to the downward movement (*avakṛṣṭagati*). Regarding "of the withered" (*jarjarasya*): it is a residual part of the very limb characterized as dry and downward-turned.
Then, the verse that demonstrates the praise of the Worn-Out One (*jarjara*) will be stated; thereafter, one should recite a single verse (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 5.118).
Its purpose is this: Vināyaka, who is the warder-off of obstacles, becomes pleased.
Virūpākṣa and the others are the obstacle-Vināyakas because they are incited by the equipment used for warding them off. They...

"They do not cause obstruction. Some say that this very contentment belongs to them because of the equality of their fruit. "Umā" is mentioned because it is a mention of her essential nature. (45–52) To summarize all of this, he says: "From the proclamation [of the name], etc., up to 'but those performed,' etc."
These four verses [state that] pratyāhāra and the other [preliminary elements] are included within āśrāvaṇā.

Here, by the word *cārī*, the *mahācārī* is intended. The purport is that for *trigata* and *prarocanā*, there is only a single observed purpose. Regarding the term *pūrvaraṅga*: the meaning is that it is connected with that [performance].

By the word "renowned" (*khyātam*), there is the designation (*uddeśa*); the meaning is that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) consists in the conceptual differentiation (*vikalpana*) of these limbs. The conclusion regarding the purpose (*prayojana*) is made by the words "the deity is pleased," and so forth. The phrase "whatever is dear to one's mind" means [it is obtained] through the power of grasping based on self-conceit (*abhimānika*).

He demonstrates praise for this [practice]: it is worthy of worship and praiseworthy by all the deities. The reason for this is that the deities themselves are worshipped by means of it. For this very reason, it belongs specifically to the patron, the performer, and others. It is excellent regarding wealth, fame, and longevity, because it brings those about. Indeed, in this matter, no one [at all]...
Regarding "detachment" (*virakti*): the *nirgīta* [melody] such as *daityadānava* brings satisfaction to the Daityas and others, while the *gītakā* and so forth belong to the gods.
224) It is worthy of worship by all deities; it is the worship of all deities.
This opening of the prologue brings merit, renown, and long life. || 55 ||
For the sake of pleasing the Daityas, Dānavas, and all the inhabitants of heaven,
the preliminary rites were performed, accompanied by both instrumental and vocal music.
Whatever knowledge, whatever crafts, whatever destiny, and whatever activity there is in this world and the world beyond— all that is contained within this drama. Indeed,
it includes those things without song and those with song, as well as the increasing [scale].
I shall indeed describe the characteristics and the ritual procedure for the installation of the Dhruva [pole].
Having performed the ritual for the *gītaka* and likewise the *vardhamāna*,
at the conclusion of the *gītaka*, the *dhruvā* known as the *utthāpanī* should indeed be performed.
One should know that in a foot of eleven syllables, there are heavy syllables at the beginning, the second, the fourth, as well as the eighth and the eleventh. (59)

[Objection: "From where is its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) to be known? For it has not been stated here [in this context], nor do we perceive its definition through the incidental mention of its constituent parts (*aṅga*). Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "of those that have been sung" (*nirgītānām*) in order to show the occasion for the incidental discussion, thinking, "I shall state its definition here [or elsewhere] as the occasion arises. Of those...

The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is likewise [stated] as "it obstructs" (*rundhre*), whereas the illustration (*udāharaṇa*) of the defined object (*lakṣya*)—namely, that it is "soft" (*ṛdu*)—I shall state later. The "object" (*karma*) refers to the defined object. The meaning is: "when the prescription of the *dhruvās* is to be performed" (Nāṭyaśāstra 31.122), and not in the chapter on the *dhruvās* (*dhruvādhyāya*).

This is what is meant: because the *dhruvā* song is the most prominent element here for providing aesthetic appeal (*uparañjaka*), I shall explain its characteristics—insofar as it constitutes the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) of that which is to be expressed—within the section on the types of musical instruments (*tātodya-vidhāna*) and in the chapter on rhythm (*tālādhyāya*). [Thinking: "I shall speak of this," [and] because of not knowing this... [or] having not known this...

As for the claim that the word *dhruvā* here refers to being sung without [specific] metrical constraints (*chandonibaddha-nirgītatva*), that is incorrect; for this [usage] is equivalent to what has not been explicitly stated. To say, "I shall state its definition when prescribing that," amounts to nothing.
Furthermore, to claim that this verse is non-Vedic (*anārṣa*) is a great act of audacity. (57)

Now, the remaining characteristics of the *utthāpana* (arousing) and other [rituals] must be completed. Regarding that, in order to provide the definition of the *dhruvā* (the constant chant) by means of its application, preceded by a restatement of the *utthāpana*, he says the four verses beginning with "having employed" (*prayujya*) and ending with "one should join" (*yojayet*). Therein:
It shall consist of four feet and likewise have moving pauses;
it possesses four combinations [of syllables], three tempos, and three metrical patterns.
There are four *parivartas* and exactly three *pāṇis*; indeed, they are distinguished by their *jāti*, and one should apply them with the *tāla*. (61)
The *śamyā* should be made of two *kalās*, and the *tāla* likewise consists of two *kalās*.
Again, the *śamyā* is one *kalā*, and the *sannipāta* consists of three *kalās*.

The first verse is a restatement (*anuvādaka*). One of the two—either *gītaka* or *vardhamāna*—is employed at the end of the *gītaka*. Then, immediately after the *vardhamāna*, the *dhruvā* known as *utthāpanī* is to be performed; this is the restatement. The particle *ca* is displaced in its position and has the sense of "or" (*vā*), though others take it as a conjunction (*samuccaya*). [This refers to] the collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāyam*).
With the intention of demonstrating the simultaneous application of *gītakas* and *vardhamānas*, they state:
"The definition of the *dhruvā* is: 'If there are two at the beginning... The remaining [syllables] are short (*laghu*).
Such are its four feet (*pādas*). Its rhythm (*tāla*) is *cañcatpuṭa* with two beats (*dvikala*).

Even though it is obtained through the method of future [application], the mention of "four-square" (caturaśra) is for the purpose of relying on the rules of finger-movement (*aṅgulinyāsa*) to be described later, concerning the two-measure *cañcatpuṭa* and the quarter-measures (*pādabhāga*).
It is called "four-fold conjunction" (*catuḥsannipātā*) because its conjunction occurs at the end of every foot. The tempos (*laya*) are fast (*druta*) and so forth.

The remaining point is that three types of *pāṇis*—namely, *samapāṇi*, *aparapāṇi*, and *uparipāṇi*—are to be employed in this [dhruvā].
Anticipating the objection as to why this *dhruvā* is not counted among the *vṛtta-jāti* meters, he says:
The *viśloka* class of meters is defined as follows: if,

Having taken up handfuls of flowers, consecrated by protective and auspicious rites, wearing pure garments and being well-disposed, they likewise possessed wondrous visions. (66)
With the right [hand], then stepping out with both hands, then with the left; thereafter with the right hand, then with the *śamyā*;

Regarding the phrase "four combinations" (*catvāraḥ sannipātāḥ*), he describes a rotation of all four feet. The *sthitalaya* (steady tempo) is said to be the *vilambitalaya* (slow tempo). As for the third [combination], one employs the first three feet—excluding the final beat (*antyakalā*)—accompanied by stringed instruments (*tantrīgāna*).
Then follows the final beat of the third foot; from that point onward is the application of percussion instruments (*puṣkaravādya*).

Until the completion of the fourth quarter (pāda), there is singing again with a moderate tempo (*madhyalaya*). At that time, the stage manager (*sūtradhāra*) enters. "Of that" refers to the first act (*parivarta*). Furthermore, even though it is the first singing, it is called an "act" (*parivarta*) by virtue of its association with the second and subsequent ones. "Another" [act]—as in the expression "he cooks twice"—refers to three.
The [grammatical] operations (*pāka*) would occur; from the expression "he cooks once" (*sakṛt pacati*), two [operations] would result. Regarding the phrase "the entrance of the *sūtradhāra*":

by the word *sūtradhāra*, through association with him, the *pāripārśvika*s are also included. He states the procedure for their entrance with the words beginning "a handful of flowers" (*puṣpāñjali*). First, there is the handful of flowers.
This applies specifically to the Sūtradhāra; as for the positions of the other two, having assumed the Vaiṣṇava stance, they should be preceded by graceful bodily movements.
Having been initiated and being pure, the three should enter together.
The two attendants (pāripārśvika) should hold water-pitchers (bhṛṅgāra) and wear garlands;
meanwhile, the director (sūtrabhṛt), surrounded by them, should walk five steps between them.
Five steps may be taken by a Brahmin with the desire to perform a sacrifice;
I shall now explain the measurement of those steps in their proper sequence.
This is because it will be described later as having a ground shattered by the jar of the *rbhṛṅgāra* [demon]. "Pure" means white.

"Those of beautiful minds" (*sumanasaḥ*) refers to those whose minds are excellent and filled with wonder. And this wonder arises from the thought: "Those who are difficult to discipline through the Vedas and other means are easily disciplined by us."

"That gaze which has the tips of its lashes slightly contracted, whose pupil is turned upward with wonder, and which is gentle yet wide-open, is the 'Adbhuta' (wonderful) gaze used for the marvelous sentiment. (Nāṭyaśāstra 8.51).
By the partial definition beginning with "sauṣṭhava" and so forth, he clarifies that it is specifically the Vaiṣṇava [gaze]; otherwise...
Even in the case of Viṣṇutva and other such [forms], there might be a possibility for someone [to perceive them] based on their literal meaning.

There should be a distance of two *tālas* and a half-*tāla* between the feet; one [foot] should be positioned straight, while the other, triangular, should be directed toward the side. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.52)
"With the shanks slightly bent and the limbs arranged with graceful poise—this indeed is the Vaiṣṇava posture" (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.53).
"The initiated ones" means those who have observed the fast. (66–67)

The *bhṛṅgāra* (water-pot) is for purification; the *jarjara* (the wooden beam) is for the pacification of obstacles. The two attendants (*pāripārśvika*) are at the sides. For this very reason, the stage-manager (*sūtradhāra*), being surrounded by the two, [stands] in the middle; thus, the meaning is that all three should walk five steps. He states the purpose of that: "the steps. There is an interval of three *tāla*s.

One should place that foot—whose width is such as to have a corresponding height in its upward movement—by raising it from the side, rather than rising with a more distinct verticality; one should drop it between the two feet, since the act of walking has already commenced. In this same manner, four other steps should be taken slightly forward.
The steps: (68–70) p. 228) One should slowly lift the foot at an interval of three *tālas*.
And having risen from the side, one should cause it to fall back again into the middle.
Having thus moved five steps, the master of the cord, together with the other,
should place the needle on the left foot and make a movement with the right.
Furthermore, the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) should be performed in the Brahma-maṇḍala;
for Brahmā himself is established in the center of the colored-pedestal.
Then, having paid homage to the Grandfather with graceful hand gestures,
one should perform three salutations with the hand upon the ground.
And due to the duration of time, it is divided into sections, beginning with the entry of the stage director and ending with the performance of salutation. (74)
The second chapter, however, should be performed based on a medium tempo;

Now, he describes the scattering of handfuls of flowers along with its ritual procedure— the purpose for which the five-step movement was performed— beginning with the words "the needle," and so forth:

"One should cause it to fall by means of the foremost yoga; that is proclaimed as the *sūcī*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 10.34).

The word "back" (*pṛṣṭhadeśa*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The outward casting of that foot is the *maṇḍala* position. What is that? He says it is the *brāhma*. Regarding the phrase "of the stage-platform" (*raṅgapīṭhasya*), the meaning is "for the purposes of salutation" (*abhivādanāni*). As for the word "three," [it refers to] each one individually.

He explains how the salutation (vandana) should be performed: "In that [salutation], regarding the excellence of time—that is, its greater duration—one relies upon the cause consisting of the application of dance-hand gestures (nṛtta-hasta-karaṇa). Anticipating the objection, "But how can there be such an excellence of time? he says: "Of the feet," meaning of the rhythmic units (kalās) characterized by them. As for that...

The differentiation [of the rites] depends on the interval of time and measure. Now, as to the question "What is the rule for those [rites]?", he says: "Beginning with the entry of the Sūtradhāra," etc.
There should be sipping of water (ācamana) as well as the grasping of a worn-out rag;
then, having risen quickly from the mandala, one should lift up the right foot.
One should perform the piercing with that very [foot] and the throwing-out with the left;
then again, one should lift up the right foot, keeping it positioned at the side.
Then, having performed the piercing on the left and the casting away of the right according to this procedure, one should properly circumambulate [the deity] from left to right.
Having summoned one who holds a water-pitcher, he should also perform purification;
indeed, the rite of sipping water (ācamana) must be performed by him according to the prescribed rule.
The self-sprinkling with water must indeed be performed in the proper sequence, with great care by the Sūtradhāra who has already undertaken purification through diligent effort. (80)

This is what is meant: among the thirty-two *kalās*, one must perform the entry, the walking of five steps, the offering of flowers, and the three prostrations. Among those *kalās*, as many as remain after the ritual action ending with the walking of five steps has been completed, [those are the ones remaining].

Having adopted the appropriate artistic gestures (*kalā*) for that salutation— such as the *vyāvartita*, *parivartita*, and other hand-movements, or the various dance-hand postures (*nṛttahasta*) like the upturned lotus bud (*udvṛttanalinīpadmakośa*)— one should perform three graceful salutations.

Thus, having demonstrated the three types of ritual action (*karmatraya*) in the second chapter, he teaches the collection of ritual actions for the fast-paced (*druta-laya*) [mode] in the third chapter, beginning with the words "Thereafter" (*tataḥ param*). Regarding the phrase "of the mandala": it refers to the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*).
While characterizing those three rituals in sequence, he states the definition of the first: "Having risen" (*utthāya*).

For in the act of salutation, the bending of the knee and head is performed until it reaches contact with the ground. "He should raise" refers to the bent foot; this indicates the *sūcī* gesture according to the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (10.34). "Piercing" (*vedha*) refers to the striking down upon the back of the heel of the second foot. "Situated on the side" refers to the *pārśvakrāntā* gesture (according to the *Nāṭyaśāstra*).

[The author] speaks of the *cārī* (footwork). Concluding this ritual action (*karman*), he defines the second [requirement], called "purity" (*śauca*), with the words "by this [means]" (*ity anena*). Because of the expression "having summoned" (*āhūya*), it follows that while the bearer of the water-pot (*bhṛṅgāra-dhārin*) performs the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa-bhramaṇa*), one should remain silent.

It is observed that the purpose regarding purity will be stated later. Since, according to the logic of the *Smṛti* texts such as "the head is joined during salutation," one should sit facing east with the knees not protruding, and so forth; this is the sequence [of actions].

It should be grasped when the conjunction is equal; it is worn out by obstacles and worn out by circumambulations and the like; it should be known that its end comes with the grasping of the worn-out state. || 81 ||
The third chapter, however, should be understood as being performed at a rapid tempo;

In that case as well, there is a piercing from the left, while the distraction belongs to the right;

The fourth section, moreover, should be performed at a fast tempo; here, there are sixteen beats of the hands and feet. (85)

He shows the third activity with the words "with effort" (*prayatna*). To dispel the doubt as to at what conjunction that [activity] is grasped, he says "beginning with circumambulation" (*pradakṣiṇādya*).
By this, it is stated that there is no grasping of it at the time of the conjunction of the fourth quarter (*turyapāda*).
Now, in the fourth cycle at a rapid tempo (*drutalaya*) alone, he demonstrates two ritual acts with the words "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*). "Taking" means holding.

"Here, eight *kalās*" means up until the falling of the first foot-step. "To be recited" (*japyam*) refers to that which is to be chanted as stated in the third chapter [of the *Nāṭyaśāstra*]. Here, it is for the purpose of destroying obstacles (*vighnavināśārtham*). (Nā. Śā. 3.78)

One should join and recite these four verses, beginning with "ityādi," by means of this half-verse per beat (*pratikalamardhaśloka*), that is to say, with a high degree of rhythmic precision. Here too, "grasping" means "retaining. The intended meaning is that one should effect the transition to the *kutapa* by means of twenty-four *kalās*. Regarding "sixteen": this means that one "falling" (*patana*) consists of two *kalās*. (83–85) p.

It is square in its middle cadence due to eight *sannipātas*;

In the Atijagatī meter, that [song] should be performed as a *dhruvā* with variations, following the path of the *vārtika* and accompanied by instrumental music.

In each [step], there should likewise be two combinations (sannipāta).

"Triangular"—this was stated incidentally. To show that this auxiliary element does not consist of such a performance alone, he says "evam" and so forth: "When such a procedure (itikartavyatā) has been performed here, the reciters of the *nāndī* raise the performance; however, [the action] was already [performed] previously on this stage."

Thus, as characterized by the verse (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.22), the "raising" (*utthāpana*) of the drama—the performance of the *pratyāhāra* and so forth up to the end of the *gītaka* rules—is the task whose form has been explained.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). Therefore, however, there is a transition (*parivartana*), and not immediately after the performance of the *dhruvā*.
Then one should walk five steps with strides that have transcended [the ordinary],

One should first salute the eastern direction, of which Śakra is the presiding deity;
one should then salute the second, the southern quarter, of which Yama is the presiding deity.
Then one should salute the western direction, whose presiding deity is Varuṇa;
thereafter, one should salute the fourth direction, the north, which is the refuge of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).

Those, however, who explain this as a concluding passage (*upasaṃhāra-grantha*) stating "therefore they cause [the text] to arise" have clearly not grasped anything; for nothing whatsoever is caused to arise merely by the recitation of mantras worn out by the salutation to Brahmā. Its status as a "causer of arising" consists in its utility for the pacification of obstacles.

It may also occur at the beginning of a *parivartana* (transition) and so forth, because the term "arousing" (*utthāpanī*) is etymologically significant. Furthermore, through the dramatic performance (*nāṭyāyita*), there is an implication of a suitable meaning, since everything from the commencement of the performance up to its conclusion consists of *dhruvā* singing and gestural expression (*abhinaya*).
As for the statement that "what is not expressed by the poetry (*kāvyam*) should be [expressed] by song (*gītam*)," [this is the case here].
Thus it has been sung: "The vital breaths are for the performance," according to the sequence of the stage and likewise by the force of the meaning;
as for the transitions—

By this statement, it is understood that in the *dhruvā* song, the *parivarta*s are like those of the *gāndharva* [tradition], because they lack the nature of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Furthermore, this [work] is clearly endowed with the fourfold purpose as prescribed by the appropriate means by a skilled poet.

The elders say that the *dhruvā* must be performed; hence [the phrase] "and then. Because it is joined with a square *tāla* and associated with the *dhruvā*, the modulation (*parivartana*) is square. It is sung in quarters (*pāda*), and because of the combination (*sannipāta*) of four quarters, there is an eightfold combination (*sannipātāṣṭaka*) here, which he characterizes by the words "of which... (*yasyāḥ*).

The *atijagatī* consists of thirteen syllables; by that [measure], there are four *parivartanas*. Where the *guru* is the path of the *vārtika*, the *kalā* consists of four *mātrās*. That instrumental music (*vādya*) which follows the song (*gīta*) becomes "anugata. When a foot-step (*pādacārī*) is to be performed—whether on the ground (*bhaumī*) or in the air (*ākāśikī*)—the falling of the foot constitutes two *kalās*.

It pervades; that is to say, there is a lifting in one [foot] and a falling in the other. Others, however, describing two foot-falls in the *kalā* for the sake of beauty on the path of the *vārttika*, explain it thus:
"One who turns [the foot] creates duality, while the other follows; there is no *kalā* for such a falling of the foot."
"Deficient in that" means: those who speak thus [are as stated] previously; that is to say, they are ignorant of the contradiction between what precedes and what follows. (86–92) p.
Having performed the salutation to the directions, one should employ the leftward piercing; the shifting of the gaze should be performed with the right hand. 95.

Then, facing eastward, the man should perform salutations to Rudra, Brahmā, and Upendra by means of the three-footed [Gayatrī] mantra, while holding the thread with the masculine, feminine, and neuter forms.
The right foot is prescribed for men and the left for women;
for a neuter, it should be the right foot again, neither raised too high.
One should worship the Lord with the word "puruṣa," Janārdana with the word "strī," and likewise the Lotus-born One with the word "napuṃsaka. (98)

The fourth officiant, having taken up flowers according to the prescribed rite, [should proceed].

meaning he connects it with a qualification— it is understood that Śakra is to be worshipped as being endowed with specific attributes (*saviśeṣa*).

Turning about preceded by a movement away [from one's current position]. By means of this, one who was standing facing north turns around and becomes facing east. To the question of what one should do therein, he says: "But facing east" (*prāṅmukhas tu*). He shows the three steps with this triad of verses beginning with "the right foot" (*dakṣiṇam tu*). He shows the salutation with the word "one should salute" (*vandeta*).

In this manner, the salutation to the deities of the directions is to be performed by the *parivartinī* while the *dhruvā* sings the verses of the *udgītha*. Regarding the phrase "at its end" and so forth: "of that" refers to the *parivarta*. There are three actions for the *sūtradhāra* and the two *pāripārśvika*s; because he performs a fourth action distinct from those, he is called the "performer of the fourth" (*caturthakāra*). This is the rule (*vidhi*).

"The Vaiṣṇava station," and so forth, is stated by the architect (*sūtradhāra*) [in *Nāṭyaśāstra* 5.67]. The movement and progression of that [drum] should be made like a vessel by those who know it;

then the square [mandala], drawn with song, remains fixed and stable.

(The fourth, fifth, seventh, and likewise the eighth syllables are short in the *paṅkti* meter; this is known as the *sāvakṛṣṭā dhruvā*). Therein, the *sūtradhāra* should recite while relying on the middle pitch (*madhyama-svara*).

"Equal to the vessel itself": for the purpose of its movement, the *puṣkara* drum alone should be employed in succession all around.

"Singing" (*gāna*) refers to a meaningful sentence; it means the performance of the *stobhas*, which are dry syllables. "Established" means with a slow tempo (*vilambita-laya*). "Abounding in long [syllables]" means there are nine long syllables at the beginning.
(NAŚĀ 5.111) That which will be the characteristic of the *śuṣkāvakṛṣṭā* [rhythm] shall indeed be present in this [rhythm]. Where the vowels (*svara*) remain equal, that is called the *sthāyī-varṇa*.
Endowed with those ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) which will be described as depending upon that [vowel], [there is] the eight-part (*kalāṣṭaka*) *dvikalacañcatpuṭa*.
Having thus described the preceding ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as previously stated (5-62; 101-103), he speaks of the *nāndī*: "The *sūtradhāra*," etc.
Therein, the word "there" (*tatra*) means when the song has been concluded. It refers to the middle pitch (*madhyama-svara*) contained within that *dhruvā* chant.
In the recitation from this point, the middle portion of that *dhruvā* (p.
235) is as follows: "Homage be to all the gods, and likewise may there be welfare for the twice-born."
Victory has indeed been won by King Soma; may there be welfare for the cows and the Brahmins.
"May there likewise be the preeminence of Brahman, and may those who hate Brahman be slain;
may the great king rule this earth together with its oceans. (106)
May the kingdom flourish, may the hopes of the theater company be fulfilled, and may the great merit spoken of by Brahmā accrue to the patron of the performance. (107)
"May the fame of the author of this poem increase, may his merit also flourish, and may the deities be eternally pleased by this sacrifice. (108)
In these intervals between the *nāndī* verses, those two attendants (*pāripārśvika*) should always address her as "Noble Lady" (*āryā*), speaking with words that are properly articulated. (109)
It is thus stated that the *jātyaṃśaka* has been grasped. Relying upon this, the teacher Kaśyapa has stated in the *pūrvaraṅga*: "The *ṣāḍava* [is employed].
He recites the *nāndī*, beginning with "Salutation be... and ending with "...the deities. Here, a *pada* refers to an intermediate sentence.

Due to the use of "or" (*vā*) and "also" (*api*), there are sixteen words in the square (*caturaśra*) preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*), and thirteen in the triangular (*tryaśra*).

However, the state of being a "six-fifth" (or *triṣaṭpada*) is also obtained. This has already been stated by us in the first chapter itself (pp. 25–26). Regarding the phrase "of the stage" (*raṅgasya*): it refers to the class of actors and performers (*naṭakuśilavavarga*). Regarding "duty" (*dharma*):
it is that which will be described as "this preliminary rite" (*pūrvaraṅga*) in [Nāṭyaśāstra] 5.170. (104–109)

Then she would become withered and drawn out, revealing worn-out verses.

Just so, O best of the twice-born, having properly performed the drying and extraction of the *tecām* [substance] from the *digle*, *digle*, *digle*, and *digle* [parts] that have been turned grey like a jackal; || 112 ||

Having thus fulfilled the *nāndī* according to its characteristics, he fulfills the limb known as *śuṣkāvakṛṣṭa* with the words "Then, *śuṣkāvakṛṣṭa*" and so forth. (The word) "then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after this performance; since a verse of praise for the worn-out [actor] is recited by the *sūtradhāra*, it is called *jayate* because it reveals that [actor], meaning it precedes him.

"Only the dry and extracted portions; nine heavy syllables"—this is the example he recites, beginning with "idaṃ digle" and so forth. By the word "yathāvat" (accordingly), he indicates the subsequent recitation of the *jarjara* verse, since that is stated upon seeing it.
