He explains: Having first performed a hymn of praise (*stotra*) to the god Viṣṇu, whichever deity was the object of the dance performed at a festival or similar occasion should be praised therein; or else, it may be done in this very manner. [The deity to be praised is] the worshipful deity of the king who initiates the dance—that is, the patron of the performance (*tatprekṣāpati*). If he is indifferent (*udāsīna*), then [the deity to be praised is] that of Brahmā.

In order to fulfill the *aṅga* known as *āryā* by concluding the *raṅgadvāra*, he states the preliminary procedure there with the words "having spoken" (*gaditvā*). Having spoken the *jarjara-śloka*—that is, having spoken the verse at the *raṅgadvāra*—the *jarjara* is also bent down; for it is bent by means of the form of the *tulādhṛta* which is about to be described.
One should recite another such verse; here, for the sake of destroying obstacles,
one should again recite another verse that destroys decrepitude.
Having bent the jarjara, one should then employ the cārī. || 115 ||
The two attendants (pāripārśvika) should withdraw to the rear;
here, the Dhruvā song should be performed in a slow tempo (madhyalaya).
By the combination of four [syllables], it is a square in its measurement;
likewise, the first, the last, the fourth, and the fifth [syllables] are heavy. 117.
That [meter] in which the remaining [syllables] are short is to be known by the wise as *tvaḍḍitā*.
I shall describe its application just as Maheśvara did previously. (118)
This means that one should recite the verse beginning with *nā. śā. 3-78*, which expresses a meaning distinct from its name, as an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual.
Others, however, maintain that after the *śuṣkāvakṛṣṭa* [mantra], there is the verse for the praise of the deity (*devatāstotra*), and after that, the *jarjara* verse. Then...
The verse for the entrance door composed as a hymn to Viṣṇu is as follows: "Then they call it the *jarjara* verse" (110–115).
Regarding the phrase "by the western [door]," it means that the two attendants (*pāripārśvika*) should withdraw by turning their backs with steps while facing eastward.
The *cārīs* and *mahācārīs* to be employed solely by the *sūtradhāra* have been indicated; he now speaks of the *dhruvā*:
"And here, the *aḍḍitā*. Some say it is performed at the stage-door (*raṅgadvāra*) and during the *cārī*.
Others, however, maintain that because of its proximity, it is performed only at the stage-door as an *avakṛṣṭā*. Some say the stage-door itself is the non-fixed (*adhruva*) [part].
Regarding "square" (*caturaśrā*): it occurs in the *cañcatpuṭa* rhythm when the *prastāra* is bent (*añcita*) (Nāṭya Śāstra 31, p.

522, Kāmamālā edition). Although specific meters (*chandas*) such as *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, *bṛhatī*, and *paṅkti* will be mentioned here [in verses 32–36], a rule will also be stated. Regarding "the *jāti* is doubled": [this refers to the doubling of the *jāti*].
Others, however, read it thus: "The first, fourth, tenth, eighth, and likewise the eleventh syllables are heavy in the Dodhaka; that which possesses these is known by the name Aḍḍitā."
Together with Umā, he sported with various playful gestures; adopting a pose of feigned indifference (*avahittha*), he placed his left arm downward. (119)
The chest should be made square and the head slightly bent;
having placed the worn-out [cloth] upon the region of the navel, it should be held on a scale.
With the left hand like a sprout and feet rising at intervals of a *tāla*,
she should walk five steps with graceful movements of her limbs.
The piercing with the left hand should be performed, as well as the casting away of the right;
the wise one should recite an Āryā verse imbued with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa). || 122 ||
"The first, the last, the fourth, and likewise the fifth [syllable] are heavy"—so say others.
"Of her" refers to Umā. "Together with Umā" is because of the prevalence of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). The intention is that it has been stated [in the *Nāṭyaśāstra*]:
"Umā was pleased" (NS 5.52). "He played" means by means of feminine gestures; this is the intention.
"Having assumed the *avahittha* posture" refers to the *avahittha* stance of women.
The first [hand] is arranged as *viracita*, while the other is drawn back and level;
the foot is placed at the interval of a *tāla* and the three [parts of the body] are slightly raised.
(Nāṭyaśāstra 12.168) Where one hand is called *latā* and the other is placed upon the hip.
"Avahittha is thus defined" (Nāṭya Śāstra 12.169).

Regarding "jarjara": it will indeed be stated concerning the female gait that the *khaṭakāmukha* [hand] is placed in the middle—namely, "having placed the left *khaṭakāmukha* upon the region of the navel" (Nāṭya Śāstra 12.179).

Regarding "with the hand [having] a left sprout": *vāmapallava* refers to the hand with the fingers extended like leaves, as stated in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* (9.196): "The *patāka* and *pallava* [hand gestures] are those with the wrist unbound.

This recalls the five-line verse mentioned previously. Regarding "the left piercing" (*vāmavedhas*) and "the noble lady" (*āryā*): this refers to where the affectionate anger (*praṇayakopa*) and other emotions of the Lord, the beloved of Pārvatī, together with the Goddess, are described.
Regarding the word "tena" (by that): here, in the *Āryā* meter (pp.
239–240), having recited the *cārī* verse and performed the transition, [the following is said]:
And with those very same words, one should perform the final withdrawal. || 123 ||
Having placed the excellent *jarjara* in the hand of the *pāripārśvika*,
one should then employ the *mahācārī* according to the prescribed rule.
There, the *dhruvā* is square and likewise possesses a quick tempo;
by means of four *saṃnipātas*, it measures eight *kalās* in extent.

In the quarter-verse of the *dhruvā* consisting of twenty-four syllables, the first, fourth, last (twenty-fourth), seventh, and tenth syllables shall be long, while the remaining syllables shall be short. (126)
Just as when a mountain, struck by the blow of his foot,
causes the entire ocean and its inhabitants to tremble;
May this Tandava dance of Hara, which bestows happiness upon the world at the end of the dissolution, protect [us]. 127.
Then, with the face turned toward the vessel, one should perform the throwing of the feet;
having formed the needle (sūcī), one should again perform the turning of the throw.
Now he introduces the performance of the *mahācārī*: "In the hand of the *pāripārśvika*," and so forth. Regarding that, he states the *dhruvā* melody:
"Square-shaped" (*caturaśra*), performed with the *cañcatpuṭa* rhythm in two beats (*dvikalā*). The definition of a *dhruvā* is that its first and fourth [parts] are identical.
He describes its application: "With the face turned toward the *bhāṇḍa*," meaning facing westward.

For one who, desiring to deposit the state of Maheśvara within his own self, [attains] a height of three and three-quarter *tālas*—and because he follows that [divine] activity even in his intermediate state, he possesses two *tālas* [of height] according to propriety; thus, the distinctness of the *tāla* measure is stated.

Then, with graceful steps that have transcended [the initial tempo] and are endowed with a quick rhythm (*drutalaya*), one should proceed through five steps, raising the feet at intervals of three beats (*tritāla*). || 129 ||
Then, there should be a piercing with the left foot and a displacement of the right;
with those very same steps, one should perform the withdrawal while facing eastward.
Again, he should take exactly three steps facing east;
then there shall be the piercing with the left and the casting away of the right.
Then one should recite a verse of the *raudra* (fierce) sentiment with its lines joined together;
at the end of that, however, two attendants (*pāripārśvika*) should speak three verses.
Upon their arrival, the wise should employ the *narkuṭaka* song;
likewise, in the division of the *bhāratī* style, one should apply the *trigata*.
Then the Vidūṣaka should deliver a monologue (kathanikā) consisting mostly of incoherent talk, which elicits a smile from the Sūtradhāra and is delivered in a single breath. || 134 ||

Then the Mahācārya indicates [the next section] with the words: "Then, the Furious Sentiment (raudrarasa). This refers to that sentiment which consists primarily of Rudra. Where there is the withdrawal of the feet (*pādānām*) through the unification achieved by the application of compounds—that demonstrates the predominance of *ojas* (vigor). Regarding the word "of that" (*tasya*): it refers to the end of the recitation. Regarding the word "tripadyā": [it refers to the three-footed verse].
The two attendants (*pāripārśvikau*) [speak] with a form that is not loud. And here, since the *dhruvā* has not been mentioned, the previously stated *āḍillā* alone should be adopted.
Now, he demonstrates the *trigata* member [of the drama] with the words beginning "of those two" (*tayoḥ*), etc.; [this refers to] those two attendants.
The *narkuṭaka-dhruvā* will now be described.
241) One should employ the *vitaṇḍā*, the *gaṇḍa-saṃyuktā*, and the *tālikā*.
[She spoke] the verse beginning with "Who remains? By whom is victory won? and so forth.
The dialogue of the attendants, rendered humorous by the *vidūṣaka*,
is established by the *sūtradhāra* and joined with the *tri-gata*.
Furthermore, the *prarocanā* (prologue) should be performed as an invitation by one who has attained success (*siddha*).
Once the stage is established, however, the delineation of the subject matter of the poem must be undertaken. || 135 ||
Then, having performed the entire ritual according to the rules, the three should exit together with steps that have not been pierced by needles and whose gait is even.
In this manner, O best of the twice-born, this preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) is to be performed according to the rules; having understood the square form, now learn also the triangular one.
This indeed shall be the practice, and these are the constituent parts;
however, the specific distinction lies solely in the concise measurement of the *tāla*. (138)
The *śamyā* should be made of two *kalās*, while the *tāla* is indeed one *kalā*.
Again, the *śamyā* is one *kalā*, and the *sannipāta* consists of two *kalās*. (139)
It should be understood that there are eight root types of *narkuṭaka*:
*rathoddhatā*, *budbudaka*, and so forth (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 32.280).
A song characterized by any one of these *dhruva* measures is called a *narkuṭaka*.
Regarding the phrase "the division of Bhāratī": he concludes the constituent elements of the Bhāratī style with the words "thus this.
The *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite) is fourfold: square (*caturaśra*), triangular (*tryaśra*), pure (*śuddha*), and variegated (*cita*). As he will state on page 242:

By this very means of measurement, the preliminary ritual (pūrvaraṅga)—including the three acts such as the *utthāpana* and so forth—must be performed in accordance with the musical divisions (*kalā*), beats (*tāla*), and rhythms (*laya*). || 140 ||
That Jagaṭī meter in which the first, fourth, tenth, eighth, and final syllables are heavy is known as Tryaśrothāpinī and is considered fixed (dhruvā). || 141 ||

Musical instruments, the movement of the gait, the *dhruvā* songs, and likewise the rhythmic beats (*tāla*)—these actions should be performed in a concise manner by those expert in the triangular dance (*tryaśra-nṛtta*). || 142 ||
One should perform the movements of the limbs according to the measure of instrumental music and song,
whether they are extensive or concise, fashioned according to these two measures.
The movement of the hands and feet is proclaimed to take two *kalās*;
when moving in a square formation, there should be exactly sixteen *pātas*.
In the triangular [hand gesture], there are twelve finger-widths for the hands and feet;
this measurement is to be understood as applying to both preliminary stages.
In the case of a simple circumambulation, there should be three steps;
for the salutation of the directions, five steps are prescribed in a square formation.
It should be made with the thought that it is the Preceptor, triangular in shape and according to the measure of a tāla;
therefore, no further characteristic is mentioned here, as it would otherwise be redundant.
O best of the twice-born, this preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) should be performed in this manner: it may be triangular or square, pure, and based upon the Bhāratī style. (148)
p. 243) Thus far, this pure preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) has been described by me;
I shall now explain its various forms as they are to be employed by performers according to the requirements of the work. || 149 ||

When the rite of raising [the image] has been performed, O Brahmins, and the turning around has been completed, and it has been adorned with flowers offered by those who have performed the fourth ritual action. || 150 ||
Then, as the Gandharvas sang with sublime melodies according to the proper measure,
the celestial drums resounded loudly.
The Siddhas should scatter flower garlands all around,
and those goddesses should dance before him with graceful movements of their limbs.
The procedure for the *tāṇḍava* dance that has been described is accompanied by *piṇḍī* formations, as well as *recaka*, *aṅgahāra*, *nyāsa*, and *upanyāsa*. (153)
Among the various types of *nāndī* verses, each one should be employed separately by the wise who desire to achieve a diverse aesthetic effect (*citrabhāva*). || 154 ||

Whether triangular or quadrangular, plain or variegated—thus it becomes variegated, enriched with specific details. Then, at the time of departure; immediately thereafter, when the female dancers have exited, following that, by means of those very same [elements] beginning with the "dry" (*śuṣka*) and "withdrawn" (*avakṛṣṭa*) gestures up to the "enthusiasm" (*prarocanā*).
Thereafter, the stage director and others, having performed that [preliminary], and having executed a painting (citra) superior to the pure [performance],
should perform it with a mixture of *aṅgahāras*.
Furthermore, with the intention that "there is no dance (*nṛtta*) for a man other than this," [the term] "in all" (*sarvāsu*) is used here.

The exit of those very [singers] who have entered for the sake of the variety of the *nāndīpada* constitutes the [exit] here for the first four; therefore, they consider that the very singing performed by them constitutes the "variety" (*citratva*) in those [verses]. (132–157) p.
Having thus prepared the pure and variegated [stage] according to rule with great effort,
one should thereafter employ a drama endowed with all its defining characteristics.
Then all those divine women would vanish;
and after all the female dancers had departed, thereafter—
After this, the collection of ancillary elements (aṅgas) should be performed during the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga).
In this manner, the pure and variegated preliminary rite is completed according to the prescribed rule. || 157 ||
One should not allow excessive indulgence here regarding the practice of dance and song;
for when one is engaged in singing, instrumental music, and dancing, there arises the danger of overindulgence.
There would be weariness for both the performers and likewise for the spectators;
and for those who are weary, clarity regarding the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas) does not arise. (159)
"One should not overextend [the application]" means that in this context, only the performance of a single *aṅgahāra* is required.

For this very reason, by counting the constituent parts (*aṅga*), there are exactly sixteen *aṅgahāras*. Thus, [they are]: rising (*utthāpana*), turning (*parivartana*), drawing back (*avakṛṣṭa*), singing (*gāna*), dramatic performance (*nāṭya*), and the recitation of the *nāndī* (*nāndīpāṭha*).

The *dhruvā* consists of dry, extracted, and worn-out verses; the recitation of *āryā* verses at the entrance of the stage; the recitation of *raudra* (fierce) verses; the *narkuṭaka*, the *trigata*, and the *prarocanā*—these are the components.
Furthermore, the sixteen *aṅgahāras* are employed even in the triangular dance (*tryaśra*); thus, there is extensive dancing within the intervals of the *nāndī* verses.

Others, however, desire that dancing (*nṛtta*) occur in those very [verses] through different paths (or *mārga*s), rather than different limbs (*aṅga*s). But that is inconsistent. For if that were the case, then [the rules regarding] "in the *vṛtta* indeed, at the rising," and so forth, as well as "when all have exited," and so forth, would be equivalent to what has not been prescribed. It is not [so].

Furthermore, because of the variety of *aṅgahāras* even when only one limb is involved, the designation "mixed" (*vimiśra*) and "variegated" (*citra*) is observed; for just as there might be a designation [of variegation] on a cloth due to the variety of colors and parts in a single thread, so too is this designation applied here.
This has already been stated previously [in Nāṭyaśāstra 4.16]: "This is the mixed [type]. Enough of this.

By the phrase "of the spectators," he shows that for the members of the audience, the cognition of the actor as such is indeed clear during the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite). However, because their minds are refined by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that [performance], it indicates that their cognition—though involving error and the like—becomes the cognition of the drama (*nāṭyadhi*). For if, in those [spectators]...

On the contrary, one should instead strive with effort to produce the cognition of drama, rather than the cognition of an actor, through the preliminary rites (*pūrvaraṅga*), the prologue (*prastāvanā*), and so forth.
Consequently, the remaining application would not produce passion.
[Without its defining characteristic, it would become extensive due to external characteristics;
therefore, drama proceeds in accordance with worldly conventions and treatises.]
It may be triangular or quadrangular, and either plain or variegated. || 160 ||
Having performed [the invocation] with the colors, the director should exit together with his followers,
[uttering] words of benediction appropriate for gods, kings, and the audience.
It is endowed with the name and qualities of the poet, consisting of the presentation of the subject matter, composed of concise syllables and words, and adorned with various metrical forms.
Then, standing behind the inner curtain, he should perform the call for attention;
and at the conclusion of that call, having uttered the *nāndī*, he becomes the *sūtradhṛt*.
Having entered the stage again, one should then perform the *prastāvanā* (prologue), after having duly performed the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite) according to the prescribed rule. (161)
This must be kept secret from them. We have already demonstrated this in the first chapter (p. 3).

Since performers become weary during the performance of the *karaṇas* and other elements, and since the spectators likewise [become weary] at the outset, the remaining portion of the performance would not produce delight. Furthermore, this drama (*nāṭya*) has that [delight] as its primary purpose.
It has been stated that this provides proficiency.
Regarding "pure" (*śuddha*): in this case, dance occurs only within the *gītaka* and *vardhamāna* modes, and not in a manner that is entirely pure and suitable for performance at present. (158–160)
Having thus explained the constituent elements up to the *prarocanā* (the prologue), he now elaborates upon what was stated previously—

"Once the stage is established, the subject matter of the poem must again be determined" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 5.135)— with the words "by means of the performance" (*prayogeṇa*). [The author] establishes everything through the performance (*prayoga*).

The Sthāpaka [announces] "the representation of the form. The qualities of the Sūtradhāra consist of cheerfulness, wonder, the state of having a marvelous gaze, training, and so forth; as well as his physical appearance.
Then the Sthāpaka, possessing the qualities and appearance of a Sūtradhāra, should enter there;
having assumed the Vaiṣṇava posture, preceded by graceful gestures and bodily movements. (162)
Having entered the stage, one should proceed using those very same words of the *sūtradhāra*;
however, upon the entrance of the *sthāpaka*, a *dhruvā* verse that follows the meaning [of the play] must be performed.
Whether triangular or square, provided with a medium tempo by those who know it, one should thereafter perform the *cārī* that proclaims the gods and the Brahmins. (164)
Having propitiated the audience according to the rules with verses that are sweet with beautiful words and imbued with various emotions and sentiments, one should proclaim the name of the poet.

The phrase "such as Vaiṣṇava" applies even to one who has reached the rank of a *sthāpaka* (director). He clarifies this very point with the words beginning "But the installation," and so forth. Since the *sūtradhāra* (stage-manager) himself is the *sthāpaka*, the rule that "the *sūtradhāra*, having performed the *pūrvaraṅga*, shall enter as the *sthāpaka*" does not imply a difference in the agent. [This is] because it follows the sense of the matter.
In that context, the introductory [performance] proceeds by means of comparisons such as the *sārasa* crane and the *cakravāka* ruddy goose;

for that purpose, the *utthāpanī* and other [elements] should likewise be employed. This is because the present-day practitioners prefer [performances] endowed with a medium tempo (*madhyalaya*). Indeed, when one is overcome by grief and the like, a slow tempo (*vilambitalaya*) is used, and when one is overcome by anger and the like, [a fast tempo is used].

The introductory song (*prāveśikī*) is performed at a rapid tempo (*druta-laya*). From that point onward, it is proper to employ three tempos (*laya*) so that the hearts of the audience may be refined for the capacity to experience the appropriate aesthetic relish (*rasāsvādana*). Otherwise, the singing of all introductory songs would be intended as an act of independence.

This should be understood as merely a conventional expression (*prasiddhi*) for that which has not been critically examined (*avicārita-bhāṇa*). "Thereafter, one should perform a *cārī*" means that two verses regarding the movement of the *mahācārī* will be stated later; therefore, the meaning is that one should recite a verse intended for the praise of gods or brahmins, whether it primarily concerns the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) or the sentiments of heroism and so forth (*vīrādi-rasa*).

Others read "antaracārī" and explain it as follows: one who moves elsewhere from his own place, like the *anantara-pratihāra-āsani* and others. In that regard, for the sake of further encouragement, one should recite a verse directed toward the praise of gods and the twice-born (*dvija*) in order to please the assembly of spectators present on the stage, following the sequence of blessings for victory and so forth.

One should perform the *prasādana* (purification), which is the clearing of the heart, for the purpose of bestowing upon it the fitness for reception through the refinement appropriate for tasting the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Thereafter, one should proclaim the name of the poet;
by the word "and" (*ca*), his qualities and so forth are also included, whereby a state of well-known respectability arises. (161–165)
Then one should compose the prologue (prastāvanā), which serves as the basis for announcing the poem;
the "opening" (udghātyaka) and other such elements should be employed as the basis for introducing the subject matter of the poem. (166)
In a divine [state], having become one with a divine basis; in a human [state], having a human basis;
or in the conjunction of the divine and human, being either divine or even human. (167)
The introduction of a poetic work may occur through various introductory devices that resemble the seed-syllable of the plot and rely upon diverse paths. (168)
Having thus introduced [the performance], the narrator of the poem should then exit;
in this manner, the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) is to be performed according to the rules. (169)
Then, by relying on the manifestation of a specific poetic figure (*rūpaka*), one should, under the pretext of manifesting that [figure],
initiate the *upakṣepa*— a synonym for *prastāvanā* (the prologue)— concerning the future dramatic action (*rūpakārtha*).
By means of this, from the very beginning, the members of the audience become briefly refined (*saṃskāravantaḥ*).

And they possess the refinement of expressing common worldly conduct. For instance, in a divine poetic subject such as a *ḍima* and so forth, there is the introduction of objects similar to that [divine] reality. Rāma and others are divine-human. The mention of "and" (*vā*) is for the purpose of conjunction.

Now, one might object: "How does the *upakṣepa* (the 'throwing-in'), which is the *prastāvanā* (prologue), differ from the *upakṣepa* that is a limb (*aṅga*) of the *mukha-sandhi* (opening juncture), and from the *arthaprakṛti* (element of the plot) characterized as the 'seed' (*bīja*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "resembling the seed of the opening. Here, *mukha* refers to the *mukha-sandhi* limb; and *bīja* is like a seed—a small, indicated cause for the effect.

In the *mukha* (opening) juncture, during the *upakṣepa* (introduction), that very [matter] is introduced; and in the *bīja* (seed), that same [matter] is present only in a very small measure. Here, however, it is equal to that. For instance—by means of the *naṭī*, the *vidūṣaka*, and the *pārṣvika* from all sides, through various distinctions under the pretext of describing their own business, those various introductions (*upakṣepas*) which are characterized by being whispered or concealed...
Having cast the seed of the meaning of the drama upon the ground of the hearts of the audience, the introducer (prastāvakasthāpaka),
having introduced the play, should exit. Now,
if the introduction here is a remnant of the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite), then, by virtue of being a constituent part of the *bhāratī* style...
Furthermore, why will the *āmukha* and the *prarocanā* be mentioned [in Nāṭyaśāstra 20–27]? It is said:

the *prastāvanā* is of two kinds—that which is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *pūrvaraṅga*, or that which belongs to another [variety of dramatic style, namely] the *vṛtti* (specifically the *bhāratī*). Among these, in this *prastāvanā* which is a constituent part of the *pūrvaraṅga*:
The poet is indifferent [to this]. (Regarding this *prastāvanā*, which is a constituent part of the *pūrvaraṅga*:

the *sthāpaka* alone is the independent creator, whether he be the poet himself or another; this is likewise true for the *dhruvā* songs and so forth. As Śrī Harṣa has said: "For this very reason, the poet named Bhāsa [composed] in a certain drama... [divaṃ]...
Those who have been driven mad by the fever of passion should perform this preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) according to the prescribed rule. (p. 248)
He shall not encounter anything inauspicious and goes to the heavenly world. || 170 ||
Furthermore, he who abandons the prescribed rule and acts according to his own whims incurs terrible decline and goes to the womb of an animal. || 171 ||
Fire, even when fanned by the wind, does not burn as intensely as a wrongly applied [mantra], when employed, consumes [everything] in an instant. (172)
In this very manner, the preliminary ritual (pūrvaraṅga), performed by two Brahmins, should be carried out by those from Avantī, Pañcāla, the Deccan, Oḍhra, and Magadha. (173)
O Brahmins, this rule concerning the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) has been told to you.
What further should be correctly explained regarding the rules of the science of drama (nāṭyaveda)? 174.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Application of the Preliminary Rite" (*pūrvaraṅgaprayoga*), in the *Bhāratīya-nāṭyaśāstra*. [The passage] beginning with "It is impossible to stand before this... refers to that second [element], which is listed among the varieties of *vṛtti*. The same should be understood regarding the *prarocanā* (prologue) and other such elements. As it is said therein:

A certain [introductory rite] leads toward the poetry; this is the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga-vidhi*). (Its twofold nature: whether it faces toward that [performance] or is the commencement of the poetry itself, it is thus twofold, and so forth. This will be explained in the chapter on dramatic styles (*vṛtti-adhyāya*), starting with the passage: "The *naṭī* or the *vidūṣaka* also... (Nāṭyaśāstra 20.30). Regarding the abandonment of the treatise (*śāstra*):
To show that one must not act even in the slightest [contrary manner], he says, "Thus is this" (166–169).

He states, "He who this... regarding how prosperity (*abhyudaya*) arises from practice according to the rule; and he speaks of the transgression (*pratyavāya*) that results from practicing otherwise, with the words beginning "And he who... and "Not unwholesome," etc., where "wholesome" (*śubha*) refers to [the prescribed conduct].

In the visible world there is prosperity; "heaven" refers to the invisible world. "Decline" refers to the visible world as "transgression," and "animal birth" refers to the invisible world. Since the world is for the most part afraid of visible transgressions, he shows that very [invisible transgression] to be even more certain to occur: "Fire is not like that."
Now, raising the objection that the arrangement of the recitation and so forth, as well as the arrangement of costume and conduct, have not been mentioned here in the *pūrvaraṅga*,

[the author] provides a fitting conclusion to state them by way of restatement and to declare that [the *pūrvaraṅga*] is to be employed as something distinct— namely, as the "pure" (*śuddha*) [form]. He does so as follows:
249) Furthermore, I shall speak regarding the *citra*, the *miśra*, and the *śuddha* [melodies];
I shall explain in accordance with reality how the five *dhruvās* are to be applied.
First, the *utthāpanī* (raising) should be performed; likewise, there should be the *parivarta* (turning).
Then the *avakṛṣṭā* (drawn down), the *āḍḍitā* (contracted), and the *vikṣiptā* (cast aside) as the fifth.
Thus, these five fixed elements (dhruvas), accompanied by the introductory sections (upohana),
should be performed with great effort by the performers during the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga).
Hereafter, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the *hyupohana* (the re-awakening).
The rite of *utthāpana* consists of eight parts, while that of *parivarta* consists of six parts.
Furthermore, the *avakṛṣṭa* should be performed with five *kalās*;
likewise, when the *dhruvā* is doubled, it should consist of four *kalās*.
And when it has been cast [into the sequence], it should be understood as being endowed with three *kalās*.
Thus indeed has the measure of the *upohanas* been declared.

The preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) should always be understood as being joined with gravity and lightness, endowed with rhythmic units (kalā) and tempo (tāla), and characterized by the introductory section (upohana) in the Citra style.
In the *citra* [style], the arts of Caitra are to be known; in the *miśra* [style], they are based on the *vārtika*;
in the *śuddha* [style], they are to be employed by practitioners according to the Southern Path (*dakṣiṇamārga*).
Four types of song (gītis) are to be performed: namely, Māgadhī, Ardhamāgadhī, Saṃbhāvitā, and likewise Pṛthulā, as they are proclaimed.

Thus, [the phrase] "of Avanti, Pañcāla," and so forth; by those beginning with the *sūtradhāra* and ending with the *sthāpaka*, who conform to the dress, speech, conduct, gestures, and other elements appropriate to the specific activity in which the dramatic hero will be fixed, [the performance proceeds]. The *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite) is of two kinds: triangular (*tryaśra*) and square (*caturaśra*).

"This" refers precisely to the nature just described as that which is to be performed, not the pure [nature]. Others, such as the Āvantyas, consider it to be a mixture of *sāttvikī* and *kaiśikī*. "That [speech] of the stage director (*sūtradhāra*) shall be *pāñcālī-madhyamā*"—thus [ends the section] from the *Nāṭyavedavivṛtti* composed by the great teacher of Maheshvara, Abhinavagupta.
The fifth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Preliminary Performance."
Furthermore, it should be performed either in the Māgadhī or the Ardhamāgadhī style;
in the *pūrvaraṅga*, it should be varied, relying upon the diverse paths of performance.
Just as the mixed [performance] should be employed here in the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga),
so too in the mixed [drama], the Sambhāvitā should be performed, relying upon the Vārtika.
On the pure [side], a broad [line] should be made, following the southern path;
hereafter, I shall explain the ritual procedure according to its gravity and lightness.
In the act of *upohana*, however, the performers should apply it as appropriate;
furthermore, at the end of each *digla*, the wise should always employ the *jhaṇṭu* sound.
In the middle, there should always be exactly sixteen short syllables;
having thus performed the *upohana*, one should likewise proceed with the *vastu*.
In this performance of the *utthāpanī*, one must attend to the proper measure of time,
as well as the weight and lightness of the syllables and their rhythmic units (*kalā*).
However, because it was already mentioned previously, it need not be stated here.
For example:
"The Lord, the all-pervading Sovereign of the three worlds, who delights in the caves of Mount Kailāsa."
I bow my head to the beloved of the daughter of the King of Mountains, the destroyer of the cities.
Thus should the *utthāpanī* be performed by those who employ the *pūrvaraṅga*;
beyond this, the definition of the *parivartikā* is now set forth.
Its *tūpothana* (suppression) should be performed with six beats in number;
at the beginning, the syllable *digle* is repeated twice, and at the end, *jhaṇṭum* should always be placed.
In the middle, one should employ exactly twelve short syllables;
here I shall explain the sequence of long and short syllables for the subject matter.
The second, the first, the fourth, the eighth, the tenth,
as well as the fourteenth and fifteenth syllables in the quarter-verse (pāda) are indeed long (guru).
That [performance] is fixed, known as *parivarta*, and likewise possesses three tempos (*trilaya*) and three pauses (*triyati*).
There are four *parivartas* and exactly three *pāṇis*.
Accompanied by thirty-two *kalikās* and four *sannipātas*,
the *parivarta* should be performed by the performers during the *pūrvaraṅga*.
For example:
[I bow] to the excellent one who has matted hair adorned with the crescent moon, whose banner is the bull,
who dwells on Mount Kailāsa, and who is the most eminent among the gods.
I bow my head to the beloved of the daughter of the mountain king, the lord of the Pramathas, the destroyer of Tripura, the supreme yogi.
Now, however, listen to the *avakṛṣṭā* being described;
its introductory prelude (*upohana*) should be performed with five *kalās*.
One should apply *digle digle* again at the end, followed by *jhaṇṭumasya*; furthermore, there should be exactly eight syllables in the middle, consisting of short vowels.
The third and the sixth, as well as the ninth and the eleventh,
and likewise the fifteenth and the sixteenth syllables in the foot, should be heavy.
O wise ones, the rule for the extraction [of the syllables] is by groups of sixty-eight feet,
by four combinations (sannipātas), and by three hands.
p. 252) For example:
[I bow to] the Bestower of Boons, together with his retinue, the Destroyer of Tripura, whose banner is the bull.
I bow to you, the Lord of Umā, who wears an elephant hide as a garment, whose eyes are fierce, who is the sovereign of the worlds,
adorned with serpents, the benefactor of the worlds,
the source of the universe, and the dark-throated one.
The third, the sixth, and the thirteenth syllables in the quarter of the Guru—these should be joined with four morae (guṇas) and doubled; that is the *dhruvā*.
In that case as well, the *upohana* should be performed, consisting of four *kalās*,
adorned at the end with the *jhaṇṭu* by those skilled in its application for the *aḍḍitā*.
Furthermore, the wise should always place *digle* and *tataḥ* at the end;
however, exactly four short syllables should be placed in the middle.
Constantly prostrate before the supreme granter of boons,
who is accompanied by the host of sages and clad in an elephant hide.
I bow to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, who wears a serpent as a bracelet, and who is the sustainer of the three worlds.
Thus, the *prayojyā* should indeed be employed in the *pūrvaraṅga* according to its true purpose.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the *vikṣiptā*.
That [verse] in which the third, sixth, ninth,
and likewise the tenth syllables in the quarter-verse are long syllables is the Vikṣiptakā.
The directions are indeed his feet, endowed with three qualities;
furthermore, the *upohana* is specified as having three parts.
The syllables *digle digle* should again be employed at the end by the performers, followed by *jhaṇṭu*;
however, if it is devoid of short syllables, it becomes a *vikṣiptopohana*.
Just so:
"I always bow down to the Supreme Lord, the Destroyer of Tripura, who possesses manifold sports, who is accompanied by Umā, who has many forms, and whose ornaments are serpents."

In this manner, all the *dhruvās* should be composed in even and odd meters according to the *gītaka* style; they must be performed according to the rules during the *pūrvaraṅga* with the intention of honoring the teacher.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, I have correctly explained to you the threefold preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga). What else that is desired by you shall I further declare?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Pūrvaraṅga," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Śrī. Now begins the sixth chapter.
Having heard the rules for the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga), the great sages spoke again.
O Bharata, all the sages say: "Tell us the five questions."

(Having heard the rule for the preliminary rite [pūrvaraṅga]—namely, "the five questions": the first question is "By what do the aesthetic flavors [rasas] possess the nature of rasa?"]—nevertheless, it is only when the true essence of drama [nāṭyatattva] is thoroughly understood that [the answer] becomes determined; not by mere words alone.

With this very intention, the meaning of the first question will be concluded in the exposition of the ten types of drama (*daśarūpaka*), beginning with: "In the future age, for the most part, there will be ignorant men" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 19.150), and so forth.
Likewise:
"Intellects, crafts, skills, and proficiency in the arts."
(Nā. Śā. 19.151), and so forth.
Furthermore, the subject matter concerning the second question in the *Siddhyadhyāya* will be determined [later]: "The young are satisfied with desire" (Nā. Śā.
19.151), and so forth.

And in the chapter on accomplishment (*siddhyadhyāya*), the subject matter of the second question will be determined by the passage beginning with "The young ones are satisfied by desire" (*kāme*, Nā. Śā. 27.58). Likewise in other places here and there; and we shall demonstrate this in the course of explaining those very passages. Therefore...

The intended meaning is that the determination of the true nature of the matters previously questioned should now be made. Regarding the phrase "the five questions" and so forth, concerning the three questions beginning with "those which are the *rasas*," the point here is this: in such passages as "In this [treatise] on the collection of dramatic elements, he took up the recited (*pāṭhya*)" (Nāṭyaśāstra 1.17), the distinction between the recited and the sung (*gīta*) is already well known.
"Regarding form: you shall indeed correctly represent the meanings of even the gestures and the great songs. (Nāṭyaśāstra, p.
255) "Those which are recited as 'rasas' in drama by those expert in drama..."
By what means indeed do they possess the nature of rasa? You ought to explain this to me.
And how are the existents (bhāva) described? What do they bring about as well?
[Explain] the compendium, the summary verses (kārikā), and the etymological explanation (nirukta) according to reality.
Having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata replied once more with speech characterized by various sentiments and emotional nuances.

Furthermore, by the force of such statements as "When the experts [in drama] have performed a representation (*abhinaya*) for the sake of attaining the objects [of experience]" (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.261), the [actual] nature [of these objects] is not particularly heart-pleasing. As for those "flavors" (*rasas*) mentioned in the passage "The flavors [are derived] from the Atharva[veda]" (Nāṭyaśāstra 1.17), they are indeed well-known.
The *ṣāḍava* and other such [flavors] are neither appropriate in the primary form (*prakṛti*) nor in the modified form (*vikṛti*). As for those others, such as *śṛṅgāra* and so forth,

which are employed together with the word "rasa"— for instance in the phrases *śṛṅgārarasabhavaḥ* (Nāṭyaśāstra 4.269) and *tato raudrarasaṃ ślokam* (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.132)— how is it that [the term is used] even in those cases of *śṛṅgāra* and the rest?

The term *rasa* is not [the only] word to denote it. The word *vai* signifies "tolerance" (*akṣamāyām*). For the word *rasa* is well-known as denoting that which is perceivable by the sense of taste. Nor is this subject a matter for disregard such that it might be neglected without investigation, for it is said:
"For those who are weary, there is no state other than *rasa*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 5.159).

Because an exceeding degree of reverence is perceived in such passages as these, for this very reason it is stated that "the manifestation of sound" and "the sounds are the aesthetic flavors (*rasas*)" are recited. Therefore, the meaning is that although this [topic] is already included within the inquiry concerning the subsidiary elements of dramatic representation (*aṅgābhinaya*), it is asked again because of its primary importance.
It is thus appropriate that he says, "you ought to explain," with the intention of posing a further question.
However, since it has been stated in the previous explanations, "Speak again, for you have already spoken," [the author replies:
the word *ca* in the phrase *bhāvāśca* (and the emotions) has the sense of the word *tu* (but/rather). But how can the emotions (*bhāvas*) be said to have been taught when they were not recited?

If it is argued that the recitations and so forth are themselves the emotions, then what is their nature? Therefore, because they are objects of reverence, [they are included] within the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Another question: (a? There is a set of four questions regarding the *bhāvas* because they are a source of wonder due to their manifestation as real entities.

For instance, it was stated in the verse beginning with "khinnānām" that some *bhāvas* exist simultaneously with the *rasas*. In what manner were they stated? For in the passage beginning with "jagrāha," not even their names were heard. Now, [if one asks] regarding these very same [passages]...

The word "bhāva" has been employed. Regarding that as well, O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall tell you everything in its entirety: "they exist" (bhavanti). p. 256) I shall relate it to you in full.
The compendium, the causal agent, and the etymological explanation, respectively. || 5 ||
It is not possible to reach the end of this dramatic art in any way;
why? Because of the multiplicity of branches of knowledge and the infinity of the arts.

[The word] *vyutpattiḥ* [is explained]. Regarding the phrase "they cultivate" (*bhāvayanti*): what does this mean? Do they produce [it], or do they pervade [it]? By means of the words *vā*, *ca*, and *api*, there are four questions concerning the two objects [of action].
Thus, due to their predominance, there is another set of five questions; however, in reality, there are again five questions.

This very [point] previously stated is being expanded upon. And you should say "because of reproach. But surely, what is the purpose of that here? He says: "In reality" (*tattvataḥ*). The word *tu* indicates a reason. The word *tat* refers back to the narrative (*ākhyāna*). Since that is the narrative, therefore...

Since these [topics], beginning with compendium (saṅgraha), are primary in the context of enumeration, definition, and investigation, the entire subject matter is introduced precisely by means of them. Thus he says: "In its entirety, the triad beginning with compendium is characterized by the nature of being compendious, definable, and expressible."

"I shall speak" refers to the three types of correct means (*sadupāya*). Therefore, [the request] "please tell us. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is displaced in its order; Bharata Muni spoke such words by which *rasas* and *bhāvas* are conceptualized—that is, determined—but it was not his own [work].

The word "again" (*punaḥ*) signifies that the speech was honored by being answered. The particle "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of the Sage" (*muneśca*) has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) regarding the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth. The word "only" (*eva*) implies that once this has been expressed, nothing else remains to be said. The phrase "in due order" (*yathākramam*) refers to what precedes.

[He] has attained the compendium (*saṅgraha*). With the intention that those who take great interest in the subject matter of his own intellect—following the sequence beginning with "because it is a mode of enumeration" (*uddeśaprakāratvāt*)—might grasp it, he said, "This was rightly stated by you," starting with "the compendium" (*saṅgraham*). Showing them that [point], the Sage said: "It is not possible for this... as for the word "possible" (*śakyam*).
Because the discussion begins with generalities, there is an intention to maintain neutrality. "To go" means to attain. "End" means certainty.

"By any means whatsoever" means by some method other than this approach of summary and so forth—namely, by the detailed examination of each individual word. For indeed, it is impossible to examine every single word.

It is stated by way of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). For the indication (*uddeśa*) and the examination (*parīkṣā*) are themselves limbs of the characteristic; their function consists in demonstrating its object and in its purification. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to provide a detailed definition for every single word here.
Indeed, it is impossible to reach the end of even a single ocean of knowledge;
how much more so for other forms of knowledge in their true essence? (7)
However, I shall proclaim this compendium of rasa, bhāva, and the rest for this drama, which establishes the meaning of the brief sūtra-text through inference.
The wise know that "Compendium" (saṅgraha) is that which is a concise summary of the meanings taught in detail within the Sūtras and Bhāṣyas. || 9 ||

The sentiments (rasas), the emotions (bhāvas), the dramatic representations (abhinayas), the essential qualities (dharmī), the modes of conduct (vṛtti) and their applications (pravṛttis), the accomplishment (siddhi), the musical notes (svaras), as well as the instruments (todya), the singing (gāna), and the stage (raṅga)—this is the compendium (saṅgraha). || 10 ||

He states the reason for this: "Because of their multiplicity. The sciences known as *jñāna* refer to treatises such as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth; the arts (*śilpa*) refer to crafts such as painting and sculpture. Because these are infinite—that is, because they lack an end—[it is impossible for one person to master them all]. He reinforces this very point with the words "of a single [person]," the ellipsis being "of some [person] who has become a constituent part of drama" (*nāṭyāṅgabhūta*).

"Of the meaning," that is, of the subject matter, "in its true nature. "Expansion" means extension; "by that. "Of others" means those which come as subordinate members (*aṅga*) even though they are themselves [the subject].
He shows that the compendium (*saṅgraha*) and so forth are here the correct means (*sadupāya*) with the words "but rather" (*kiṃ tu*). Not [of] the *naya*.

I shall state that summary (uddeśa), by which the subject matter of drama is grasped in its condensed form. How so? It means that, because rasa, bhāva, and so forth are primary, the exposition begins with them.
He asks, "What is the use of that? and replies: it is the definition (lakṣaṇa) that establishes [the nature of] inference, for it takes the form of a purely negative reason (kevalavyatireki-hetu).
And its indication (*uddeśa*) is the preeminent means of establishing the subject (*dharmin*), yet it is also [the basis for] the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Because it dispels doubt, it nourishes the fundamental limb rooted in the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). He states the nature of that summary: "The meaning of the definition and examination in the Sūtra and the treatise, which is the object of the definition and the examined."

The "concise definition" (*lakṣaṇasaṃkṣepa*) refers to that which is brief and contracted, being designated merely by name. He shows that others also think in this very way with the words "in detail" (*vistareṇa*). The *sūtra* is the definition; the *bhāṣya* is the examination (*parīkṣā*) consisting of its elucidation. As for the phrase "that meaning in which the two Sūtra-texts are brief," it means that the subject matter (*artha*) is such that the Sūtra compositions therein are concise.
The explanation does not accord with this verse: (7–9) p.
258) "That meaning which is expressed by the wise in brief through a concise statement..."
This [work], which elucidates the meaning of the *kārikās*, has been recited (or studied) by Sūtrata; it should be approved. || 11 ||
He shows the summary with the words "the rasas, the bhāvas," and so forth. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of the word *iti*.

Drama (*nāṭya*) consists of five components: the three types of *abhinaya*, song, and instrumental music. For if a dancer were to possess the actual *rasas* and *bhāvas*, there would occur a real immersion into death and the like, as well as a dissolution and destruction [of the self]. However, such a cognition is observed in the dancer [only as a representation].
[This is] an error. However, by this verse, the state of having eleven limbs (*ekādaśāṅgatva*) is stated according to the opinion of Kohala, but not according to Bharata.
For even that which was included [by Bharata] is mentioned here again; and because the order is reversed in this enumeration, so say the followers of Udbhaṭa. "This is not so," says Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa.

Since even the *rasas* and *bhāvas* can occur in an actor by virtue of the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and obsession, and because of the power of connection through the pursuit of *laya* (dissolution) and so forth; and since that which is already included may be mentioned again for a specific purpose,
and because the sequence is not intended to be significant— let us leave this matter aside, as we shall expand upon the truth here later on.

Thus far. Now he defines the *kārikā*: "by means of a brief statement. By this, he shows that the nature of a *kārikā* consists in its meaning (*artha*) being of the form of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). [He then refers to] the *sūtra* which expresses that [meaning].

And regarding this verse, which consists of both a concise statement and its explanation, the intended meaning is that the definition-statement is twofold. That meaning which is expressed by means of few words through a summary that encompasses a great many objects of definition, relying upon a *sūtra* as its expressive vehicle—that meaning is a *kārikā*. It is called a *kārikā* because it seeks [to convey] that [meaning] by establishing it through cognition.

"According to the *sūtra*" means by means of the *sūtra*. Therefore, a *sūtra* is also a *kārikā*. Furthermore, that which is recited subsequently (*anu*) after that *sūtra* in the form of a verse (*śloka*) is also a *kārikā*. For it is thus:
the very meaning obtained from the *sūtra*—which consists of indication (*sūcana*)—and which is of the nature of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), is precisely what is correct.

Because it is composed of syllables that are pleasant to hear (*śravyatā*), and because it is expressed through metrical composition (*vṛttabandha*) by means of this [work], and because it is defined by few words while demonstrating the excellence of the subject matter (*artha*)— that is, its distinction from other entities— it is called a *kārikā*. By means of this, a property (*dharma*) is established.
"Kārikā" means a formal statement; that is to say, a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Because it illuminates its meaning, a verse (*śloka*) is also metaphorically called a "kārikā.
What is intended by this is as follows: a definition must be stated that excludes [the subject] from other properties once it has been indicated.

And that [is explained] by the preceding sūtra; furthermore, it is elucidated by a verse that is easy to grasp, consisting merely of an expansion upon the objection raised therein. For the definition of both is indeed what is to be understood. That very [definition] is stated in the kārikā: "Because the sūtra and the verse are to be held together" (10–11).
Next, he defines *nirukta* as having an investigative nature through two verses, beginning with "nānānāma" and so forth.

In brief—that is, in a concise manner—the meaning that indicates the object to be defined, which is distinguished by the differences among many individual instances, is that which consists of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). That [is *nirukta*].

(259) Arising from various names and sources, it is endowed with glossaries and Vedic citations; it is joined with the meanings of roots and their causes, and established through various philosophical systems. || 12 ||

When there exists a subject matter characterized by objection and resolution, that which is established therein is called an "explanation by way of examination" (*parīkṣārūpanirukta*). This is not a mere technical convention; rather, it is the statement of a definition through objection and resolution by means of analyzing this very meaning. Thus he says:
Regarding the phrase "by the expression of the meaning of the verbal root":
having raised the doubt as to how its definition is established, he demonstrates the manner of the objection and its resolution by means of expressing an adverbial modifier of the action:

By the phrase "various names" (*nānānāma*) and so forth: those various kinds of names are the inflected words (*subanta*) that convey meaning within the defining statements (*lakṣaṇavākya*). Arising (*utpāda*) occurs there by depending upon these, in the context of posing a challenge (*ākṣepa*) and providing a resolution (*pratisamādhāna*). Now, one might ask: how can there be a challenge and a resolution regarding nominal words (*nāmapada*)?

He says: regarding conventional meanings, [one relies] on a *nighaṇṭu*, that is, a dictionary; regarding others, [one relies] on the method of determining the division between root and suffix. "Where there is a connection" (*anvita-anvaya*)—these two words are adverbs. And as for those verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) found in a definitional statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), he states the manner [of their application]:

Furthermore, the investigation into the connection of the object (*artha*), the action (*kriyā*), and the causal factors (*hetu*)—that is, the *kārakas* which are the causes of the action—insofar as they are established therein, is also a qualification of the action. By this much, the prior examination of words (*śabda*) has been shown within the definition-statement. This refers to the objection: "In what manner does this word function with respect to this meaning?"
"And thus" (*ittham*) refers to the resolution. This is precisely that which has been set forth by the subject matter demonstrated [above].

He also demonstrates the examination of the meaning: "by means of various kinds of tenets, such as those common to all systems (*sarvatantropasaṃgraha*) and those specific to individual systems (*pratitantra*), wherein the proof for both the objection and the response is established through meanings rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

In the section on "Establishment" (*sthāpana*), the method of investigation (*parīkṣā*) is thus demonstrated by this [verse]. The principles of grammar and so forth are its auxiliary components, as is etymology (*nirukta*). That [etymology] is fourfold: by means of a noun (*nāman*), a verbal root (*dhātu*), both a noun and a root, and by means of convention (*samaya*).

Among these, an example by means of a noun is: "The mortar (*ulūkhala*) is that which has a cavity (*kha*) above. An example by means of a verbal root is: "It is tasted (*ras-yate*); therefore, it is 'taste' (*rasa*)."

By two [definitions]: he who eats flesh (*piśita*) is a *piśāca*. Regarding the convention (*samaya*), that too is threefold: worldly (*laukika*), Vedic (*vaidika*), and specific to each treatise (*pratiśāstrapārṣada*). Regarding this, the venerable Śaṅkuka says: "In the absence of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, there is no permanent emotion (*sthāyin*)."

Because comprehension is impossible in the absence of a defining characteristic (*liṅga*), it would follow that entities must be denotable prior [to their manifestation]; because in a state of full manifestation, other characteristics would be redundant;
because there would result an infinite regress of degrees such as "slight," "more intense," and "neutral"; and because the sixfold nature of the comic sentiment (*hāsya-rasa*) would be lost.

Because there is the possibility of innumerable rasas, bhāvas, and so forth within the ten states of desire (*kāma-avasthā*), there is first an intensity of sorrow which is seen to diminish over time; and in the case of anger, energy, and passion, there is a diminution when their opposites—namely, resentment, steadfastness, and devotion—are present. This constitutes "reversal" (*viparyaya*).

And because it is directly perceived. Therefore, by means of the causes known as the *vibhāvas*, the effects consisting of the *anubhāvas*, and the concomitants in the form of the *vyabhicāribhāvas*— which, though artificial due to being produced through effort— [the rasa is manifested].

Thus, by those who do not identify with the characters, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*)—perceived through the power of the dramatic signs (*liṅga*) as residing in the performer—is essentially the imitation of the stable emotion belonging to the primary characters such as Rāma. And precisely because it takes the form of an imitation, it is designated by another name: *rasa*.
For the determinants (*vibhāva*) are to be pursued through the power of poetry; the consequents (*anubhāva*) through training; and the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) through artifice. (p.

[The permanent emotion] is to be apprehended through the power of acquiring one's own experience; however, it need not even be traced through the power of the poem itself. For words such as "love" (*rati*) and "sorrow" (*śoka*) denote love and so forth by way of denotation (*abhidhā*), but they do not cause them to be understood in the form of verbal representation (*vācikābhinaya*). For verbal representation is not merely speech itself, but rather that which is [conveyed] by it.
It has come to pass; it is as if the body itself were composed of its own limbs. For it is said:
"Though it has grown vast, though it is unfathomable, though it is endless, and though it is great—sorrow is swallowed up by anger, just as the ocean is by the submarine fire."
Likewise:
"The paralysis caused by grief remains as it was,
even though he is entreated by his ministers— who themselves suffer from the fear of their own hearts bursting— to weep with unrestrained lamentations."

(In the *Tāpasavatsarāja-nāṭaka*, the speech of Vinītadeva: "In such passages as these, sorrow is not to be represented through performance (*abhineya*), but rather expressed through description (*abhidheya*). 'As she writes, the flood of droplets from her tears falls [upon the leaf] like scattered spray.'"
"Like the breaking out of perspiration upon the mere touch of my palm, [it arises] within my body. (Ratnāvalī 2.11).

By this sentence, which expresses its own meaning, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*rati*), consisting of bliss, residing in Udayana, is enacted (*abhinīyate*); it is not merely described. For enactment is the capacity for comprehension.
It is distinct from denotative power (*vācakatva*). For this very reason, the term "permanent emotion" (*sthāyin*) is not included in the aphorism even with a different case-ending.
Consequently, it is logical that love (*rati*), when being imitated, is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), as it consists of that [imitation] and originates from that.
Even purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) may arise from false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), as for example:
"Between one who runs toward the light of a jewel and another who runs toward the light of a lamp, both perceiving it with the cognition that it is a jewel—
though there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a difference regarding purposeful action.
(Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣapariccheda, verse 77)

And here, there is no cognition that "only the dancer is happy," nor that "this is Rāma himself," nor that "this one is not happy," nor that "Rāma might be this one or he might not," nor even that "he is similar to him. Rather,
[it is a cognition] distinct from right knowledge, false knowledge, doubt, and the cognition of similarity, according to the analogy of the painted horse and so forth.
There is the cognition: "This is that very Rāma who was happy. As it has been said:
"It appears; there is no doubt, no [cognition of] reality, nor is it error.
There is the thought 'this is he,' but not even the thought 'this is not he.'"
"Since there is no confusion of contradictory cognitions, how could an unexamined confluence [of perceptions] be subjected to logical inquiry while it is manifesting as experience?
"The teacher [says]: 'This too is internally devoid of reality and is incapable of withstanding critical scrutiny. For instance:

when it is said that rasa is of the nature of imitation, does this refer to the cognition of the audience, or to the intention of the actor, or perhaps to the understanding of a commentator who discerns the actual state of things?"
As the commentators indeed analyze it thus (*Pramāṇavārttika*, *Svavṛtti*, p. 39, Nidiś edition):
"Now, according to the words of the sage Bharata, the first position therein is inconsistent; for something indeed..."

It can be said that what is perceived through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). For example, when it is observed directly that "this person drinks milk in this manner," the drinking of milk appears as an imitation of the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*).
But in the present case, one must consider what is perceived within the actor (*naṭa*) that appears as an imitation of passion (*rati*).
That body, its various parts such as the head and so forth,

and its states such as horripilation, stammering, the tossing and turning of the arms, the knitting of the brows, and the casting of side-long glances— none of these appear to anyone as an imitation of the mental state of *rati*, because they are insentient (*jaḍa*).

Because they are apprehended by different sense organs and have different substrata, there is a great disparity between them; furthermore, the appearance of an imitation occurs only when the original is perceived. Moreover, no one has ever previously experienced the love residing in Rāma. By this, the popular saying that "the actor is an imitator of Rāma" is also refuted.

Now, if it is argued that the very mental state residing in the actor, when it is perceived as such, is called the Erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) as an imitation of love (*rati*), then even in that case, it must be considered: in what form is that [state] perceived? Is it not the worldly [mental state] which, by means of causes such as the presence of a beautiful woman, effects such as side-long glances, and concomitants such as steadfastness—all of which serve as its signs—is [perceived]?
The mental state (*cittavṛtti*), whether in the form of an effect, a cause, or a concomitant, is capable of being perceived;

thus, the mental state of the actor appears as identical with that [original mental state]. Alas! In that case, since it is apprehended precisely in the form of *rati* (love), the verbal claim of it being an "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*) of love is far removed from the truth.

Is it not the case that those excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth are real in the object of imitation (*anukārya*), whereas here, in the imitator (*anukartṛ*), they are not so? Let this be granted; however, even though those excitants and so forth do not possess the nature of its [the emotion's] cause, effect, or concomitants, being artificial as they are fashioned by the power of poetic training and the like, why would they be perceived as such by the audience (*sāmājika*) because of their artificiality?
Are they perceived or not? If they are perceived, then how can there be an apprehension of *rati* (love) through them?
Is it not precisely because of this that the imitation of *rati*, being thus cognized, is the cause for one of dull intellect?
For when an effect arises from a different cause, it is only when it is recognized as such by one who is well-trained [in the distinction] that it serves as a cause.

Inference of another object is indeed logical; however, for one who is poorly trained, it is merely an inference of that very well-known cause—for instance, inferring cow-dung from a particular kind of scorpion, or rather, it is simply a subsequent false cognition regarding the scorpion itself. Even in cases where the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) is false, there too [the same applies].
Therefore, an inference based on that appearance is improper. For an inference of fire does not arise from mist when it is known as smoke;
nor is an inference of that which is imitated justified even from a mark (liṅga) that appears as an imitation of it. This is because [it is] by virtue of being an imitation of smoke...
It is observed that from mist being perceived [as such], there arises the cognition of a *japā* flower resembling fire.
But surely, even when not angry, an actor appears as if he were angry. True; he is merely similar to one who is angry.

And there is a similarity with the frown and so forth, as in the case of a cow being similar to a gavaya by way of its face and other features; yet, by this much alone, no imitation [of the original] occurs. Nor, moreover, does the audience possess a cognition of similarity. Furthermore, it is said that the audience’s perception of the dancer is not devoid of the [original] emotion (*bhāva*). And yet...
The expression "an appearance resembling that" is an empty verbal construction.

Furthermore, as for what was said— that there is a cognition [of the form] "This is Rāma"— if that were determined at that very time, how could it not be a cognition of reality (*tattvajñāna*), given the absence of any sublation occurring at a later time?

Or, if a sublater (bādhaka) exists, how could it not be false cognition? Furthermore, even if no sublater arises due to the actual state of affairs, it would still be nothing but false cognition. Therefore, the claim that "it is because there is no intermingling with a contradictory cognition" is incorrect; for even in the case of another dancer, there is the recognition, "This is Rāma."

Consequently, it follows that the state of being Rāma is of a generic nature. Furthermore, as for what is said—that the excitants (*vibhāvas*) are inferred from the poem—that too we do not understand.
For the actor has no realization of her as his own, such as "This Sītā is mine"; nor does the spectator have such a realization.

If it is argued that "anusandhāna" (synthetic unification) merely means that things are rendered capable of being perceived [as one], then there would be an even greater degree of anusandhāna regarding the *sthāyin* (the permanent emotion). For it is precisely of that [permanent emotion] that the audience has the cognition "this is that" by virtue of its primacy.

As for the extensive analysis regarding the nature of abhinaya, which contains an intense exposition on its various divisions beginning with the words "that which is vocal" (*vāgvācika*) and so forth, that will be discussed later in its own proper context (Nāṭyaśāstra, Chapter 14).

Therefore, the claim that rasa is the imitation of the stable emotion (sthāyin) according to the perception of the audience is untenable. Furthermore, the actor does not have the realization, "I am imitating Rāma or his mental state.
For imitation consists in making something similar, and that cannot be performed by one who has not perceived the original nature of the object being imitated.

Now, if it is imitation—that is, following after something—then that nature of imitation would lead to an over-extension even to worldly things. If, on the other hand, it is not an imitation of any specific fixed thing, but rather [the thought], "I am imitating the sorrow of a noble character," then one must consider by what means this is done. It cannot be by sorrow itself, because that [sorrow] is absent [in the actor]; nor can it be by the shedding of tears and so forth.

It has been stated that this is an imitation of sorrow because of its difference from it. However, one might argue: "I am imitating those emotional expressions of sorrow belonging to a person of noble character (*uttama-prakṛti*). Even so, [one must ask]: "Of which noble character? If you say, "Of any [such character]," then how can that person be brought to mind without some specific distinction? It would simply be someone who "is weeping in this manner."

If his own self also enters into the midst [of the performance] as the actor, then the distinction between the object of imitation and the imitator dissolves. Furthermore, by virtue of training and the recollection of his own corresponding excitants (*vibhāva*), the actor, through the commonality of mental states arising from sympathetic resonance (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*), manifests only the consequents (*anubhāva*).

When one recites poetry with embellishments such as modulated intonation (*kākuprabhṛti*) and so forth, the spectator perceives only this much—that the poet is acting; they do not perceive it as a representation (*anukāra*).
The increase [of aesthetic flavor] occurs through the imitation of the beloved’s attire, not through the imitation of Rāma’s own conduct;

this has also been demonstrated by us in the first chapter. Nor does its status as an imitation follow from the actual facts of the matter (*vastuvṛtta*), because that which is being experienced cannot logically constitute the actual facts of the matter. And as for that which...

We shall demonstrate the actual state of affairs: there is no statement of the Sage anywhere to the effect that "rasas are the imitation of stable emotions" (sthāyin); nor is any indicative mark (liṅga) of the Sage found regarding this point. On the contrary, there is evidence to the contrary, such as the description of the dependence on the variety of *dhruvā* singing, rhythmic beats (*tāla*), and the limbs of dance (*lāsya*).

We shall elaborate on the term *liṅga* at the end of the chapter on the *saṃdhy-aṅgas*. As for the passage beginning with "the imitation of the seven continents" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 1.117), it can be understood in other ways as well. Furthermore, even in such imitations, what difference is there in the creation of lovely dress, gait, and so forth?

As for what is said—that [the universal] such as "white" is being conjoined with pigments like yellow orpiment and so forth—that is incorrect if the intended meaning is that it is being manifested (*abhivyajyamāna*). For a real white object is not manifested by vermilion and the like in the way it is by lamps and such; rather, a particular aggregate similar to it is produced. Ta...

For indeed, vermilion and other such things, when situated in a particular configuration resembling the configuration of the parts of a cow, are the objects of the appearance "this resembles a cow. It is not so with the collection of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and the rest, which cannot be grasped as being apprehended through a cognition of similarity to love (*rati*). Therefore, the claim that "rasas are imitations of emotional states" (*bhāva-anukaraṇa*) is incorrect.

As for that which was asserted [by others]: "The external collection of objects (*viṣayasāmagrī*), endowed with the power to produce pleasure and pain, is itself—according to the Sāṅkhya view—the aesthetic essence (*rasa*) whose nature is pleasure and pain;

and within that collection, the determinants (*vibhāvas*) occupy the position of the petals, while the consequents (*anubhāvas*) and transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) are the embellishments; as for the permanent moods (*sthāyins*)..."

"Internal [states] such as pleasure and pain are produced by that causal complex. By thus accepting a metaphorical usage in passages such as "thereby we shall bring the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) to the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasatva*)," the author— realizing for himself the contradiction with his own text—
has spared the authoritative scholar from the clamor of exposing his own flaws.

What is said regarding this? As for the objections concerning the undesirable consequence of a discrepancy with the understanding of other systems (*tantra*) and so forth—how much more could be said here on that score?

Bhaṭṭanāyaka, however, says: "The rasa is neither cognized, nor produced, nor manifested. For if it were cognized as belonging to oneself, there would be suffering in the case of the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa; and such a cognition is not tenable, because Sītā and others would not then function as aesthetic determinants (*vibhāva*)."

Because there is no perception of the memory of his own beloved, because he is unfit for making [the experience] common to deities and others, and because such acts as leaping across the ocean are unique [to him]; nor is there a memory of Rāma who possesses those qualities, since he is not perceived; and it is not reasonable that the world should feel aesthetic delight (*sarasatā*) upon the cognition of him through words, inference, or other means.

For if there were a manifestation of the pair of lovers as if they were directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), there would instead be a preoccupation with the arising of other mental states appropriate to them—such as shame, disgust, or desire—and what talk could there be of aesthetic relish (*sarasatva*)?
If they were perceived as belonging to another, there would be only a state of detachment (*tāṭasthya*). In that case, how could there be aesthetic enjoyment?
The cognition of rasa, consisting of the forms of experience, memory, and so forth, is logical; however, this same objection applies equally even to its production.

If it is argued that what previously existed in the form of a latent power (*śakti*) is later manifested, then the consequence follows that there would be a gradation in the acquisition of the object. Furthermore, distinctions such as being "inherent in oneself" (*svagata*) or "inherent in another" (*paragata*) must be analyzed in the same manner as before.

Therefore, in poetry, by means of its nature consisting of the absence of defects, excellences (*guṇas*), and ornaments (*alaṃkāras*); and in drama, by means of its fourfold form of representation (*abhinaya*) which effects the removal of the dense confinement of one's own delusion; [it serves as the means].

Through the second aspect, the operation of *bhāvakatva* (the act of evoking), which consists in the common internalization (*sādhāraṇīkaraṇa*) of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)— being brought into being— is experienced in a manner distinct from ordinary perception, memory, and the like, characterized by rapidity, expansion, and blossoming due to the power of the diversity inherent in the interpenetration of *rajas* and *tamas*.

It is enjoyed supremely through an enjoyment that is proximate to the savoring of the Supreme Brahman, characterized by resting in one's own consciousness— which consists of light and bliss due to the predominance of *sattva*—
as it is said: "The denotation (*abhidhā*), the creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), and another [the *bhoga*], which is indeed made into that enjoyment."
Consequently, word and meaning become the locus of expression;
for this entire group of sentiments, beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), is that which is to be brought to being by the creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
Thus, the perfected person is pervaded by the process of experiencing them.

In this regard, since this prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is not accepted precisely because it does not accept the position of Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa, its refutation is undermined by the fact that it never even arose as a viable argument. Furthermore, we do not know what "enjoyment" (bhoga) could be in the world of transmigration (saṃsāra) apart from cognition and so forth. If you say it is "tasting" (rasanā), that too is simply a form of apprehension (pratipatti); it merely has a different name due to the distinctness of its means.
Let it be understood that [the term] is merely another name for perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, intuition, and so forth.
Furthermore, if one does not accept both production (*niṣpādana*) and manifestation (*abhivyakti*), there would be no third possibility other than that the *rasa* is either eternal or non-existent;
nor is an unperceived object fit for the conventional usage of its existence.
Now it is said: "Apprehension" (*pratīti*) is the enjoyment (*bhogīkaraṇa*) of rasa, and that consists in the nature of melting (*druti*) and so forth. Let that be so;

nevertheless, it is not merely that much. For as many rasas as there are, there are just as many apprehensions whose essence is tasting and whose nature is enjoyment. Furthermore, the variety of the relationship between the primary and secondary elements among the qualities such as *sattva* is infinite.

Regarding the statement "it is to be conceptualized" (*kalpyam*), which implies a limitation by way of its being an agent— namely, when it is said that "the aesthetic flavors (*rasas*) are brought about by poetry"— if therein [the process] consists merely in bringing [the flavors] within the scope of a cognition (*pratyaya*) whose nature is the relish (*carvaṇā*) produced by the excitants (*vibhāvas*) and so forth;
That [process of] cultivation is indeed accepted.
As for what was said:
