Therefore, in the phrase "an imitation of *śṛṅgāra*," the word *tu* (but/however) is used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). The second [particle] indicates the reason. Thus, the construction is as follows:
that which is an imitation is the *hāsya* (comic), because it is proclaimed as such; therefore, the *hāsya* is characterized by such *vibhāvas*.
The remainder [of the commentary] is as follows: *śṛṅgāra* is formed by adding the suffix *ac* according to the *arśa-ādi* group; the meaning is "an imitation characterized by *śṛṅgāra*.

As for the doubt raised here regarding the emergence of *śṛṅgāra* and *adbhuta* in passages such as "the gaze was made even wider due to the arising of *śṛṅgāra* and *adbhuta*" (*Ratnāvalī* 2.15), that is entirely groundless. For in Udayana, there is *śṛṅgāra*, while in Brahmā, there is the possibility of *vismaya* (wonder).
And that [succession] is neither simultaneous nor subsequent; rather, it occurs precisely prior [to the rasa]. Thus, this [objection] is of no consequence.

Regarding the suggestion of another rasa by virtue of being a mutual result, *raudra* (the Furious) is the example. Of *raudra*, there is the action consisting of its fruit, such as killing, and by the word "and" (*ca*), there is also its action which takes the form of its fruit—that very same [action].
The word *karaṇaḥ* [is used]. By means of the particle *eva*, he rejects a succession that is extremely remote.

(40) Because it is the immediate fruit (*samanantaraphala*) in the context of introducing another rasa, there is also an example of the heroic (*vīra*). The particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*sanniyoge*);
the fruit which is properly proximate to the heroic is the marvelous (*adbhuta*). That fame (*kīrti*) or glory (*yaśas*) which extends everywhere, on all sides—[that is the marvelous].

Therefore, it consists of the form of majesty (*pratāpa*). By the force of the word "also" (*api*), the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) is also a result immediately following the heroic, as seen in the Svayaṃvara of Draupadī and similar instances. When there is an evocation of another rasa through coexistence, the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) serves as the illustration.
That very perception of the loathsome, consisting of its determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, is itself the fearful (*bhayānaka*).
Because the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) consists of that [concomitance] as its basis; the result is the cognition of coexistence. And the word "ca" (and) illuminates precisely that.

The particle "tu" (but) expresses a distinction from what precedes. Furthermore, this very mode of implication (*ākṣepaprakāra*) is possible in only four ways and not more; however, although it exists even here, it has not been mentioned. And those which are the causes of origination (*utpattihetu*) in this context...

It has been stated how they themselves pervade the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*); for that [pervasion] consists in generating an excellence of beauty. Therefore, the coloring elements such as *bhāva* (emotional states) and so forth should be composed within poetic figures (*rūpaka*) by way of following that [beauty].

It has already been stated that there are only this many *rasas*. Therefore, although they are infinite, Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa’s assertion—that only this many are to be employed because they are well-known among the *pārṣadas*—is to be disregarded as mere arrogance; enough of this. (41)

The description of the colors is useful for worship and other rites, as well as for meditation; others say it is also useful for determining facial expressions. "Clear and yellow correspond to tranquility and wonder"—this is the reading of those who teach the Śānta-rasa. Regarding the determination of the deities: whichever deity is established through a particular rasa, that deity is to be worshipped. Viṣṇu is Kāmadeva. The Pramathas are the attendants of the Lord.

They are intent on play. Rudra is the agent of the destruction of the three worlds; for this very reason, he impels [them], and thus, by means of *yama* (restraint), he restrains them in acts such as killing.
Now, the colors:
the erotic sentiment is dark; the comic is proclaimed to be white;
the pathetic is dove-colored (grey); and the furious is proclaimed to be red. (42)
The fair-complexioned one is to be known as the Heroic; the black one is the Terrible;
the blue-colored one is the Disgusting; and the yellow one is remembered as the Marvelous. (43)
Now, as for the presiding deities:
the erotic sentiment has Viṣṇu as its deity; the comic has the Pramathas as its deity;
the furious has Rudra as its presiding deity; and the pathetic has Yama as its deity.
For the *bībhatsa* [sentiment], Mahākāla is the presiding deity; for the *bhayānaka*, Kāladaiva; for the *vīra*, Mahendradeva; and for the *adbhuta*, Brahmadaivata. (45)

Thus, the origins, colors, and presiding deities of these aesthetic sentiments (rasas) have been fully explained. Now, we shall explain the definitions and illustrations of those [sentiments] when they are conjoined with the ensuants (anubhāvas), the determinants (vibhāvas), and the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas), as well as the permanent states (sthāyibhāvas).
We shall bring it to the state of rasa.

When accomplished, it is the *karuṇa* (the pathetic). Mahākāla is its presiding deity (*adhidaivata*)—this is the ellipsis. For he frequents its excitants (*vibhāva*), such as skeletons, cemeteries, and the like. Mahendra is the king of the three worlds. Brahmā...
The creator of the inconceivable and marvelous.

(45) Some proponents of the Śānta [doctrine] read: "The Buddha is in the peaceful; the Lotus-born is in the marvelous. Or, the Buddha is the Victor (*jina*), one solely intent on benefiting others, or the fully awakened one (*prabuddha*). In that regard, the characteristic of origination does not [apply], because of mutual dependence.
It brings about certainty.
Because it is established by scripture (*āgama*), it also consists of the deities of the phonemes;
thus he concludes with the section beginning "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth. "Of these" means "of all of them."
Now, with the words "at this point," etc., he introduces [the topic] in order to state the definitions of the particulars (*viśeṣa*).

A particular is that which excludes [an object] from its own class (*sajātīya*). There can be no exclusion from one's own class without [first] excluding it from other classes (*vijātīya*). Nor can there be exclusion from other classes without the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, in order to show that the definition of the particular follows immediately after that [general definition], [the author says...]

He restates the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) with the words "the manifestations" (*anubhāva*) and so forth. These definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) are also illustrations (*nidarśana*), being specific in nature. Therefore, the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇaviśeṣa*) are stated individually.
Among these, that which is called *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) originates from the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*rati*). Its essence consists of brilliant attire.
Whatever in the world is pure, sanctifying, brilliant, or beautiful is compared to the *śṛṅgāra*.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) are illustrations of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); for the general characteristic is applied to and exemplified by them, since it is impossible to illustrate it without them. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates respect due to its supramundane nature (*lokottaratā*). Those stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) which, in the world, consist of mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), [are so called].

We shall indeed designate even those compositions—which describe a continuous series of duties resulting from efforts of many kinds—as *rasa* (aesthetic flavor), by way of their being the primary locus of repose. For it is through poets and actors presenting the *vibhāvas* (determinants) as appropriate that these [compositions] are led to the state of *rasa*. As it has been said:
Relying upon both that certain new vision of poets which is active in savoring aesthetic flavors,
and that scholarly vision which unfolds its focus upon established subjects,
we incessantly contemplate the entire universe.
"Exhausted, yet we have not obtained even a happiness equal to a fraction of yours, O You who recline upon the ocean" (Dhvanyāloka 3.43).
As for actors, however, because they subsist upon that [art], their vision does not see it as new, nor do they relish it as new; therefore, it is not "new" to them.

Therefore, by our teaching that the appropriateness (*aucitya*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors conducive to aesthetic relish leads the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) to the state of rasa, he demonstrates the fruit of this definition.
(Now begins the section on the Erotic Rasa.)

In this context, because desire (*kāma*) is the fruit [of all experience] and because it resonates with the entire heart, he defines *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment), which is predominant therein, by means of the sūtra beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and ending with "consisting of brilliant attire" (*ujjvalaveṣātmaka*). The word "therein" (*tatra*) serves to determine the sequence, or it has the sense of "this being so. This is made clear by the commentary on this sūtra. As for the term that is to be defined, it is called "name" (*nāma*).

He explains this with the words "whatever it may be," and so forth. Adorned with bracelets, necklaces, and the like, he is possessed of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic charm). By that, he is compared to something pure and sanctified (*medhya*). Thus, the word *śṛṅgāra* refers to a resplendent appearance. And there is no over-extension [of the term's application], because the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*) serves as the regulator; so say the ancients. That, however, is untenable.

Thus, because there is no manifestation of a distinction between the specific domains of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), this is the meaning here: *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) is primarily the relish of *rati* (passionate love) itself.
One who is intent on honoring that [relish] while tasting *rati* is called a *śṛṅgārī* (one characterized by the erotic sentiment). As for one who [is devoted to] a virtuous person and so forth...

On the contrary, that which is characterized by addiction (*vyasani*) is indeed [the true aesthetic state]. That condition of tasting the aesthetic flavor (*rasanāsvāda-dāśā*) does not endure for long even in this world. Furthermore, what is required for that tasting is the set of determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, each according to its own nature.

That which possesses a radiant appearance is called "possessing the erotic" (śṛṅgāravat). Just as men have names that arise from their lineage, family, and conduct, and are established through the instruction of authoritative teachers,
so too are the names of these rasas and bhāvas that depend upon drama.

And names are established for objects through usage, proven by the instruction of authoritative persons (*āptopadeśa*). Thus, this erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) is established by usage because it consists of a charming and radiant appearance;
and it has women and men as its cause, with the nature of excellent youths.

Likewise, that which is not prohibited by the scriptures, is not loathsome, and is clearly manifest and captivating, is designated by the term *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) through figurative usage (*upacāra*). Thus it is said: "It is compared. By virtue of its utility, it is so measured—that is to say, characterized.

He shows where [the term] "so be it" applies—namely, with the words "he who... By the use of the particle *tāvat*, which expresses restriction, he shows that the primary meaning denoted by *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) does not exist there; thus he says, "he is possessed of *śṛṅgāra*. He states that, consequently, the word *śṛṅgāra* is used figuratively (*upacarita*) in reference to a brilliant costume (*ujjvalaveṣa*). But is it not [used] in its primary sense?
Anticipating the question, "What is the basis for applying the word *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) to the tasting of pleasure (*ratyāsvāda*)?

he says: "And just as... and so forth. *Gotra* refers to the paternal lineage and so on. *Kula* indicates the maternal lineage. *Ācāra* is conduct or worldly practice. Those [terms] have arisen from that and become established in the world, but not at their very root; rather, they are based on the original instruction of a trustworthy person (*āpta*).

They are accomplished by means of the convention characterized by naming. "Of men" refers to those of the human species, both males and females. For the names of males follow the paternal lineage, such as Viṣṇuśarman and so forth;
whereas for females, they follow the maternal line, such as Kanakaprabhā, Candraprabhā, and so on. The same applies to tastes and the rest.
These names are established through the usage of elders who are learned in those scriptures, having been composed by ancient authorities such as Brahmā and others.
He concludes that very point: "Thus, the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) is established even in the world through customary practice."
For what reason? Because it consists of the dress and so forth of the heart. This is what is meant:

even words that follow the conventions of specific treatises are well-known in the world through the tradition of usage by those who are proficient in them, and they are employed elsewhere by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). For example: "This is a Sāṅkhya *puruṣa*. It is not...
It performs something; by that, the preliminary stage (*pūrvaraṅga*) has been composed for me here. In this regard, "of this great one" refers to their mutual relationship.

Likewise, these words such as *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and so forth are primary (*mukhya*) with respect to the aesthetic flavors (*rasas*) in this very context, but in common worldly usage they are metaphorical (*aupacārika*), like the word "Sāṅkhya-puruṣa" (the person of Sāṅkhya).

As for the one who explains the derivation of the word *śṛṅgāra* by means of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), he has even forgotten its actual form; for the suffix *-āraka* was introduced [in the rule] beginning with that: "The suffix *-āraka* after *śṛṅga* and *vṛnda*" (*vārttika* 5.2.121), as in the example *vṛndāraka*. Therefore...
This word is established as an irregular form (*nipātita*) in *evoṇādi* and other such lists (cf. *Śṛṅgārabhṛṅgārau*, Uṇādisūtra).

As for those who explain the names of lineages (*gotra*) and so forth as being distinct entities, their [explanations] are merely based on individual observation (*tattadīkṣitāni*), since there is no basis for exclusion (*vyāvartyābhāvāt*).

In the present context, this [argument] is of no use whatsoever. Furthermore, let us leave aside the point that in the world there is no authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) to restrict a name arising from the conduct of a lineage (*gotra*).
Now, he clarifies the portion of the Sūtra stating "and delight is the permanent emotion" (*sthāyin*) with the following commentary, beginning with the words "And that... (*sa ca*).

By the term "woman and man," there is the worldly notion characterized by mutual longing and sexual enjoyment, such as the thought, "this is her woman" or "this is his man. Therefore, this [rasa], which is of a distinct nature as a stable state (*sthāyin*), differs from those forms of transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) that follow the stages of desire and have mere longing as their essence.

The pervasive aesthetic relish (*rati*), which extends from the initial undertaking to the attainment of its fruit and has the singular fruit of perfect bliss, is declared to be the cause of this [drama]. For the poet, permeated by the latent impressions of worldly relish, thus brings forth the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth for the drama.

And through the [actor's] consequents (*anubhāva*), the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) arises as the relish of passion (*ratyāsvāda*). It was stated previously that even for the relisher (*āsvādayitṛ*), the comprehension of passion in the preceding stage is useful.
This is what is meant: passion and play (*rati-krīḍā*)—and that [play]—are, in the ultimate sense...

This applies only to the two lovers, because it is precisely therein that the stream of pleasure finds its rest. As for the other—the beauty of objects such as garlands and so forth—this is merely a mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) fashioned by the poet.
For the supreme enjoyment consists in the fusion (*mīlana*) characterized by the mutual immersion of the two cognitions. This is consciousness (*saṃvit*).
This is because [the self] is primary, whereas elsewhere the insentient [body] is merely an object of enjoyment.
For this very reason, it is said: "The vital breaths in the body are nothing but a mockery of labored breathing; they are, however, Janakī.
It is for this reason that some have raised the objection: "Since Rati is differentiated by the difference in her substrates, how can there be a single Rasa?"
This is due to a lack of familiarity with that [reality]. For this delight is indeed one and the same, wherein there is no separation from one another through mutual consciousness;
for this very reason, it is the nature of the supreme youth (*uttamayuvaprakṛti*). "Supreme" (*uttama*) and "supreme" (*uttamā*) form the compound *uttamau*; likewise for "youths" (*yuvānau*).
In this context, by the term "supreme youth," their mutual consciousness is meant, not the body, for it is of consciousness alone [that this is said].

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the distinction is the state of being a supreme young woman (*uttamayuvatva*). She, possessing various states, is the very nature (*prakṛti*) of that [experience] because conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) arises therein. Because she is fit to be relished through consciousness (*saṃvid-āsvāda*), she becomes the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). However, in the absence of unsurpassedness and the lack of firmness, there is no such consciousness of passion (*rati-saṃvit*).
This is because of the possibility of separation; however, *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) consists of consciousness and vital breath that are inseparable. As it is said:
"By the flow of water from the eye, the moon-like face is moistened;
in the root of the cheek, the lotus-stalk of the lower lip appears as if trembling. Thus.
It has been explained that [this] consists of mutual pride regarding one's life and all one's possessions;
it envelops and pervades.

It has two bases: enjoyment (*sambhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*). Of these, enjoyment arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as the season, garlands, ointments, ornaments, beloved persons, excellent dwellings, the enjoyment of pleasure gardens, and the experiences of wandering, hearing, seeing, play, and sport.
"Costume" (*veṣa*) consists of the *vibhāvas* and *anubhāvas*, because it transfers the movement of the mind elsewhere by means of making [the emotion] known.

"Transitory states" (*vyabhicārin*) are so called because they pervade (*veṣayanti*) or permeate the permanent emotion (*sthāyī*). He whose self (*ātman*) is such that it possesses these [transitory states] which are "resplendent," meaning excellent (*ujjvala*), is [described as such].

With the intention that what was described in the Sūtra in brief—beginning with its divisions (vibhāva) and so forth—should now be explained through detailed analysis, he states the different states of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) starting with "Of that, there are two," and so on. The meaning is that these are the two "bases" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is to say, the two states (*avasthā*).
Here, the state is "based upon" (*adhiṣṭhīyate*) by way of the form of *śṛṅgāra*. Therefore, it is not...

These two are varieties of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic), just as *śābaleyatva* and *bāhuleyatva* are of the universal "cowness" (*gotva*). However, *śṛṅgāra* is the form of that passion (*rati*)—which consists of a firm attachment (*āsthābandha*)—that persists through both those states and is being relished. As they say:

"Knowing from this gift of a token that I am well, O dark-eyed one, do not become distrustful of me because of rumors. For they say that affections diminish during separation, even though they are not actually enjoyed."
"In an object of destiny, when the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) has accumulated, it becomes a mass of love. (Meghadūta 2.45).

For this very reason, the fear of the possibility of separation even during union, and the persistence of the mental projection of union even during separation—this much constitutes the body of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

States such as longing (*abhilāṣa*), jealousy (*īrṣyā*), and separation (*pravāsa*) are included within the three [types of love] when love consists of a firm bond of attachment (*āsthābandha*). Therefore, designations such as "the erotic sentiment of union" (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) are applied even to non-union through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Consequently, it is only in the actual conjunction of these two states that [the sentiment exists] in reality.
It possesses an extraordinary charm, as for example:
"On a single bed, they lay with their faces turned away, suffering in silence; though the conciliation was held within each other's hearts, they both guarded their dignity."

In that [state], the strife of pride was broken between the husband and wife as their eyes mingled through the slow turning of sidelong glances, while they were seized by the neck with laughter and impetuous haste. (Amaru-śataka 23) Therein...

The extraordinary experience of rasa consists precisely in the union of jealousy, separation, and enjoyment, brought about by the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) residing in both [lovers] who have become as one life-force. Therefore, as for what was raised by Śrī Śaṅkuka regarding the lack of brilliance in dress in the case of Purūravas during his madness and the King of Vatsa in his state as an ascetic— how [could this be]?

Even in the case of *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation), [the objection] remains without any scope; for enjoyment (*bhoga*) lacks the quality of being an aesthetic flavor (*rasatva*), just like the state of bathing and so forth. As for the answer given in this regard:

The statement of that Yakṣa—that supreme delight does not abandon her because of her steadfastness even in the absence of a brilliant appearance—is incorrect, for it fails to resolve the objection at hand. For was it not objected: "How can there be the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) in one who is not brilliantly attired? If you say, "Let that very objection remain," we reply: no.
This is an excessive burden for the statement. However, the Sage did not say that "the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) exists when the dress is bright"; rather, it is the opposite—let this matter rest.
Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): between the two states, the state of union (sambhogāvasthā) is first described. Therein, in this context, in reality...

The beloved person refers to the Vidūṣaka and others. Both of these indicate the highest excellence. As it has been said:

The experiencing or hearing of a grove or garden, even while staying in a magnificent palace;

For this very reason, even by means of a syntactical split, the poet did not mention death [explicitly]. Others, however, say that "death" does not refer to the mere separation from life; rather, it should be understood as a state of consciousness characterized by the act of relinquishing the vital breath (*prāṇatyāga*), occurring at the moment of being bound by the fetters (*pāśabandha*) and so forth, functioning as an *vyabhicāribhāva* (transitory emotion). This is an easily available example. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), wretchedness, delusion, and others are included.

Although these are transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), when they are themselves manifested by their own attendant expressions (*anubhāva*), they bring about the manifestation of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation);

Here it is asked: "If I am *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) originating from pleasure (*rati*), how can its emotional states (*bhāva*) be based on pathos (*karuṇa*)? To this it is replied: It was already stated previously that *śṛṅgāra* is produced by both union (*sambhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).

Others, however, relying on the word *ādi* (and so forth) as denoting compassion (*karuṇa*), primarily demonstrate its attendant emotional states (*anubhāvas*). Others [explain] both by means of the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa*. Here, "deception" (*vipralambha*) is commonly understood as mockery; however, it is taken here figuratively (*upacārāt*) to mean its result, namely separation (*viraha*). For by that [separation], they [the lovers] toward one another—
In this regard, there is a mockery of the lover; by showing that he has been thoroughly nourished by that separation,
the sage demonstrates that erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) does not attain aesthetic charm in poetry unless it is employed in its proper context.

For instance, even in the context of enjoyment (*sambhoga*), poets describe discord, a slip of the tongue regarding family name, envy, or other causes of quarrel and separation, in order to avoid a state comparable to the taste of a single solid lump of sugar. This has been stated by Vātsyāyana and others, and will also be taught by the Sage [Bharata]: "That which is adherence to the contrary" (Nāṭya Śāstra 22.207). "Dear person" refers to Vidūṣaka and others. The word "gāndharva" is an indicator for charming objects such as song and so forth. By the term "devotion to poetry," one should understand the conceptualization of sense-objects.
He defines [rasa] by way of its manifestation (*vibhāva*).

As for the one who says that from the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which has become the meaning of the poem, another state (*bhāva*) arises in those who know the meaning of the poem—and therefore, because it generates pleasure, the meaning of the poem is *rasa*—he is refuted. For it is not the case that the totality of objective conditions (*viṣaya-sāmagrī*) is *rasa*.

This has been shown previously. By the words "steadfastness" (*dhṛti*) and "joy" (*pramoda*), he indicates the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*). And with the intention that, in ultimate reality, there is only one *śṛṅgāra*, it should be understood that all [the other rasas] are included at the outset by means of the indication of their respective stages (*avasthā*).
Thus ends the section on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
Now begins the section on the comic and the pathetic sentiments.
Now, he speaks with "atha" (then) in order to define laughter (*hāsa*). By the word "ātman" (self), he means this:

while *rati* (love) produces a cognition called "tasting," it does not establish that [cognition] as being of the very nature of love itself, because at the outset—namely, in the case of the *vibhāvas* and so forth—it is characterized by universality (*sādhāraṇya*). However, as for the tasting that occurs in laughter, that too...
Since distorted dress and the like become causes of laughter for the audience through worldly convention,
they possess the nature of that [laughter] alone by way of being common to the excitants (*vibhāva*);
and because they are to be relished through the act of aesthetic tasting known as *rasana*, which consists of laughter, they are nothing other than love (*rati*) and sorrow (*śoka*).

The relish of consciousness belonging to another and that which is of a similar kind arise solely by the power of a cause grasped through the apprehension of a rule regarding their own unique nature, characterized as a continuous stream of pleasure and pain; for this reason, the Sage has designated these two as "origins" (*prabhava*). However, in the case of other *vibhāvas*...

Because it is possible for them to be common [to all], they are grasped as being of that nature. This is because factors such as policy (*naya*) and discipline (*vinaya*), when practiced improperly, as well as time and the like, and unprecedented objects, serve as common determinants (*sādhāraṇya-vibhāva*) by acting as causes of enthusiasm, anger, fear, disgust, and wonder for everyone; so, enough with further prolixity.
...is produced by these determinants (*vibhāva*).
Of that [state], there are trembling of the lips, nose, and cheeks; dilation and contraction of the eyes; perspiration; and redness of the face.
The dramatic representation (abhinaya) should be performed through the indicative emotions (anubhāva), such as the seizing of one's own [belongings] and so forth.
Its transitory mental states (vyabhicārin) include dissimulation (avahittha), lassitude (ālasya), drowsiness (tandrā), sleep (nidrā), dreaming (svapna), waking (prabodha), envy (asūyā), and others.
Furthermore, this [laughter] is of two kinds: residing in oneself (ātmastha) and residing in another (parastha). When one laughs by oneself...
When [the actor] is situated within himself, he is "self-abiding" (*ātma-stha*); but when he causes another to laugh, he is "other-abiding" (*para-stha*).

In this context, "costume" (*veṣa*) refers to the arrangement of hair and so forth, while "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) refers to bracelets and the like. Both of these, when distorted—that is, contrary to the requirements of place, time, temperament, age, and condition—constitute the determinants (*vibhāva*) of laughter. By this, all aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) are [explained].

It has been shown that these are included within *hāsya* (the comic). Furthermore, it was already stated previously that even the *vidūṣaka*, by assuming that disguise, spreads a semblance of laughter (*hāsyābhāsa*). "Belonging to another" means *para*.
Thus, [the definition is: "this is the dress or ornament belonging to Devadatta"—this is the *udghaṭṭaka* (Nāṭya Śāstra).

4-187) When displayed during the performance of juggling, dancing, and the like, it produces laughter. Costume and ornamentation are indicative of [other elements] such as coming and going. Audacity is shamelessness. Fickleness is instability regarding sense objects. Deceit is the touching of the armpits, neck, and so forth, as is well known from the methods of producing wonder.
"Of the ignorant" (bālānām). "Devoid of limbs" (vyaṅgam) refers to those whose limbs have been severed by weapons and so forth. The compound means "the sight of these.

"Defects" (doṣāḥ) include fear and the like, even when not of that nature [i.e., not inherent to the object], as well as the performance of improper acts and so forth, or indeed distorted dress and the like.
Their "description" (udāharaṇam) is their depiction; by the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), intention, memory, and so forth are also included.

The connection is with words such as "trembling of the lips" (*oṣṭhādeḥ spandana*). "Blossoming" (*vyākośana*) means expansion, as does "opening" (*vikāsa*), while "closing" (*nimīlana*) and "contraction" (*ākuñcana*) are slight [forms of these]. This should be applied according to what is observed. "Coloring of the mouth" (*āsyarāga*) is the coloring of the face. "Grasping the sides" (*pārśvayor grahaṇa*) is pressing. By the word "drowsiness" (*tandrā*), "delusion" (*moha*) is meant. And these are the excitants (*vibhāva*).

The *anubhāvas* and *vyabhicāribhāvas*, as well as the various types of smiles and so forth that will be described according to the distinctions of the three *prakṛtis*, should be applied to these [situations] as appropriate.
This [laughter] is of two kinds: first, the *vidūṣaka* himself, through internal *vibhāvas* such as distorted dress and the like;...
"He laughs while remaining within himself; and he makes the Goddess laugh, thus being outside of her"—this is incorrect.
For it is thus [that the] determinants (*vibhāva*)...
In this regard, O Noble Lady, there are two types of followers:
through ornaments that are contrary [to the norm], and through distorted conduct, speech, and dress;
because one laughs at these distorted particularities of meaning, it is known as the Comic sentiment (hāsya-rasa). || 49 ||
Because it causes people to laugh through distorted behaviors, speech, contortions of the limbs, and eccentric dress, it should be known as the Comic sentiment (hāsya-rasa). || 50 ||
This sentiment (rasa) is most frequently observed in women and those of a lowly nature;
its six varieties should be understood, and I shall describe them again. (51)

Smile, laughter, chuckle, derisive laughter, mocking laughter, and excessive laughter—these six types occur in pairs according to the superior, middling, and inferior natures [of the characters]. (52)

In this regard, among the superior and the middling, there are smiling and laughing, as well as gentle laughter and derisive laughter; whereas among the inferior, one should recognize both scornful laughter and excessive laughter. (53)

There would be no distinction regarding its being situated within oneself; nor would there be any for laughter. Furthermore, since the master’s grief causes grief among his subordinates, it would follow that [the emotion] is situated elsewhere in all cases. If it is argued that the Self-born (Svayambhū) is indeed "situated elsewhere" when manifested in others such as goddesses, then even the anger of a profound lord, when manifested through the influence present in his subordinates, would likewise be "situated elsewhere."

[It might be argued: "That [laughter] resides within oneself as its determinants (*vibhāva*), whereas another [person's laughter] is the determinant for that [internal one]. This too is incorrect; for even the laughter of another would then be a determinant for one's own laughter. And this is the case for all emotions, such as love (*rati*) and the rest. Therefore, the meaning here is this:
in the world, it is observed that one laughs upon seeing another laughing, even while not perceiving the [external] determinants for oneself.

Likewise, even when observing the laughter of others, although one's own laughter does not arise due to one's gravity, it is indeed one's nature that at that very moment one becomes overwhelmed by laughter upon seeing the laughter of another;
just as the tasting of the juice of sour pomegranate and the like possesses the inherent quality of being transmissible.
Regarding this, there are verses:
With cheeks slightly blossoming and side-long glances endowed with elegance...
The smile of the most excellent ones is steady and does not reveal their teeth.
That smile is performed wherein the face and eyes are blossomed, the cheeks are expanded, and the teeth are slightly visible. (55)
Now, regarding the middle [type of laughter]:

that which involves the contraction of the eyes and cheeks, is accompanied by sound, is sweet, occurs at the appropriate time, and possesses the glow of the mouth—that indeed is *vihasita* (the smile). || 56 ||

In other cases as well, [the emotion] transfers precisely because one observes a transition corresponding to the modification of the teeth and saliva; thus, laughter is by its very nature prone to transfer, which is why wood is its most abundant material.
He speaks of its various divisions, saying "and six types," meaning two pairs, respectively.

Some say that [the verse beginning with] "the gradation of manifestation" (*vibhāvatāratamya*) refers to this; however, that is incorrect, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of other distinctions as well.

Therefore, this is intended with reference to the transition (*saṅkramaṇa*). For when a smile (*smita*) occurs in a person of superior character, it becomes laughter (*hasita*) once it has been transferred [to another]. It is for this very reason that it will be stated that "laughter is established in six stages. Otherwise, there would be only six stages.
It may be so.

When the slightness of the smile has vanished, it becomes laughter (*hasita*); from that, it becomes especially distinct; and when it has gone even further toward another, it becomes another, namely *apahasita*, which is characterized by an exceeding degree. Thus, there is a difference in meaning due to the difference in prefixes. (53)

*Sauṣṭhava* (excellence) is the absence of excessiveness (*anulbaṇatā*). *Dvijāḥ* means teeth. Having rendered [the smile] slow (*dhīram*) as "gradual" (*mantharam*), he says "with blossoming" (*vikasitaiḥ*) in order to exclude slightness (*īṣattvam*).
Now (*atha*): this means at the time of transition following the smile. "That" (*tat*):
the meaning is that the very smile, having been transferred, attains such a form.
That [expression] in which the nose is expanded, the gaze is sidelong,
and the limbs and head are contracted, is the "derisive smile" (upahasita). (57)
Now, regarding the lowest [types]:
that which is a laugh out of place, accompanied by tears in the eyes, and likewise with the shoulders and head trembling—that shall be known as *apahasita* (the derisive laugh). || 58 ||
That which is performed with agitation and tearful eyes, in a loud and elevated tone, with the sides of the body embraced by the arms, is called *atihasita* (excessive laughter). || 59 ||
Whatever occasions for laughter may arise from the action in a drama, one should employ them in this manner among characters of high, low, and middle status. (60)
Thus, this comic sentiment (hāsya-rasa) is to be understood as being twofold—arising from oneself and arising from another—and as existing in three temperaments and three stages. (61)

Where there is a gazing with a glance called *jihmā* (sidelong), which is appropriate for the time and occasion, [but] in terms of posture and so forth—(57)—"in an improper place" means at an inappropriate time, such as on an occasion of grief; "harsh" means grating to the ear; "in a drama" refers to [the context of a play].

The word *nāṭaka* refers exclusively to dramatic representation (*rūpaka*). "Arising from oneself" is characterized by smiles, laughter, and derisive laughter that have not been transmitted [to others]; "arising from another" consists of laughter, derisive laughter, and excessive laughter that have been transmitted. This [latter] occurs in a superior nature due to the very transmission of the forms of laughter and so forth.

The form [of the rasa] consists of smiles and so forth. It has already been stated that there is no transference (*saṃkramaṇa*) of love, anger, grief, and the like. For in that case, either that very excitant (*vibhāva*) simultaneously becomes the excitant, or the person possessing that mental state (*cittavṛtti*) attains the status of an excitant. However, those same excitants do not, having presented their own mental state, cause it to be transferred to another.

[Regarding] the *pratibimba* (reflection): others [hold that] this very thing is merely an indication of the distinction between what resides within oneself and what resides in another for all [beings], like laughter (*hāsa*). But this is incorrect;
for it is established by direct experience that laughter is indeed transmitted.

311) Now, that which is called *karuṇa* (compassion/pity) arises from the stable emotional state (*sthāyibhāva*) of sorrow (*śoka*). And it [arises] from the fall [of beings] due to curses or afflictions, separation from beloved persons, the destruction of wealth, execution, imprisonment, flight, or injury.
This [sorrow] arises from determinants such as the misfortune of living in a forest or the loss of wealth;

its representation through performance should be executed by means of consequents such as shedding tears, lamentation, parching of the mouth, change of complexion, drooping of the limbs, sighing, fainting, and death. And its transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas) are as follows:
Disgust, languor, anxiety, longing, agitation, confusion, delusion, fatigue, fear, despondency, wretchedness, disease, stupor, madness,
epilepsy, terror, indolence, death, paralysis, trembling, change of color, tears, hoarseness of voice, and so forth.

But another says: "In the three natures (*prakṛti*), there are three states; due to the gradation of manifestation (*vibhāva*), they are of two forms. Furthermore, by virtue of being situated in oneself or in another, they are twofold; thus, this [manifestation] has twelve divisions—this is the intended meaning of the *kārikā*. And here, there is also a separate analysis of each. However, that opinion leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding reality (*tattva*), and therefore it has not been cited. (61)
Thus ends the section on the comic sentiment (hāsya-rasa).
Now begins the section on the aesthetic flavor of compassion (karuṇa-rasa).
Now, he defines *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment), which has arrived at its proper occasion—namely, "Now, as for what is called *karuṇa*. The word "now" (*atha*) indicates sequence.

And the sequence here is as follows: the *hāsya* (comic) sentiment was required as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) by means of *sambhoga* (union); and because it shares the same transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) with *vipralambha* (separation), the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment [is required]—so says the commentator.
And this is contradictory to what precedes and follows. We have, however, demonstrated that the sequence consists merely in the division of the enumeration.
Its enactment should be employed such that, when it is being tasted, it receives the designation "karuṇa" (the pathetic).
For in the world, *karuṇā* is well known as a state of compassionate heart; and that [compassion] is [to be inferred] by signs in the actor who is imitating grief.
"It is designated as 'compassion' (karuṇa) because it is to be experienced by the audience," says the illustrious Śaṅkuka.

This, however, is merely a manifestation of his failure to remember what precedes and follows; for that which is a counteraction of sorrow is compassion, whereas mercy (dayā) is the desire to protect. How could that [mercy] be an imitation of sorrow? And toward what [object] would they [the audience] have it?
We do not know [how] it is day.
Regarding this, there are these two verses: (p.
312) — [The verses follow].
Whether from witnessing the slaughter of a loved one, or even from hearing unpleasant words—
through these particular conditions, that which is called the flavor of compassion (karuṇarasa) arises.
The pathetic sentiment (karuṇa-rasa) is to be represented through moaning, weeping, the onset of delusion, lamentations, wailings, and the exhaustion and affliction of the body. 63.

Therefore, "karuṇa" (the pathetic sentiment) is the designation for sorrow because it is common to all, according to the reasoning previously stated; for that very reason, the word "nāma" (namely) is used. Its arising [from causes] is to be explained in the same manner as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). The mention of a "curse" (*śāpa*) serves as an illustration of a cause for which there is no remedy. Regarding the affliction of a curse...

Regarding the separation and other afflictions of one’s fallen loved ones: here, "separation" (*viprayoga*) refers to this [present] disjunction; "union" (*saṅgama*) is its opposite (*asaṅgama*). The loss of wealth and so forth is well known. "Flight" (*vidrava*) is expulsion from one’s country; and that [flight] also occurs during separation—this is the distinction. "Affliction" (*upaghāta*) is the death of sons and others. "Flight" caused by fire and the like is also included.

The claim that there is injury caused by thieves and the like is incorrect, because such things have already been accounted for under the destruction of wealth. "Calamity" refers to association with ruinous vices such as hunting, gambling, and so forth. Even the loss of wealth and other such misfortunes would not cause grief to one of superior character who has internalized [the truth], but they do affect those of middling and inferior characters.
The inclusion of the phrase "they should indeed do" and so forth [is for the sake of emphasis]. Lamentation (*paridevana*) is the reproaching of oneself, of fate, or of another.
By the term "sighing" (*niśvāsa*), the inhalation (*ucchvāsa*) that immediately follows it—consisting of upward breathing—is also indicated.
Through the loss of memory (*smṛtilopa*), paralysis (*stambha*) and fainting (*pralaya*) are indicated. Here, there are changes in complexion, tears, and alterations in the voice.

Those whose nature is manifested externally are apprehended as being of the essence of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*). For instance, speakers say, "His throat is full of tears, yet no water from his eyes is seen. We have already stated that these [manifestations], such as tears and the like, are mentioned in the middle precisely for the sake of supporting their status as transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) and as objects of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*).

And we shall explain [this] later; therefore, there is no tautology. The same applies elsewhere as well. We shall explain insanity (*unmāda*) and epilepsy (*apasmāra*) separately from disease (*vyādhi*).
The word "killing" (*vadha*) is also indicative of imprisonment and so forth—that by which the death of a beloved person and the like is brought about.

It is expressed by the word because it is heard from him; therefore, the meaning is that poets should represent the loss of wealth and so forth experienced by a loved one—whether seen or heard—as the excitants (*vibhāva*) of the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*).
"By these" means by such types as these. In this *āryā* verse, the word *bhāva* denotes the excitant (*vibhāva*).

And by means of those [physical] manifestations (*anubhāva*), one should also discern the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*); thus, another *āryā* verse beginning with "with sound" (*sasvana*) and so forth is provided. The plural number is used to indicate that there are many varieties due to differences in nature, place, time, condition, cause, and so on. [The first transitory state is] delusion (*moha*).
Inertness.
313) Now, the Furious [sentiment] (*raudra*) consists of anger as its dominant emotional state (*sthāyibhāva*).
It has as its nature fierce *rakṣas*, *dānava*, and human beings; it is caused by battle.
And it arises through such determinants (*vibhāva*) as anger, assault, insult, false speech, injury, verbal harshness, malice, envy, and so forth. And of that...
By means of beating, tearing, pressing, cutting, piercing, striking, seizing, the falling of weapons, blows, and the drawing out of blood,
other deviant [actions] are indicated; as well as the exhaustion of the body through casting down, binding, and so forth.

"Assault" refers to such acts as beating the chest and so forth. These secondary emotions (anubhāvas) are to be distributed according to their appropriate application based on the distinction of the [original] nature, as it was stated:
"The pathetic (karuṇa) [arises] from the furious (raudra)," and so on. Some say that the sequence [of the original natures] is as follows: "What kind of furious [nature is it]? [and so forth].
Thus ends the chapter on compassion.
Now begins the section on the Furious Sentiment (raudrarasa).

Now he defines the Furious Sentiment (*raudra-rasa*)—beginning with "Next, that which is called the Furious. The intention behind the inclusion of the word "self" (*ātman*) is as follows: the commission of injustice is primarily the object of anger; and toward such a person, everyone—even in their innermost thoughts—would not hesitate even to drink blood. Thus says the world: "If such a one..."
Even by drinking that very blood of his, one is not satiated. This was also stated by the great poet Bhāsa in his own composition: "That was indeed the Tretā age, for she was Maithilī."
"Rāma’s path is one of passion and his heart is tender;
yet even if someone were to obtain Rāvaṇa’s body and cut it into pieces as small as sesame seeds, he would not reach satiety. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, because it possesses common excitants (*vibhāva*) such as laughter and the like, its aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*) consists precisely of anger; thus, the *raudra* rasa is essentially of the nature of wrath. Those in whom the quality of "slaying" is intensified are called "haughty" (*uddhata*). The actors who assume their dress constitute its natural cause for the emergence of this aesthetic relish.

Regarding this, some explain: [The *raudra-rasa*] caused by battle is characterized by the drinking of blood and so forth among those such as Bhīmasena, who are of a haughty nature; whereas *rakṣasas* and *dānavas* are *raudra* by their very nature. That is incorrect. Bhīma’s drinking of blood is not caused by battle, but rather by the opposite; it is precisely because of his haughty nature.
For he, being under the sway of anger,
performed such deeds; and furthermore—

The performance should be enacted through such *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions) as bloodshot eyes, the knitting of eyebrows, the biting of lips, the quivering of the cheeks, and the clenching of the fists.
He has made a vow even though it was improper; and for the fulfillment of that very vow, he is under the influence of Rākṣasa.

It has been described by the poet in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "Therefore, all these [heroes] are wrathful by their very nature (*svabhāvāt*). When this is imitated by the actor (*naṭa*), the Furious (*raudra*) sentiment is relished; thus, that [wrathfulness] is his innate disposition (*prakṛti*). And the meaning of the phrase "having battle as its cause" (*saṅgrāmahetuka*) is this: the battle, which is displayed by the poet and the actor, is the cause—the causal basis—of the Heroic (*vīra*), for the Hero is indeed...

Anger is not the appropriate cause for that [heroism]. Thus, he will be designated primarily as a *vīra* (hero) on account of his combat. [Objection: But even those who are naturally prone to anger require an incitement; [the author] says "yes," namely: "and he... Anger and so forth are caused by another; "insult" (*ādharṣaṇa*) refers to the humiliation of one's wife and so on. "Undistractedness" (*avikṣepa*).
Censuring one's country, caste, lineage, learning, or occupation; speaking falsehoods—that is, any untruthful speech;

causing injury, such as the oppression of one's household or servants; verbal cruelty, which is threatening by means of mentioning killing and so forth; malice, which is the desire to harm; and envy, which is intolerance toward the virtues of others.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [acts such as] the seizure of a kingdom are intended. These, when described by the poet as being in the state of an excitant (*vibhāva*), give rise to this [emotion].
His actions, such as beating and so forth, and his physical manifestations, such as bloodshot eyes and so forth, are the ensuants (*anubhāvas*); thus they are defined separately.

This is for the purpose of indicating a distinction, even though the status of being an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) is equal. The distinction, however, lies in the fact that for the former [emotions], it is described merely through words, because they cannot be shown directly on the stage. As it will be said:
"Battle, loss of kingdom, death, and the siege of a city."
"Those things not performed on stage are to be conveyed by means of *praveśakas*. (Nāṭyaśāstra 18.38).
[In this verse,] "red eyes" and so forth are performed directly on the stage;
however, some maintain that "the seizing and brandishing of weapons" was erroneously included in the previous [list]. But this—
There is no purpose in mentioning them separately. This is the underlying intention here:

even when Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and arrogant humans act merely through physical gestures—even in jesting conversations and the like—without the presence of excitants (uddīpana-hetu), the striking and so forth constitute the primary element. As he will state: "And that which..."

“They undertake something” means they undertake an incitement; even while seized by beating and so forth, their eyes become bloodshot and the like. For this very reason, there is the word “again. In that context, “beating” (*tāḍana*) is the striking with the palm of the hand or similar implements; “tearing” (*pāṭana*) is making into two parts; “crushing” (*pīḍana*) is grinding; and “cutting” (*chedana*)— [Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.]
Cutting; splitting; the mutual separation of friends and others—these are formed with the suffix *lyuṅ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
The complete seizing of weapons from all sides.
And its constituent states (bhāvas) are non-delusion, enthusiasm, impetuosity, indignation, fickleness, ferocity, pride, perspiration, trembling, horripilation, stammering, and so forth.
Here it is asked: as for what was stated—that the *raudra* (fierce) rasa belongs to Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and the like—is this the case for others as well?
It does not exist. It is said: The *raudra* (fierce) sentiment exists in others as well; however, it is the one under discussion here that is being taken up.

For they are fierce by their very nature. Why? Because they possess many arms and many faces, and even without splitting [the enemy], they cause the falling of weapons; they strike and split [them] apart, and thus [they bring about] the felling. By that...
The extraction of blood: for demons and the like strike even in jest; however, their result is merely the flow of blood and nothing more. And those two eyes are filled with blood.
The raising of the roots of the eyebrows is the frown. The pressing of the teeth and lips as appropriate [is the biting].

The mutual pressing of the tips of the hands is *saṅgharṣaṇa* (rubbing). "States" (*bhāvāḥ*) refers to the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*). *Asaṃmoha* (non-delusion) is the opposite of *saṃmoha* (delusion); here the negative particle (*nañ*) implies opposition. In this context, it comprises correct cognition (*samyagbodha*) through non-repetition. *Utsāha* (exertion) is a transitory emotion here [in relation] to anger.

Because they are primarily characterized by their capacity to be tasted (rasanīyatva). Perspiration and the like are external; even in the absence of internal *sāttvika* [emotions], they occur due to contact with poison, fever, and so forth. Therefore, they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Internal [emotions] are unmanifest, but they become manifest through external means such as the fanning with a fan and the like, which bring about perspiration and other physical effects.
The transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) have been enumerated.

Taking it as his intention that the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*) exists within these very [states], the challenger says: "As for what was stated... The proponent, however, with the intention that the Furious Sentiment indeed exists among these, says: "It exists in others. [This refers to] "others."

The connection of those [words] being employed by poets and actors is by way of being produced (*janya*). "Adhikāra" means continuity (*anuvṛtti*). "In this context"—that is, regarding kings and so forth. He clarifies this very point with the words "for they... By the particle *eva* immediately following the word "svabhāva," the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is indicated, meaning that they "indeed exist. Their own coming into being (*bhavana*) from that...

This is the meaning. Therefore, the mention of Aṅga and Raudra is also not contradictory. Otherwise, only those who are naturally fierce, such as Raktākṣa and others, would be intended; not those with many arms, faces, and so forth. With the intention that even among them, the Rākṣasas and others are not always angry toward their own attendants, he asks, "Why? (kasmāt).
With their tawny hair tossed upward and scattered, their bloodshot eyes wide and rolling, and possessing terrifying dark forms, whatever they undertake as their natural behavior—

For them, everything such as speech and physical gestures is indeed fierce (raudra), and they generally indulge forcefully in the erotic (śṛṅgāra) sentiment. Furthermore, the fierce sentiment produced by battles and combat should be recognized in those men who imitate them.
In this regard, there are two traditional verses: "Here [are] the noble ones with many arms"— for their form is indeed contrary to what is commonly known in the world— and in that case,
their visible actions consist of ascetic practices and the like, produced by the intent to destroy others.

It is active; therefore, in such well-performed [representations], that very intention consisting of anger is perceived, and thus the aesthetic relish (*rasa*) of the Furious (*raudra*) is not hidden from the spectators. And by means of that, just as passion and so forth [are experienced], that which was seen at the time of anger is always manifested for them in their two eyes.

"Red-eyed. For this very reason, they possess a form that is always "terrible" (*bhīma*) and "black" (*asita*); the suffix *-ini* is used here to denote a constant connection (*nityayoga*). Consequently, a *bahuvrīhi* compound has not been employed here. (The meaning is that the use of the *bahuvrīhi* term *bhīmāsitarūpāḥ* was not made.)
He shows that not only is his body thus, but even his visible activity produces nothing but the aesthetic flavor of the Furious (raudra): "And whatever... [and] "by its very nature.
Even when there is no change in the mind, whatever activity—whether vocal or physical—there is of these [beings], that...

That which is characterized primarily by beating and so forth, as seen both in poetry and in performance, is the cause of the *raudra* (furious) aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). That whose verbal and physical [expressions] are its primary instruments—mental activity, however, is not mentioned because it is imperceptible.
He clarifies what was stated as "all" with the words "and the *śṛṅgāra*": here, by the word *śṛṅgāra*,...
Its excitant (*vibhāva*) consists of the pleasure garden and so forth; that too is "forcibly" (*prasabham*) resorted to by them in its cruel form.

The meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is: "if even the avoidance of ferocity has been mentioned [in such cases], how much more so anything else? Likewise: "O Sītā, whose brows wander with the weight of the graceful pride of her husband... (*Udāttarāghava-nāṭaka*).

This is an example, beginning with "ityādi. Likewise, even the service of various deities is shown— through intense repetition, as in "O Malaya breeze, give me a chain of fetters" (*Bālarāmāyaṇa* 5.51)— to sometimes occur through conciliation as well, by virtue of being the *raudra-rasa* (the Furious sentiment), as indicated by the word "prāyaśaḥ" (mostly).

Through the striking, killing, mutilating, cutting, and tearing apart [of enemies] in battle, as well as through the agitation of combat and other such factors, the *raudra* (fierce) [rasa] arises. (64)
The enactment of this [sentiment] should be performed through these specific dramatic means: the hurling of various weapons, and the severing of heads, headless trunks, and arms. || 65 ||
Thus is the Furious Sentiment (raudrarasa) seen, characterized by fierce speech, limbs, and gestures;
it abounds in the striking of weapons and consists essentially of the performance of terrible deeds. (66)

Now, one might object: "In that case, how can there be transformations such as ferocity among arrogant humans? For they do not possess many arms and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And of them," meaning of the *rākṣasas* and others. "Imitators" means that, by virtue of having a *tāmasa* (dark) nature, they should be understood as followers who resemble those [beings].

To the question "How so?", he says: by the mention of "battle" (*saṅgrāma*), the previously mentioned acts such as striking and tearing are included. By this, even in the absence of many arms and so forth, those of a fierce nature (*raudraprakṛti*) are characterized as arrogant men through speech and bodily gestures appropriate to anger. Thus...

In passages such as "the Rākṣasas, Dānavas," and so forth, the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is certain. However, there are others who are primarily heroic, such as Aśvatthāman and Paraśurāma; in them, anger—which is suitable for the aesthetic flavor of the Furious (*raudra*)—does indeed arise by virtue of the power of the cause. Furthermore, even among Rākṣasas and the like, there exist laughter, sorrow, and so on.
One whose anger has been overcome by its own causes may indeed experience a connection with humor, compassion, and so forth here;

therefore, for these [characters], the sentiment is not exclusively the Furious (raudra). Now, one might ask: how can there be a relish consisting of anger among the members of the audience (*sāmājika*) upon seeing such beings as Rākṣasas? It is said in reply:

The "taste" (*āsvāda*) consists in the resonance with one's own heart (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*). Furthermore, this resonance with the heart occurs only among spectators who possess a *tāmasa* (dark) nature; thus, there is nothing objectionable in the fact that those similar to Dānavas and others, having become identified with the [characters], experience the taste of anger directed toward wrongdoers.
"Distortion" (*vikṛtam*) refers to mutilation, such as causing a limb to be deformed and so forth. "Battle and the like" (*yuddhādi*) refers to what is being performed by another;

by this, it is stated that the anger of the enemy and so forth, which is inferred from the battle and other such acts, functions as the *vibhāva*. "Agitation for battle" (*saṅgrāmāya saṃbhramaḥ*) is the haste in seizing weapons.
He describes the majestic powers (*anubhāva*) with the word "various" (*nānā*). He demonstrates the predominance of the act of killing through various weapons.
By indicating the excess of wrath even in a dead body—such as by the decapitation of the head—he states the distinction from the heroic (*vīra*) [sentiment].
For that [wrath] does not exist even in the case of the martial hero (*yuddhavīra*), but here it does.
318) Now, the hero (*vīra*) is a superior character type whose essence is energy (*utsāha*).
He is characterized by freedom from delusion, resolve, policy, discipline, strength, valor, power, majesty, and influence.
It arises through these determinants (*vibhāva*).

Its representation (*abhinaya*) should be performed through its consequents (*anubhāva*), such as steadfastness, fortitude, heroism, renunciation, and self-confidence; and its transitory states (*bhāva*) are as follows:

Fortitude, intelligence, pride, impetuosity, ferocity, indignation, mindfulness, horripilation, and so forth. Regarding this noble theme—the introduction to the analysis of rasa—it will be stated: "of fierce deeds. Fierce deeds are those such as the decapitation [of enemies] which are characterized primarily by ferocity (*augrya*). Of these...
That action which is its own method is that of which the self is the primary element. The sage Bharata, however, concludes with a single verse: "Thus is the Furious Sentiment" (66).
Thus ends the section on the Furious Sentiment.

Now begins the section on the Heroic Sentiment (*vīrarasa*). He defines the Heroic, which follows in sequence: "(Now the Heroic... [The phrase] "the engagement in combat and striking" applies to the Furious (*raudra*) as well; thus, for the Heroic, it specifies "the desire not to kill. The word *atha* indicates immediate succession. It is the nature of superior beings.

Since enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is likewise so named; or rather, when employed in poetry and drama, it has a character of the highest order as its cause. For among those of the highest caste, enthusiasm is everywhere to be savored. It is for this very reason that heroism will be described as following along with all four types of heroes.

Regarding the passage beginning with "dhīrodātta" (the noble and self-controlled): although all people possess energy (*utsāha*), nevertheless, because that energy is directed toward improper objects, their conduct is not fit to be taught in poetry or drama. However, as for those whose conduct is worthy of instruction, the manifestation of their energy occurs only at its appropriate time.
Appropriateness (*ucitatva*) consists in the perfection of non-delusion and so forth at the proper occasion; thus, that very [perfection] is taught as the *vibhāva* (the determinant cause).
For determination through non-delusion is the ascertainment of the true nature of reality; thus, the power of the mantra (*mantra-śakti*) is demonstrated.
It is incorrect to claim that non-delusion regarding an unreal object—such as the enthusiasm found in Rāvaṇa and others—is the *vibhāva*, because it is not the meaning of the word [in this context].

In that case as well, the determinants (*vibhāva*) consist precisely of valor, policy (*naya*), and so forth. Policy (*naya*) is the correct application of the qualities such as diplomacy (*sandhi*). Discipline (*vinaya*) is the conquest of the senses. Force (*bala*) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
From enthusiasm, resolute effort, freedom from despondency, absence of wonder and delusion, and various specific objects, that which is called the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) arises. (67)

The heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) should be properly enacted through steadfastness, fortitude, vigor, and pride, as well as through enthusiasm, prowess, majesty, and speech that is full of challenge. 68.

*Parākrama* is the assault resulting from the invasion of another's territory and so forth; *śakti* is the capacity for battle and other such activities; *pratāpa* is the renown that causes distress among the enemies; and *prabhāva* is the excellence of one's lineage, wealth, and ministers. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), fame and other qualities are meant. And these—

The *vibhāvas* (determinants) possess a complete nature; therefore, it is incorrect to provide separate examples for each, suggesting that for the highest hero (*uttama-nāyaka*) some [determinant] might occasionally be additional. In reality, every life-story of Rāma and others serves as an example here.
Furthermore, when the success of the plot depends upon ministers—as is the case with a hero like the King of Vatsa—these [determinants] may also reside in the ministers, as appropriate.

These [qualities] are to be considered. Furthermore, since even those residing in the antagonist (*pratināyaka*) manifest energy (*utsāha*), the poet should conceive of their distinctions—whether taken individually or collectively—as appropriate to the context.
Steadfastness (*sthairya*) is the absence of wavering. Fortitude (*dhairya*) is the concealment [of emotion] produced by gravity (*gāmbhīrya*). Valor (*śaurya*)...

Action refers to activities such as warfare. Renunciation is giving. Confidence (*vaiśāradya*) is the application of the four means—conciliation and so forth—to their respective objects according to their divisions into one, two, three, four, and so on.

It is called "artha" because it is sought after (*arthyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The fourfold set beginning with Dharma is [the goal]. For it is precisely through the etymological derivation from action (*karman*) that...

Dharma and the others are called "human goals" (*puruṣārtha*) because they are sought after by the person. The diversity of these specific goals arises from the distinctions among dharma and the rest. Thus, the meaning is this: with reference to the various specific goals consisting of dharma and so forth, [the term is used] because of its non-contradictory nature.

The term *avismayāsaṃmoha* is a *dvandva* compound treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*). Because of the absence of astonishment (*avismaya*) and the absence of delusion (*asaṃmoha*), there arises a resolve (*adhyavasāya*), which is a certainty; and because it incites (*utsāhayati*)—derived from the causative form (*ṇijanta*) with the suffix *pacādyac* added—it is the cause of enthusiasm (*utsāha*). This is then a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "enthusiasm" (*utsāha*) and "resolve" (*adhyavasāya*).

This is what is meant: in times of adversity, the heart’s sinking, its being under the sway of others, despondency, contentment with even a little, and astonishment—having cast aside these three, namely delusion which is false knowledge—that very determination of reality is the primary cause of enthusiasm. However, in the case of the Furious (raudra) sentiment...
Because of the predominance of possessiveness (*mamatā*), even unscriptural and improper acts such as fighting may occur; thus, there is a predominance of delusion (*moha*) and wonder (*vismaya*).

And so, the enthusiasm (*utsāha*) that arises by means of a mental resolve (*adhyavasāya*) produced after first dispelling the triad beginning with despondency (*viṣāditva*) is what is called the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).

*Sthiti* is steadfastness; *vīrya* is heroism. By the word "pride" (*garva*), its outward manifestation is indicated. *Utsāha* is enthusiasm, which is the incitement of one who is weak or despondent, as in the *Setubandha-kāvya*. *Parākrama* is valor; it is the exertion of force, such as [the command]: "In this manner you must remain here, you must fight."
The "manifestation of power" (*prabhāvanā*) refers to the accomplishment of power through the performance of duties such as employment.

"Suggestion" (*ākṣepa*) is the indication of another matter; by means of this, those sentences which are made to have that [suggested matter] as their primary focus are described as having meanings that are profound and difficult to fathom. (68)
Thus ends the section on the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).
Now follows the so-called *bhayānaka* (the terrible), which consists of the transitory mental state (*sthāyibhāva*) of fear. And that—

It arises from determinants (*vibhāvas*) such as seeing beings making distorted sounds, the fear and agitation caused by jackals and owls, entering empty houses or forests, and witnessing or hearing accounts of the killing and binding of one's own kin.
Its [consequent] states (*anubhāvas*) are manifested through trembling of the hands, feet, and eyes; flickering; horripilation; discoloration of the face; and changes in the voice.
The enactment [of the drama] should be performed through the *bhāvas* (emotional states).
And its *bhāvas* are:

paralysis (*stambha*), perspiration (*sveda*), faltering voice (*gadgada*), horripilation (*romāñca*), trembling (*vepathu*), change of voice (*svarabheda*), change of color (*vaivarṇya*), apprehension (*śaṅkā*), delusion (*moha*), and dejection (*dainya*).
Haste, fickleness, dullness, terror, epilepsy, death, and so forth.
Here are the Āryā verses— now begins the section on the Frightful Sentiment (bhayānaka-rasa).
Because the limbs of the hero are primarily characterized by fear and its absence, he defines the *bhayānaka* (the terrible sentiment) with the word "atha" (*now*).
"Distorted sound" refers to things such as loud, mocking laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*). "The sight of beings" refers to the sight of *piśācas*. "Terror and agitation" are states occurring in others.
"Going to" means reaching an empty house or a forest. Regarding one's own kin...
For those two, "killing" and "binding" are perceived through direct observation; they are heard through traditional testimony (āgama);
and there is "recollection" through the reconnection with events long past. Furthermore, the very act of the hands and feet beginning to tremble is itself an indicator of fear.

This is because it indicates a distinction from [the causes of fear such as] disease and so forth. "Pulaka" is the bristling of the hair on the body. "Change of voice" (svarabheda) is a deviation from one's natural state.
Regarding the phrase "of the teacher and the king," the underlying intention is this: fear, for its part, will be described [as occurring] toward women, low-caste persons, children, and the like.

[This applies] to those of superior and middling natures. Even they (the superior and middling natures) should display feigned fear toward their teachers and the king. Even in the absence of such [actual] danger, their status as superior becomes even more pronounced, while the ministers' lack of authority is established. As it has been said:

"I am indeed afraid of one who acts according to his own whims" (Ratnāvalī 1.7). Furthermore, the *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions) are similarly associated there [with fear] due to the hearing of distorted sounds,
the sight of living beings, battle, wandering in the forest, and entering empty houses.
And that which is feigned due to an offense against the teacher or the king should be known as "terrifying. || 69 ||

Fear is recognized by changes in the body, face, and gaze; by stiffness of the thighs, staring, and agitation; and by a drooping face, dryness of the mouth, palpitations of the heart, and the bristling of the hair.
This should be performed as arising from one's own nature and likewise originating from one's disposition;
furthermore, by means of these very states, the task should be accomplished through gentle actions.
With trembling hands and feet, stiffness of the limbs, and a quivering heart, with parched lips, palate, and throat, one should always perform the terrifying [mudrā]. (72)
In this world, they are performed such that people truly perceive them with the thought, "This person is afraid," regarding elders and others.

Because they are not innate, they possess the quality of being produced (*kṛtakatva*); because they persist for a considerable length of time and are relished, they possess the quality of aesthetic flavor (*rasatva*).
Nor do they possess the quality of transience (*vyabhicāritva*), for that would only be the case if [the emotion] existed by its very nature.
For a brief moment,

there arises a transformation of the limbs and so forth— a reversal of color, action, configuration, and so on. The gaze, having strayed due to being overwhelmed by panic, becomes aimless and devoid of focus.
Agitation is trembling; depression is the drooping of the limbs; dryness in the palate of the mouth;
and the heart throbbing with excessive force. Here, "fear" is to be enacted; this is connected to the verse [beginning] "in the heroic sentiment" (*vīrarasa*).
Indeed, these noble verses were recited by the former teachers as a single continuous unit (ekapraghaṭṭaka) for the sake of defining their characteristics;
however, the Sage (Muni) has arranged them in their proper places for the sake of easy comprehension.
Regarding the phrase "arisen from courage" (sattvasamuttham): "courage" (sattva) refers to the concentration of the mind; that which is produced from it is this training of the actor.

And the commentator [Vallabha] maintains that this [rasa] pertains to all objects; however, this is incorrect. For this entire treatise is intended solely for the instruction of poets and actors, since in the world there is no such technical usage of *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *abhinayas*.
Therefore, the meaning here is as follows:
322) Now, that which is called *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) consists of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of disgust (*jugupsā*).
And it arises through excitants (*vibhāva*), such as hearing, seeing, or speaking of things that are unattractive, unpleasant, impure, or undesirable.

Thus, the performance of the dramatic representation of enmity should be executed through the contraction of all limbs, the contortion of the face, the spitting, the causing of agitation, and so forth.
And its manifestations include epilepsy, agitation, impetuosity, delusion, disease, death, and so forth.

Regarding this, there are two traditional verses (āryās): "This much, then, is for those of low birth—meaning those whose nature is characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*—who are born of such a disposition. As for those who...

And since those [characters] are dominated by *sattva* (goodness), their action—produced from *sattva* and performed with effort—must be enacted through these very *anubhāvas*, yet with gentle gestures, because it is artificial (*kṛtaka*). The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a distinction.
Now, why does the king and so forth display fear caused by teachers and others? Having displayed it...

Why does he display such gentle things as the trembling of the limbs? And why is artificiality mentioned specifically regarding the terrifying [sentiment]? For artificiality is said to apply to everything—for instance, a courtesan seeking wealth displays feigned passion. Anticipating this objection, he provides a general answer: "In the same way."

Regarding the word "body": for when fear is displayed, the teacher knows him to be disciplined; and because of his mild conduct, he does not consider him to be of inferior nature. Furthermore, no attainment of the human goals (puruṣārtha) results from the taught [practices] such as artificial passion and love. For it is by that very method which has been stated that the specific human goal of action is achieved.

It is obtained. However, where a king does not display artificial anger, wonder, and so forth for the sake of favoring others, there those emotions are merely transitory (*vyabhicārin*) and not permanent (*sthāyin*). To indicate this meaning, he recites an *āryā* verse well-known in another lineage of teachers, beginning with "hands and feet," and [the word] "always."
Whether it be produced or unproduced.
(72) Thus ends the section on the Furious Sentiment (*bhayānaka-rasa*).
Now begins the section on the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsarasa*).

He now characterizes the *bībhatsa-rasa* (the sentiment of disgust), which has reached its proper occasion, with the word "atha" (now). That which is unlovely (*ahṛdya*)—even if something is lovely, it may be naturally impure or unpleasant to someone, like garlic to the twice-born (*dvija*s); or unpleasant due to defects such as caste, like milk to one afflicted by phlegm; or unclean (*acokṣa*), even if not defective in its own nature.
"Defiled" means impaired by impurities and the like. "Unwanted" refers to that from which desire has ceased because it has been consumed incessantly.
"Destruction" (saṃhāra) means making into a lump; "of the mouth" implies the contraction of its parts. "Scraping" (ullekhana) means cleansing. "Spitting" (niṣṭhivana) is the expulsion of phlegm.
The sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsa-rasa*) arises through the sight of what is undesirable, through defects in odor, taste, touch, and sound, and through many causes of agitation. (73)
The *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) rasa is to be properly enacted by contorting the face and eyes, covering the nose, lowering the head, and performing indistinct prostrations at the feet. 74.
Now, the marvelous (*adbhuta*) rasa consists of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of wonder (*vismaya*).
