It arises from such determinants (*vibhāvas*) as the sight of divine beings, the fulfillment of desired longings, visiting gardens and temples, witnessing assemblies of the virtuous, and the perception of illusions, sorcery, and magical displays. Of this [rasa]...

The performance should be enacted through the following consequent expressions (*anubhāvas*): the expansion of the eyes, fixed gazing, horripilation, tears, perspiration, joy, shouts of "Well done!", the continuous offering of gifts, cries of "Hā hā!", and the waving of arms, faces, garments, fingers, and limbs. And its emotional states (*bhāvas*) are as follows:

Stiffness is the trembling of the limbs. Covering the nose is observed when there is a predominance of foul odors. Due to repulsion, there are indistinct falls of the feet; or [it occurs] when the ground is strewn with bones, skeletons, and the like.
As he wanders through the cemetery, there are uncrushed footprints—somewhere long, elsewhere short.
Thus ends the section on the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsa-rasa*).

Now begins the section on the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*). Since it has been stated that the marvelous occurs at the conclusion of all [sentiments], he says "now" (*atha*) in order to define it. "Divine beings" refers to Gandharvas and others.
"Desired" refers to an object that is capable of being attained; "other" refers to a wish (*manoratha*). The attainment of these two [is the marvelous]. [This occurs] in a grove or a temple.

Going; its nature as a marvelous manifestation is such that the arrangement of the lake and other features therein have never been seen anywhere else. A *sabhā* is a particular kind of hall. *Vimānas* and so forth are celestial chariots. *Māyā* consists of the transformation of forms and the like. *Indrajāla* refers to [the use of] spells and substances held in the hand.
324) Upon hearing [this], there arise choking of the voice, horripilation, agitation, bewilderment, fainting, and so forth.
Regarding this, there are two traditional verses (anuvaṃśya-āryā):

Any statement endowed with extraordinary meaning, as well as any craft or form of action, should all be understood as being of the nature of a determinative factor (*vibhāva*) within the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*). (75)

The representation of that [state] is performed through the seizing of contact, leaping up, cries of "Alas! Alas!", shouts of "Well done!", trembling, faltering speech, perspiration, and so forth. (76)

The demonstration of a thing that has never occurred before by means of reasoning and so forth; "of that" refers to that marvelous event. Here, the word "joy" (*harṣa*) denotes its consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*). "Saying 'well done'" (*sādhu*) is the expression of praise (*sādhuvāda*). "Giving" is the bestowing of wealth and the like. Having made a continuous series of sounds, one utters the cry "Hā hā! There is also the waving of garments and the twirling of fingers.

*Atiśaya* means "surpassing" (*atiśete*). It refers to an object that is superior in comparison to others. A sentence endowed with such a meaning as its expressed content (*vācya*), as well as a craft (*śilpa*)—meaning an action (*karman*) consisting of a praiseworthy deed (the suffix *-rūpa* is used here in the sense of praise)—all of this, in short, constitutes [the *atiśayokti*]. By the term "perception of touch" (*sparśagraha*), its *vibhāvas* and other [poetic elements] are implied.
The *abhinaya* (gesticulation) is characterized as follows:
having slightly contracted the eyes and raised the eyebrows,
one should likewise cast a touch by touching the shoulders and cheeks.
(Nā. Śā. 22.77). Thus:
"The shaking of the limbs with joy is *ullukasanam*. The plural number indicates a variety of types due to differences in their fundamental nature. (76)
Thus ends the section on the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*).

Now, by means of demonstrating its divisions, he explains the subordinate states (*bhāva*) that are consistent with the predominant determinants (*vibhāva*), beginning with the words "the erotic" (*śṛṅgāram*) and so forth. For in that context, the "fierce" (*raudra*) [sentiment] is indeed fierce by its very nature (*svabhāva-raudra*).
It will be discussed. Or, because it follows its own nature:
one should know that the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is threefold, consisting of speech, costume, and action. (p. 325)
The comic (hāsya) and the furious (raudra) rasas are each remembered as being threefold by means of gestures, dress, and speech. || 77 ||
Furthermore, that which arises from the destruction of dharma, as well as that produced by the loss of wealth, and likewise that caused by grief—compassion is thus remembered as being threefold. (78)

Brahmā has indeed declared that there are three types of heroes: the hero of generosity, the hero of righteousness, and likewise the hero of battle; he has also spoken of the hero of aesthetic flavor.

Of what [is it the cause]? It is born from the obstruction of *dharma*, for even among the highest [beings], it serves as a cause of beauty. By the word "sorrow" (*śoka*), the destruction of one's kinsmen and so forth is also included; these three are the *vibhāvas*. By the word "*dharma*," rituals such as the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice are meant.
Therefore, this sacrifice and so forth are not necessarily of the nature of an *anubhāva*. However, that which resides in the antagonist (*pratināyaka*)...

"Even in the form of a disguise" (*vibhāvarūpam api*). "By means of a pretext" (*vyājāt*) means "artificial. By this, the softness of the emotional response (*anubhāva-mārdavam*) is shown. "Those who offend" (*aparāddhāḥ*) refers to thieves and the like.
As for those whose hearts are naturally timid, such as women, children, and others, they feel fear even when a blade of grass trembles.
*Tadvitrāsitaka* (The Terrifying): One who is especially terrified is *vitrāsita*, such as a child and so forth.
Because it has that as its nature, the *bhayānaka* (the terrifying) is described in that way. The suffix *-kan* is added here to form a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
To claim that even for the most excellent persons there is an onset of fear in reality due to offenses against teachers and the like is incorrect; for fear is—
The nature of apprehension regarding destruction does not occur among the highest [beings]. Furthermore, fear is generally characterized as belonging to women and those of base nature.
That which is the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) arising from the sight of blood, entrails, and so forth, is "pure" (*śuddha*) because of its capacity to cause agitation. As for that which...
That which causes agitation toward excrement and the like, and makes the heart tremble, is impure; this is because it evokes the impure.

However, the Teacher says: "The *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) is of two kinds due to the distinction of its excitants (*vibhāva*). But that which serves as a means to liberation by acting as an antidote to passion—the protagonist of the drama of worldly existence—is pure."
As they say: "From grief comes self-disgust for one's own body," and likewise, "When discursive thoughts cause affliction, there is the cultivation of their opposites" (Yoga Sūtra 2.40, 33).
Therefore, even that [distraction] is ultimately of only three kinds. By the term "the second type," he indicates its rarity due to its difficulty of occurrence.
One should know that the *bhayānaka* (terrible) rasa is likewise of three kinds: arising from deceit, from an offense, and from being terrified. (80)
The loathsome (bībhatsa) rasa is pure when born from agitation; the second type is agitating.
That which is agitating arises from excrement and worms, while that born from blood and the like is born from agitation.
The marvelous rasa (adbhuta-rasa) is known to be twofold: that born of the divine and that born of bliss.
That which arises from a divine vision is called "divine," while that which arises from joy is considered "born of bliss. (82)
Now, that which is called *śānta* (the peaceful) consists of the stable emotion of tranquility (*śama*) and is the instigator of liberation.
It arises through determinants (*vibhāva*) such as knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and purity of disposition (*āśaya-śuddhi*).

Its indicators (*liṅga*) include the observances (*yama*), restraints (*niyama*), internal meditation (*adhyātma-dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), worship (*upāsana*), compassion for all beings (*sarvabhūta-dayā*), and the assumption of [auspicious] marks.

The dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) is called "divine" (*divya*) by virtue of its primary *anubhāvas*. In this context, the *anubhāvas* consist of the assembly hall, celestial palaces, and so forth. It is called "bliss" (*ānanda*) because it causes one to rejoice;
bliss (*ānanda*) refers to the attainment of one's heart's desires and the like. That very same state is called "joy" (*harṣa*) because it gladdens.

And in these verses beginning with "śṛṅgāram," the word *ca* (and) is used to dispel the suspicion that other excitants (*vibhāva*) or ensuants (*anubhāva*) might be excluded; the words *eva* (only/just) are for the purpose of showing that only these many [factors] are connected as being primary; and likewise the word *tathā*...
The phrase "for the purpose of inferring the unmentioned excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth" is to be applied as appropriate.
(82) Thus ends the section on the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*). Now follows the investigation of the tranquil sentiment (*śānta-rasa*).

Furthermore, according to those who recite "nine rasas," the nature of the *śānta* (the peaceful) is now described. Regarding this, some say: *Śānta* consists of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of tranquility (*śama*), and it arises through determinants (*vibhāvas*) such as asceticism and contact with yogis. Its representation is performed through consequents (*anubhāvas*) consisting of the absence of desire, anger, and so forth.
"The transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) are *dhṛti*, *mati*, and so forth"—this [definition] others do not accept, because *śama* and *śānti* are synonyms;
because it abandons the number [of fifty-three], stating that there are forty-nine states; and furthermore, because of the *vibhāvas*...
It is logical that seasonal flowers and the like are associated with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others which arise immediately thereafter;
however, asceticism, Vedic study, and so forth are not the immediate causes of the tranquil sentiment (*śānta*).

It should be employed. Its transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) include despondency, recollection, fortitude, all stages of life, purity, paralysis, horripilation, and so forth. On this subject, there are these noble verses (*āryā*) and *śloka*s:
Arising from liberation and the inner self, joined with the purpose and cause of the knowledge of reality,
and taught for the sake of the supreme good, there exists that which is called the flavor of tranquility (śāntarasa).

If it is argued that [austerity, study, and so forth] are the immediate causes of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), then they would have to be employed even for the knowledge of reality mentioned previously;

thus, the status of austerity, study, and so forth as *vibhāvas* (determinants) would be abandoned. Furthermore, the absence of desire and the like is not an *anubhāva* (consequent), because it does not exclude its opposite, namely, the state of being unpeaceful (*aśānta*).
Because it is non-informative and because it does not coexist with the performance [of an action]. Indeed, the cessation of activity is not suitable for performance;
for even sleep, fainting, and so forth, are experienced through activities such as breathing in and out, falling, and lying on the ground.

Furthermore, how could even one who possesses fortitude and enjoys sense objects be at peace? Nor are disciples instructed in the means for the knowledge of reality merely by [pointing out] its inefficacy. These [disciples], whose minds are pained by the suffering of others, are not seen to have attained the state of perfect vision. Moreover...
"But [this] is within saṃsāra; therefore, that is not the peaceful flavor.

To this it is replied: It is well known that just as the triad beginning with dharma exists here, so too liberation (mokṣa) is a human goal (puruṣārtha), and it is primarily explained through its means in the scriptures, such as the Smṛtis and Itihāsas.

And just as mental states such as love (*rati*) and others, which are habitually associated with objects like women, are denoted by words such as "love," they attain the status of *rasa*— as *śṛṅgāra* and so forth— for members of the audience who possess a corresponding resonance in their hearts, by means of being rendered fit for aesthetic relish through the activity of the poet and the actor.

It must be explained why the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) appropriate for the supreme human goal called liberation (*mokṣa*) is not likewise brought to the status of *rasa*. And that very mental state which is of such a nature is the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) here. However, this requires reflection: what indeed is it? Some say it is "disgust" (*nirveda*) arising from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). For instance: [The verse: "O King, you have conquered the earth; your enemies have been slain; your son has attained youth; your wife is devoted to you; yet, O Lord of the Earth, you are still unhappy. In this case, the mental state of disgust arising from the knowledge of reality is the permanent emotion. From that [permanent emotion], the *rasa* of tranquility (*śāntarasa*) arises. Therefore, it is established that the *rasa* of tranquility exists. Furthermore, it is said: "The *rasas* are nine, beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāvas*) are likewise nine, beginning with love (*rati*). This is stated by some. Others, however, say there are eight *rasas*, excluding the tranquil (*śānta*). This is because the tranquil is not mentioned among the *rasas* in the following passage: "The *rasas* are the erotic, the heroic, the comic, the odious, the pathetic, the furious, the terrible, and the marvelous. And because the tranquil is not included among the *sthāyibhāvas* in the following passage: "Love, mirth, resentment, grief, fear, disgust, wonder, and heroism are the eight permanent emotions. Therefore, they maintain that the tranquil is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, they argue that the tranquil cannot be a *rasa* because it lacks the necessary substratum (*āśraya*). For a *rasa* must have a substratum, whether it be a character (*nāyaka*) or a character in a drama (*nāṭakīyanāyaka*). Since the tranquil is devoid of passion (*vītarāga*), it cannot have either of these as its substratum. Moreover, the tranquil is not a *rasa* because it lacks the requisite transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*). For a *rasa* is produced through the combination of a permanent emotion, transitory emotions, and the like. Since the tranquil is free from all passions, it is devoid of transitory emotions and so forth. Consequently, it cannot be a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not mentioned in the authoritative texts (*śāstra*). For it is said: "The *rasas* are the erotic, the heroic, the comic, the odious, the pathetic, the furious, the terrible, and the marvelous. Since the tranquil is not mentioned therein, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not experienced by the audience (*sāmājika*). For a *rasa* is that which is tasted (*āsvādya*) by the audience through the power of suggestion (*vyañjanā*). Since the tranquil is free from passion, it is not tasted by the audience. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a source of aesthetic delight (*camatkāra*). For a *rasa* is defined as that which produces a unique, indescribable aesthetic delight. Since the tranquil is characterized by the cessation of all mental activity, it does not produce such delight. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a transformation of the mind (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*). For a *rasa* is a specific transformation of the mind. Since the tranquil is the cessation of all transformations of the mind, it is not a transformation of the mind. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of equilibrium (*samāveśa*). For a *rasa* is a state of intense absorption. Since the tranquil is a state of total detachment, it is not a state of absorption. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of expansion (*vikāsa*). For a *rasa* is a state of expansion of the consciousness. Since the tranquil is a state of contraction of the consciousness, it is not a state of expansion. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of relish (*carvaṇā*). For a *rasa* is that which is relished. Since the tranquil is the absence of all relish, it is not a state of relish. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of enjoyment (*bhoga*). For a *rasa* is that which is enjoyed. Since the tranquil is the cessation of all enjoyment, it is not a state of enjoyment. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of bliss (*ānanda*). For a *rasa* is a state of bliss. Since the tranquil is the cessation of all worldly pleasure, it is not a state of bliss. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of wonder (*camatkṛti*). For a *rasa* is a state of wonder. Since the tranquil is a state of indifference, it is not a state of wonder. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of aesthetic experience (*rasanā*). For a *rasa* is that which is experienced aesthetically. Since the tranquil is beyond all experience, it is not an aesthetic experience. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of emotional resonance (*saṃvāda*). For a *rasa* is that which resonates with the spectator's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Since the tranquil is devoid of all latent impressions, it does not resonate. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of identification (*tanmayībhāva*). For a *rasa* is that which leads to identification with the dramatic situation. Since the tranquil is a state of withdrawal from all objects, it does not lead to identification. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of expansion of the heart (*hṛdayapravistāra*). For a *rasa* is that which expands the heart. Since the tranquil is a state of contraction of the heart, it does not expand it. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of overflowing joy (*ullāsa*). For a *rasa* is a state of overflowing joy. Since the tranquil is a state of total quiescence, it is not overflowing joy. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of radiance (*prakāśa*). For a *rasa* is a state of radiance. Since the tranquil is a state of darkness (*tamas*), it is not radiance. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of manifestation (*abhivyakti*). For a *rasa* is that which is manifested. Since the tranquil is unmanifest, it is not a manifestation. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of relishable flavor (*rasanīyatva*). For a *rasa* is that which is relishable. Since the tranquil is tasteless (*nīrasa*), it is not relishable. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of aesthetic satisfaction (*tṛpti*). For a *rasa* is that which satisfies. Since the tranquil is the cessation of all desires, it does not satisfy. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of aesthetic transport (*vismaya*). For a *rasa* is a state of transport. Since the tranquil is a state of indifference, it is not transport. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore, it is not a *rasa* because it is not a state of aesthetic rapture (*āhlāda*). For a *rasa* is a state of rapture. Since the tranquil is the absence of all rapture, it is not rapture. Therefore, it is not a *rasa*. Furthermore

The despondency (*nirveda*) that arises from poverty and the like is entirely different from this [despondency arising from *tattvajñāna*], because of the difference in their causes. It is for this very reason that it is recited among the permanent (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*sañcārin*) emotions; otherwise, the auspicious Sage would not have recited it there. Furthermore, he would not have included loathing (*jugupsā*) as a transitory emotion within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

The Sage, while negating all [transient] states (bhāvas), nevertheless permits their status as states— whether as permanent emotions (sthāyibhāvas), transitory moods (vyabhicāribhāvas), those grasped by the mind, or those existing as consequents (anubhāvas)— as they are brought forth by the power of words and meanings through the force of their inherent fitness.
And the detachment born from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the sublater of other stable emotions (*sthāyin*).

For that which is the supreme stable emotion among passion (*rati*) and the rest—capable of enduring the diversity of emotional states—is indeed the sublater of other stable emotions. This too [is so].
One who is endowed with internal composure through the restraint of the faculties of cognition and action,
and who is devoted to the welfare and happiness of all living beings, is to be known as the "Flavor of Tranquility" (śāntarasa).
Where there is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither hatred nor even envy, but equanimity toward all beings— that is the celebrated flavor of peace.

The *bhāvas* (emotional states) are modifications such as love (*rati*) and so forth, while the *śānta* (the peaceful) is considered the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*). They raise this objection: "If it is said that detachment (*nirveda*) born from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is its stable emotion (*sthāyin*), then the knowledge of reality itself must be stated here as the determinant cause (*vibhāva*). How [then] could there be detachment in the presence of seeds for passion and the like?"

[If it is argued that] it possesses the nature of a *vibhāva* because it is a means (*upāya*) [to that], then this designation of "vibhāva" would apply to the cause of the cause; and that leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, what is called *nirveda* is the cognition that nothing is to be grasped anywhere, and it is characterized by dispassion (*vairāgya*).

And that [vairāgya] is useful for the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). For one who is dispassionate (*virakta*) strives in such a way that the knowledge of reality arises for him;

for liberation comes from the knowledge of reality. It is not the case that one becomes disenchanted after knowing reality, and from disenchantment comes liberation. Rather, from dispassion comes dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*). Thus it is said there by the venerable ones (in the *Iṣṭasiddhi-kārikā*).
*Sāṃkhyakārikā* 45):
Now, it is observed that one who possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*) exhibits a far more firm dispassion (*vairāgya*) in all circumstances.
This has also been stated by your honors: "That supreme dispassion toward the *guṇas* arises from the discernment of the *puruṣa*" (*Yogasūtra* 1.16).

(1-16) "It is indeed so; but such dispassion (*vairāgya*) is merely the supreme limit of knowledge. Thus it was declared by the Lord Himself, the Master of the Serpents (*bhujaṅgavibhu*). Consequently, this is simply the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is being nourished by the substrate of the knowledge of reality; therefore, there is no cause for world-weariness (*nirveda*).
[The opponent says: "It is permanent. [The author replies: But it must be the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone that is permanent.

As for what will be stated during the explanation of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), that is intended to remove the sense of acceptability in one who has been deceived by long-standing delusion. As for that which is correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)—
For example: "The cow, though her udders droop with the weight of milk, has yielded its milk in vain; the eunuch is embraced by a young woman, yet he is devoid of beauty."
"I, a fool, have placed my hope in a piece of glass with shimmering rays, mistaking it for lapis lazuli, while bowing down to you—a wretched man who knows nothing of virtue.
A modification born from primordial nature dissolves back into that very same source.
Having encountered its respective cause, the tranquil state arises;
and when that cause ceases, it dissolves back into the tranquil state itself.

Thus, the nine rasas have been observed by those learned in drama as endowed with their defining characteristics. Among them, [the rasa of] nirveda, which consists of weariness, serves as a *vibhāva* (excitant). We shall explain this very point in that same context.
Now, one might object: "The scent of sense-objects, which is rooted in false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), is pacified through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)."

In the *Duḥkha-janma-sūtra*, the venerable Akṣapāda stated that the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) is the cause for the diminution of false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*), and that it is the cause of detachment (*vairāgya*), which is characterized by the removal of defects (*doṣa*). But what follows from this?
Is detachment not indeed disillusionment (*nirveda*)? Who says so? For disillusionment is...
It is a specific modification of the mind characterized by the outward flow of a stream of sorrow. Detachment (*vairāgya*), however, is the complete destruction of passion and the like.
Or, let it be that detachment itself is despondency (*nirveda*); nevertheless, of that—

The Teacher has not established that even those factors existing in the middle [stage], by virtue of their own causes, serve as the "sūtra-like" (foundational) means for achieving liberation. Furthermore, the statement "disgust arises from the knowledge of reality" would merely be a renaming of *śama* (tranquility) as *nirveda* (disgust). Nor should one suspect that *śama* and *śānti* are synonyms.

Because there is a distinction between *hāsa* (laughter) and *hāsya* (the comic) in terms of being established (*siddha*) versus that which is to be established (*sādhya*), worldly versus non-worldly, and common versus uncommon; the same applies easily to *śama* (tranquility) and *śānta* (the peaceful).
Therefore, *nirveda* (disgust/disillusionment) is not the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*).

Others consider that only the eight mental fluctuations, beginning with love (*rati*), have been mentioned; these very same [fluctuations] become truly manifold when they rely upon specific extraordinary *vibhāvas* such as hearing [the poem], which are distinct from the previously described *vibhāvas*. Consequently, one among those very [fluctuations] is the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) in this context.

In this context, the very delight (*rati*) whose object is one's own self—which consists of bliss and is unimpeded—is the means to liberation; therefore, that alone is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of "delight" (*rati*) in the scripture. As it has been said:
"The person who finds delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self..."
"And for one who is content in the Self alone, there is no duty to be performed" (Gītā 3.17).
Thus, for one who perceives the entire universe as a mere transformation, who beholds the world as something to be pitied, and who views all worldly affairs as detrimental;
For one who relies on an extraordinary vigor characterized primarily by non-delusion,

who fears all objects of sense, and who feels revulsion even for things such as young women that are coveted by the whole world— [this occurs] due to the attainment of an unprecedented excellence of the self.

330) "Liberation is achieved through wonder. [In this view,] one of the states beginning with love and laughter and ending with wonder must be established as the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). However, this is not approved by the Sage (Bharata). For, as long as only those who are distinguished...
When one enumerates the mental states (bhāvas) by means of terms such as "love" (*rati*) and so forth, and includes their specific varieties, one thereby necessarily allows that love and the rest—
when produced by extraordinary causes distinct from those [ordinary ones]—
have liberation (*apavarga*) as their object. However, for those who speak in this manner, there is mutual contradiction.

The stability of that which is subject to disintegration is itself destroyed. Even the claim that its stability is maintained through various means is refuted; for if there were a difference in the stable substrates (*sthāyin*), it would follow that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is infinite, as it would vary with every individual. If it is argued that there is only one flavor because liberation is its sole fruit, [we reply] that this applies only if the fruit is non-perishable. If the fruit were perishable...

There would also be a unity between the heroic (*vīra*) and the furious (*raudra*). Others, however, say that all these permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāvas*), beginning with love (*rati*), reach a state of non-distinction here, like the flavor of a mixed beverage (*pānakarasa*). This too is not pleasing, because mental states do not exist simultaneously and because they are mutually contradictory.

What, then, is the permanent factor here? It is said: since, in this system, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone is the means to liberation, it is logical that this very knowledge possesses permanence in liberation. And what is called the "knowledge of reality" is precisely the knowledge of the self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, is not the knowledge of this [self] non-different from the self itself? [The opponent asks: Is there another...?
In this way, the Self would indeed become non-Self. This has been elaborated upon by our teachers, and we shall expand upon it elsewhere; therefore, no excessive insistence is made here.
Consequently, it is the Self alone—endowed with pure attributes such as knowledge and bliss, and free from the taint of imagined objects—that is [the subject] here.

It is the permanent (sthāyin). Nor should its non-permanence be asserted on account of its being permanent; for love and the other [emotions], whose functions arise and perish as various distinct causes emerge and dissolve, remain for some time in a relatively stable form, resting upon the foundation of the self. These six—[love, laughter, sorrow, anger, fear, and disgust]—are the permanent emotions.

These are called the permanent emotions (*sthāyins*). However, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which serves as the foundation for all other internal states, is the most permanent of all permanent emotions;
it naturally causes all mental fluctuations such as love (*rati*) and the rest to become transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*).

By the statement of the Tantra, "the established state" (*siddhasthāyibhāva*), its separate enumeration is not appropriate. For one does not count a third "cowness" between a hornless cow and a horned cow.
Therefore, the number of fifty minus one (forty-nine) states remains entirely uncontradicted.

If it is asked why this [rasa] is not counted separately—our reply is that it is because it cannot be tasted separately. For, unlike *rati* and the other [transitory emotions], its own nature in such a state does not come within the range of worldly perception in a form unmixed with the others; even when it is internal, it is of a non-conceptual nature.
When reflected upon at the moment of emergence, it appears as nothing but defiled by other mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*).

Or let it appear so in the world; nevertheless, those that exist merely as possibilities are not counted among the [permanent] emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), because they would serve no purpose once the [eight] *rasas* have been defined. Rather, it is understood that they are not to be defined [as *sthāyibhāvas*] precisely because they are transitory (*vyabhicārin*) states.
For thus is established the validity of this section [of the text]: "by forty-nine states" (*bhāva*).
Nor can there be any deviation from this essential nature of the self, because such deviation is impossible, as it would fail to produce variety and would be improper. *Śama*.

That which is the self-nature [of phenomena] has been designated by the Sage with the word "tranquility" (śama). If, however, that very same thing is designated by the word "tranquility," it is also designated by the word "disenchantment" (nirveda).

Or rather, there is no contradiction therein; for tranquility (*śama*) is merely another mental state (*cittavṛtti*). Even despondency (*nirveda*) does not belong to the same category as the despondency arising from other determinants (*vibhāva*) such as poverty; it belongs to that very same category.
Even when the causes differ, it is still designated by that [same name], just like love (*rati*), fear (*bhaya*), and so forth.

This very knowledge of reality is tranquility (*śama*) within the very nature of the self (*ātman*). Thus, attachment and the other emotions are merely specific stains of impurity upon the self. Even while those [emotions] persist, by resting in its pure form through the power of uninterrupted meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one attains a state of profound peace even during the period of post-meditative activity (*vyutthāna*).
As it has been said: "From the [accumulation of] latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is a flow of tranquility" (Yogasūtra 3.10).

And for this stable state characterized by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), this entire collection of worldly and transcendental mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) becomes merely a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*). Furthermore, those very [fluctuations], when assisted by the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, become the determinants (*anubhāva*).

Furthermore, those natural expressions (*svabhāvābhinaya*) which will be described in the three chapters beginning with the *Upāṅgābhinaya* are likewise restricted to this very subject; for this alone is the "natural state" (*svabhāva*). As for the determinants (*vibhāva*), how could things such as the grace of the Lord (*īśvarānugraha*) and the like, as well as the emotions (*rasa*) such as love (*rati*) when they are on the verge of subsiding, be the objects of aesthetic relish (*āsvādya*) here?

It is solely because, as in the case of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), there is longing (*autsukya*), and even in *saṃbhoga* (union), there is love whose festival remains unfulfilled (*Tāpasavatsarāja* 1.17); and as in the case of *raudra* (the furious), there is ferocity (*augrya*);
and as in the cases of *karuṇa*, *vīra*, *bhayānaka*, and *adbhuta*, there are the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of despondency, fortitude, terror, and joy.
In that same way, loathing and so forth manifest predominantly in the state of tranquility (*śānta*), because they are in every respect the antidotes to passion (*rāga*).
For instance, there is the wearing of human skulls and other such items during the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*), which involves association with impure women and the like.
For the performance of acts such as expansion and contraction serves as a cause for revulsion toward worldly phenomena (*dharma*).
Anointing oneself with oil, [the story of] Devarāta, and the birth of a son have been taught [as examples].
Furthermore, for one who has accomplished his own purpose, effort is directed solely toward the accomplishment of the welfare of others; this is his *utsāha* (enthusiasm).

The internal [heroism] is superior, consisting of desire and effort directed toward the welfare of others, and is synonymous with compassion (*dayā*). For this very reason— due to the power of its concomitant factors— some designate it as the "heroism of compassion" (*dayāvīra*), while others designate it as the "heroism of dharma" (*dharmavīra*).
Now, enthusiasm has *ahaṅkāra* (ego) as its life-force, whereas tranquility consists in the loosening of *ahaṅkāra*.
It is not improper for even contradictory states to function as transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), just as *nirveda* (disgust) and others are appropriate in the context of love (*rati*).
[The poet describes: "The bed is a grassy meadow; the seat is a pure rock; the home is beneath the trees."
The water of mountain torrents is cool for drinking, roots are the food, and deer are the companions;
thus, in this forest where all things are obtainable without being sought, there is only this one drawback:
that one dwells in vain among those who are barren in their efforts to accomplish the welfare of others, while those in need are difficult to find. (Nāgānanda 4.2)
For in such passages (p.
it is precisely the excellence of enthusiasm (*utsāha*) that is observed in performing service for others, and not [a state] devoid of enthusiasm.
There is no state whatsoever that does not involve desire and effort, for otherwise one would fall into the condition of being like a stone.
Precisely because there remains no other duty to be performed with reference to one's own self once the higher and lower goals have been fully perceived,
it is therefore not contrary to the scriptures for those whose hearts are peaceful to give away their bodies, all their possessions, and so forth for the sake of helping others.

For by the passage beginning with "One should protect oneself" (Gautama Dharmasūtra 9.35), the protection of the body is taught as pertaining to those who have not yet accomplished their purpose; this is because renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) lack any intent toward such protection. Thus it is said:
"The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are the cause for the maintenance of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa."
"By slaying them, what has not been slain? By protecting them, what has not been protected? (Hitopadeśa 1.83).
Thus, it is shown that the very means for accomplishing the four aims of human life (caturvarga) is the primary reason for protecting the body.
This is because it is heard in the context of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) that one who has fulfilled his duties may fall into water, fire, or a pit.

In whatever manner this body must eventually be relinquished, if it is sacrificed for the sake of others, what could possibly remain unaccomplished? If you argue that Jīmūtavāhana and others were not true *yatis* (ascetics), what does that matter to us?
They certainly possessed the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Otherwise, for those who identify the self with the body, the body itself [would be their only concern].

For it is impossible to renounce everything for the sake of others without aiming at dharma and other such goals; even in battle, a hero does not exert himself merely for the sake of abandoning his body, since he engages in it solely with the aim of defeating the enemy.
Even in cases such as leaping from a cliff, it is the desire to attain another, more auspicious body that manifests most prominently.
Whatever they have performed for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others— without aiming for their own self-interest—

from the giving of instruction up to the ultimate sacrifice of the body, all that would be utterly impossible for those who have not attained knowledge of the reality of the Self; therefore, they too are knowers of reality.
"For the wise, liberation exists in all stages of life (*āśrama*)," so it is stated in the Smṛtis and in the Śruti. As it has been said:

"One devoted to the worship of the gods, established in the knowledge of reality, fond of guests, and who, having performed the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), bestows wealth—even such a householder is indeed liberated."

For Bodhisattvas and others, the manifestation of a body suited to that very purpose occurs once again solely from the Dharma born of the intention for the welfare of others, which is intended as having the fruit of benefiting others.

Even for those who possess knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*), a state of repose is observed even within the subordinate elements (*aṅga*) due to the natural fitness of their disposition. For example, in the case of Rāma, while fulfilling his father’s command, this repose was found even within the heroic element (*vīrāṅga*). The same should be understood regarding the subordinate elements of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other sentiments. For this very reason, although tranquility (*śānta*) is a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), it lacks primacy [in dramatic representation]. As in the case of Jīmūtavāhana...

This is because the attainment of the *trivarga* itself is the fruit of that which is primarily devoted to the service of others. With this very intention, it will be stated in the definition of the *nāṭaka*: "by means of qualities such as prosperity (*ṛddhi*) and elegance (*vilāsa*)" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 18.11). For by this [definition], the entire course of action, characterized primarily by prosperity and elegance, culminates in the goals of wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*).
It has been stated that the purpose of a drama must be one that is beautiful because it resonates with the hearts of all people;
we shall describe this very point in that same place.

And with this very intention, it was stated by the Sage that "no one shall be employed as a *jātyaṅgaka* in a peaceful [state]" (*Nāṭyaśāstra* 29.1–4). Therefore, the argument that its non-existence follows from the absence of employment as a *jātyaṅgaka* has been refuted.
Others, however, cite: "O Jīmūtavāhana, who will be your protector, your son? (*Nāgānanda* 4.9).

He protected an old woman who was seeking refuge; yet they say that he possessed no power whatsoever and committed no violence against others. And this is indeed approved [or: this is indeed consistent], for the life of Bodhisattvas does not consist of a mere resuscitation nor is it entered into with a specific intent.

The power (śakti) impels [the teaching], and the scripture does not teach by way of mere chance (kākatālīya). Thus it is established that here, enthusiasm characterized by compassion is the primary factor;
the others, however, are transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) as they appropriately occur. As it has been said: "In its gaps..."

"Other conditions [arise] from the latent impressions" (Yoga Sūtra 4.27). For this very reason, the objection that there is an absence of aesthetic experience (*anubhāva*) due to the lack of physical activity is refuted. However, when there is an absence of aesthetic experience upon reaching the final stage, then it is not brought about by effort; this applies even in cases such as love (*rati*) or grief (*śoka*).

Because non-application alone is appropriate at the final stage, even the "correspondence with the heart" occurs for those who have been cultivated by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the seeds of such knowledge of reality. As he will say:
"And even regarding liberation, for one who is dispassionate... (Nāṭyaśāstra 27.58). It is not the case that everyone has a correspondence with the heart in every respect.
Because there is an absence of the heroic nature (*vīraprakṛti*) in what is terrifying.

[Objection: But in such a performance, what is the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) for the hero? [Response: It is said—in whatever [work] this [heroism] is composed, there must necessarily be one or another of the sentiments (*rasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) or the heroic (*vīra*), which is conducive to human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

The aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) for them is centered upon that [primary rasa]. Even in cases such as the comic play (*prahasana*), where humor and the like are predominant, the relish is nonetheless centered upon another rasa that is produced as a secondary consequence.
Some maintain that the very purpose of considering the different types of dramatic forms (*rūpaka*) is based on the aim of providing distinct aesthetic relishes for different classes of spectators.

Therefore, the *śānta* (peaceful) rasa exists. Accordingly, in ancient manuscripts, after the passage stating, "We shall bring the permanent moods (*sthāyibhāva*) to the state of rasa" (*Nāṭyaśāstra*, p. 299), the definition of the *śānta* is recited as, "The *śānta* is that which consists of the permanent mood of tranquility (*śama*)" (*Nāṭyaśāstra*, p. 332), and so forth.

In that state, the taste of all flavors is essentially quiescent because of the turning away from sense objects and the attainment of inwardness; it is merely conditioned by other latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
This is stated first in order to designate it as the "universal source" (*sarvaprakṛti*). And in the world:
Since there is no separate enumeration of each individual universal (*sāmānya*), the *sthāyin* (the permanent emotion) is not mentioned separately;

however, because even a universal must be enumerated separately by the discerning critic (*vivecaka*), it remains distinct as the object of the realization characterized by the aesthetic relish (*rasāsvāda*) of the audience intended by that discernment.
Furthermore, nine rasas are heard of in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, lexicons, and so forth, as well as in the venerable Siddhānta scriptures. And thus it has been said:
In this [mandala], one should display the erotic and other [rasas] of the eight deities;
and in the center, one should fashion the peaceful form of the God of Gods. Its determinants (*vibhāva*) are detachment, fear of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and so forth; for he is indeed...
Through these [emotions] thus expressed, it is understood that the contemplation of the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) and so forth are the *anubhāvas* (consequents);

while detachment (*nirveda*), intelligence (*mati*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and so forth are the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory states). For this very reason, devotion (*bhakti*) and faith (*śraddhā*) are present in relation to the object of devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*).

Because [the factors] such as mindfulness, intelligence, fortitude, and enthusiasm have entered into [the other limbs] in a different manner, they are not counted as separate *rasas* (flavors). Here is the summary verse (*saṅgrahakārikā*):
"It is connected with the cause for the purpose of knowledge of reality, which has liberation and the inner self as its objective."
That which is endowed with the dharma of the highest good (niḥśreyasa) is to be known by the name "the sentiment of tranquility" (śāntarasa).
The conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*), and the consequents (*anubhāva*) has been shown by the three qualifiers in their respective order.
Having encountered its own respective cause, the emotion (*bhāva*) proceeds;
but when that cause ceases, it dissolves back into the state of quiescence.
By these and other such statements, the fact that [the *ḍima*] has other *rasas* as its constituent nature is concluded.

As for the statement that will be made later—that in the *ḍima* there are six *rasas* excluding the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the comic (*hāsya*), or rather, by the exclusion of the comic and the erotic—the intention there is this: [it is so stated] because of the forthcoming rule, "The source of a drama is a poetic work characterized by intense *rasas*" (Nāṭyaśāstra 18.85).

First, regarding a *vaṭṭima* (a type of dramatic composition) in which the fierce (*raudra*) sentiment predominates by definition, there is not even the possibility of the existence of its opposite, the peaceful (*śānta*) sentiment;

what, then, is the point of its exclusion? But if the peaceful sentiment were impossible, what would be excluded by the statement that [the *vaṭṭima*] "is the source for poetry characterized by the intense (*dīpta*) sentiments" (Nāṭyaśāstra 18.84)? For it has been stated: "Excluding the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the comic (*hāsya*), it is endowed with six sentiments. (Nāṭyaśāstra 18.84).

What is the relevance here? Is it not the case that the predominance of the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) sentiments is excluded by this quarter [of the verse]? No, that is not so;
for that has already been ruled out by the statement "endowed with the *sāttvatī* and *ārabhaṭī* styles" (18.88). However, in the case of the peaceful (*śānta*) sentiment...

The statement "the path belongs only to the *sāttvika* [nature]" is merely intended to exclude that [other possibility]. Therefore, the definition of *ḍima*, on the contrary, is a sign of the presence of the *śānta-rasa* (the peaceful sentiment). As for *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment), it is certainly to be expected when being intensely cultivated;
and since *hāsya* (the comic) is its subordinate element (*aṅga*), the prohibition was made specifically against those two, as they were already applicable. That...

Furthermore, because of its total similarity [to other rasas], it should be understood that the specific designation of this [śānta] as having a deity and a caste (varṇa) is improper, yet it has been so postulated.
Its origin, however, has already been shown even for the śānta. For the absence of *sattva* is laughable (*hāsya*).
And because of its co-existence with the *vibhāvas*, the *vīra* and *bībhatsa* [rasas] belong to it. Precisely for this reason, of this rasa—

The instruction regarding the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and devotion to the Lord (īśvara-praṇidhāna), as well as its great fruitfulness due to being unexhausted [by worldly enjoyment], its supreme primacy, and its pervasiveness over all that has occurred, are thus established; enough with this digression.
What is the nature of the savoring of reality (tattvāsvāda) for this? It is said:

The very nature of the Self, when colored by enthusiasm, passion, and so forth—which impart their own hue—is that same nature which appears like a brilliantly white thread shining through the intervals between gems set at sparse distances.
Thus these eight rasas are to be known as characterized by their defining marks;
hereafter, I shall also declare the definition of the bhāvas.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on Rasa, in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.

Even while all coloring factors such as passion (*rati*) and the rest are present, this Self shines forth by the principle that "it has shone once and for all"; thus, through the application of poetic compositions and their continuous practice, it manifests as a single consciousness consisting of the attainment of supreme bliss, free from the state of being directed toward others and devoid of the entire web of one's own suffering.
Manifesting in a common manner, it establishes such a heart as a mass of supramundane bliss through the distinction of its inward-turned state;
thus, there are exactly nine rasas, either by virtue of their utility for human goals or due to their excellence in delighting the soul.

This is because only this many [rasas] are fit to be taught. Therefore, the claim made by others—that even though other rasas may exist, their number is fixed due to traditional consensus (*pārṣadaprasiddhi*)—is refuted. This will also be stated in the chapter on *bhāva*. Furthermore, the assertion that "the rasa called *sneha* (affection) has *ārdratā* (moistness/tenderness) as its *sthāyibhāva*" is incorrect; for *sneha* is indeed attachment (*abhiṣaṅga*), and that...

Everything culminates precisely in pleasure (*rati*), enthusiasm (*utsāha*), and so forth. To illustrate: a child’s affection for his mother, father, and others rests upon [the protection from] fear; that of a youth for his friends rests upon pleasure; the affection of Lakṣmaṇa and others for their brother rests upon the heroic sentiment of righteousness (*dharmavīra*) alone;
and in the same way, it should be understood that an elder’s affection for his son and so on [rests upon the same]. This very [principle] applies to one whose dominant emotion is greed (*gardha*).

In the rejection of the flavor of greed (*laulyarasa*), one must consider the recourse (*saraṇi*) [to another], because it culminates either in laughter or in pleasure elsewhere. The same should be stated regarding the speaker as well.
Concluding the meaning of the chapter while providing space for what is to come, he states the connection (*saṅgati*).
To make this clear, he says: "Thus these rasas are to be known as nine" (though some say eight).

They are praised by such designations as "the song is *rasavat*," and so forth. He shows that these [qualities] are merely figurative applications based on the very root of the *rasas* themselves—namely, that they are "characterized by their defining marks. The definition of the *bhāvas* is also simply the definition of the *rasas*.
It fulfills [the definition]. It is precisely the definition of rasa that is fulfilled by means of the determinants (*vibhāva*), transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), and consequents (*anubhāva*).

Even though it has been stated that [rasa] originates from the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*rati*), has seasonal flowers and garlands as its determinants, and has the cleverness of the eyes and so forth as its consequents, this remains incomplete. For what kind of love is it? What is the determinant? And what is the consequent?
Therefore, although this definition of the *bhāvas* appears at first glance to belong to the Great Teacher [Bharata] due to their association (*sāhacaryāt*),
nevertheless, by virtue of the syntactic unity of the entire passage, the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that this is indeed the definition of *rasa*.
May there be auspiciousness!

By him whose mental activity is centered within the eightfold powers beginning with *īra*, and who has established Śiva as the permanent resident in his heart through the application of his own heart-mandala, this treatise on rasa has been composed here in due order.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on Rasa, in the Abhinavabhārati, a commentary on the Nāṭyaveda composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Abhinavagupta.
Śrī. Now begins the seventh chapter.
We shall now explain the factors (bhāva). Here it is asked: why are they called "factors" (bhāva)? What...
They are called *bhāvas* because they come into being (*bhavanti*), or alternatively, they are called *bhāvas* because they bring something into being (*bhāvayanti*). It is said:
they are called *bhāvas* because they bring into being the meanings of poetry, which are endowed with speech, gesture, and the inner state of being (*sattva*).
The permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) is awakened in the heart and becomes a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*).

May the glorious Three-eyed One, of great majesty, whose form consists of pure aesthetic flavor (rasa) alone and who is the object of internal contemplation, be gracious of heart toward me amidst people agitated by desires.

Regarding the phrase "Now, as for the states of being" (*bhāvānidānīm*): one might ask, "Since this was already aphorized at the very end of the previous chapter, what is the purpose of this repetition?

Furthermore, since the question 'And how are the states of being described? (*bhāvāścāpi kathaṃ proktāḥ*) was already posed there, why is it stated again here in this chapter, 'What do they become? (*kiṃ bhavanti*) and so forth? [This is the objection.]

Regarding this, some say: at the beginning of the chapter, "The entities as well," and at the end of the chapter, "The definition of the entities as well," there is a general inquiry and formal proposition concerning all [the factors], such as the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth;
however, now that the excitants and others are to be discussed, first—

Since they are predominant, the permanent (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*vyabhicārin*) mental states, which take the form of fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*), must be defined; therefore, this proposition and inquiry concern them alone.
We, however, say: by the word *bhāva*, specifically particular fluctuations of the mind are intended. Likewise...
In the passage beginning with "and by forty-nine states," he will summarize those very [states] later on.

However, by virtue of their suitability, they can respectively take the form of the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), the transitory emotions (*saṃcārībhāva*), the determinants (*vibhāva*), or the consequents (*anubhāva*).
As for these external determinants such as seasons and garlands, and the external consequents such as tears and so forth—
Those things whose nature is exclusively inert are not to be designated by the word "existence" (bhāva).
But surely, because they immerse themselves in the nature of the consciousness of aesthetic relish (rasa) and likewise emerge from it, they too are essentially consciousness.
If that were so, then the entire universe would consist of existence (bhāvamaya) by way of metaphorical designation.

Alternatively, because they are based on the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*), the separate existence of the *abhinaya*, *dharmya*, and so forth is untenable. Therefore, the *bhāvas* consist solely of the stable (*sthāyin*), the transitory (*vyabhicārin*), and the involuntary (*sāttvika*).
We shall also explain the incidental definition of the *vibhāvas* and *anubhāvas*.

As for the objection regarding redundancy that was raised—that since the *bhāvas* were not mentioned among the *aṅgas* at the beginning of the chapter on *rasas*, how is it that they are mentioned here and there?—that is incorrect. For it is as follows: [the *bhāvas* were not mentioned] because they were not yet indicated among the *aṅgas* at the start of the chapter on *rasas*.

To refute that [objection], he says: "the emotions" (*bhāvān*). Since at the end of the previous chapter the definition of emotions was indeed the definition of rasa, therefore now, on this occasion when the points of contention have been resolved, we shall speak of the emotions because they are recited among the constituents (*aṅga*) of the rasas.

Now, if entities are indeed of the nature of mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), then two derivations of the term *bhāva* are possible in their case. For instance, the root *bhū* signifies "the manifestation of what was previously non-existent" (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*), and it also signifies "reaching excellence" (*prakarṣagati*) due to its repeated mention [in grammatical treatises]. Therefore, those [entities] which manifest internally as something entirely new and do not persist for even a moment—[from these...]

The *bhāvas* consist of the activity of the mind (*cittavṛtti*), because they exist for only a limited duration within the knowledge of aesthetic experience (*anubhāva*). Alternatively, they are so called because they "cultivate" (*bhāvayanti*)—that is, they produce relish or pervade the heart. Thus, since there are two possible etymologies, one need not even entertain the doubt as to how they come to be; or rather, what are they?

With the intention that the question "they cultivate" (*bhāvayanti*) is improper, [the author] restates the very meaning of the question while disclosing its underlying sense—which had not yet been made explicit—beginning with "What do they become? and so forth. Do they "become" (*bhavanti*) or do they "cultivate" (*bhāvayanti*)?
And regarding "they cultivate," what do they do: do they act (*kurvanti*) or do they pervade (*vyāpnuvanti*)? Furthermore, in both of these cases, what is the object (*karman*)?

Having thus restated the meaning of the question, he states the answer: "Endowed with speech, limbs, and character," and so forth. [The word *kāvyam*] is derived from the root *ku-* or *kavi-*, meaning that which is to be praised (*kavanīyam*). In that context, since the meanings of words and the meanings of sentences culminate precisely in the *rasas*, the *rasas* are the "meanings" (*arthāḥ*) of poetry because of their unique and preeminent status. They are sought after (*arthyante*).

The meaning is "by way of predominance"; however, the word *artha* here does not signify "the denotable object. For the fact that rasa and the like are not denotable by their own words has been demonstrated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* and others. This should be ascertained from my own commentary on that work, the *Sahṛdayālokalocana*. But here, [the point is as follows:]...
This will indeed be explained at the appropriate occasion.

In this way, they cultivate—that is, they bring to perfection—the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) which constitute the meaning of poetry. For it is precisely through the combination of the permanent moods (*sthāyibhāvas*) and the transitory moods (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) that the extraordinary object of relish is brought into being. Previously, indeed...
One perceives the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) and so forth, and subsequently relishes it through its universal nature.

Therefore, having been the object of prior cognition, one is called the "cultivator" (*bhāvaka*)—the producer—of the relishable aesthetic state (*āsvādya*) which partakes in the subsequent stage. To show the instrument by which one cultivates it, he says: "by means of voice, limbs," and so on.

Speech and the other [organs] are engaged in their respective functions; thus, they are endowed with— that is, connected to— the instruments consisting of vocal elements such as phonation, bodily elements such as the arrangement and movement [of limbs], and internal-external elements such as the *sāttvika* [emotions].

The root *bhū* (in its causative form, *bhāvaya-*) has the sense of "making" (*karaṇa*). Thus, "perfumed" (*bhāvita*), "scented" (*vāsita*), and "made" (*kṛta*) are synonymous. This is also well-known in common worldly usage. Indeed, by this—
Although the instrument (*karaṇa*) is connected both to the action (*karman*) and to the agent (*kartṛ*), nevertheless,
because it is predominant here, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used specifically to show its status as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) in the perception of the connection.

It is explained as "by means of the vocal and physical expressions of the face. Here, although the *nṛtyakalā* and *dhruvāpāta* are internal (*antaraṅga*) to the [performance], nevertheless, immediately following that, in the comprehension of the mental states (*cittavṛtti*), the vocal and other [expressions] alone are internal. For instance:

It has been stated that the tasting of rasa (aesthetic flavor) arises even from poetry (*kāvya*). In that case, however, there is no fullness of the "artificial" (*āhārya*); therefore, it is not included here.
What is meant is this: only worldly mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) [are intended].

Because they bring their own self into the state of being tasted within the extraordinary condition (*alaukikadaśā*) by means of being established in the process of dramatic representation through speech and so forth, they alone are the *bhāvas*. He shows that the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*) expresses the sense of "making the subject at hand [tasted]" by saying "the root *bhū*. The letter *ca* is for the sake of pronunciation. [The phrase] "by connection with the causative suffix" (*ṇic-sambandhena*).
When the suffix *ika* is present, the root *bhū* functions in the sense of "to do. He concludes this very point with the words "(it is brought about).
"Not a different thing" means, in short, that it is one and the same thing.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of vocal and other [forms of recitation], the instrument (*karaṇa*) is included within the objects of experience, while the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) constitutes a distinct part.
Anticipating the objection that this must be explained, he states [the following] to show another etymology by means of a *tantra* (common application): "And even in the world...

Not only is it well-known in the world that *bhāvita* means "performed," but it also means "pervaded. This is what is expressed by the phrase "and even this. The word "all" (*sarva*) includes even smell and taste.

Anticipating the objection that "in that case too, let the meaning simply be 'it has been produced' (kṛtam)," he says: "And that [is] for the sake of pervasion. For a cloth is not made by the scent of musk; this is because a quality does not transfer [to another substance], nor is there the production of another similar quality, since scents and the like persist as long as the substance itself exists, and [this is true] in the case of cloth and so forth.

Because [the consciousness] is perceived as perishing. It is simply that the substance of musk itself, possessing the nature of pervading the space of form and consciousness, produces a corresponding perception even in things such as cloth; so it is in the present case as well. For those very same [expressions] are the vocal and other gestures (abhinaya).
Although they appear in the state of the primary [characters] as being situated in specific places and times, nevertheless—

because the actor here is devoid of qualities (and because Rāma and others are not [actually] present), because Rāma and others possess ultimate reality, and because there is an absence of erroneous cognition— they do not abandon their fixed nature and instead attain a state of commonality (*sādhāraṇībhāva*).
"Even every member of the assembly is thus purified. And that is for the sake of pervasion (*vyāpti*). There are also verses on this point:
That meaning which is brought forth by *vibhāva* and understood through *anubhāvas*, by means of the dramatic representations (*abhinaya*) of speech, body, and spirit, is designated as *bhāva*. (1)

They pervade [the audience] like the fragrance of musk through the medium of the activity of their own mental states; therefore, they "cultivate" (*bhāvayanti*) the self of the spectators, and thus they are called *bhāvas* (emotions).
Now, he speaks in order to show another etymology while also summarizing the previous one:

And here are the verses: "Vibhāva" means the object. That which is brought forth or produced by it is called "bhāva," because it is brought into being (bhāvyate) or created in relation to that vibhāva. He defines the "anubhāvas" through these [verses], beginning with "vāgaṅga... and so on.

Others, however, maintain that by the *bahuvrīhi* compound "those which possess speech, limbs, sattva, and so forth," the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) accompanied by their own specific expressions are included. By the word "by them" (*taiḥ*), it is meant that [the stable emotions] are manifested—that is, mixed—with the transitory states; thus, even among the transitory states, there are further transitory states. For example:

They define [the states] as "reflection on despondency," "despondency resulting from mental exertion," and so forth; however, that is incorrect. For while a permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) may become a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*), a transitory emotion cannot become a permanent emotion. If this were the case, there would have to be another aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) even in the relish of that [transitory state]. This is because one might also conceive of another transitory emotion within a given transitory emotion.

For example, even in the case of Purūravas’s madness (*unmāda*), there is still reflection and deliberation (*tarkacintā*); therein, it is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love itself that is joined with other transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*). That [love] is merely colored by madness, which occupies the position of a minister.
We shall explain this further in the passage beginning with "Just as a king" (*yathā narendra*, Nāṭyaśāstra 7.10).

Having thus explained another kind of proficiency (vyutpatti) useful for the instruction of poets and actors in accordance with worldly convention, he speaks two verses to summarize that meaning which has been defined through the two types of proficiency according to the perspective of the audience: "By means of speech, gestures, and facial coloration," and so forth.

Through the representation consisting of speech, limbs, facial expressions, and gestures, as well as through the representation characterized by inner emotion (*sattva*) and the technical means (*karaṇa*),
that [rasa] of the poet— which, even at that time, is common to the audience— is internal,
composed of beginningless prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and creative intuition (*pratibhāna*), and not born from worldly objects.
Because there is no distinction of place, time, and so forth for one who has reached the end of passion, it is fit to be savored as something common to all.
One who brings to life the internal emotion of the poet through speech, physical gestures, facial expression, spirit, and dramatic representation is called a *bhāva* (an actor). || 2 ||
Since they bring these aesthetic sentiments (rasas) into being through connection with various types of dramatic gestures (abhinaya),
therefore these should be understood as "bhāvas" by those who perform the drama.
Now, why is it called *vibhāva*? It is said: *vibhāva* has the meaning of "that which makes known" (*vijñāna*).

*Vibhāva*, *kāraṇa*, *nimitta*, and *hetu* are synonyms. It is called *vibhāva* because by means of it the representations of speech, body, and spirit (*vāgaṅgasattvābhinaya*) are made manifest (*vibhāvyante*). As it has been made manifest:
"Known" (*vijñāta*) is not different in meaning [from "realized"].
"Cultivating" (*bhāvayan*) means making it palatable; "cultivation" (*bhāva*) is said to be characterized precisely by the activity of the mind (*cittavṛtti*).

Furthermore, "being" (*sattva*) refers to one-pointedness of mind (*citaikāgrya*), as well as that which is produced therefrom—namely, the artificial state consisting of the attainment of tears and so forth.

This should be understood according to the appropriate application. Although it is included within that [category], the change of facial color (*mukharāga*), which consists of pallor, is mentioned again because of its predominance. As he will say:
"Even if a performance is executed with the primary limbs, the secondary limbs, and the minor limbs joined together, it is auspicious [only when this is present]."
"But one devoid of facial coloration would not possess beauty at all" (Nāṭyaśāstra 8.165).
Now, in order to define the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), he states a summary verse beginning with "nānābhinaya":
they cultivate, convey, and bring to awareness those specific mental states (*cittavṛtti*) suitable for aesthetic relish (*rasa*), making them objects of the intellect.
They cause these members of the assembly to attain [the aesthetic experience]. Since the root *bhū* (to become) has the sense of "cognition," it takes two objects.

By the phrase "accompanied by dramatic representation" (*abhinayasahitān*), even the representations themselves are brought within the range of cognition. And this very cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which consists of mental saturation (*adhivāsanā*), transforms the aesthetic flavors (*rasas*)—which are suitable for being tasted—into their own appropriate forms in various ways.

It cultivates [the mind] such that the passion colored by detachment becomes colored by longing; likewise, it permeates the stable emotions (*sthāyins*) which have the extraordinary aesthetic relish (*alaukikāsvāda*) of rasa as their object. For the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*), and so forth, is indeed permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of worldly passion.
p. 341) Here is a verse:
Many meanings are manifested based on the gestures of speech and body.
For this reason, it is designated by him as "vibhāva. || 4 ||
Now, why is it called "anubhāva" (consequent emotion)? It is said:
because by means of it, the representation (*abhinaya*) produced through speech, limbs, and inner being (*sattva*) is experienced.
On this point, there is a verse:

Since the meaning is here made manifest through the representation of speech and limbs, it is therefore known as *anubhāva* (the ensuant), being joined with the major, minor, and subsidiary limbs [of the body]. || 5 ||

It was stated that [the emotion] is brought forth by the *vibhāva*. Although it is understood from the context that the meaning of the word *vibhāva* here is the object that causes the arousal of a mental state (*cittavṛtti*), nevertheless, desiring to know the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in this case, he asks about that very point: "Why is it called *vibhāva*? Why? Because the season, garlands, and so forth are referred to here by the word *vibhāva*.
The sense is: "In what way are they designated?
To this, the answer is given: "They are manifested," and so forth.

Those permanent (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*vyabhicārin*) emotions, which possess the dramatic representations (*abhinaya*) of speech and the rest, are manifested—that is, they are perceived with distinctness—along with those dramatic representations of speech and the rest.
Those by which [emotions] are known are the *vibhāvas*. The various causes from which the *abhinayas* (gestures) arise are as follows:

laughter arises from joy and the like; tears arise from heat, smoke, disease, and so forth. From those [tears], what could be inferred? However, from the *vibhāva*, there is immediate certainty. For this very reason...

Regarding the term "bases" (*āśrayāḥ*): because the permanent (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*vyabhicārin*) emotions are perceived precisely through the medium of the representation of gestures such as those of the body (*āṅgika*), he therefore explains [the term] as "the causes of perception. The meaning is that they are manifested only when they have speech and other gestures as their bases, and not when they are baseless or solitary. For if speech and other gestures were not known in their specific forms, [the emotions could not be perceived].
At that time, even the permanent (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*vyabhicārin*) emotions are not known in such a manner.
Thus, these have been explained as "emotions" (*bhāva*) conjoined with the determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*). Therefore, for these—

The establishment of these emotional states occurs. Therefore, we shall provide a detailed exposition of the definitions and illustrations of these states, which are associated with the determinants (*vibhāva*) and the consequents (*anubhāva*). Among them, the determinants and the consequents—

These two are well-known in the world; furthermore, their definition is not stated because they conform to the nature of worldly convention, and this is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And on this point there is a verse:

The experienced emotions (anubhāvas) and the determinants (vibhāvas), which are established by the very nature of the world and follow the course of worldly life, should be understood by the wise in dramatic representation.

In this regard, there are eight stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), thirty-three transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), and eight involuntary emotions (*sāttvikabhāva*); these are the divisions. Thus, these forty-nine emotional states (*bhāva*) should be understood as the causes for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in poetry. And from these—
Flavors are produced through the combination of general qualities.
On this point, there is a verse: "That meaning which resonates with the heart, its aesthetic state (*bhāva*) gives rise to flavor (*rasa*)."
The body is pervaded by it, just as dry wood is by fire.
(343) Here it is asked:

if [the rasa] is produced by the forty-nine emotions manifested through the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) which are based on the meaning of the poem—

If flavors (*rasas*) are produced through the conjunction of common qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*), how then do the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāvas*) alone attain the state of being flavors? It is said: [It is] so.
For just as [beings] may have identical characteristics, with equal hands, feet, bellies, and bodies, and even equal major and minor limbs, yet...
Just as men attain the status of kings due to their proficiency in lineage, character, learning, action, and arts,
while others of lesser intellect remain their followers; so too do the transitory (vibhāva), ensuant (anubhāva), and inconstant (vyabhicārin) states depend upon the permanent (sthāyibhāva) state.
Because they have many supports, the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) are the masters;
likewise, other emotions that serve as their attributes depend upon them as qualities.
The stable emotions attain the state of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). The transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) are like attendants. Regarding this, it is said:

"What is the illustration? [The answer is: Just as a lord of men receives that very name [of "king"] even when surrounded by a great multitude of people, and no other man does, however great he may be; so too, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), when surrounded by the transitory (*vibhāva*), the consequential (*anubhāva*), and the involuntary (*vyabhicāribhāva*) emotions, receives the name "rasa."
And there is a verse on this point:
Just as a king is to men, and as a teacher is to his disciples.
For thus, in this world, the existence of all things is a great and enduring state.
Indeed, the definition of these [emotions] designated as *rasas* has already been stated previously.
Now we shall state the general definition of the *bhāvas*. Among them, we shall first describe the permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāvas*).

That which is called *rati* (love) consists of the nature of delight; it arises through such determinants (*vibhāva*) as the experience of the proper season, garlands, ointments, ornaments, excellent food, and magnificent dwellings, as well as the absence of anything disagreeable.
One should represent her through consequential emotions (*anubhāvas*) such as a smiling face, sweet speech, the raising of eyebrows, and side-long glances.
On this point, there is a verse:
Delight arises from the attainment of objects that are desired;
because of its gentle nature, it is to be represented through the sweetness of speech and the movements of the limbs. (9)
That which is called laughter arises from such determinants (vibhāvas) as the imitation of another's actions, deceit, incoherent prattle, self-aggrandizement, and folly.
One should represent that [laughter] through the previously mentioned attendant emotions (*anubhāva*), such as smiling and so forth. And there is a verse on this point:
"Laughter arises from the imitation of another's actions."
That [laughter] is to be expressed by the wise through smiles, laughs, and loud bursts of laughter. || 10 ||
