Sorrow (śoka) arises from determinants (vibhāva) such as separation from beloved persons, the loss of wealth, execution, imprisonment, and the experience of suffering.

The performance of this [grief] should be enacted through various manifestations such as shedding tears, lamentation, wailing, change of complexion, hoarseness of voice, drooping of the limbs, falling to the ground, moaning, weeping, crying out, long sighs, numbness, insanity, delusion, death, and so forth.

Weeping here is of three kinds: that born of joy, that born of affliction, and that arising from envy. Regarding this, there are these Āryā verses: "Even in [a state of] joy, weeping caused by affliction is always to be understood by the wise as being of three kinds."
I shall now describe the applications of its representation according to the nature of the determinants (*vibhāva*):

arising from joy, with cheeks blooming, with tears flowing from the corners of the eyes due to recollection, and with the limbs trembling with horripilation, it becomes the manifestation of bliss. (11)

Exhausted, liberated from restraint, making sounds, with movements and postures of the limbs that are unsteady, and uttering lamentations upon falling to the ground— such is that which arises from suffering.
With quivering lips and cheeks, accompanied by shaking of the head as well as sighing,
and characterized by frowns and sidelong glances, this occurs in women born of jealousy. (13)
This grief arising from calamity is natural for women and those of base nature; for the noble and the middling, it is countered by fortitude, while for the base, it is expressed through weeping. (14)

What is called anger arises from such determinants (vibhāvas) as insults, verbal abuse, quarrels, disputes, and oppositions. Its [consequent] manifestations (anubhāvas) include the dilation of the nostrils, the rolling of the eyes, the biting of the lips, and the throbbing of the cheeks.
The dramatic representation should be performed through these internal states (*bhāva*).
Anger is traditionally held to be of five kinds: that arising from an enemy, that arising from a superior, that arising from a loved one, that arising from a servant, and the feigned. (15)
Regarding this, there are these verses:
With a face fierce and contorted by a frown, biting his lip, touching hand to hand with his gesture, looking at his own arm in anger, he should rage unrestrainedly against the enemy. (16)
With his gaze slightly cast downward, intent on wiping away tears and sweat, his movements indistinct yet intense, he may show anger while constrained by discipline toward his teacher. (17)
With little deliberation, scattering tears with sidelong glances, his brow knit and his lips quivering, he should show anger toward the beloved who has approached him with affection. (18)
Now, in the case of servants, anger—devoid of cruelty—is to be represented through threats, reproaches, wide gestures of the eyes, and various glances. (19)

When observing the underlying cause, anger that generally manifests with the signs of physical exertion and occurs within the context of the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) is considered "artificial" (kṛtaka). || 20 ||
Enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is the highest *prakṛti*. It arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as freedom from despondency, capability, fortitude, and heroism.
Its representation (*abhinaya*) should be performed through consequents (*anubhāva*) such as steadfastness, non-abandonment [of the task], and confidence.

Regarding this, there is a verse: "Enthusiasm, which consists of resolve and method, is manifested through non-delusion and so forth; it should be represented on stage through such means as the arising of vigilance. (21)
Fear is of the nature of women and the base;
it consists of offenses against teachers and kings, the sight of wild beasts, empty houses, forests, mountain thickets, elephants, and snakes;
being reviled, traversing deserts, foul weather, the darkness of night, seeing ghosts, and hearing the cries of nocturnal wanderers.
It arises from the determinants (*vibhāva*) such as these: its [manifestation] consists of trembling of the hands and feet,
agitation of the heart, paralysis, dryness of the mouth, licking of the tongue, perspiration, trembling, fear, and seeking protection.
The performance should be enacted through the following expressive states (*anubhāva*): searching, running, crying out, and so forth.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"Due to an offense against a teacher or a king, and also from the sight of those who are fierce..."
Even from merely hearing of terrible things, fear arises through delusion.
The action should be performed through the qualities of dramatic representation, such as trembling of the limbs, expressions of terror, parching of the mouth, agitation, and wide-opening of the eyes.
Fear arises in men produced by the terror of living beings;
that [fear] is to be expressed by dancers through drooping limbs and the closing of their eyes. 24.

Regarding this, there is an Āryā verse: "The representation of this [state] is performed through trembling of the hands, feet, and heart; through the parching of the mouth, licking the face, and paralysis;
and through a bewildered expression, quivering, and the manifestation of terror. (25)
Disgust (*jugupsā*) is characterized by a loathing for women and those of base nature. It arises through determinants (*vibhāva*) such as the sight or hearing of what is unattractive.
Its manifestations (*anubhāva*) include the contraction of all the limbs, spitting, contorting the face, and internal distress.
The inferior [method] should be employed.
And there is a verse on this point:
One should indicate disgust by covering the nose, by contracting the limbs, and by expressions of agitation accompanied by loathing. (26)

What is called "astonishment" (vismaya) arises from various manifestations such as illusions, sorcery, superhuman feats, or the excellence of craftsmanship in painting, sculpture, and the arts. Of that—

The performance should be enacted through expressive states (anubhāvas) such as wide-eyed gazing, unblinking looks, the movement of eyebrows, the bristling of hair, shaking the head, and the utterance of "Excellent!
And on this point, there is a verse:
Amarvement arising from the excellence of the ritual action is born of joy;
however, this [state] is to be accomplished at the stage of *siddhi* by means of intense delight, horripilation, and so forth. (27)
Thus, these permanent emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) are to be understood as being designated by the term "rasa.

Now we shall explain the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*). Here it is asked: why are they called "transitory"? It is said in reply: *vi* and *abhi* are two prefixes; *cara* is a verbal root meaning "to move" or "to go."
They are called *vyabhicārins* (transitory states) because they move in various ways directly toward the *rasas*.
They are called *vyabhicārins* because, when endowed with speech, physical gestures, and internal disposition (*sattva*), they lead one to the *rasas* during performance. Here it is asked:
how?

"It leads," it is said. The reply is: this is a conventional worldly expression, such as when one says "the sun leads this day or that constellation. And yet, it is not led by him with his arms or upon his shoulders; rather—

This is well known in the world, such as when one says, "The sun leads the asterism or the day. In this same way, these [emotions] should be understood as transitory. We shall now describe those thirty-three transitory mental states (bhāvas) mentioned here in summary.

In that regard, what is called "disenchantment" arises among women and base beings due to such conditions as poverty, illness, contempt, abuse, reviling, anger, being beaten, separation from beloved ones, and lack of knowledge of reality.
One should represent that [state of despondency] through such consequent emotions (*anubhāva*) as weeping, sighing, gasping, and deep reflection.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Despondency (*nirveda*), by name, arises from poverty, separation from what is beloved, and other such causes."
But his representation [of the emotion] should be performed through deliberation and sighs. || 28 ||
In this regard, there are two traditional verses:

"From separation from beloved ones, from poverty, from being afflicted by disease, or likewise from suffering, or upon seeing the prosperity of others, that which is called world-weariness (nirveda) arises. (29)
With eyes overflowing with tears and eyes distressed by repeated sighs,
the man filled with world-weariness becomes like a yogi absorbed in meditation. (30)

Illness (*glāni*) is defined by such determinants (*vibhāva*) as vomiting, purging, disease, ascetic observances, fasting, mental anguish, excessive drinking, intoxication, the consumption of liquor, over-exertion, traveling on foot, hunger, thirst, and the deprivation of sleep.
It arises.

Its representation (*abhinaya*) should be performed through its attendant emotional expressions (*anubhāvas*), such as emaciated speech, eyes, cheeks, slow lifting of the feet, trembling, lack of enthusiasm, discoloration of the limbs, and a change in the voice. In this regard, it is said in the *Anuvaṃśya*:
Noble ladies, in those who have vomited or been purged, or who suffer from disease, exhaustion arises due to asceticism and old age;
it is manifested through emaciation, slow wandering, and trembling. (31)

Despair (*nirveda*) is a particular state of mind, a transformation of the intellect in the form of suffering, produced by causes such as poverty or disease, and which is the cause of weeping, sighing, and so forth. The same explanation applies to the remaining [emotions] as well.
And the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the cessation of the long-continued stream of grasping and rejecting based on delusion.
When delusion ceases, it generates world-weariness (*nirveda*), such that one thinks: "Fie upon me for having wandered in vain! For example:

"In vain was the ox milked; for a long time was the cow, though burdened by the weight of her udders, embraced as if she were a young woman; and he who lacked beauty [was loved as if he were a lover]."
I, a fool, placed my hope in lapis lazuli upon a fragment of glass that merely radiates light, as I bowed down to you— a miserable man ignorant of true merit.
Even though "deliberation" (*sampradhāraṇa*) is a distinct state of mind from "doubt" (*vitarka*), [it was nevertheless directed toward you].

The status of these as *anubhāvas* (consequents) here should be understood as being due to their influence upon that [primary emotion]. It is not, however, the case that one transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) can be joined with another transitory emotion; rather, since "disgust (*nirveda*)" arises from seeing, the single agency of the act of seeing is required in relation to the verbal action contained within the word *nirveda* ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*).

The suffix *ktvā* [is used here]. By means of the possessive suffix *matup* in the phrase "a person possessing detachment" (*nirvedavān puruṣa*), he shows this: these states such as detachment do not indeed appear as "this-ness" like a jar or other objects; rather, they appear solely through dependence on a substratum, as in "I am detached. However, when extracted by means of discrimination (*viveka*), that internal modification (*vikāra*) is that in whose very presence there is cognition.

Disgust (*nirveda*). The same applies elsewhere. Furthermore, this disgust, unlike enthusiasm, despondency, and so forth, does not by itself suffice for the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), nor, like laughter, wonder, and so forth, does it suffice for extreme attachment; thus, because it depends on another [permanent emotion], it is merely a transitory state (*vyabhicārin*). The same should be stated for the remaining [transitory states] as well.

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the action (*bhāve*); thus, *vāntam* means "vomited" and *viriktam* means "purged. *Madanasevana* refers to the practice of sexual intercourse. [Regarding] the speech, the eyes, and the cheeks...
One should indicate exhaustion by means of extremely feeble speech, changes in the eyes, dejected movements, and the constant looseness of the limbs.

Doubt (*śaṅkā*) is of the nature of uncertainty; it arises from women or low-born persons and is produced by such determinants (*vibhāva*) as apprehension of theft, arrest, offenses against the king, or the commission of sinful deeds.

In that [state], the performance should be enacted through following emotions (*anubhāvas*) such as repeated glancing, covering [the face], parching of the mouth, licking the tongue, discoloration of the face, hoarseness of voice, trembling, dryness of the palate and throat, and resemblance to a crow.

Suspicion arising from theft and the like is generally considered to belong to the Frightful sentiment; likewise, that arising from the betrayal of a beloved is regarded as belonging to the Erotic. (33)

And these are the attenuated [states]. The attenuation of the sentence is due to the low pitch of the tone. Having made the lifting of the foot slow, there is also the placement of it which accompanies that. The locative case in "vānta" and so forth is a causal locative (*nimitta-saptamī*).
Regarding "repeatedly" (*muhurmuhuḥ*): even when there is merely a flow of homogeneous mental states, the transitory mental factors (*vyabhicārin*) may still occur.
This indicates that no single person remains [in a state of suspicion] for long.

Regarding "the apprehension of a thief": when others are apprehended for theft and identified, then even one who was not apprehended at that time becomes the subject of suspicion, which by its very nature consists of the uncertainty of impending misfortune for that accomplice.

The mention of "theft" is an illustration for any improper act; by this, it is meant that when several people have committed the same improper act, suspicion arises toward any one among them—even if the other person's guilt is not yet known—upon the apprehension of one of them. Therefore, the demonstration of offenses against the king and so forth applies specifically to this case.

This is an elaboration. Regarding the phrase "of women and low-born persons": although there is no improper act for women of superior nature, those of inferior status are already included by the mention of "low-born" (*nīca*);
nevertheless, the specific mention of "women" is made so that even for women who have not committed a sin, [the rule applies] when another woman who has committed an offense is held in the mind.
Suspicion certainly arises; this is for the purpose of demonstrating that it exists because it is a remnant of fear and because they are timid by nature.
Thus, such apprehensive suspicion belongs to women and low-born persons.
By showing this, he demonstrates that even for superior persons, doubt arises from offenses such as acquaintance with other women;

for there is no rule here that these alone are the excitants (*vibhāva*), nor that from these excitants only doubt arises, nor that from these [excitants] only doubt necessarily arises. Rather, doubt first arises from its own specific causal complex (*svasāmagrī*).

It arises as something to be personally realized within oneself; and it is said here that there is an entry into this [state] by them. For this very reason, there may be a suspicion that [the emotion] belongs to another, such as the suspicion of love for Nandayantī in Samudradatta (in the *Puṣpadūṣitaka*), or [the suspicion of love] in Duryodhana for Bhānumatī (in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*).
That [state] too is indeed accepted here as being of the nature of doubt; however, because it would be utterly improper for the hero in this context, such a description is not appropriate.
In this regard, some also maintain that there is a concealment of one's outward appearance; and that [concealment] is to be discerned through wholesome attributes and gestures.
On this point, there are two verses by the Noble One:
For two kinds of suspicion must be entertained: that arising from oneself and that arising from another.
Of these, that which arises from oneself is to be known by one's views and actions. (34)
With his limbs slightly trembling, looking downward and glancing at his sides, with a heavy and faltering tongue and a darkened face, such a man is apprehensive. (35)

What is called *asūyā* (envy) arises from such determinants (*vibhāva*) as various offenses, hatred, the sovereignty of others, their good fortune, intelligence, learning, playful charm, and so forth; and of this [envy], in an assembly...

The representation (abhinaya) should be performed through such transitory emotions (anubhāvas) as the proclamation of faults, the disparagement of virtues, envy, the showing of the eyes, looking downward, knitting the brows, contempt, and reproach.
Regarding "the concealment of outward appearance" (ākārasaṃvaraṇa): that which is commonly observed in the context of dissimulation (avahittha) is also applicable here.

He states the application of its influence: "Or rather, it demonstrates that there is dissimulation (*avahittha*) here; since doubt (*śaṅkā*) becomes a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) in this stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), dissimulation is necessarily demonstrated there as well. But it is not another transitory emotion [that arises] in a transitory emotion. For if that were the case, then by the sequence beginning with 'whatever else in that,' [the rule would be violated]."

Then that first [emotion] would become a transitory state (*vyabhicārin*). For example, as there is anxiety (*cintā*) in fear (*śaṅkā*), so too there is despondency (*nirveda*) therein, and languor (*glāni*) therein, and indolence (*ālasya*) therein, and so forth. In this way, in every case where the definition of a transitory emotion applies, the inclusion of another transitory emotion is to be explained. By the phrase "some say" (*kecit*), he intends to say this:
Anticipating the question of how the concealment of the subject matter (*vastu-saṃvaraṇa*) gives rise to doubt, he says: "And that...
The *upādhis* are the means of concealment, such as the interruption of the discourse or excessive prolixity;
they are so called because by them the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) is covered (*upādhīyate*), or because they are applied elsewhere, being joined to a different context.

Gestures (*iṅgita*) are the subtle movements of the limbs and minor members that cannot be concealed, as well as those preceding a concealment that were intended to be concealed; by means of these, which serve as instruments,
skillful agents effect the concealment of their outward appearance through such factors as dress and so forth.
It is indeed possible to characterize [the state] by means of the manifestation of apprehension (*śaṅkā*).
Regarding the phrase "of two kinds": that twofold nature mentioned by others exists for all transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*).
For despondency (*nirveda*) residing within oneself is sometimes perceived through the eyes, gestures, and so forth when it resides in another; [as in the thought] "I..."
This person is "disgusted" because of the cognition "I am disgusted. Therefore, this is the meaning here:

by the word *ātman* (self), the fault residing in one's own self is expressed; by the word *para* (other), the fault residing in another is expressed. In that regard, even though a fault residing in another is impossible, [it may still occur] due to some cause.

The doubt that was shown in the case of Nandayantī when she had attained a state of high esteem is what is intended here as being "arisen from another. This is what is meant: those very same excitants (*vibhāva*) produce within oneself a doubt concerning a potential punishment or similar consequence; these same [excitants], at other times...
Even those [cognitions] whose function is directed toward their own nature produce doubt concerning things such as a staff or the like that might be expected;
indeed, they sometimes produce even a doubt regarding their own nature, such as "Could this person be a thief?
Now, one might ask: "Even so, how does a suspicion of theft and the like arise with respect to another? To this he says: "By means of observed behavior."

Thus it is said: for when another person looks upon or acts toward one as if they have committed an offense— whether that person has actually committed an offense or not, due to some other cause such as timidity or fearfulness— then a suspicion regarding an offense such as theft arises in that regard.
Regarding the term "sides" (*pārśvāni*): by means of the suffix *-as*, it shows repeated looking back. And this very thing constitutes the similarity with a crow.
Regarding this, there are two noble verses:

"Indeed, envy arises upon seeing the sovereign power over another's fortune, the excellence of their intellect, and the height of their playful charms; and so too does it arise in one who has committed an offense. (36)

In that [performance], the dramatic representation should be employed by those with faces fierce and distorted by frowns, whose eyes are rolling with envy and anger, and who are hostile toward the destruction of virtues. (37)

"Intoxication" (mada) is that which arises from the consumption of intoxicants. It is threefold and consists of five states. Regarding this, there are these verses: "Intoxication should be known as threefold: youthful, middling, and inferior."
The instrument is of five kinds; its representation (abhinaya) should be employed. || 38 ||
One sings in intoxication, another likewise weeps or laughs; one utters harsh words, while another sleeps. (39)
The person of superior nature sleeps, laughs, and sings; the one of middling nature does the same; but the one of inferior nature speaks harsh words and even weeps. (40)
With a sweet passion in his smiling speech, his body thrilled, his words slightly agitated, his gait delicate yet unrestrained, he is a youth intoxicated with the pride of his noble nature. (41)
With eyes stumbling and rolling, with arms drooping and flailing in confusion, and with a crooked and winding gait, one of middle nature is in the state of middling intoxication. || 42 ||
With lost memory and destroyed gait, loathsome due to vomiting phlegm and hiccups, his tongue heavy and stuck, he spits out like one of the lowest nature. (43)

That by which a virtue is destroyed or made into a fault is described as such; for example, "this person is a hypocrite" when [his] austerity and recitation are [thus characterized]. "Depressed" (avakṛṣṭa) means inferior. "Instrument" (karaṇa) refers to action or effort; by that, there is indeed the fivefold [action].
This very [state] is the representation (*abhinaya*) of intoxication (*mada*); and it is precisely this that is designated by the term "emotion" (*bhāva*) in the Sūtra.

He describes these five types of action with the words beginning "Someone... and so forth. By doing so, he demonstrates that joy, sorrow, laughter, anger, and delusion share a single underlying stable state (*sthāyibhāva*) through intoxication.
On the stage, one should increase intoxication while engaged in the performance of drama;
however, for one who has actually entered [the performance] after having drunk, a decrease in intoxication must indeed be effected. (44)
Whether due to terror, grief, fear, or joy arising from a cause, those who know the truth should gradually effect the destruction of intoxication, even by means of a leap. 45.
Through these specific reflections, intoxication quickly comes to total destruction, just as grief is brought to an end by words concerning the joys of prosperity. (46)
Fatigue (śrama) arises from determinants such as traveling long distances, physical exertion, and so forth.

Its representation should be performed through consequents such as rubbing and massaging the limbs, sighing, yawning, slow lifting of the feet, closing the eyes, contorting the face, and hissing sounds.
In this context, what is called "fatigue" arises in a man from dancing, walking, and physical exercise;
its representation should be performed through sighing, perspiration, and labored movement. (47)
Due to the difference in temperament (*prakṛti*), there is no fixed rule that the "young" intoxication is only for the superior type or the "middle" intoxication only for the middle type;

however, it is the inferior temperament alone that possesses the nature of lost memory and so forth. By this, it is shown that the "young" intoxication is common to all, the "middle" is for both the middle and the low, and the "excellent" is for the low alone. [He] sleeps...

The meaning is: "this being the case due to excessive drinking. Her body is thrilled, meaning it is covered with horripilation. Having made it delicate, it is "twisted," meaning it stumbles slightly. For the instruction of the poet and the actor, he says: "drink on the stage. This is approached through a causal impulsion—a deliberate effort intended to signal the cause of alarm and so forth.

"Having come. This is what is meant: how could one whose intoxication has been destroyed by fear and so forth become free from intoxication if one does not understand the very cause of that fear and so forth? Therefore, the thorough knowledge of those causes must be applied with effort.
By the word "quickly," it is shown that one has "transcended"; he explains this as the abandonment of sequential order. Incidentally, something else is also mentioned.

He shows that it is of such a kind by the phrase "with the pleasures of worldly prosperity" (*abhyudayasukhaiḥ*). They are so called because they cause happiness through what is expressed by "worldly prosperity. The mention of "statements" (*vākya*) is an indication for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That which is called indolence arises among women and low-born persons through such determinants (vibhāvas) as exhaustion, disease, pregnancy, natural lethargy, satiety, and the like.
One should act that out through the following consequent emotions (*anubhāvas*): the non-utterance of any ritual action, lying down, sitting, sleeping, drowsiness, and so forth.
On this point, there is an *āryā* verse:
Laziness, however, should be represented as arising from exhaustion, as being innate, or from the failure to undertake undertakings that were previously free from food. (48)
Dejection (*dainya*) arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as poverty and mental anguish.
Its representation (*abhinaya*) should be performed through consequents (*anubhāva*) such as lack of fortitude, headache, heaviness of the limbs, distraction, and the abandonment of cleanliness.
On this point, there is an Āryā verse:
"The dejection of men arising from anxiety and longing consists of suffering and the like;
its various modes of representation (abhinaya) occur through the avoidance of all straightforwardness. (49)
What is called *cintā* (anxiety) arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as the loss of power, the seizure of beloved objects, poverty, and so forth.
One should represent it through such [consequents] as sighing, heaving, distress, brooding, looking downward, and emaciation.
[It arises] through such dominant emotions (*anubhāva*) as despair and the like.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"But [sorrow] born from the loss of sovereignty or the depletion of beloved possessions is of many kinds."
In humans, thought arises accompanied by mental discursive reflections within the heart. || 50 ||

"Fatigue" (*kheda*) here refers to exhaustion; by this it is shown that one emotion indeed becomes the determinant cause (*vibhāva*) for another emotion. "Satiety" (*sauhitya*) means the state of being fully satiated. Regarding the phrase "devoid of food": even a lazy person necessarily takes food.

"Enterprises" refers to the engagement in the means for attaining the four aims of human life; "by the non-enterprise of these" means by that which is distinct from enterprise, such as lying down, reclining, and so forth.
"Mṛjā" (cleansing) refers to the refinement of the body.

The loss of sovereignty is temporary, whereas poverty may be inherited through family lineage; this is the distinction. "Cintana" (thinking) should be understood as "smaraṇa" (recollection). Recollection is indeed distinct from anxiety (*cintā*). [This is supported by] such [Vedic] passages as "in *citi*, which means recollection," and so forth.
Anxiety is to be enacted through labored inhalations and exhalations, through fevers, through a sense of emptiness in the heart,
and through a lack of cleanliness and lack of fortitude. (51)
Delusion (moha) arises through such mental states as the stroke of fate, calamity, assault, the onset of disease, fear, agitation, and the recollection of former enmities. Of this—

The performance should be enacted through the following consequent emotions (*anubhāvas*): unconsciousness, wandering, falling, reeling, and so forth. Regarding this, there is both a verse (*śloka*) and an *āryā*:
Seeing thieves in an improper place, even though one employs various means of intimidation, delusion arises in one who lacks the means to counter them. (52)
Delusion arises from calamity, assault, fear, the recollection of former enmity, or disease;
its representation should be performed through the total confusion of all the senses. (53)

Memory (smṛti) is the recollection of things experienced as pleasure or pain. It arises from such determinants (vibhāva) as physical well-being, the interruption of sleep during the latter part of the night, witnessing similar sights, recounting [past events], reflection, and repeated practice.
One should represent that [intention] through expressive gestures (*anubhāva*) such as shaking the head, looking about, and raising the eyebrows.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"The indication of meaning occurs through proximity to you; for the meaning of all verbal roots differs from one another."

Indeed; for although the root *kheḷ* is recited as meaning "to go," nevertheless, in common usage—as in the expression *khelagāmī* ("one who moves with a playful gait")—it is well known to signify a specific, graceful movement. Furthermore, "swallowing" (*grasana*) refers to a form of sexual union characterized by a forceful, prideful, and passionate outburst of anger that swallows [the partner] entirely, and not merely eating.

The same should be understood for other cases as well. "In whose presence there is the approach of discursive thought (*vitarka*) in the heart," or "from whom, that is, from which discursive thought, there is the approach"— by this, he teaches that discursive thought occurs during both the preceding and succeeding stages of reflection (*cintā*).

"Divine affliction" (*daivopaghāta*) refers to calamities such as fire or water. "Misfortune" (*vyasana*) refers to suffering and the like; some say it is the injury caused by that. However, "injury" (*abhighāta*), such as a blow to a vital spot (*marmaprahāra*), has its own distinct meaning as a *puṣkala* (contributory factor).

With the intention that even one emotional state may become a *vibhāva* (excitant), he says "fear," etc. And although a stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) [is present] within a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*)...
It is indeed a transitory emotion (*vibhāva*). Nevertheless, the mention of "fear" is for the purpose of indicating the predominance of delusion (*moha*) in fear.
Wandering is the instability of the mind, while reeling is that of the body.
By the phrase "of one devoid of a remedy for that," the prior stage of delusion is indicated.

By the phrase "due to the delusion of all the senses," he shows that even what is designated by the word "delusion" (moha) is characterized by a state of not knowing what ought to be done; and by demonstrating that the internal consciousness remains undestroyed even when one is deluded,
he explains that delusion consists in the mind's falling into a state of bewilderment.
By the phrase "since the accomplishment of pleasure and pain belongs to them," he states that memory pervades all objects. The "lowest" refers to the final portion of the night.
It is said to be the cause of memory by balancing the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), as it has been stated: "The fourth watch of the night is the time [for this]" (*Vāmanapurāṇa*).
[As stated] in the *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti*: "The interruption of sleep occurs even at midnight and other such times;
[the causes are] the sight or hearing of something similar, reflection, concentration, repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), and constant study (*pariśīlana*) or observation."

He who remembers, as it actually occurred, that which has transcended pleasure and pain and has been thus mentally visualized, even though long forgotten— he is to be known as one possessed of mindfulness (smṛtimān). || 54 ||
Memory arising from health, practice, learning, and vision should be represented by skillful actors through gestures such as shaking the head, waving it about, and raising the eyebrows. (55)

That which is called *dhṛti* (fortitude) arises from such determinants (*vibhāva*) as valor, wisdom, the abundance of learning, purity, conduct, devotion to one's guru, the attainment of desired objects through great resolve, and play. One should represent that [fortitude] in those who have attained it.
Through the non-attachment to the enjoyment of sense objects— whether unattained, past, impaired, or destroyed— and through such secondary emotions as the absence of lamentation;
regarding this point, there are two verses:

Fortitude, which arises from the power of learning and the abundance of purity of consciousness, should always be practiced by the virtuous, being free from fear, grief, despondency, and the like. (56)
It is that state in which there is the enjoyment of sounds, tastes, touches, forms, and smells when they are obtained, and no sorrow regarding those not yet obtained; indeed, that is steadfastness.

"Of a similar [nature]" means that which produces pleasure and pain. "Cultivated" indicates being grasped by sharp cognition. "Discriminative knowledge" is *vijñāna*; "abundance of learning" is great erudition; and "practice of purity" is the observance of cleanliness.

The attainment of a superior object beyond the scope of one's desires, as well as the attainment of an object that is the very content of one's desire—that which is desired is the "manoratha. Here, the mind (*manas*) is the "chariot" (*ratha*), meaning it is the means of attainment;

for in this context, someone [the mind] functions as the subject (*viṣayatā*) because one becomes satisfied upon the attainment of what was desired, while someone else [the mind] functions as the instrument (*karaṇatā*).

Being entertained by play, one who is suffering attains fortitude. For some, there is a state of possessing both [aspects], as in the case of the abundance of knowledge, learning, and wealth; the connection is that this [fortitude] arises through such attendant moods (*anubhāva*) as the absence of grieving for things not yet obtained, based on the enjoyment of objects already acquired. By that [means].

It is stated that all experiences are preceded by what has already been attained; however, that which has been attained as an experience does not constitute a separate category of experience. That which is unattained remains outside its scope even if it persists; that which is past has departed from its scope even if it persists. That which is impaired has reached a state of decay and so forth; that which is destroyed... [is no longer present].
Destroyed. (p.
359) That which is called shame (*vrīḍā*) consists in the non-performance of what ought not to be done; and that—

It arises from such determinants (*vibhāva*) as the transgression against a guru, contempt, the failure to fulfill a promise, and subsequent remorse; it is manifested by such consequents (*anubhāva*) as hiding the face, looking downward, brooding, scratching the ground, touching the fingers on a garment, and so forth.
One should represent this through the consequent emotions (*anubhāvas*) such as self-reproach and the like.
On this point, there are two verses: "When one is seen by others who are pure while performing some improper act..."
One who is possessed of remorse should be understood as being "ashamed. || 58 ||
With his face hidden out of shame, scratching the ground and tearing at his nails,
he would touch the rings on her fingers, feeling abashed.
What is called fickleness arises from such determinants (vibhāva) as passion, hatred, envy, resentment, jealousy, and hostility;
and of that—
The performance is to be enacted through the following attendant emotions (anubhāvas): verbal abuse, threats, killing, binding, striking, beating, and so forth.
On this subject, there is a verse in the Āryā meter:

By the term "non-performance of what should not be done" (akāryakaraṇa), that knowledge is expressed; the meaning is that its essential nature is the awareness: "I have thus performed what ought not to be performed.
For this very reason, shame is observed even in women, children, and others when in the presence of a person they have never met before, even in the absence of having actually committed such an act.

Others hold that the self is one who performs what ought not to be done. According to that view, when one feels remorse for having previously abandoned a mere elaboration—such as transgressing against a guru—and subsequently regrets it, shame arises in one possessed of discrimination; [this occurs] in one who is devoid of reflection upon what preceded and what followed.

"Scratching the earth and so forth" refers to the thought, "The world suspects me. "By those who are pure" means by those who perform their proper duties; for among those who perform improper acts, there arises no such realization as, "This improper act was committed by me alone. That mental remorse which follows later is indeed discernment (*viveka*) at that time.
Since it is impossible to undo what has already been done, [the verb] merely indicates causing distress.

In the case of *vinikṛntan kuryāt*, the simultaneity of the two senses expressed by the suffix *śatṛ* is not intended; rather, this is clearly understood as meaning either "he cuts his nails and so forth" or "he touches his clothes and so forth."
But that person who, without reflection, begins to carry out an action such as killing or beating,
should indeed be known by the wise as fickle, because he acts without certainty. (60)

That which is called joy (*harṣa*) arises from such determinants (*vibhāva*) as the attainment of one's desires, reunion with beloved persons, mental satisfaction, the favor of gods, teachers, kings, or husbands, and the acquisition and enjoyment of food, clothing, and other such things.

One should represent that [state] through such consequent emotions (anubhāvas) as the dilation of the eyes, graciousness, pleasant speech, embracing, horripilation, and perspiration. Regarding this, there are two verses by Ārya: [Verse 1] When a woman, having seen her beloved who has arrived unexpectedly, experiences joy, she displays a state of mind characterized by horripilation, tears, and perspiration, and she speaks with words that are both gentle and firm. [Verse 2] The expansion of the eyes, the breaking forth of tears, the manifestation of joy, and the shedding of tears— these are the signs of love; they are the very essence of the heart.
Whether an unattainable object is attained, or when a desired goal is reached, or even upon meeting with a beloved, joy arises in men when the heart's desire is fulfilled. (61)
His representation [of emotion] is achieved through the clarity of his eyes and face, affectionate speech, embraces, horripilation, graceful movements of the limbs, perspiration, and so forth. (62)

Regarding "killing and beating": by the phrase "even that which is of the nature of sin and ought not to be done impulsively," other [faults] are also indicated. He is indeed "impetuous" (*capala*); thus, acting without reflection or deliberation—that is, the performance of an action out of impulsiveness—is what is meant. Regarding "contentment": this refers to the fact that joy residing in one's son or others serves as the cause of one's own joy.

It indicates that even an entity belonging to a different class (*niḥsajātīya*) can indeed be the cause of another entity when it is situated elsewhere; for example, the despondency, anxiety, and so forth residing in Rāma are the cause for the arising of despondency, anxiety, and so forth in Lakṣmaṇa. The term "without reaching" (*aprāpya*) means that the attainment [of the object] is impossible. "The heart" (*hṛdayam*) refers to that which constitutes the essential core (*sārabhūta*) in this matter.

Upon obtaining that gain, joy arises. For example, it is like one seeking gold who, while wandering through various regions, obtains a jewel of infinite gold value; yet it is not reasonable to say that this [joy] serves to set aside the mental aspirations, the seizing of the heart, and the physical activities [previously directed toward gold].
Because it is impossible within one's desires.
361) What is called *āvega* (agitation)—

It arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as portents, wind, rain, fire, the wandering of elephants, hearing what is pleasant or unpleasant, calamities, and physical affliction. Among these, that produced by portents (*utpātakṛta*) is caused by lightning, meteors, thunderclaps, eclipses of the moon and sun, and the appearance of comets.
One should represent that [state] through drooping of all the limbs, dejection, discoloration of the face, despondency, astonishment, and so forth;
whereas that caused by wind (vāta) is represented by covering the head,
wiping the eyes, clutching at the clothes, hurried walking, and the like.
Furthermore, that caused by rain occurs through the contraction of all limbs, running about, seeking shelter, and so forth;
whereas that caused by fire—
[The state] named "the confusion caused by the wandering of elephants" [is characterized] by eyes clouded with smoke, contraction of the limbs, shaking, fleeing,
retreating, and so forth; it consists of haste, crawling like a snake, restless movement, fear, paralysis, trembling, looking back, and astonishment.
[The first type is] caused by hearing what is pleasant,
characterized by rising from one's seat, embracing, giving garments and ornaments, shedding tears, horripilation, and so forth.
[The second type is] caused by hearing what is unpleasant.

[The pain] born from the onset of calamity arises through falling to the ground, rolling about in distress, running hither and thither, lamenting, wailing, and so forth; as well as through sudden retreating, wielding weapons, shields, and armor, and mounting elephants, horses, and chariots.

Because those whose hearts are possessed [by love] alone are fit for the performance [of this art], and because agitation (*āvega*) is the very lifeblood of every performance, there is a variety of performance according to the specific variations of the emotional states (*anubhāva*) corresponding to each particular object of emotion (*vibhāva*). This is the intended meaning regarding the use of necklaces (*hāra*), ornaments (*ābharaṇa*), and so forth.

He demonstrates this with the words beginning "In that regard, that which is caused by rising," and so forth. The meaning is that one should move away from those two noble ones when they have transgressed or departed from the bounds of propriety (*maryādā*). *Udbhramaṇa* (agitated wandering) is wandering that has overstepped the limits of decorum.
Upon hearing something unpleasant, someone experiences agitation; in that state, the manifestations of grief (*śokānubhāva*) fall one after another in succession.

And [the grief of] one who is not firm-minded (*adhīra*) has a swift onset; however, according to Śrī Śaṅkuka, for the firm-minded (*dhīra*), grief occurs first. But that is incorrect. For in that case, agitation (*āvega*) would become the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), and grief would become a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Therefore, for one of a non-firm nature, there is grief...
Thus, this eightfold agitation, consisting of bewilderment,
is manifested through the composure of the high and middle classes, and by the flight of the low. (63)

Regarding this, your venerable selves have stated: "Whether due to the announcement of something unpleasant, or from suddenly grasping the words of an enemy, or from the brandishing of a weapon, or from fear, that which arises is called *āvega* (agitation). (64)

The emotional state (bhāva) of despondency (viṣāda), which arises from reporting unpleasant news and so forth, has as its external manifestation (anubhāva) such actions as the sudden clashing of weapons upon seeing an enemy. (65)
Inertness (*jaḍatā*) is defined as the failure to engage in any activity.
It arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as hearing or seeing the desirable or undesirable, or from illness and the like.
One should represent it through non-speaking, silence, lack of eloquence, and gazing with unblinking eyes.
Through such consequential emotions (*anubhāva*) as lack of dependence on others and so forth;
regarding this, there is a verse in the Āryā meter:
"He who, through delusion, does not perceive what is desired or undesired, or pleasure and pain..."
He who remains silent while under the control of another is known as a dull-witted man. || 66 ||

It is overcome by a surge of emotion in the very second moment immediately after it has arisen. However, in one of a steadfast nature, even though the surge occurs, it is concealed by composure through a display of feigned indifference; it does not fail to arise at all.
And so the author will say: "By means of steadfastness, [the passion of] the superior and middling types. Nor is it ever devoid of association with the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*).

There is no state whatsoever that exists independently of the permanent emotions (*sthāyin*). Nor can the variegated condition of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) exist without the foundation provided by the permanent emotions. Regarding the term "by means of withdrawals" (*apasarpaṇaiḥ*): the plural number indicates various modes;
the meaning is "by means of modes such as flight and so forth. Furthermore, withdrawal occurs when there is agitation caused by elephants, fire, and the like.

The phrase "it becomes more frequent" is included [in the definition]. By stating that agitation (*āvega*)—arising from the announcement of something unpleasant—is the determinate emotion (*anubhāva*) upon which despondency (*viṣāda*) relies, he demonstrates that one transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) can exist within another transitory emotion. And this has already been shown by us at the very beginning with the words "suddenly" (*sahasā*).
When a sudden agitation arises from seeing an enemy who was previously unperceived, then one must perform the movement of brandishing a weapon or a club;
by the phrase "lack of comprehension regarding what is to be done," insensibility due to a lack of discernment is indicated— even for one who sees with both eyes.
The phrase "even while hearing with the ears" shows that [the author] demonstrates another aspect of her nature due to delusion (*moha*).

"Non-speaking" refers generally to the failure to provide an answer even when a question has been asked; it is the non-engagement in speech toward friends and others. Regarding the phrase "due to delusion," the connection is that this occurs either before or after the delusion.
p. 363) Pride (*garva*) is defined by such determinants (*vibhāva*) as sovereignty, noble lineage, beauty, youth, learning, strength, wealth, and gain.
It arises through [actions such as] envy, contempt, insult, not giving instruction, refusing to converse, looking askance at the limbs,
mocking, derision, verbal harshness, transgressing against the guru, reviling speech, and interrupting [the discourse].
The enactment [of drama] is performed through the powers of expression.
On this matter, there is a verse:
"Whether through the acquisition of knowledge, or from beauty, sovereignty, or even from the arrival of wealth..."
And that pride of base men should be provoked by the observation of their glances and bodily gestures. || 67 ||

Confusion (*vibhrama*) is a state of pride in women; its characteristic is as follows: confusion is to be understood as a disordered transposition of various objects—consisting of speech, limbs, costumes, and inner disposition—produced by intoxication, passion, and joy.
Since intoxication (*mada*) and the like are used as illustrations, pride (*garva*) is also certainly included here. Regarding the word "and" (*ca*): it serves to emphasize.
For those low individuals who were previously deemed unfit for knowledge and so forth, pride alone arises upon attaining that [knowledge].
And indeed, for those whose limbs are [merely] for display, there is movement characterized by various transformations.

Therefore, it has already been explained that for those [beings] who abide in the highest state, it exists as a continuous flow, whereas for others, it occurs only momentarily, like a flash of lightning.
Despair (*viṣāda*) is that which arises from the failure to accomplish a task or from the adverse turn of fate.

It should be represented among the *uttama* (highest) and *madhyama* (middle) characters by means of *anubhāvas* such as the search for companions, the devising of expedients, the frustration of one's resolve, dejection, and sighing. However, for the *adhama* (lowest) characters:
[This is expressed] through such consequential expressions as wandering about, looking [desperately], parching of the mouth, licking the corners of the lips, sleep, sighing, and meditating.
On this subject, there are two Āryā verses:
Whether due to the failure to accomplish a task, or being caught in a theft, or through some fault before the king, or from the loss of wealth by fate, despondency always arises for men. (68)
One should employ the thought of various means for the superior and middling tasks; however, one should apply sleep, sighing, and meditation for those of inferior capacity.

By stating that "despair" (*viṣāda*) is the failure to accomplish a task that has been undertaken through various means— that is, the non-attainment of the fruit— due to such an operation of destiny (*daiva*) as the opposition of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), he indicates that the failure to attain the fruit even from proper means, when born of a defect in destiny, serves as a determinant emotion (*vibhāva*) for despair. This [occurs] in anger.
Some claim that [the rasa] is not inconsistent; that is incorrect. For even those of a fierce nature (*raudraprakṛti*) are seen to experience despondency (*viṣāda*), as in the *Rāmābhyudaya*:
"But this causes a wound to the mind—that which is marked by the edge of a thunderbolt..."
"The desire for cruelty, like the claw of a monkey, has struck Prahasta’s chest.

For mental injury is dejection, which is the manifest sign (*anubhāva*) of despondency. Moreover, it is improper for those monkeys—who are but beasts whose sole refuge is flight—to harbor such a desire for cruelty; however—

As long as his affection remains unfulfilled regarding the desired object, this failure to achieve the fruit—even through a proper means—due to the power of destiny, is what is called "anubhāva" (the external manifestation). Nor does this [manifestation] contradict reason, scripture, or experience in its being a transitory state (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of dejection (*viṣāda*) associated with anger; so, enough of this.
What is called longing (*autsukya*) arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as the recollection of separation from a beloved person or the sight of a garden.
The performance of this [sorrow] should be enacted through such consequent expressions as long sighing, looking downward, brooding, sleepiness, lethargy, and the desire for reclining.
On this point, there is an Āryā verse:
"Indeed, longing arises from the recollection of separation from beloved people;
its representation [is performed] through anxiety, sleeplessness, lethargy, and heaviness of the limbs. (70)
Sleep is that which arises from such determinants (vibhāva) as weakness, fatigue, exhaustion, intoxication, indolence, anxiety, overeating, and innate disposition.

One should represent that [state] through such *anubhāvas* (consequent expressions) as gravity of countenance, gazing at the body, rolling of the eyes, stretching of the limbs, slowness of movement, labored breathing, a sense of physical exhaustion, and the closing of the eyes.
By the word *utsūyate*, the term *utsū* refers to seeds and the like that have begun to sprout; from that, [the representation] is formed in its likeness (*pratikṛti*).

The form *autsuka* arises from the word *utsuka* with a short vowel; its state is *autsukya*. The mention of "separation" (*viyoga*) indicates that this [longing] is predominant in the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) type. It shows through the mention of "recollection" (*smaraṇa*) that the beloved person serves as the objective basis (*ālambana*), while memory acts as the excitant (*uddīpana*). This includes even the longing for a bed [in the absence of the beloved].
It is categorized as distinct because it arises from sleep.
Debility (*daurbalyam*) is the state of having one's strength depleted by disease and so forth; exhaustion (*klamaḥ*) is that caused by heat and the like.
Regarding this, there are these two verses:
"From laziness, from weakness of the limbs, from exhaustion, from fatigue, from anxiety, and from one's own nature;
and also from staying awake at night, sleep occurs for a person. (71)

A wise person should represent that [state] through the following indicative expressions (anubhāvas): heaviness of the face, tossing of the limbs, closing of the eyes, lassitude, yawning, and the stretching of the body.
What is called epilepsy (*apasmāra*) arises from various conditions such as: the recollection of gods, yakṣas, nāgas, brahmarākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, or possessing spirits;
the consumption of leftovers; dwelling in empty houses; impurity; falling at improper times; and diseases and so forth.
It arises;

its representation should be performed through the following expressive gestures (anubhāvas): heaving sighs, trembling, running, falling, perspiration, paralysis, frothing at the mouth, licking the corners of the mouth with the tongue, and so forth.
In this regard, O Noble Ones, [it is said]:
"Epilepsy arises from remembering spirits, piśācas, or seizing demons; from going to an empty house while still impure from food remnants; and from the lapse of the proper time. (73)
Sudden falling to the ground, trembling, the spitting of foam from the mouth,
and rising while unconscious— these are the symptoms of epilepsy (apasmāra).

That which is called "sleep" arises from the dominant emotion of sleep, produced by such determinants as being overcome by drowsiness, approaching a place for rest, delusion, lying upon the ground, stretching out, and drawing oneself together.

The "seizing" (*graha*) by deities and others, ending with *piśācas*, refers to the obsession (*anusmaraṇa*) for the sake of possession; or, one of inferior character becomes possessed (*apasmārī*) by recollecting them. "Seizing," however, is well known [as the act of possessing]. "Impurity" (*aśuci*) is the prolonged duration of its presence over time. It occurs when there is an imbalance of the elements (*dhātu*), namely wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
When the locus of the intellect (*buddhi*) is obstructed by *sati*, there occurs what they call epilepsy (*apasmāra*), arising from the agitation of the intellect and the vital essence (*sattva*).
This is characterized by the swelling of the limbs, the closing of the eyes, the delusion of all the sense faculties, and involuntary movements resembling sleep-walking (*utsvapnāyita*). (p. 367)
One should represent it through the manifestations of joy.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"Sleep arises from the overcoming of wakefulness, the cessation of the senses, and delusion."
[The state of being asleep] should be produced by closing the eyes, breathing, and speaking as if in a dream. || 75 ||
With labored inhalations and exhalations, with the closing of the eyes,
and motionless due to the delusion of all the senses, one should practice sleep and dream-states.
Awakening, by name,
arises through such conditions as the transformation of food, the interruption of sleep, and the hearing of intense sounds or tactile sensations during the end of a dream.
One should represent that [state] through such *anubhāvas* (consequent actions) as yawning, rubbing the eyes, lying down, and stretching out.
On this point, there is an *āryā* verse:
"It arises from the transformation of food and from sounds, touches, and so forth."
Awakening, however, is to be represented through yawning, facial expressions, and rubbing the eyes. || 77 ||
What is called indignation (*amarṣa*) arises when one is insulted or humiliated by those superior in learning, sovereignty, heroism, or strength.
One should represent it through gestures such as shaking the head, perspiring, looking downward, reflecting, meditating, and making a firm resolve.
Through the *anubhāvas* (consequent states) such as the search for companions and so forth;

by the phrase "arisen from sleep" (*nidrāsamuttham*), he shows that "sleep" (*suptam*) is the deep state of sleep itself, and thus states its essential nature (*svarūpa*) as consisting in the desire to withdraw from sense objects—this is expressed by the term "dreaming" (*svapnāyitam*). "Muttering" (*pralapanam*)...

In the world, it is well known that dream-cognition is indeed distinct from ordinary cognition of objects occurring at that very moment, because dream-cognition is not consistent with reality. For in a dream, one speaks while recollecting something;
and from such incoherent speech, people infer that there was a corresponding recollection.

Because sleep may be interrupted even without the digestion of food and so forth due to the force of its fixed limits, the interruption of sleep is mentioned separately. As for "the end of dream," which is its completion: Ghaṇṭuka maintains that sound and the other [objects] are indeed included therein; however, it is more logical that they are external.

*Amarṣa* (resentment) is distinct from *krodha* (anger); it consists of the desire for retaliation. Regarding *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) as being without a specific object—on this point there are two verses:
(368) Here are the two verses:
When those who are superior in learning, heroism, and strength are challenged in the midst of an assembly, indignation arises from the conjunction of their human energy. (78)
Through enthusiasm and resolve, by means of downward-looking reflections, and by shaking the head, perspiring, and so forth, the wise man should employ that [method]. (79)
*Avahittha* (concealment) is defined as the act of hiding one's outward appearance.

It arises from such determinants (*vibhāva*) as shame, fear, defeat, respect, or deceit. Its manifestations (*anubhāva*) include speaking otherwise than one feels, avoiding eye contact, interrupting the conversation, and feigning composure.
—the appropriate gesture (*abhinaya*) should be employed.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Hypocrisy (*avahittha*) arises from audacity, deceit, and so forth; it is characterized by fear."
And that should be performed by means of non-counting, rather than through further verbalization.
What is called *ugratā* (fierceness) arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as the apprehension of thieves, offenses against the king, and harsh speech.
One should represent it through consequents (*anubhāva*) such as execution, imprisonment, beating, and threats.

Regarding this, there is an Āryā verse: "When ferocity arises due to being caught in the act of theft or through an offense against the king, its representation is performed through expressive effects such as execution, imprisonment, and flogging. (81)

The term "establishment" (*avasthāna*) is distinguished from mere "thought" (*cintā*). "Endowed with enthusiasm" (*utsāhasampanna*) means that it does not belong to ordinary people who lack enthusiasm; by the words "enthusiasm" (*utsāha*) and "resolute determination" (*adhyavasāya*), its external manifestations (*anubhāva*) are indicated—namely, those such as the movements of the eyebrows and the coloring of the face, by which the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) is acted out and manifested externally.

*Avahittha* is that form of mental activity which performs concealment or covering; they say its etymology is "that by which the mind is not situated externally," and its form [is derived] according to the *pṛṣodarādi* rule. *Jaihmya* is the state of having a crooked disposition characterized by the desire to conceal what ought to be hidden; for one who is *pragalbha* (bold/arrogant) knows how to conceal their outward appearance.

The term "boldness" (*dhārṣṭya*) is used for emphasis; for even one who possesses shame, if he is lacking in boldness, does not act. Therefore, it should be understood that boldness is a constant follower of this [shamelessness] across all its manifestations. "Disregard" (*agaṇanā*) is the setting aside of an object due to arrogance.

Theft is an illustration of improper acts; when people are apprehended on that account, there is cruelty—that is, mercilessness—on the part of kings and others. Thus, it applies to one who offends the king, such as one who utters false speech or speaks of unfounded faults.
That which is called *mati* (intellection) arises through various mental states such as the investigation of diverse scriptures and the processes of inclusion and exclusion (*ūha-apoha*).
One should represent it through *anubhāvas* (consequents), such as instructing disciples, deliberation on meaning, and the cutting away of doubt.
And there is a verse on this point:
Through the understanding of the meanings of various scriptures, an intellect arises in men;
for one who acts for the sake of instructing disciples, there should be a dramatic representation of that [intellect]. (82)

Disease is defined as that which originates from the humors of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), or their combination (sannipāta). Its specific manifestations include fever and other such conditions. Fever, moreover, is of two kinds: accompanied by cold shivering and accompanied by burning heat. Among these, that which is accompanied by cold shivering is as follows:

It is to be enacted through such *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) as trembling of all limbs, quivering and contraction, longing for fire, horripilation, gnashing of the teeth, contraction of the nose, parching of the mouth, and lamentation.
That which is called "fever with burning" (*sadāha*) is as follows:

[These are manifested] through such secondary expressions as the tossing of limbs, hands, and feet; longing for the ground; desire for ointments and coolness; lamentation; parching of the mouth; and shrieking. Furthermore, whatever other diseases there may be, they too are indeed characterized by such [expressions] as the contortion of the face, stiffness of the limbs, drooping of the eyes, sighing, groaning, shrieking, and trembling.
These are the gestures for those to be instructed by means of gold.
On this point, there is a verse:
"In brief, the wise should perform the gestures for diseases."
With the tossing of his drooping limbs and the contortion of his face, || 83 ||

"Intellect" (*mati*) means having the nature of unprecedented intuition (*apūrva-pratibhāna*). "Reasoning" (*ūha*) and "elimination" (*apoha*) refer to the cognitions of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or alternatively, the cognitions of possibility regarding the objects of injunction and prohibition. That which has arisen or been produced from the meaning and purpose of various scriptures—the attainment of discernment—is [the result] characterized by the instruction of disciples.
The *abhinaya* (representation) of this [fever] consists of those bodily modifications such as the knitting of the eyebrows and so forth, which arise from its purpose.

Fever is mentioned because it is the foremost among all diseases, and because fever can occur during the state of passion (*madana*). Furthermore, it refers to that mental state of the afflicted person which is appropriate to each specific disease at the time of illness.
That very [state] is intended here by the term "disease," for in the presence of disease, the mind does not abide in its own true nature.
What is called insanity arises from determinants such as separation from beloved persons, loss of wealth, physical injury, and the provocation of the bodily humors— wind, bile, and phlegm.
He observed their various unstable behaviors, such as making gestures, laughing, weeping, shouting, and uttering incoherent chatter; lying down, sitting, standing, and running about;

dancing, singing, and reciting; smearing themselves with ashes and dust; wearing grass, discarded flower-garlands, rags, bark garments, pots, skulls, bowls, and ornaments; and indulging in other such diverse activities.
One should represent this through the secondary emotions (*anubhāva*) such as weeping and so forth.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"From the loss of a beloved person or wealth, from injury, or from the agitation of wind, bile, and phlegm..."
From various disturbances of the mind, that which is called insanity arises. || 84 ||
One should induce insanity through groundless weeping, laughing, sitting, singing, running, and shouting, as well as by other such artificial distortions of behavior. (85)
Death is of two kinds: that born of disease and that born of injury.

Among these, that which arises from intestinal colic, liver pain, disorders of the humors, boils, pustules, fever, cholera, and so forth, is produced by disease. That which is born of injury is as follows:
[This pertains to] that which arises from weapons, snakebites, poison-drinking, wild beasts, elephants, horses, chariots, falling from vehicles, or destruction.

Now, we shall describe the specific modes of representation (*abhinaya*) for these: therein, [the representation of] that born of disease consists of observing those whose limbs are dejected, whose bodily movements are protracted, whose eyes are closed, and who are possessed of hiccups and labored breathing.
One should represent this through such *anubhāvas* (consequent actions) as the speaking of indistinct syllables by a white-clad attendant and so forth.
On this point there is a verse:
"In the case of separation from a beloved person, even for a person of the highest status (*uttama*), madness arises, as in the case of Purūravas."

However, because it is the destruction of existence (*vibhava*), it is inconsistent with the sorrow of worldly existence (*bhavana-śoka*) in the case of the Unsurpassed One (*anuttama*). For this very reason, the attendant moods (*anubhāvas*) must be differentiated according to the propriety of the nature [of the character]. The commentators state that "cognitive transformation" (*cittavikāra*) means that which transforms the mind.
Bhaṭṭatauta, however, says: "It is that transformation of the mind, its scattering, its lack of rest in one place when there is no certainty; from that..."

"Insanity occurs. For instance, Purūravas, suddenly not seeing his beloved and finding no cause whatsoever for it, fell into a state of madness. This very point was indeed recognized by the sovereign of the circle of poets, Kālidāsa, in such verses as "He might remain under the sway of anger... (*Vikramorvaśīya*). Thus, there is the absence of a [specific] cause.

Because there is an absence of well-known causes [for it]. Although madness (*unmāda*) is included within disease (*vyādhi*), it is mentioned separately because it produces effects such as deception through the beauty of its performance and various gestures. The same should be said for epilepsy (*apasmāra*);
for that indeed brings about variety in the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome), *bhayānaka* (the terrible), and other sentiments.
For the unification of all diseases is known as the simulation of death;
it is characterized by dejected limbs, lack of movement, and the withdrawal of the sense faculties. (86)

In the case of [emotions] arising from injury (*abhighātaja*), however, there are various types of specific dramatic representations (*abhinaya-viśeṣa*), such as those caused by wounds from weapons, being bitten by snakes, seeing venomous creatures, drinking poison, falling from elephants and the like, or being killed by wild beasts. For instance, regarding a wound from a weapon, the representation is first performed by suddenly falling to the ground, trembling, convulsing, and so forth.
It should be administered. In one bitten by a snake or who has drunk poison, there arise various stages of the poison's onset (*viṣavega*). They are as follows:
emaciation, trembling, burning sensation, hiccups, frothing at the mouth, breaking pain in the shoulders, numbness, and death—these are the eight stages of the poison's onset.
Regarding this, there are two verses: "In the first stage, emaciation occurs; in the second, trembling arises;
in the third, burning sensations; and in the fourth, one should apply [remedies for] hiccup. (87)
One should produce froth in the fifth [day], the breaking of the aggregates in the sixth;
one should produce numbness in the seventh, and death occurs in the eighth. (88)
Regarding this, there is an Āryā verse:

"One should act as if wounded by a weapon toward any injury arising from wild beasts, elephants, horses, or chariots, or even from falling while riding an animal or a vehicle; one must not move one's limbs without careful observation. (89)
Thus, death should be understood as consisting of various internal states; it must be properly enacted by the wise through the movements of the limbs and the expression of emotions. (90)
What is called "terror" arises through various manifestations such as lightning, meteors, the falling of thunderbolts, hurricanes, and the roars of great beings, wild animals, and so forth.
One should represent that [state] through such *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) as the contraction of limbs, trembling, shaking, paralysis, horripilation, and faltering speech.
Regarding the phrase "the singular state (*ekabhāva*) of diseases": by this expression, "becoming one" or "being equal," it is meant that [it is distinct] from all [other states].

It is said that death is manifested precisely as a single form of existence. Alternatively, the very state of mind that contemplates diseases as a unity and without opposition—thinking, "I must not be turned back by this disease"—is what is called the manifestation of death. That itself...

For the abandonment of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is death; therefore, what is intended here is the state of the mind during the process of dying, and not the state of being already dead, because in that [latter] state there is an absence of the *anubhāva* (consequent emotions) and so forth. And those limbs are "dejected" precisely for this reason—namely, they are motionless. By the phrase "acting devoid of the senses," he expresses the total delusion of all the sense organs.
In the case of *viṣapīta*, the compound means "by him poison was drunk. According to the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ*, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is placed at the end of the compound.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Terror arises from the great Bhairava-sounds and the like;
his dramatic representation (abhinaya) should consist of drooping limbs and the closing of the eyes. (91)
What is called *vitarka* (deliberation) arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as doubt, reflection, and misconception;
it should be enacted through consequents (*anubhāva*) such as various forms of inquiry, questioning, deliberation, and the concealment of counsel.
On this point there is a verse:
"Vitarka, which arises from deliberation and the like, and consists of an excess of doubt, is to be represented by shaking and trembling of the head and eyebrows. (92)
Thus, these thirty-three transitory emotions (bhāvas),

according to the suitability of place, time, and circumstance, may belong to oneself, to another, or to a neutral party; they are to be produced by superior, middling, or inferior women and men through the power of their own application.

He is called *bhairava* because he terrifies timid people; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*). [The author] indicates by means of the plural number in the word *akṣinimeṣaiḥ* that the sudden, startling fear produced by the act of shaking is entirely different from the kind of fear preceded by deliberation on what comes before and after.

Doubt (*saṃdeha*) is a cognition that rests upon both [alternatives] in the form of "it might be this" or "it might be that. Deliberation (*vimarśa*) is a desire consisting of the longing for a specific cognition. Contradiction (*vipratyaya*) is merely the cognition of the non-existence of the other alternative by means of a subverting proof, or it is a conflict of opinions (*vipratipatti*). Immediately after these—

Reasoning (*tarka*) has the nature of a causal condition for what is to be (*bhavitavyatā*); it causes laxity in one side [of a dichotomy], displaces the other side from its state of equal status, and demonstrates the emergence of the alternative. Furthermore, it is distinct from doubt (*saṃśaya*), because through doubt there arises an inquiry (*vimarśa*) characterized by the desire to know the truth and so forth.

Even if [the term *saṃdeha*] is accepted [as the name for this figure], it is analyzed by breaking it down for the sake of poetic instruction. Others, however, say that while there is doubt regarding the substratum (*dharmī*), the "deliberation" (*vimarśa*) concerns the attribute (*dharma*), which is a cognition of error or a misconception. The term "alternating" (*vihṛtā*) is intended when there is a repeated relinquishing and attaining of various effects through the intellect.

By means of concealing and grasping the mantras, and by his focused application (*avahittha*), he speaks of their equal duration. "Deliberation" (*vicāraṇā*) refers to the consideration of sequence, priority, and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), obstructive means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) and the like are intended;
for from those, the weakening of one side arises. Thus it is said to be "preceded by deliberation and so forth. This is the method (*naya*).

The self of the application of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) is that from which [it arises], for every application of political science proceeds solely from the conviction of possibility derived from the perceived strength of the opposing side. Thus, by stating that "fate is inconceivable,
whereas human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is conceivable," the teacher Cāṇakya [demonstrates] that everything is preceded by reasoning (*tarka*).
He states the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). And it has been said by Bhaṭṭa Tauta:
"Even one of sharp intellect, if he speaks on the basis of mere probability (*sambhāvanā-pramāṇa*), let him not say: 'The sky is pervaded by clouds, dense with the weight of water.'"
These thirty-three states are to be known as the transitory (vyabhicārin).
Now, however, I shall describe the involuntary (sāttvika) states in their proper order. (93)
Here it is asked: Are other states manifested without *sattva*, such that they are called "pertaining to *sattva*"? To this it is replied:

For here, that which is called *sattva* (sentiment) originates from the mind, and it is so designated because of the state of mental composure (*samāhita-manas*). When the mind is composed, the perfection of *sattva* occurs; and its inherent nature—characterized by horripilation, tears, change of color, and so forth, as it arises according to the specific emotion—is not [artificially produced].

"It can be performed with another state of mind. Furthermore, because drama imitates the nature of the world, *sattva* (inner essence) is desired. What is the illustration? For here, the states (*bhāvas*) produced by pleasure and pain that arise through the dramatic elements (*nāṭyadharmin*) must be rendered pure in *sattva*, just as follows:
They become similar in form. In that regard, what is called suffering consists of weeping;

how, then, could it be enacted by one who is not suffering? And joy consists of exultation; how could it be enacted by one who is not joyful? This alone is his true essence: that through being either suffering or joyful, tears and horripilation arise.
Having established that they are to be manifested, the sattvic states (*sāttvikā bhāvāḥ*) have been thus explained—on the grounds that "the essence (*sattva*) is desired. These are as follows;
he concludes this by stating: "these thirty-three states. Other [states] are, however, included within these very ones.
For example: hypocrisy [is the cause] of dissimulation; agitation [is the cause] of despondency; hunger, thirst, and so forth [are the causes] of physical exhaustion.
In this way, other cases are also to be inferred. Others, however, think: "Who indeed is capable of comprehending the fluctuations of the mind? Or, even in the case of counting them..."

Whether by the nine qualities of the self as conceived by logicians, or by the four types of cognition— such as error and the rest— as enumerated among the eight properties of the intellect in Sāṃkhya,
or by the distinction between mind and mental factors as taught by the Śākyas, what is the point of this [limited] enumeration when everything is included? Or rather...

If it is argued that for the sake of training poets and actors, this much must be defined, then others [states] must indeed be mentioned; or rather, they have already been stated by the Sage (Bharata) in the general theory of representation (*sāmānyābhinaya*) through the definition of the emotions, gestures, and ornaments pertaining to men and women.

They are also indicated here in the enumeration of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*). For instance, in the case of lassitude (*glāni*): [The text continues with examples of these states.]

Hunger and thirst are mentioned merely as manifestations [of suffering] because they are so well known. Their definition, which pertains to poets and actors, is not of much utility here; therefore, they have not been defined. Others, however, say: "In performance, beauty arises only through these many [manifestations]; for it is only in these many that [beauty exists]. Thus, in these very cases...
When the specific attendant conditions (*sahacārin*) have been demonstrated through their application, the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) becomes fit for aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*).
However, some maintain that these [emotions] are merely to be understood as examples; by this method of cognition, the definitions of others should be inferred.
Stupefaction, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, trembling,
