change of color, tears, and fainting— these eight are considered the *sāttvika* [emotions]. (94)
Regarding this, the noble ones say: therein, sweat arises from anger, fear, joy, shame, pain, fatigue, hunger, thirst, physical injury, exertion, exhaustion, and heat, as well as from pressure. (95)
Stupor (stambha) arises from joy, fear, grief, amazement, despondency, anger, and so forth.
Trembling (kampa) is born of cold, fear, joy, anger, touch, old age, and disease. || 96 ||
Tears arise from joy, indignation, smoking, collyrium, yawning, fear, grief, the act of gazing without blinking, and diseases caused by cold.
And discoloration arises from cold, anger, fear, fatigue, disease, exhaustion, and heat;
horripilation arises from touch, fear, cold, joy, anger, and disease. (98)
Change of voice is produced by fear, joy, anger, old age, dryness, disease, and intoxication;
dissolution [of the voice] occurs through exhaustion, fainting, passion, sleep, injury, delusion, and so forth. (99)
Thus, these eight sattvic states (bhāvas) are to be known by the wise;
I shall now describe their functions, which bring about the experience of rasa and bhāva.

Devoid of consciousness and motionless, remaining with the appearance of a void and an insentient form, the wise man should enact the state of a pillar (stambha) by means of his limbs being rigidly fixed. 101.
The representation of perspiration should be employed by means of taking up a fan and by the removal of sweat, as well as through the longing for wind. (102)
One should indicate horripilation by means of frequent bristling of the skin, as well as by shivering and by the standing on end of the body hairs upon being touched. (103)
A variation in tone should be enacted through broken and faltering sounds;
one should demonstrate trembling through quivering, throbbing, and shaking. (104)

Through a change in the complexion of the face and by means of the practice of constricting the channels, a state of discoloration should be skillfully enacted; for that is indeed difficult to achieve.
A wise performer should represent tears by wiping the eyes because they are flooded with the water of tears, and by the frequent falling of drops of tears. 106.
Being motionless due to being without tremor, and even from imperceptible breathing as well as from falling to the ground, there should be the representation of dissolution (pralaya). || 107 ||
These forty-nine states of being, existing as they truly are across three stages, have been described by me here;
furthermore, those which are to be applied to each respective rasa—
And the foremost of Brahmins ought to listen to them. || 108 ||
In this regard, there are these verses: Doubt, disease, as well as languor, anxiety, envy, fear,
as well as wonder, discursive thought, rigidity, and likewise fickleness.
Horripilation, joy, sleep, as well as madness and intoxication;
perspiration, concealment of emotion, fainting, and trembling.
Despair, fatigue, despondency, pride, agitation, fortitude, memory, intelligence, delusion, and awakening— these [states] exist in sleep, with the exception of longing.
Anger, resentment, laughter, sorrow, epilepsy,
dejection, death, and passion conjoined with energy.
Terror, change of complexion, weeping, alteration of voice, and even fainting,
as well as numbness— these six are proclaimed as the forty-six [anubhāvas].
Excluding those states known as indolence, ferocity, and disgust,
all other emotional states (bhāvas) manifest the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) by their own respective names.
"For when these [emotions], born of the permanent and transitory states, reach their proper occasion,
they intensify the rasa designated as the Erotic.
Languor, apprehension, envy, fatigue, and likewise fickleness;
Sleep and the concealment of sleep through drowsiness are proclaimed as the internal states (bhāvas) in the comic sentiment (hāsya). || 110 ||
Despair, anxiety, dejection, exhaustion, fatigue, numbness, death, and disease are recorded as the [stable] states in the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa). || 111 ||
Pride, envy, intoxication, enthusiasm, agitation, resentment, anger, fickleness, and ferocity are to be known as arising from the Furious (raudra) sentiment. 112.
Absence of delusion, as well as enthusiasm, agitation, joy, intelligence, as well as ferocity, indignation, and pride; || 113 ||
Horripilation, change of voice, anger, envy, fortitude, as well as pride and deliberation—these indeed are the emotions present in the heroic sentiment. (114)
Perspiration, trembling, horripilation, and stammering, as well as terror, death, and change of complexion, occur in the Frightful [sentiment]. (115)
Epilepsy, insanity, despondency, and intoxication, as well as death, disease, and fear— these are the states that depend upon the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome). (116)
Stupefaction, perspiration, delusion, horripilation, and amazement, as well as agitation, numbness, joy, and fainting, are the bases of the marvelous sentiment. (117)
However, all these sattvic states (bhāvas) which are based on various modes of dramatic representation (abhinaya) should be understood by practitioners of drama within these [nine] rasas. (118)
For in practice, there is no poetic composition whatsoever that arises from a single rasa;
this applies equally to the emotion (bhāva), the sentiment (rasa), the activity (pravṛtti), and even the dramatic style (vṛtti). 119.
Among many emotions combined together, that whose form appears most frequently should be considered the permanent emotion (sthāyībhāva); the rest are regarded as transitory emotions (saṃcārībhāvas).
Furthermore, those which proceed while illuminating the stable rasa should be known as transitory (saṃcārins), for they have attained the state of being stable.
Indeed, when the permanent emotion (sthāyī), supported by the limbs and the subject matter, is joined with the determinants (vibhāva) and consequents (anubhāva),
and further conjoined with the transitory emotions (saṃcārī), it becomes rasa.
The permanent emotion (sthāyin) should be employed by practitioners as something exceeding the sentient being [in intensity],
because the permanent emotion exists only through the form of the transitory emotions (sañcārin).
Those sattvic states which are employed through various modes of representation (abhinaya) should be understood by experts in drama as belonging to all these aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
For poetry is not born of a single flavor, nor does it consist of a single sentiment or a single mode;
indeed, when applied with effort, it attains aesthetic resonance through the process of friction.
Whether they be emotions (*bhāva*), sentiments (*rasa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), or even conduct (*vṛtti*),
the threefold nature of the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful is not discussed here.
The six flavors are threefold and endowed with various emotional sentiments;
for the purpose of the *sattva* (the audience's mind) is the aim here, and thus the dramatic application shines forth.
For when they are understood, the aesthetic flavors (rasas) shine forth in the world; indeed, it is wonderful and rare [to achieve this].

Endowed with various states of being and meanings, possessing stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas) and transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas), the wise should indeed scatter these aesthetic flavors like flowers throughout their poetic compositions. (120)
Thus, the rasas and the bhāvas are recorded in drama as having three states;
he who understands these shall attain the highest perfection.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Emotions," in the glorious *Nāṭyaśāstra* of Bharata.
